===== lecture 1: General Intro to XR

1/A0  quiz  1/S0  "Quick quiz"  (1 facts, 7 concepts)
  Q Why might the abbreviations XR, VR, AR, and MR be understood differently by different listeners?  [1/S0/F1]
    - Because each abbreviation names a different type of display
    * Because listeners may connect them with films, games, documentaries, or headsets
    - Because each abbreviation points to a different part of the reality-virtuality continuum
    - Because each abbreviation is fixed by a single official standard
    because: The abbreviations can trigger different media associations, so one listener may think of movies, another of games, and another of a vision-blocking headset. The ambiguity comes from these associations, not from displays, standards, or positions on a continuum.
  Q What is distinctive about the Pokémon Go–style association compared with a vision-blocking headset?  [1/S0/F1]
    * A real-world view on a screen plus virtual objects on that screen
    - Only virtual objects on a screen without any real-world view
    - Internal body structures visualized in a virtual room
    - A virtual world on a screen that hides the real world
    because: In the Pokémon Go–style association, the real world is visible on a device screen and virtual objects that are not in the real world can also be seen on that screen. A vision-blocking headset instead transports the user to a virtual world.
  judge round 1: 1 of 2 failed
    1 FAIL no_giveaway  (Why might the abbreviations XR, VR, AR, and MR be understood differently by different …)
      check: B
      reason: Fact [2] supports B by saying listeners may associate the terms with movie scenes, games, documentaries, or headsets. However, B reuses the question’s key word “listeners” and is the only hedged option (“may”), while A/C/D use “each” or “fixed”; a repaired question should remove that keyword from the option and make all options similarly neutral/qualified.
    2 pass  (What is distinctive about the Pokémon Go–style association compared with a vision-blocking headset?)
      check: A
      reason: Fact [2] states that in Pokémon Go the “real world is visible on a device screen and virtual objects that do not exist in the real world can also be seen on that screen,” which matches A and contrasts with a vision-blocking headset.
  judge round 2 (rewrite, ok): 1 of 2 failed
    1 FAIL one_answer,no_giveaway  (Why might the abbreviations XR, VR, AR, and MR be understood differently by different …)
      check: A, C
      reason: C follows directly from fact [2], but A is also defensible because fact [2] includes associations with 'a headset' and 'a device screen', which are particular display types, so the question admits more than one answer. A repair should ask for the exact associations named in the fact and remove the display abstraction, or make the options mutually exclusive and not let the correct one be a concrete list while the others are abstract categories.
    2 pass  (What is distinctive about the Pokémon Go–style association compared with a vision-blocking headset?)
      check: A
      reason: Fact [2] states that in the Pokémon Go association 'the real world is visible on a device screen and virtual objects that do not exist in the real world can also be seen on that screen', while the headset 'blocks vision and transports the user to a virtual world', making A the only correct option. 1/A1  recap  1/S0  "Recap"  (2 facts, 7 concepts)
  The names XR, VR, AR, and MR are defined by their full forms. These terms can be ambiguous because different people associate them with different immersive experiences, such as virtual worlds, games, or visualizations.
  - XR, VR, AR, and MR stand for extended reality, virtual reality, augmented reality, and mixed reality.
  - When people hear XR, VR, AR, or MR, they can picture movies, games, headsets, or screen overlays, causing ambiguity.
  judge round 1: 1 of 3 failed
    1 pass  (XR, VR, AR, and MR stand for extended reality, virtual reality, augmented reality, and …)
      check: none
      reason: The point directly restates fact [1] without adding or narrowing anything.
    2 pass  (When people hear XR, VR, AR, or MR, they can picture movies, games, headsets …)
      check: none
      reason: The point is supported by fact [2] and the segment’s stated purpose: different hearers may associate the terms with movie-like scenes, games, headsets, or on-screen virtual objects, creating ambiguity. “Screen overlays” is a reasonable shorthand for the fact’s description of virtual objects seen on a device screen alongside the real world.
    0 FAIL supported,faithful  (The names XR, VR, AR, and MR are defined by their full forms.)
      check: magical movie scenes such as Avatar, interactive video games, 3D or 4D movie-theater documentaries about extinct animals, a user wearing a headset ... virtual world, games such as Pokémon Go ... visualizations of internal body structures [2]
      reason: It fails on supported/faithful because “different immersive experiences” adds a category not stated in the facts; fact [2] lists possible associations but does not call them immersive experiences. A repaired version would say “different associations or examples, such as virtual worlds, games, or visualizations.”

1/A2  quiz  1/S1  "Quick quiz"  (3 facts, 6 concepts)
  Q What best describes Extended Reality (XR)?  [1/S1/F0]
    - XR is a standard for virtual scene display and object placement
    - XR is a particular category of headset hardware used for immersive training
    - XR is a method for blending real footage with virtual content
    * XR is an umbrella term for present or future immersive technologies
    because: XR is not itself a specific technology; it is an umbrella term that covers present or future immersive technologies. A display standard, headset category, or blending method would be a specific part of an XR system, not the umbrella term.
  Q What is the effect of treating the X in Extended Reality as a variable?  [1/S1/F1]
    - It can stand for a particular display format
    * It can stand for different immersive reality types
    - It can stand for a fixed set of present technologies
    - It can stand for a hardware sensor channel
    because: The X can be read as a variable whose values, such as A, V, and M, denote different immersive reality types. A display format, sensor channel, or fixed set is not what the variable values denote.
  Q What makes a produced environment count as an immersive experience?  [1/S1/F2]
    - when a system tracks the user's motion in a virtual environment
    - when a display overlays virtual objects onto the visible real environment
    * when the user's senses cannot separate it from a real environment
    - when a headset hides the surrounding real environment
    because: An experience is immersive when the person's sensory perception of the produced environment is taken to be real. Overlaying content, hiding the room, or tracking motion may support an XR system, but by themselves they do not make the experience immersive.
  judge round 1: 1 of 3 failed
    1 pass  (What best describes Extended Reality (XR)?)
      check: D
      reason: Fact 1 states that XR is “an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies,” which directly supports D and makes A, B, and C too specific to be the answer.
    2 FAIL no_giveaway  (What does reading the X in Extended Reality as a variable indicate?)
      check: B
      reason: Fact 2 supports B because the X “can be read as a variable” with values such as A, V, and M for AR, VR, and MR, but no_giveaway fails because B alone contains the hedge “can” while A, C, and D make unqualified assertions. A repaired version would give all options the same modal/qualifier shape or otherwise avoid making B uniquely cautious.
    3 pass  (What makes a produced environment count as an immersive experience?)
      check: C
      reason: Fact 3 says an immersive experience occurs when a person “fails to distinguish that environment from the person's real environment, perceiving it as the real environment,” which C paraphrases as the senses not separating it from a real environment.
  judge round 2 (rewrite, ok): 0 of 3 failed
    1 pass  (What best describes Extended Reality (XR)?)
      check: D
      reason: Fact [1] states that XR is “an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies,” which directly supports D and contradicts the specific-technology options.
    2 pass  (What is the effect of treating the X in Extended Reality as a variable?)
      check: B
      reason: Fact [2] states that the X “can be read as a variable” and its values “such as A, V, and M denote augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR),” supporting B. The other options describe formats, fixed sets, or hardware channels not stated by the fact.
    3 pass  (What makes a produced environment count as an immersive experience?)
      check: C
      reason: Fact [3] defines an immersive experience as one in which a person “fails to distinguish that environment from the person's real environment, perceiving it as the real environment,” which is paraphrased by C. The other options name mechanisms that are not the stated condition for immersiveness.

1/A3  recap  1/S1  "Recap"  (3 facts, 6 concepts)
  Extended Reality groups present and future immersive technologies under one umbrella name rather than naming a single technology. The variable X in the name allows it to refer to augmented, virtual, and mixed reality, among related possibilities. These technologies are called immersive because they make a sensed environment appear real, so the person cannot distinguish it from the real environment.
  - Extended Reality is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, covering present or future immersive technologies.
  - The X in Extended Reality is a variable whose values denote augmented, virtual, and mixed reality.
  - An immersive technology makes an environment experienced through the senses appear real because the person cannot distinguish it from reality.
  judge round 1: 2 of 4 failed
    1 pass  (Extended Reality is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, covering present or future …)
      check: none
      reason: Fact [1] states that Extended Reality is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers present or future immersive technologies; the point omits optional examples but otherwise says the same.
    2 FAIL supported,faithful  (The X in Extended Reality is a variable whose values denote augmented, virtual, and …)
      check: can be read as a variable [2], such as A, V, and M [2]
      reason: It says the X “is a variable,” whereas fact [2] only says it “can be read as a variable,” and it presents augmented, virtual, and mixed reality as the values rather than examples among many possible values. A repaired version should keep the hedge and the example status, e.g. “The X in Extended Reality can be read as a variable with values such as A, V, and M.”
    3 pass  (An immersive technology makes an environment experienced through the senses appear real because the …)
      check: none
      reason: Fact [3] supports the core idea that an immersive technology produces a sensory experience that appears real because the person cannot distinguish it from the real environment.
    0 FAIL supported,faithful  (Extended Reality groups present and future immersive technologies under one umbrella name rather than …)
      check: can be read as a variable [2], such as A, V, and M [2]
      reason: The text says “The variable X,” while fact [2] only supports that X “can be read as a variable,” and it says X “allows it to refer to” the three named technologies, which restates the example values as the main referents. A repaired version should keep the hedge and mark the three technologies as examples among other possible immersive technologies.
  judge kept: original; still failing: [2, 0]

1/A4  quiz  1/S2  "Quick quiz"  (3 facts, 3 concepts)
  Q What do the two ends of the reality-virtuality continuum represent?  [1/S2/F0]
    * a completely real environment and a completely virtual environment
    - a real environment augmented with virtual content and a virtual environment augmented with real content
    - a real environment and a mixed real-virtual environment
    - a real environment with some virtual content and a virtual environment with some real content
    because: The continuum runs from a purely real environment to a purely virtual environment. The augmented real and augmented virtual states lie in the middle, not at the ends.
  Q On the reality-virtuality continuum, what is augmented reality?  [1/S2/F1]
    - the intermediate state in which the virtual environment is augmented with real-world content
    - the real extreme in which the real environment is replaced by virtual content
    - the virtual extreme in which the virtual environment is replaced by real-world content
    * the intermediate state in which the real environment is augmented with virtual content
    because: Augmented reality keeps the real environment as the base and adds virtual content to it. Augmented virtuality is the opposite intermediate state, and the extremes have no content from the other side.
  Q In a broad sense, what does mixed reality cover on the reality-virtuality continuum?  [1/S2/F3]
    - the intermediate state in which the virtual environment is augmented with real-world content
    - the intermediate state in which the real environment is augmented with virtual content
    - the two extreme states of a completely real and a completely virtual environment
    * the whole space between the real and virtual extremes
    because: In the broad sense used here, mixed reality is not just one intermediate state; it spans the entire region between the real and virtual extremes, with varying amounts of real and virtual augmentation.
  judge round 1: 0 of 3 failed
    1 pass  (What do the two ends of the reality-virtuality continuum represent?)
      check: A
      reason: Fact 1 states the extremes are “a completely real environment with nothing virtual and a completely virtual environment with nothing real,” which is exactly option A.
    2 pass  (On the reality-virtuality continuum, what is augmented reality?)
      check: D
      reason: Fact 2 defines augmented reality as “the intermediate state in which the real environment is augmented with virtual content,” which is exactly option D.
    3 pass  (In a broad sense, what does mixed reality cover on the reality-virtuality continuum?)
      check: D
      reason: Fact 4 says mixed reality, “in a broad sense, is the entire space between the real environment extreme and the virtual environment extreme,” which is exactly option D.
  judge kept: original

1/A5  recap  1/S2  "Recap"  (4 facts, 4 concepts)
  The reality-virtuality continuum gives a scale for where immersive experiences lie, with a completely real environment at one end and a completely virtual one at the other. Augmented reality and augmented virtuality are intermediate states, distinguished by whether virtual content is added to reality or real content is added to virtuality. Mixed reality, in a broad sense, covers the entire space between the extremes, so it includes those intermediate states.
  - The reality-virtuality continuum is the scale from completely real to completely virtual environments.
  - Augmented reality is the intermediate state where a real environment is augmented with virtual content.
  - Augmented virtuality is the opposite intermediate state where a virtual environment is augmented with real-world content.
  - Mixed reality, broadly, is the entire space between the real and virtual environment extremes, with varying degrees of augmentation.
  judge round 1: 0 of 5 failed
    1 pass  (The reality-virtuality continuum is the scale from completely real to completely virtual environments.)
      check: none
      reason: The point restates fact [1] as the scale between completely real and completely virtual environments, without adding or changing the claim.
    2 pass  (Augmented reality is the intermediate state where a real environment is augmented with virtual …)
      check: none
      reason: The point captures fact [2]: augmented reality is the intermediate state in which a real environment is augmented with virtual content. Omitting “on the reality-virtuality continuum” is acceptable in the point sequence and does not add a false claim.
    3 pass  (Augmented virtuality is the opposite intermediate state where a virtual environment is augmented with …)
      check: none
      reason: The point captures fact [3]: augmented virtuality is the opposite intermediate state in which a virtual environment is augmented with real-world content. The wording is concise but preserves the meaning.
    4 pass  (Mixed reality, broadly, is the entire space between the real and virtual environment extremes …)
      check: none
      reason: The point captures fact [4]: broadly, mixed reality is the entire space between the real and virtual extremes, with varying degrees of augmentation. The shorter phrase “varying degrees of augmentation” stays within the fact’s meaning.
    0 pass  (The reality-virtuality continuum gives a scale for where immersive experiences lie, with a completely …)
      check: none
      reason: The text summarizes the continuum and the positions of augmented reality, augmented virtuality, and mixed reality. It connects them as one explanation: the scale has real and virtual extremes, the two augmented states differ by direction of augmentation, and broad mixed reality spans the whole space and includes those intermediate states.
  judge kept: original

1/A7  quiz  1/S3  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 10 concepts)
  Q What pattern does the XR market-size projection from 2021 to 2030 show?  [1/S3/F1]
    - A linear increase in hardware sales
    * An exponential increase
    - A temporary spike from a single application domain
    - A steady one-percent rise each year
    because: The projected rise in XR market size from tens of billions to hundreds of billions follows an exponential pattern. A linear hardware-only rise, a temporary spike, or a one-percent annual rise does not match that scale.
  Q What is the metaverse in a broad understanding?  [1/S3/F5]
    - A system that adds virtual objects to the real world
    - A new version of a flat two-dimensional screen
    * A reimagining of how humans interact with the digital world
    - A single application of virtual reality technology
    because: The metaverse is not merely one VR, MR, or AR application; broadly, it reimagines human interaction with the digital world. A flat screen, a single VR application, or a simple overlay system describes a narrower or different idea.
  Q How is interaction in the metaverse different from most current screen interactions?  [1/S3/F6]
    * It uses natural interaction in an all-around three-dimensional environment
    - It uses mostly flat two-dimensional screens with occasional three-dimensional effects
    - It uses a single fixed camera perspective for all users
    - It uses virtual objects displayed on a handheld device screen
    because: In the metaverse, people act as they do in the real world and use natural interaction with digital content in an all-around 3D environment. The flat-screen pattern is the current interaction style, not the metaverse style.
  Q What workforce demand does the growth of XR create?  [1/S3/F8]
    - More people who can buy XR hardware for personal use
    - More people who can promote XR products in retail stores
    - More people who can consume XR content at home
    * More people who can develop and deploy XR systems
    because: XR growth creates demand for people who can develop and deploy XR systems. Consumer, purchasing, or retail-promotion roles do not fit that workforce demand.
  Q Why is the metaverse not yet fully realized?  [1/S3/F7]
    - Its growth potential is not present in hardware or software
    * Current technology is not advanced enough and has bottlenecks
    - Companies are not investing heavily in making it a reality
    - Its application domains are not broad enough to attract investment
    because: The metaverse is not yet fully realized because current technology is not advanced enough and has technological bottlenecks. The other options are false because companies are investing heavily, growth potential exists in both hardware and software, and XR has multiple application domains.

1/A8  recap  1/S3  "Recap"  (10 facts, 15 concepts)
  Extended reality is becoming an important emerging field. Broad application use, expected market growth, and the metaverse vision explain the expanding interest. The metaverse adds a longer-term driver, though it still faces technological limits and heavy investment. Finally, this growth creates demand for skilled practitioners and is recognized by governments as an emerging area.
  - A 2022 forecast placed extended-reality content in video games, healthcare, engineering, live events, video entertainment, real estate, retail, and military.
  - The extended-reality market is expected to grow exponentially, with hardware larger than software and India's market projected to grow.
  - The thirty-year-old metaverse term is a broader natural 3D digital-interaction vision, not merely an XR application, and has stimulated growth.
  - The metaverse is not fully realized because current technology is not advanced enough, but companies are investing heavily in it.
  - Extended-reality growth creates demand for skilled XR developers and deployers, while many national governments identify XR as an emerging field.
  judge round 1: 2 of 6 failed
    1 pass  (A 2022 forecast placed extended-reality content in video games, healthcare, engineering, live events, video …)
      check: none
      reason: The point is carried by fact [1], which names the same 2022 forecast and the same application domains; leaving out the percentages and the caveat that figures may now be larger is acceptable because it does not add or alter the core claim.
    2 pass  (The extended-reality market is expected to grow exponentially, with hardware larger than software and …)
      check: none
      reason: Facts [2], [3], and [4] support the global exponential growth claim, the hardware/software comparison, and the projected growth of India's market. The point is dense but remains one broad market-growth idea rather than unrelated ideas.
    3 FAIL faithful  (The thirty-year-old metaverse term is a broader natural 3D digital-interaction vision, not merely an …)
      check: more than 30 years [5]; heavily [5]; one broad view [6]
      reason: The point says the term is “thirty-year-old” rather than in use for “more than 30 years” [5], says it “has stimulated growth” rather than “heavily stimulated growth” [5], and asserts the metaverse “is a broader ... vision” rather than presenting it as “one broad view” [6]. A repair should preserve “more than 30 years,” “heavily,” and the fact that this is one broad view rather than the only characterization.
    4 pass  (The metaverse is not fully realized because current technology is not advanced enough, but …)
      check: none
      reason: Fact [8] states that the metaverse is not yet fully realized because current technology is not advanced enough and that companies are investing heavily; the point faithfully compresses this without adding unsupported claims.
    5 pass  (Extended-reality growth creates demand for skilled XR developers and deployers, while many national governments …)

      reason: Fact [9] supports the demand for skilled people who develop and deploy XR systems, and fact [10] supports the claim that many national governments identify XR as an emerging area. 1/A15  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (10 facts, 12 concepts)
  Q How do augmented reality, augmented virtuality, and mixed reality relate to one another on the reality-virtuality continuum?  [1/S2/F0, 1/S2/F1, 1/S2/F2, 1/S2/F3; augmented reality, augmented virtuality, mixed reality, reality-virtuality continuum]
    A They occupy different positions or ranges on the continuum. Augmented reality is an intermediate state in which a real environment is augmented with virtual content. Augmented virtuality is the opposite intermediate state in which a virtual environment is augmented with real-world content. Mixed reality broadly covers the entire space between the completely real and completely virtual extremes, so it includes both forms of augmentation.
  Q How does reading the letter X in extended reality as a variable explain why extended reality is an umbrella term rather than a specific technology?  [1/S1/F0, 1/S1/F1; extended reality, immersive technology]
    A Because extended reality is not a single technology, but an umbrella term covering all present or future immersive technologies. The letter X can be read as a variable whose values include A, V, and M for augmented reality, virtual reality, and mixed reality, as well as many possible values for future immersive technologies. Thus extended reality names the whole class of immersive technologies rather than one particular type.
  Q How does the metaverse relate to extended reality growth and to specific XR technologies such as virtual reality, augmented reality, or mixed reality?  [1/S3/F4, 1/S3/F5, 1/S3/F6, 1/S3/F7; metaverse, extended reality, three-dimensional environment, natural interaction]
    A The metaverse has heavily stimulated extended reality growth while being characterized as more than just an application of virtual reality, augmented reality, or mixed reality. One broad view is that it reimagines how humans interact with the digital world. In the metaverse, people act in an all-around three-dimensional environment and use natural interaction. It is not yet fully realized, but companies are investing heavily, with growth potential in hardware and software.

===== lecture 2: Application Domains and System Categories

2/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (7 facts, 5 concepts)
  What is extended reality (XR)? (lecture 1) -> Extended reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR).
  What is augmented reality (AR)? (lecture 1) -> Augmented reality (AR) is an enhanced version of reality created by technology, in which computer-generated digital content is overlaid on the real world in real time and registered in 3D, so the user perceives and interacts with the enhanced environment.
  What is mixed reality (MR)? (lecture 1) -> Mixed reality (MR) is an immersive technology that is the same as augmented reality, in which digital content is overlaid on the view of reality and can be interacted with.
  What is immersive technology? (lecture 1) -> Immersive technology is a technology that produces an experience in which a person perceives an environment through sensory organs as real, so that they cannot distinguish it from their real environment.
  What is immersive experience? (lecture 1) -> An immersive experience is a perceived experience through sensory organs that appears real, because a person cannot distinguish the experienced environment from their real environment and perceives it as that real environment.

  Q Which sensory arrangement characterizes a non-immersive VR system?  [2/S1/F0, 2/S1/F1, 2/S1/F2, 2/S1/F3]
    * unblocked access to real-world senses
    - partial blocking of real-world senses
    - virtual replacement of real-world senses
    - complete blocking of real-world senses
    because: A non-immersive VR system keeps the user's eyes, ears, and other sensory organs open to the real world. Semi-immersive systems block some real-world senses, while fully immersive systems block them completely.
  Q What determines a VR system's immersion category?  [2/S1/F0, 2/S1/F1]
    - the number of devices worn by the user
    - the price paid by the user
    * the degree of sensory blocking
    - the industry sector chosen by the user

    - they give no immersion while keeping the user on a regular screen

    because: A fully immersive VR system blocks the user's ability to sense the real world, so the user feels physically present in the virtual world. Leaving some senses exposed or using a common headset for a virtual tour describes semi-immersive VR, not fully immersive VR.

2/A4  recap  2/S1  "Recap"  (10 facts, 24 concepts)
  VR immersion is defined by the degree to which real-world sensory input is blocked. This sensory blocking produces three VR system categories: non-immersive systems engage attention without blocking senses, semi-immersive systems block only some senses and are the common commercial form, and fully immersive systems block all real-world senses with many tracking devices. The categories thus form a spectrum from ordinary computer engagement to complete virtual presence, with full immersion being the costliest and rarest.
  - VR immersion means the user's senses are blocked, so input comes only from the virtual world.
  - VR systems are categorized as non-immersive, semi-immersive, or fully immersive by how much real-world sensory input is blocked.
  - Non-immersive VR is a limited computer application that fully engages attention, while the user's senses remain open.
  - Semi-immersive VR blocks some but not all senses, often via a headset, and is common and cost-effective commercially.
  - Fully immersive VR blocks all real-world senses, tracks body movements via many devices, and is costly and commercially rare.
  judge round 1: 0 of 6 failed
    1 pass  (VR immersion means the user's senses are blocked, so input comes only from the …)
      check: none
      reason: Point 1 directly paraphrases fact [1]: VR immersion involves blocked senses and input from only the virtual world. No criterion is violated.
    2 pass  (VR systems are categorized as non-immersive, semi-immersive, or fully immersive by how much real-world …)
      check: 1
      reason: Point 2 is carried by fact [2] for the three categories and by uncited fact [1] for the sensory-blocking meaning of immersion. The wording is supported and faithful.
    3 pass  (Non-immersive VR is a limited computer application that fully engages attention, while the user's …)
      check: none
      reason: Point 3 is supported by facts [3] and [4]: non-immersive VR is a limited computer application that captures attention while the user's sensory organs remain open. It names its subject and is one clear point.
    4 pass  (Semi-immersive VR blocks some but not all senses, often via a headset, and is …)
      check: none
      reason: Point 4 is supported by facts [6], [7], and [8]: semi-immersive VR blocks some but not all senses, headsets are a common example, and it is commonly used and cost-effective. It remains a single category point.
    5 pass  (Fully immersive VR blocks all real-world senses, tracks body movements via many devices, and …)

2/A11  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (11 facts, 40 concepts)
  Q Why are virtual reality headsets common in commercial immersive applications even though fully immersive systems provide stronger immersion?  [2/S1/F5, 2/S1/F6, 2/S1/F7, 2/S1/F8, 2/S1/F10; virtual reality headset, semi-immersive virtual reality system, fully immersive virtual reality system, immersion]
    A Virtual reality headsets are common in commercial immersive applications because most such applications are semi-immersive and cost-effective. A headset gives partial immersion by blocking some senses, such as sight, while ears and skin can still receive real-world signals. Fully immersive systems block all senses and are the costliest and commercially rare form.
  Q Why is World of Warcraft an example of a non-immersive virtual reality system even when a player is psychologically absorbed in the game?  [2/S1/F2, 2/S1/F3, 2/S1/F4; World of Warcraft, non-immersive virtual reality system, gaming application, virtual environment]
    A World of Warcraft is non-immersive because it is a specific gaming application that runs on a regular computer or console with ordinary displays and input devices. The player controls characters or activities while retaining control of the physical environment, and the virtual environment does not directly interact with the user. Although such software can take the user's attention, the user's sensory organs remain open and the user remains physically attached to the real world.
  Q How do virtual tourism and digital heritage preservation differ as immersive applications in travel and tourism?  [2/S0/F1, 2/S0/F6, 2/S0/F7; virtual tourism, digital heritage preservation, travel and tourism]
    A In travel and tourism, virtual tourism and digital heritage preservation serve different purposes. Virtual tourism lets users visit faraway places without physically going there. Digital heritage preservation targets heritage places that cannot be physically visited by large numbers of users or in all parts for preservation reasons; it lets users explore each part virtually, preserves the space digitally despite physical decay, and increases the space's lifespan and potential to be visited by more users.
  judge round 1: 1 of 3 failed
    1 pass  (Why are virtual reality headsets common in commercial immersive applications even though fully immersive …)
      check: Virtual reality headsets are common because they are a common semi-immersive form, most commercial immersive applications are semi-immersive and cost-effective, and fully immersive systems are the costliest and commercially rare.
      reason: Facts 17 and 18 carry the commercial/common link, while facts 16, 19, and 21 support the partial-versus-full immersion comparison and the cost/rarity contrast.
    2 pass  (Why is World of Warcraft an example of a non-immersive virtual reality system even …)
      check: World of Warcraft is non-immersive because it is a gaming application on a regular computer or console where the user controls characters while retaining physical control, and although attention can be captured, the user's senses remain open to the real world.
      reason: Fact 15 identifies World of Warcraft as a non-immersive gaming application on ordinary computer/console displays and input devices; facts 13 and 14 explain why psychological absorption does not make it immersive.

===== lecture 3: Application Domains and System Categories

3/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (11 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is extended reality (XR)? (lecture 1) -> Extended reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR).
  What is non-immersive virtual reality system? (lecture 2) -> A non-immersive virtual reality system is a limited class of computer application that provides a computer-generated environment in which a user controls characters or activities while retaining control of the physical environment. The user is psychologically engaged and remains physically attached to the real world, while the virtual environment does not directly interact with the user.
  What is semi-immersive virtual reality system? (lecture 2) -> Semi-immersive virtual reality system is a type of virtual reality system, positioned between non-immersive and fully immersive systems, that gives the user a partial immersive experience by blocking some but not all senses while leaving the user free to sense the real world.
  What is fully immersive virtual reality system? (lecture 2) -> Fully immersive virtual reality system is a virtual reality system that completely blocks the user's ability to sense the real world by blocking all senses, so the user senses only the virtual world and feels physically present in it.
  What is augmented reality (AR)? (lecture 1) -> Augmented reality (AR) is an enhanced version of reality created by technology, in which computer-generated digital content is overlaid on the real world in real time and registered in 3D, so the user perceives and interacts with the enhanced environment.
  What is immersive experience? (lecture 1) -> An immersive experience is a perceived experience through sensory organs that appears real, because a person cannot distinguish the experienced environment from their real environment and perceives it as that real environment.

3/A6  recap  3/S2  "Recap"  (10 facts, 19 concepts)
  Augmented reality applications divide into marker-based and markerless systems according to their technology. Marker-based systems depend on detectable markers, while markerless systems avoid physical markers and are therefore more versatile. Within markerless augmented reality, location-based, superimposition-based, projection-based, and outlining-based subtypes differ in how they detect or project digital content into the real-world view.
  - Augmented reality applications are categorized technologically as marker-based or markerless, not by psychological or immersive experience.
  - Marker-based augmented reality applications show content at detected markers such as QR codes, but damaged markers make them hard to maintain.
  - Markerless augmented reality applications are more versatile, need no physical markers, and have four recognized subtypes.
  - Location-based and superimposition-based markerless augmented reality applications use location sensors or computer-vision object recognition.
  - Projection-based and outlining-based markerless augmented reality applications use light projectors or object recognition to enhance views.
  judge round 1: 2 of 6 failed
    1 pass  (Augmented reality applications are categorized technologically as marker-based or markerless, not by psychological or …)
      check: none
      reason: The point restates the technological classification and explicitly rejects a psychological/immersive basis, both stated in fact 1.
    2 pass  (Marker-based augmented reality applications show content at detected markers such as QR codes, but …)
      check: none
      reason: Facts 3, 4, and 5 support showing content at detected markers, QR codes as one marker type, and maintenance difficulty due to damaged markers.
    3 pass  (Markerless augmented reality applications are more versatile, need no physical markers, and have four …)
      check: none
      reason: Fact 6 supports markerless applications being more versatile and not requiring physical markers; fact 2 supports four subcategories.
    4 pass  (Location-based and superimposition-based markerless augmented reality applications use location sensors or computer-vision object recognition.)
      check: none
      reason: Fact 7 supports location-based applications using a location sensor; fact 8 supports superimposition-based applications using computer-vision object recognition.
    5 FAIL supported,faithful  (Projection-based and outlining-based markerless augmented reality applications use light projectors or object recognition to …)
      check: project digital graphics, digital characters, or other digital content onto an object, a surface, or a space [9]
      reason: The phrase “to enhance views” adds an outcome for projection-based applications that fact 9 does not state; fact 9 only says they project digital content onto an object, surface, or space. A repair would say projection-based applications use light projectors to project digital content onto objects, surfaces, or spaces, while outlining-based applications use object recognition to digitally enhance the view.

3/A7  quiz  3/S3  "Quick quiz"  (6 facts, 17 concepts)
  Q Why are augmented reality systems commonly classified as marker-based or markerless rather than by the degree of immersion they provide?  [3/S3/F0, 3/S3/F1]
    - Because their categories follow the psychological experience produced by the systems
    - Because their categories follow the display hardware worn to view the systems
    - Because their categories follow the realism of the content added to the systems
    * Because their categories follow the technology used to build and deploy the systems
    because: AR categories are based primarily on the technology used to develop and deploy the system, not on psychological immersion. VR is the side where categories follow the psychological or immersion aspect.
  Q What makes marker-based augmented reality systems easy to build but difficult to maintain in many real environments?  [3/S3/F2]
    * Their simple algorithms depend on physical markers that can be damaged
    - Their holographic-projection algorithms depend on physical markers that can be damaged
    - Their location-sensor algorithms depend on physical markers that can be damaged
    - Their computer-vision algorithms depend on physical markers that can be damaged
    because: Marker-based AR is easier to make because it uses simple algorithms, but the physical markers must be maintained and can be damaged, especially outside a carefully kept environment.
  Q How do markerless augmented reality techniques reduce the maintenance problem of marker-based augmented reality?  [3/S3/F3, 3/S3/F4]
    - By detecting needed cues mainly with holographic projection and sometimes with sensors
    * By detecting needed cues mainly with computer vision and sometimes with sensors
    - By detecting needed cues mainly with immersive rendering and sometimes with sensors
    - By detecting needed cues mainly with QR-code scanning and sometimes with sensors
    because: Markerless AR avoids dependence on placed markers by relying mainly on computer vision, with other sensors such as GPS used in location-based cases.
  Q In the experience they provide, how do augmented reality applications mainly differ from virtual reality applications?  [3/S3/F7]
    - They replace the physical room with a synthetic environment in the user's real-world view
    - They hide the user's movement from the user's real-world view
    - They remove physical objects from the user's real-world view
    * They add digital content to the user's real-world view
    because: AR emphasizes augmenting the real-world view with digital content, whereas VR applications are characterized by immersion rather than by adding content to the physical view.

3/A8  recap  3/S3  "Recap"  (8 facts, 22 concepts)
  Virtual reality and augmented reality are categorized and used in contrasting ways. Virtual reality systems are grouped by how immersive the psychological experience is, while augmented reality systems are grouped mainly by the technology used, especially whether markers are required. Marker-based augmented reality is simpler but depends on markers that are hard to maintain, so markerless methods using computer vision and other techniques become important. Both technologies have overlapping application domains, but virtual reality aims to immerse the user, whereas augmented reality adds digital content to the real-world view.
  - Virtual reality system categories are based on psychological immersion: non-immersive, semi-immersive, and fully immersive.
  - Augmented reality system categories are based primarily on technology rather than psychology, and are marker-based or markerless.
  - Marker-based augmented reality is easier to make using simple algorithms, but markers need sanitized, well-attended environments.
  - Markerless augmented reality overcomes marker maintenance mainly with computer vision, sometimes GPS, superimposition, outline, or projection-based techniques.
  - Virtual reality and augmented reality share similar application domains, but virtual reality is immersive while augmented reality augments reality.
  judge round 1: 1 of 6 failed
    1 pass  (Virtual reality system categories are based on psychological immersion: non-immersive, semi-immersive, and fully immersive.)
      check: none
      reason: Fact 1 supports that VR system categories are based on the psychological/experiential aspect and lists non-immersive, semi-immersive, and fully immersive systems.
    2 pass  (Augmented reality system categories are based primarily on technology rather than psychology, and are …)
      check: none
      reason: Fact 2 supports that AR system categories are based primarily on technology rather than psychological aspect and broadly comprise marker-based and markerless systems.
    3 pass  (Marker-based augmented reality is easier to make using simple algorithms, but markers need sanitized …)
      check: none
      reason: Fact 3 supports that marker-based AR is easier to make with simple algorithms but requires well-maintained, sanitized environments to avoid marker damage.
    4 FAIL supported,faithful  (Markerless augmented reality overcomes marker maintenance mainly with computer vision, sometimes GPS, superimposition, outline …)
      check: may rely on other sensors, such as GPS sensors, in location-based applications [5]; include superimposition-based and outline-based applications [6]; can be used in AR application development [7]
      reason: The point goes beyond the facts by saying markerless AR overcomes marker maintenance with "sometimes GPS, superimposition, outline, or projection-based techniques"; fact 5 only says it may use GPS in location-based applications, fact 6 lists superimposition and outline as computer-vision-based application types, and fact 7 only says projection-based techniques can be used in AR development. A repaired point would say only that markerless AR overcomes marker maintenance by relying primarily on computer vision and may use other sensors, such as GPS, in location-based applications.
    5 pass  (Virtual reality and augmented reality share similar application domains, but virtual reality is immersive …)
      check: none
      reason: Fact 8 supports that VR and AR have broadly similar application domains, with VR characterized as immersive and AR emphasizing augmenting digital content onto the real-world view.
    0 pass  (Virtual reality and augmented reality are categorized and used in contrasting ways.)
      check: none
      reason: The text is supported by facts 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 8, reads as a coherent summary, and the points together cover the segment's main ideas without omitting a required fact.

3/A14  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (11 facts, 31 concepts)
  Q Why are augmented reality system categories based mainly on implementation technology rather than on the degree of immersion, unlike virtual reality system categories?  [3/S0/F1, 3/S3/F0, 3/S3/F1; virtual reality system category, augmented reality system category, augmented reality, virtual reality]
    A Virtual reality systems are categorized by psychological immersion, comprising non-immersive, semi-immersive, and fully immersive systems. Augmented reality does not require an immersive experience; it emphasizes augmenting real-world content with digital content. Therefore, AR system categories are based primarily on the technology used to develop and deploy them, broadly marker-based and markerless.
  Q How do markerless augmented reality techniques address the main maintenance problem of marker-based augmented reality systems?  [3/S2/F4, 3/S2/F5, 3/S3/F3; marker-based augmented reality, markerless augmented reality technique, marker, computer vision]
    A Marker-based augmented reality systems are easy to build but difficult to maintain because markers are prone to damage, and a damaged marker may make the application not work. Markerless augmented reality techniques overcome this difficulty by not requiring physical markers; they can use computer vision and allow users to decide where to place virtual objects. This makes them more versatile than marker-based systems.
  Q How does AccuVein illustrate the way augmented reality applications in healthcare support diagnosis and treatment planning?  [3/S1/F4, 3/S1/F5; augmented reality application, AccuVein, vein network, treatment plan]
    A Healthcare augmented reality applications include medical training, telemedicine options, and real-time information that supports diagnosis, surgery, and treatment plans. AccuVein is a handheld AR device that scans a patient's vein network and, by being pointed at the skin surface, lets the internal vein network be visualized. It can indicate the patient's condition, reduce escalation by 45%, and help decide the treatment course, illustrating how AR can support clinical decision-making.
  Q How do augmented reality customer-experience and try-on applications in commerce contribute to the motivation for the metaverse?  [3/S0/F5, 3/S1/F1, 3/S1/F3; metaverse, customer-experience application, try-on application]
    A Customer-experience and try-on augmented reality applications let customers preview or try a product before purchase, for example by placing IKEA objects in a scanned room, digitally painting walls, or trying cosmetic and watch models. The presence of many such augmented reality applications in commerce, particularly e-commerce, is one motivation for the metaverse concept.

===== lecture 4: Definitions

4/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (1 facts, 1 concepts)
  What is immersive experience? (lecture 1) -> An immersive experience is a perceived experience through sensory organs that appears real, because a person cannot distinguish the experienced environment from their real environment and perceives it as that real environment.

4/A1  quiz  4/S0  "Quick quiz"  (3 facts, 3 concepts)
  Q How does the dictionary sense of virtual describe something that is present?  [4/S0/F0]
    - As present in reality or appearance but not in fact
    * As present in essence or effect but not in fact
    - As present in ideas or memories but not in fact
    - As present through sights or sounds but not in fact
    because: Virtual means being in essence or effect but not in fact, so it is present without being attributable to factual things. The other options mix in ideas from reality, sensory experience, or memory, but they do not state the dictionary sense of virtual.
  Q In dictionary terms, what does reality refer to?  [4/S0/F1]
    - The state or quality of being virtual
    - The state or quality of being imagined
    - The state or quality of being apparent
    * The state or quality of being real
    because: Reality is defined as the state or quality of being real, distinguished from something merely apparent. Being apparent, virtual, or imagined are not what the dictionary term reality denotes.
  Q In the dictionary definition of virtual reality, what role do a person's actions play?  [4/S0/F2]
    * They partially determine what happens in the environment
    - They fully determine what happens in the environment
    - They select the sights and sounds provided by a computer
    - They are determined by what happens in the environment
    because: In a virtual reality environment, a person's actions partially determine what happens. They do not fully control the environment, are not themselves controlled by it, and the definition does not reduce their role to selecting sensory stimuli.

4/A2  recap  4/S0  "Recap"  (3 facts, 3 concepts)
  The dictionary meanings of virtual and reality are defined separately before being combined in the term virtual reality. Virtual describes something that is in essence or effect but not in fact, while reality describes being real, independent of ideas, and not merely apparent. Virtual reality is then defined as an artificial sensory environment with primary computer-provided sights and sounds, where actions partly determine what happens.
  - Virtual means being in essence or effect but not in fact, not attributable to any factual things.
  - Reality is the state or quality of being real, independent of ideas, and not merely apparent.
  - Virtual reality is an artificial sensory environment with primary computer-provided sights and sounds, where actions partly determine what happens.
  judge round 1: 1 of 4 failed
    1 pass  (Virtual means being in essence or effect but not in fact, not attributable to …)
      check: none
      reason: The point is supported by fact 1: it restates 'being in essence or effect but not in fact' and 'not attributable to any factual things' without adding unsupported material. It names its subject and is a single clear point.
    2 pass  (Reality is the state or quality of being real, independent of ideas, and not …)
      check: none
      reason: The point is supported by fact 2: it compresses the dictionary description of reality into 'being real, independent of ideas, and not merely apparent' without changing the meaning in a way that would mislead a learner. It stands alone and is one idea.
    3 pass  (Virtual reality is an artificial sensory environment with primary computer-provided sights and sounds, where …)
      check: none
      reason: The point is supported by fact 3: it captures an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, primary computer-provided sights and sounds, and partial determinacy by actions. It is clear, standalone, and one idea.
    0 FAIL supported,faithful  (The dictionary meanings of virtual and reality are defined separately before being combined in …)
      check: none
      reason: The text adds a meta-sequence not stated in the facts: 'defined separately before being combined' and 'then defined'. The facts give three definitions but do not say the meanings were defined separately first and then combined into virtual reality. A repair should remove the unsupported order/composition and simply summarize the three dictionary meanings.

4/A3  quiz  4/S1  "Quick quiz"  (3 facts, 9 concepts)
  Q Why can a virtual tour built from recorded real-world imagery still be a virtual reality environment?  [4/S1/F2]
    * It is a computer-generated scenario whose changes do not happen in real time
    - It is a physical space whose changes do not happen in real time
    - It is a real-world video stream whose changes do happen as they occur in real time
    - It is a real environment whose changes do not happen in real time
    because: A virtual environment may use real-world imagery, but it still counts as artificial because the scenario is computer-generated and its changes are not happening in real time. A live feed or physical space presents a real environment rather than a synthetic one.
  Q What does the sensory experience characteristic of a virtual reality system provide?  [4/S1/F3]
    - User actions on elements in the environment for an interactive experience
    - Live camera video plus computer-generated sound to the user's sensory organs for a real-time experience
    - Physical props to the user's sensory organs for a tangible experience
    * Computer-generated stimuli to the user's sensory organs for an immersive experience
    because: The sensory experience characteristic is an immersive experience produced by computer-generated stimuli reaching the user's senses. Interaction and physical props are related to different aspects, and live camera video presents a real rather than a computer-generated environment.
  Q What does the interaction characteristic of a virtual reality system require?  [4/S1/F4]
    - Preprogrammed scripted events partly determine what happens
    - Passive viewing sequences partly determine what happens
    - Fixed environmental rules partly determine what happens
    * Participant actions or inputs partly determine what happens
    because: The interaction characteristic requires that participant actions or inputs partly determine what happens, making the environment responsive to the participant. Scripted events, passive viewing, or fixed rules do not establish that responsive interactivity.

4/A4  recap  4/S1  "Recap"  (5 facts, 9 concepts)
  A virtual reality system is identified by what surrounds the user, what the user receives, and what the user can do. The environment must be artificial and computer-generated, the experience must reach the user through sensory stimuli, and the user must be able to act within the environment. These characteristics together distinguish a VR system from systems that are not VR.
  - A VR system has an artificial, computer-generated environment, even when using real-world imagery.
  - A VR system provides computer-generated sensory stimuli, creating an immersive experience.
  - A VR system is interactive, so user actions partially determine its dynamic changes.
  judge round 1: 1 of 4 failed
    1 pass  (A VR system has an artificial, computer-generated environment, even when using real-world imagery.)
      check: none
      reason: The point is carried by facts 1, 2, and 3: a VR system has an artificial environment, that environment is computer-generated, and it can still count as VR when real-world imagery is used.
    2 pass  (A VR system provides computer-generated sensory stimuli, creating an immersive experience.)
      check: none
      reason: Fact 4 states that a VR system provides computer-generated stimuli to the user's sensory organs so the user can immersively experience the environment, which supports the point.
    3 pass  (A VR system is interactive, so user actions partially determine its dynamic changes.)
      check: none
      reason: Fact 5 states that a VR system must be interactive and that user actions partially determine what happens, producing dynamic changes, which supports the point closely enough.
    0 FAIL summary  (A virtual reality system is identified by what surrounds the user, what the user …)
      check: immersive experience [4]
      reason: The text summarizes the environment and interaction but leaves out the sensory characteristic as immersion, even though the segment teaches 'sensory immersion' and fact 4 says the immersive experience is a hallmark. A repaired version would say something like 'the experience must be immersive through computer-generated sensory stimuli.'

4/A5  quiz  4/S2  "Quick quiz"  (3 facts, 9 concepts)
  Q Why is a mouse-driven CAD system not a virtual reality system?  [4/S2/F1]
    - The user remains in a synthetic room at the screen
    - The user remains viewing a live real room at the screen
    - The user remains unable to edit the model at the screen
    * The user remains in the real room at the screen
    because: A CAD system can provide a virtual environment and interaction, but it does not provide an immersive sensory experience because the user is still situated in the real world beside the screen. The tempting synthetic-room option describes immersion, which is what CAD lacks.
  Q Why is a video conferencing system not a virtual environment?  [4/S2/F2]
    - It presents an imaginary environment in real time
    * It presents a real-world environment in real time
    - It presents a synthetic environment in real time
    - It presents a simulated environment in real time
    because: Video conferencing presents the real world as a live screen view, so it is not a computer-generated synthetic environment. Although it is interactive, that alone does not make it a virtual environment.
  Q Why does a 3D movie experience not count as virtual reality?  [4/S2/F3]
    * The viewer watches without changing the displayed content
    - The viewer sees a flat picture without changing the displayed content
    - The viewer receives no sensory stimulation while changing the displayed content
    - The viewer sees the real room beside the screen while changing the displayed content
    because: A 3D movie can provide a virtual environment and a partly immersive experience, but it is not interactive because the viewer cannot alter what is shown. The missing characteristic is interaction, not visual richness or sensory stimulation.

4/A6  recap  4/S2  "Recap"  (4 facts, 9 concepts)
  The rule for VR is that a system needs a virtual environment, an immersive experience through sensory organs, and interaction. The examples test familiar systems against that rule: CAD is virtual and interactive but not immersive, video conferencing is interactive but real-world rather than virtual and immersive, and 3D movies are virtual and partly immersive but not interactive. Thus each example fails at least one VR characteristic and is non-VR.
  - A VR system requires a virtual environment, immersive experience through sensory organs, and interaction; missing one means non-VR.
  - A CAD system is not VR because it is not immersive; users see the real world while using a mouse.
  - A video conferencing system is not VR because it shows a real-world environment through a screen and is not immersive.
  - A 3D movie experience is not VR because it is not interactive; viewers only watch the content.
  judge round 1: 1 of 5 failed

    2 pass  (A CAD system is not VR because it is not immersive; users see the …)
      check: none
      reason: Supported by fact 2: CAD is not VR because it is not immersive, with the user seeing the real world while using a mouse.
    3 pass  (A video conferencing system is not VR because it shows a real-world environment through …)
      check: none
      reason: Supported by fact 3: video conferencing is not VR because it presents a real-world environment through a screen and is not immersive.
    4 pass  (A 3D movie experience is not VR because it is not interactive; viewers only …)
      check: none
      reason: Supported by fact 4: a 3D movie experience is not VR because it is not interactive; the viewer only watches.
    0 FAIL supported  (The rule for VR is that a system needs a virtual environment, an immersive …)
      check: none
      reason: Mostly supported by facts 1-4, but it adds the unsupported characterization 'familiar systems'. A repaired version could say 'The examples apply that rule to CAD, video conferencing, and 3D movies' without 'familiar'.
  judge kept: original; still failing: [0]

4/A9  match_pairs  lecture  "Match the terms"  (15 facts, 8 concepts)
  virtual reality = An artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli provided by a computer, in which a person's actions partially determine what happens and which …
  virtual environment = A non-real, computer-generated graphical representation of a real or imaginary world, populated with artificial objects, that is experienced through computer-generated sensory stimuli.
  virtual = A term that means being in essence or effect but not in fact, that is, something that is there but cannot be …
  reality = The state or quality of being real, as something that exists independently of ideas concerning it, or as something that constitutes a …
  sensory experience = A characteristic of a virtual reality system in which the system provides computer-generated stimuli to the user's sensory organs, such as eyes …
  user interaction = A characteristic of a virtual reality system in which the user can act on or interact with elements in the environment, and …
  immersive experience = A perceived experience through sensory organs that appears real, because a person cannot distinguish the experienced environment from their real environment and …
  virtual reality tour = A virtual reality experience for visiting a recreated place without physically going there, in which movement from one point to another is …

4/A12  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (7 facts, 13 concepts)
  Q Why can a virtual tour that recreates a real world using real-world imagery still count as the virtual environment of a virtual reality system?  [4/S1/F1, 4/S1/F2; virtual environment, virtual reality tour, virtual reality system, real time]
    A A virtual tour can still be the virtual environment of a virtual reality system because the environment is an artificial, computer-generated scenario rather than a real environment. It may recreate a real world using real-world imagery or video, but the representation is still computer-generated. Also, its changes are not happening in real time.
  Q Why does a computer-aided design system fail to provide the immersive experience that virtual reality systems require?  [4/S2/F0, 4/S2/F1, 1/S1/F2; computer-aided design system, immersive experience, virtual reality system]
    A A computer-aided design system does not provide an immersive experience because the user interacts with screen content through a mouse while still seeing the real world around the screen. An immersive experience means perceiving an environment through sensory organs as real and not distinguishing it from the real environment. Virtual reality systems require this immersive experience.
  Q Why is a three-dimensional movie experience not a virtual reality system even though it can provide a virtual environment and a partly immersive experience?  [4/S1/F4, 4/S2/F3; three-dimensional movie experience, virtual reality system, user interaction, immersive experience]
    A A three-dimensional movie experience is not a virtual reality system because it lacks user interaction. A virtual reality system requires user actions to partially determine what happens in the environment, producing dynamic changes. In a three-dimensional movie, the viewer only watches and cannot change the displayed content, so the environment and partly immersive experience alone are insufficient.
  judge round 1: 0 of 3 failed
    1 pass  (Why can a virtual tour that recreates a real world using real-world imagery still …)
      check: It can count because the virtual tour’s recreated real-world imagery is still an artificial, computer-generated scenario rather than a real environment, and its changes are not happening in real time.
      reason: Facts 5 and 6 carry the link: a VR environment is a computer-generated representation that is not a real environment, and a virtual tour using real-world imagery still counts because it remains computer-generated and not real-time.
    2 pass  (Why does a computer-aided design system fail to provide the immersive experience that virtual …)
      check: A CAD system fails to provide the required immersive experience because the user interacts with screen content through a mouse while still seeing the real world, so the screen content is not perceived as the real environment.
      reason: Fact 10 gives the specific CAD reason, fact 13 states that immersion requires failing to distinguish the experienced environment from the real one, and fact 9 states that VR systems require this immersive experience.
    3 pass  (Why is a three-dimensional movie experience not a virtual reality system even though it …)
      check: A 3D movie is not a VR system because, although it provides a virtual environment and a partly immersive experience, it lacks interaction since the viewer only watches and cannot change the displayed content.
      reason: Facts 8 and 12 carry the link: VR requires user actions to partially determine dynamic changes, while a 3D movie is non-interactive and therefore not VR despite providing a virtual environment and partial immersion.

===== lecture 5: Definitions

5/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (15 facts, 5 concepts)
  What is augmented reality (AR)? (lecture 1) -> Augmented reality (AR) is an enhanced version of reality created by technology, in which computer-generated digital content is overlaid on the real world in real time and registered in 3D, so the user perceives and interacts with the enhanced environment.
  What is mixed reality (MR)? (lecture 1) -> Mixed reality (MR) is an immersive technology that is the same as augmented reality, in which digital content is overlaid on the view of reality and can be interacted with.
  What is reality-virtuality continuum? (lecture 1) -> Reality-virtuality continuum is a scale whose extremes are a completely real environment with nothing virtual and a completely virtual environment with nothing real, with augmented reality and augmented virtuality as intermediate states between them.
  What is virtual reality (VR)? (lecture 4) -> Virtual reality (VR) is an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli provided by a computer, in which a person's actions partially determine what happens and which replaces the user's sense of reality without requiring the physical existence of objects or places.
  What is virtual environment? (lecture 4) -> Virtual environment is a non-real, computer-generated graphical representation of a real or imaginary world, populated with artificial objects, that is experienced through computer-generated sensory stimuli.

5/A1  quiz  5/S0  "Quick quiz"  (3 facts, 6 concepts)
  Q In the systemic definition, what must a system that combines the real world with virtual content and supports real-time interaction also do to qualify as augmented reality?  [5/S0/F1]
    * Register the virtual content in 3D
    - Replace the real view with a fully virtual environment
    - Keep the virtual content fixed to the display screen
    - Let the user choose a separate location for the virtual content
    because: The systemic definition requires an AR system to combine the real world with virtual content, be interactive in real time, and be registered in 3D. Replacing the real view or fixing content to a screen does not satisfy that 3D registration requirement.
  Q What does it mean that an augmented reality system supports interaction with the digital content in the enhanced environment rather than separately?  [5/S0/F2]
    - The user points to the content with a physical marker
    * The user interacts with it while remaining in the real world
    - The user controls the real-world view but not the digital content
    - The user switches to a separate application to touch the content
    because: One AR characteristic is that interaction with the digital content happens within the enhanced environment, giving the user the feel of being in reality at all times. A separate application or separate control channel breaks that continuity.
  Q What follows from the rule that an augmented reality system is identified only by checking the four AR characteristics one by one?  [5/S0/F3]
    - A system that fails one characteristic is still an AR system if the interaction is real time
    - A system that fails one characteristic is still an AR system if the content is visible
    * A system that fails one characteristic is not an AR system
    - A system that fails one characteristic is still an AR system if the other three are satisfied
    because: Under the four-characteristic test, all four characteristics must be satisfied for a system to be an AR system. If at least one is missing, the system is not an AR system, regardless of how well the others are met.

  - A systemic augmented reality definition requires real-world/virtual combination, real-time interaction, and 3D registration.
  - An augmented reality system has four characteristics: computer-generated enhancement, 3D registration, sensory experience, and interaction in the enhanced environment.
  - A system is augmented reality only if it satisfies all four augmented reality characteristics; one missing disqualifies it.

5/A6  recap  5/S2  "Recap"  (7 facts, 6 concepts)
  Mixed reality has no single accepted definition, and a dictionary description does not clearly separate it from augmented or virtual reality. Some definitions broaden it, treating it as the whole space between real and virtual environments or as a capability to combine augmented and virtual reality in one application or device. Other definitions narrow it to augmented reality, as a stronger form or a synonym, so the course avoids the confusion by treating mixed reality and augmented reality as the same technology.
  - Mixed reality lacks an agreed precise definition, and its dictionary definition does not distinguish it from VR or AR.
  - One definition treats mixed reality as everything between real and virtual environments, so it includes augmented reality.
  - Another definition says mixed reality means combining augmented and virtual reality in one application or device.
  - Some definitions call mixed reality stronger augmented reality or a synonym for augmented reality with overlaid, interactive digital content.
  - In this course, mixed reality is treated as the same technology as augmented reality, so the terms are interchangeable.
  judge round 1: 2 of 6 failed

    2 pass  (One definition treats mixed reality as everything between real and virtual environments, so it …)
      check: none
      reason: Fact 3 supports the point: one definition places MR between the real and virtual extremes, so it includes AR.

  real time = A condition in which interactions are reflected immediately and content loading has minimal latency.
  interaction = The activity that takes place between a user and a system, often by manipulating an image or parts of it with input …

5/A14  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (9 facts, 10 concepts)
  Q What does the position of augmented reality and virtual reality on the reality-virtuality continuum imply about whether the experienced place must exist?  [5/S1/F0, 5/S1/F1, 1/S2/F0, 1/S2/F1; augmented reality, virtual reality, reality-virtuality continuum, physical environment]
    A Augmented reality requires the place being experienced to exist, while virtual reality does not require a physical object or place. On the reality-virtuality continuum, augmented reality is the intermediate state in which the real environment is augmented with virtual content, while virtual reality replaces the user's sense of reality with a virtual environment.
  Q How does checking the four augmented reality characteristics distinguish an augmented reality system from a system that only displays digital content?  [5/S0/F2, 5/S0/F3; augmented reality system, interaction, three-dimensional, sensory organ]
    A The four characteristics make an all-or-nothing identification test: a system must enhance the real world with digital content, register that enhancement in three dimensions, provide it through the user's sensory organs, and support interaction with the content in the enhanced environment. If any one is missing, the system is not an augmented reality system, so merely displaying digital content is insufficient.
  Q Why are mixed reality and augmented reality treated as interchangeable in the course?  [5/S2/F0, 5/S2/F6, 5/S3/F0; mixed reality, augmented reality]
    A Because definitions of mixed reality are not agreed and the resulting controversy is not needed for the course, the course assumes mixed reality is the same technology and idea as augmented reality. It therefore treats the two terms as interchangeable in its later discussion.

===== lecture 6: Historical Evolution

6/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (9 facts, 5 concepts)
  What is immersion? (lecture 2) -> Immersion is the objective, quantifiable degree to which a virtual reality system projects stimuli onto the sensory receptors of users in an extensive, matching, surrounding, vivid, interactive, and plot-informing way.
  What is immersive technology? (lecture 1) -> Immersive technology is a technology that produces an experience in which a person perceives an environment through sensory organs as real, so that they cannot distinguish it from their real environment.
  What is immersive experience? (lecture 1) -> An immersive experience is a perceived experience through sensory organs that appears real, because a person cannot distinguish the experienced environment from their real environment and perceives it as that real environment.
  What is metaverse? (lecture 1) -> Metaverse is a broad view of an all-around three-dimensional environment in which people act as in the real world through natural interaction with digital content, reimagining human interaction with the digital world rather than being merely an application of virtual reality, mixed reality, or augmented reality technology.
  What is virtual reality (VR)? (lecture 4) -> Virtual reality (VR) is an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli provided by a computer, in which a person's actions partially determine what happens and which replaces the user's sense of reality without requiring the physical existence of objects or places.

6/A4  recap  6/S1  "Recap"  (5 facts, 20 concepts)
  Before digital computers appeared in the 1940s, a few developments already anticipated immersive virtual reality. Stereoscopic devices showed that the brain can perceive 2D images as 3D objects and space, the display principle later used in virtual reality. Brewster’s later stereoscope made that depth effect more practical, while Link’s flight simulator concept extended immersion through multiple sensors.
  - The early pre-computer era before 1940s digital computers included a few key developments conceptually similar to immersive virtual reality.
  - Wheatstone’s 1838 stereoscopic device first showed the brain can perceive 2D images as 3D, the principle VR uses for immersion.
  - Brewster’s 1860 compact stereoscope improved Wheatstone’s device, making stereoscopic depth a more practical step toward immersive experience.
  - Edwin A. Link’s 1928 flight simulator concept evolved into multi-sensor simulators, a precursor to modern multi-sensory immersive virtual reality.

6/A6  recap  6/S2  "Recap"  (12 facts, 36 concepts)
  The formative history of virtual reality covers its second historical phase, from roughly 1950 to 1990. It begins with head-mounted displays, then introduces immersive and haptic systems that broadened what users could experience. Later terminology, commercial head-mounted displays, and public presentations helped shape the field's modern name and visibility.
  - Virtual reality's formative years were its second phase, roughly 1950 to 1990, from early HMDs to the term virtual reality.
  - Early head-mounted displays led to Sutherland's first 1967 head-tracked, computer-generated HMD, the Sword of Damocles.
  - Heilig's Sensorama was the first immersive virtual reality system, stimulating vision, sound, smell, wind, and haptics.
  - Brooks's 1967 haptic feedback system let users feel objects on a screen while manipulating them.
  - The term changed from artificial reality to Lanier's virtual reality, while commercial HMDs and public papers also appeared.

Early advances included immersive CAVE displays and software tools for building VR applications.   - The White 5 HMD had a 150-degree field of view, while HMDs became more portable, less bulky, and more usable.
