6/A19  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (8 facts, 26 concepts)
  Q Why can Sir Charles Wheatstone's 1838 stereoscopic device be regarded as a first step toward virtual reality?  [6/S1/F1, 6/S1/F2; stereoscopic device, stereoscopic vision, virtual reality]
    A It established that the human brain can process two-dimensional images as three-dimensional objects. In virtual reality, headsets present two-dimensional images, and stereoscopic vision makes the user perceive them as three-dimensional objects and space, which is immersion. The device is therefore roughly considered a first step toward immersive experience.
  Q Why is Morton Heilig's Sensorama considered an early immersive virtual reality system rather than only a visual display?  [6/S2/F3, 6/S2/F4; Sensorama, immersive virtual reality system, stereo sound, haptics]
    A Sensorama can be considered the first immersive virtual reality system under the modern definition of virtual reality. It was publicized as having 3D, wide vision, motion, color, stereo sound, smell, wind, and vibrations, and it stimulated all sensory organs by letting a user feel pre-recorded vibrations, sounds, smells, and wind. Therefore it was more than a visual display.
  Q Why is Sutherland's Sword of Damocles an important milestone in the development of virtual reality head-mounted displays?  [6/S2/F6, 6/S3/F5; Sword of Damocles, head-mounted display, head tracking, computer-generated imagery]
    A It was the first demonstrated head-mounted display that combined head tracking with computer-generated imagery. This showed that a headset could follow the user's motion and present computer-generated content. Later head-mounted displays evolved from such early systems into more portable and usable forms.
  Q How did the 2016 commercial virtual reality headset releases extend the effect that inexpensive headsets had already had near the end of the modern phase?  [6/S3/F8, 6/S4/F0; modern phase, current growth phase, virtual reality headset, immersive experience]
    A Near the end of the modern phase, the availability of inexpensive headsets, such as the Oculus Rift, greatly spurred interest in virtual reality. In 2016, many well-known companies released commercial virtual reality headsets, making immersive experiences affordable to a large population and spurring growth. This began the current growth phase.
  judge round 1: 3 of 4 failed

      reason: Facts 3 and 4 carry the link: Wheatstone established the 2D-to-3D principle, and VR headsets use that same principle through stereoscopic vision to create immersion. The reference’s phrase “Modern virtual reality headsets still use” is not needed and is not stated by the cited facts, but the factual claim is otherwise supported.

===== lecture 7: Historial Evolution

7/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (13 facts, 5 concepts)
  What is augmented reality (AR)? (lecture 1) -> Augmented reality (AR) is an enhanced version of reality created by technology, in which computer-generated digital content is overlaid on the real world in real time and registered in 3D, so the user perceives and interacts with the enhanced environment.
  What is virtual reality (VR)? (lecture 4) -> Virtual reality (VR) is an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli provided by a computer, in which a person's actions partially determine what happens and which replaces the user's sense of reality without requiring the physical existence of objects or places.
  What is augmented reality system? (lecture 5) -> An augmented reality system is a system with four required characteristics: it enhances the real world with computer-generated digital content registered in 3D, that content is experienced through the user's sensory organs, and it supports real-time interaction with that content in the enhanced environment.
  What is head-mounted display (HMDs)? (lecture 6) -> A head-mounted display (HMD) is a wearable, mobile visual display that integrates electronic, optical, mechanical, and audio components and uses one or two small screens directly in front of the user's eyes to place images for monoscopic or stereoscopic viewing. It can be non-see-through, optical see-through, or video see-through.
  What is Virtual Visual Environment Display (VIVED)? (lecture 6) -> Virtual Visual Environment Display (VIVED) is the first commercially viable and commercially available stereoscopic, head-tracked head-mounted display with a wide field of view.

7/A2  recap  7/S0  "Recap"  (2 facts, 12 concepts)
  Augmented reality's historical development is divided into four approximate phases that may overlap, unlike the phases of virtual reality. These phases show a progression from early work that established concepts and needed technology, through research into tracking, displays, and input devices, then early applications and work on interaction, usability, and design. The timeline ends in commercial application, where AR became more widely available and newer uses appeared in domains such as gaming, medicine, mobile, commerce, and marketing.
  - Unlike virtual reality's phases, augmented reality's four phases may sometimes overlap: pre-1980s experimental, 1980s–mid-1990s basic research, mid-1990s–2007 tools/applications, 2007–present commercial.
  - Augmented reality's phases move from concepts, to research into enabling technologies, then applications, usability, and design theory, then commercial availability.
  judge round 1: 1 of 3 failed
    1 pass  (Unlike virtual reality's phases, augmented reality's four phases may sometimes overlap: pre-1980s experimental, 1980s–mid-1990s …)
      check: none
      reason: The point states the same four AR phases, their approximate periods, their possible overlap, and the contrast with VR as fact 1 does.
    2 pass  (Augmented reality's phases move from concepts, to research into enabling technologies, then applications, usability …)
      check: none
      reason: The point compresses fact 2's phase descriptions into a progression from concepts, enabling-technology research, application-related work, and commercial availability; the omitted details are not needed for this point.
    0 FAIL faithful  (Augmented reality's historical development is divided into four approximate phases that may overlap, unlike …)
      check: such as tracking, displays, and input devices in [2]
      reason: The text changes fact 2's examples by saying "research into tracking, displays, and input devices" without "such as", making the examples read as the complete set of enabling technologies. A repaired version would say "research into enabling technologies such as tracking, displays, and input devices".
  judge kept: original; still failing: [0]

These early AR experiments later led to aircraft head-mounted displays, VR displays, and input and tracking hardware.

7/A9  recap  7/S3  "Recap"  (12 facts, 41 concepts)
  During AR’s tools-and-applications phase, mid-1990s work developed core tracking, display, and interaction research while extending AR to shared views, medical uses, and related wearable displays. In 1997, computer-vision markers and GPS wearable computers brought three-dimensional registration to in-place outdoor content. Outdoor wearable AR then supported navigation, CAD, and games in 2002–2003, but its hardware remained bulky and difficult. Marker-tracking advances, including the AR Toolkit, later moved to early mobile phones, where the first mobile-phone AR application appeared in 2004.
  - Mid-1990s AR work included tracking, display, interaction, shared AR content, medical uses, and related wearable head-mounted displays.
  - In 1997, AR used computer-vision markers and GPS wearable computers to register in-place content in three dimensions.
  - 2002–2003 outdoor wearable AR supported navigation, CAD, and games, but its backpack computers, sensors, and displays were bulky and difficult.
  - Viewpoint tracking, needed for accurate 3D registration, was addressed by Rekimoto’s matrix tracking and the open-source AR Toolkit’s square-marker tracking.
  - In 2004, the first mobile-phone AR application was demonstrated, and the AR Toolkit was ported to early mobile phones.

7/A16  match_pairs  lecture  "Match the terms"  (7 facts, 8 concepts)
  experimental phase = A phase in the historical evolution of augmented reality (AR) that involved early experimentation defining AR concepts and showing the types of …
  basic research phase = A phase in the historical evolution of augmented reality that followed the experimental phase and involved research into enabling technologies such as …
  tools or applications phase = The phase of the historical evolution of augmented reality from the mid-1990s to 2007 in which early applications were developed or explored …

7/A19  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (8 facts, 25 concepts)
  Q How does the basic research phase of augmented reality extend the experimental phase?  [7/S0/F0, 7/S0/F1; experimental phase, basic research phase, augmented reality, tracking]
    A The basic research phase extends the experimental phase by moving from identifying what augmented reality requires to researching the enabling technologies that make it possible. The experimental phase defined augmented reality concepts and showed the types of technology required for augmented reality. The basic research phase then involved research into enabling technologies such as tracking, displays, and input devices.
  Q What makes Chameleon and NaviCam precursors to the kind of augmented-reality applications seen today?  [7/S2/F5, 7/S2/F6, 7/S2/F7; Chameleon, NaviCam, mobile augmented reality system, augmented reality application]
    A They were early handheld or mobile augmented-reality systems that superimposed virtual content on the real world. Chameleon allowed a user to move a liquid-crystal display over paper to see virtual content, and NaviCam superimposed virtual tags on real objects using handheld or head-mounted displays. Because both were true augmented-reality-type applications, they anticipated the kind of augmented-reality applications seen today.
  Q How did augmented reality become widely available commercial technology after The Eye of Judgment was released?  [7/S4/F0, 7/S4/F1, 7/S4/F2; commercial application phase, The Eye of Judgment, augmented reality authoring tools, smartphone-based augmented reality]
    A It became widely available because a consumer launch made augmented reality popular and later commercial factors removed its earlier barriers. The Eye of Judgment, released in 2007, began the commercial application phase and made such augmented-reality experiences popular after augmented reality had previously been neither very popular nor easily available. In 2009, Adobe Flash authoring tools, smartphone-based augmented reality, and global marketing campaigns moved augmented reality from research laboratories and specialist applications to widespread commercial use.

===== lecture 8: Issues & Challenges

8/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (10 facts, 4 concepts)
  What is immersion? (lecture 2) -> Immersion is the objective, quantifiable degree to which a virtual reality system projects stimuli onto the sensory receptors of users in an extensive, matching, surrounding, vivid, interactive, and plot-informing way.
  What is virtual reality (VR)? (lecture 4) -> Virtual reality (VR) is an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli provided by a computer, in which a person's actions partially determine what happens and which replaces the user's sense of reality without requiring the physical existence of objects or places.
  What is virtual environment? (lecture 4) -> Virtual environment is a non-real, computer-generated graphical representation of a real or imaginary world, populated with artificial objects, that is experienced through computer-generated sensory stimuli.
  What is virtual reality system? (lecture 4) -> A virtual reality system is a system that presents a computer-generated artificial environment, provides computer-generated sensory stimuli for an immersive experience, and lets the user's actions partially determine what happens in it.

8/A1  quiz  8/S0  "Quick quiz"  (3 facts, 8 concepts)
  Q What is the main objective of a virtual reality system?  [8/S0/F0]
    - Letting a user perceive suitable sensory stimuli as a human-factor issue
    * Letting a user experience an artificial environment through computer-provided sensory stimuli
    - Letting a user distinguish real-world sensory stimuli from computer-provided sensory stimuli
    - Letting a user generate suitable sensory stimuli for an artificial environment
    because: A virtual reality system aims to let a user experience an artificial environment through sensory stimuli supplied by the computer. Generating stimuli is the technological issue, not the system's objective, and distinguishing virtual stimuli from real ones is not the stated aim.
  Q Why is perceiving virtual-reality stimuli suitably treated as a psychological human-factor issue?  [8/S0/F1]
    * Technology does not address it, and it is likely to differ between users
    - Technology makes it indistinguishable from real stimuli, and it is likely to differ between users
    - Technology projects it onto sensory receptors, and it is likely to be the same for all users
    - Technology generates it suitably, and it is likely to differ between users
    because: The psychological issue is how users perceive stimuli suitably; it is a human-factor concern that technology does not solve and that can vary from person to person. Generating or projecting stimuli belongs to the technological side, not the reason this issue is psychological.
  Q What two major concerns arise from the technological and psychological issues in virtual reality?  [8/S0/F2]
    - Extensiveness and interactivity
    * Immersion and presence
    - Sight and sound
    - Technology and psychology
    because: The technological and psychological issues of virtual reality give rise to the major concerns of immersion and presence. Technology and psychology are the issues behind the concerns, while extensiveness and interactivity are qualities of immersion, and sight and sound are only two sensory modalities.

8/A3  quiz  8/S1  "Quick quiz"  (4 facts, 11 concepts)
  Q In Slater and Wilbur's definition, immersion is an objective degree describing what?  [8/S1/F0]
    * The projection of stimuli
    - The perception of stimuli
    - The control of stimuli
    - The understanding of stimuli
    because: Immersion is defined by how a VR system and application project stimuli onto users' sensory receptors. Perception, understanding, and control are not the defining objective property.
  Q When a user's physical movement is immediately reflected in the virtual world, which quality of immersion is shown?  [8/S1/F2]
    - The vivid quality
    - The surrounding quality
    * The matching quality
    - The plot-informing quality
    because: Matching refers to congruence between the user's physical movement and movement in the virtual world. Surrounding concerns panoramic coverage, vividness concerns sensory detail, and plot-informing concerns story understanding.
  Q A user can make changes, receive responses from virtual entities, and influence future events. Which quality of immersion does this describe?  [8/S1/F5]
    - The surrounding quality
    * The interactive quality
    - The matching quality
    - The vivid quality
    because: Interactivity is the user's capability to affect the virtual world and receive responses, not merely observe one-way feedback. Matching, surrounding, and vividness concern different aspects of immersion.
  Q In VR, which of these is the psychological concern rather than the technological one?  [8/S1/F7]
    - The immersion concern
    * The presence concern
    - The extensiveness concern
    - The vividness concern
    because: Immersion is the technological issue, while presence is the psychological issue. Vividness and extensiveness are qualities of immersion, not the separate psychological concern.

8/A4  recap  8/S1  "Recap"  (8 facts, 17 concepts)
  VR immersion is defined as the objective degree to which a system projects stimuli onto users' senses. Its six qualities describe that projection in terms of sensory range, movement congruence, panoramism, sensory energy, user influence, and story understandability. These qualities separate immersion, a technological system property, from presence, a psychological issue.
  - Slater and Wilbur define VR immersion as objective stimulus projection that is extensive, matching, surrounding, vivid, interactive, plot-informing.
  - Extensive, matching, surrounding, and vivid immersion mean sensory breadth, movement match, panoramic cues, and sensory energy.
  - Interactive and plot-informing immersion mean user influence and an understandable, predictable story.
  - In VR, immersion is the technological issue, while presence is the psychological issue.

8/A6  recap  8/S2  "Recap"  (4 facts, 3 concepts)
  Presence is the psychological side of an immersive experience: it is a subjective state in which the user perceives the generated experience without accurately acknowledging the technology's role. When computer-generated stimuli are indistinguishable from real-world stimuli, the user perceives them as coming from the real world rather than from a computer. Perfect presence is the state in which the virtual world and the real world cannot be distinguished.
  - Presence is the subjective psychological state in which a user perceives the generated immersive qualities without accurately acknowledging technology's role.
  - In presence, computer-generated stimuli stimulate the senses and are perceived as real because they cannot be distinguished from real-world stimuli.
  - Perfect presence is the inability to distinguish the virtual world from the real world.

    2 pass  (In presence, computer-generated stimuli stimulate the senses and are perceived as real because they …)
      check: none
      reason: Fact 3 carries the point: in presence, computer-generated stimuli stimulate the senses, and because they cannot be distinguished from real-world stimuli, they are perceived as real or as coming from the real world.
    3 pass  (Perfect presence is the inability to distinguish the virtual world from the real world.)

8/A8  recap  8/S3  "Recap"  (6 facts, 4 concepts)
  Immersion and presence are distinct qualities of a VR experience, one objective and one subjective. Immersion describes what a VR system can provide and can be measured, while presence is the user's psychological sense of being in the virtual environment. Presence can depend on both subjective experience and the system's immersion, so greater immersion raises and lesser immersion lowers the potential for presence without ensuring it. The overall goal of a VR system is to create high presence, which requires the system to provide high immersion, a systemic issue.
  - Immersion is an objective, quantifiable description of what a VR system can provide.
  - Presence is a user's subjective, hard-to-measure psychological sense of being in the virtual environment.
  - Presence can depend on subjective experience and immersion; greater immersion raises and lesser lowers presence potential, not guaranteeing it.
  - A VR system's overall goal of high presence requires high immersion, a systemic issue.

8/A15  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (9 facts, 16 concepts)
  Q Why are immersion and presence treated as different concerns in virtual reality?  [8/S0/F1, 8/S0/F2, 8/S1/F7; immersion, presence, technological issue, psychological issue]
    A The two major issues in virtual reality are technological, about generating suitable sensory stimuli, and psychological, about how a user perceives those stimuli. These issues give rise to immersion and presence as central concerns. Immersion corresponds to the technological issue, while presence corresponds to the psychological issue.
  Q How can a virtual reality system provide a high degree of immersion without guaranteeing a high degree of presence?  [8/S3/F0, 8/S3/F1, 8/S3/F2, 8/S3/F3; immersion, presence]
    A A virtual reality system can provide a high degree of immersion without guaranteeing a high degree of presence, because immersion is an objective and quantifiable description of what a system can provide or does provide, while presence is a subjective psychological state inside the user's mind. Immersion can aid an enhanced perception of presence and is capable of producing presence, but it does not ensure presence; greater immersion increases the potential for presence.
  Q How do display resolution and field of view contribute to different qualities of immersion in a virtual reality system?  [8/S1/F3, 8/S1/F4; display resolution, field of view, vivid, surrounding]
    A Display resolution affects vividness, because higher resolution increases the energy stimulated in a sensory modality and improves visual perception. Field of view affects surrounding, because a wider field of view makes the visual cues more panoramic than a narrow field of view.

===== lecture 9: Issues & Challenges

9/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (14 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is immersion? (lecture 2) -> Immersion is the objective, quantifiable degree to which a virtual reality system projects stimuli onto the sensory receptors of users in an extensive, matching, surrounding, vivid, interactive, and plot-informing way.
  What is virtual reality (VR)? (lecture 4) -> Virtual reality (VR) is an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli provided by a computer, in which a person's actions partially determine what happens and which replaces the user's sense of reality without requiring the physical existence of objects or places.
  What is three-dimensional registration? (lecture 7) -> Three-dimensional registration is the anchoring of virtual content in augmented reality at a suitable place in the real world so that it appears to be part of the physical environment and mixes seamlessly with real-world objects.
  What is presence? (lecture 8) -> Presence is a subjective psychological state in which an experience generated by human-made technology is perceived as real, because the user fails to acknowledge the technology's role and perceives computer-generated stimuli as coming from the real world.
  What is augmented reality (AR)? (lecture 1) -> Augmented reality (AR) is an enhanced version of reality created by technology, in which computer-generated digital content is overlaid on the real world in real time and registered in 3D, so the user perceives and interacts with the enhanced environment.
  What is immersive experience? (lecture 1) -> An immersive experience is a perceived experience through sensory organs that appears real, because a person cannot distinguish the experienced environment from their real environment and perceives it as that real environment.

9/A1  quiz  9/S0  "Quick quiz"  (4 facts, 4 concepts)
  Q In virtual reality, what does a high degree of presence give a user?  [9/S0/F0]
    - Belief that the real world is the virtual world
    - Belief that the virtual world is an artificial display
    * Belief that the virtual world is the real world
    - Belief that the real world is an augmented overlay
    because: Presence means the user believes they are in the real world while actually in a virtual world. The other options reverse the relationship or describe non-presence states.

9/A2  recap  9/S0  "Recap"  (4 facts, 4 concepts)
  VR systems aim for presence, the feeling that a virtual world is experienced as real. People differ in what counts as reality: some expect virtual reality to match real-world perception and sensation, while others expect it to go beyond everyday reality. This difference makes judging presence ambiguous, because a system that works for one group may not work for another.
  - A VR system aims for presence, making users believe the virtual world is real; closer to that goal, immersion improves.
  - Some people treat real-world perception and sensation as the gold standard, so virtual reality should match them closely.
  - For others, virtual reality should surpass everyday lived reality rather than imitate it exactly.
  - Different conceptions of reality make virtual reality evaluation ambiguous, because matching or surpassing reality may not satisfy all users.

  The uncanny valley effect shows that increasing human likeness does not continuously increase familiarity. It describes how almost-real digital humans can feel eerie because of subtle imperfections, with a sharp dip in familiarity in 70-85% human likeness, especially for moving objects. In VR, this makes exact realism a design risk, so the amount of realism must be chosen as a trade-off.
  - The uncanny valley effect is that almost-real digital humans can feel eerie because of subtle imperfections.
  - The uncanny valley plot shows familiarity rising, falling sharply in 70-85% human likeness, especially for moving objects, then rising again.
  - In VR, near-real human-like figures can be unpleasant, so creators must choose how much realism to include.

9/A7  recap  9/S2  "Recap"  (9 facts, 10 concepts)
  VR presence is not achieved only by making virtual objects photorealistic or human-like, because familiar cues in the virtual environment can support it. Representational, interaction, and experiential fidelity are the main design axes, each moving toward higher fidelity when virtual places, user actions, and personal experiences more closely match real-world or intended conditions. Maintaining all three fidelities as highly as possible helps keep the uncanny valley from disrupting the virtual experience.
  - Presence in VR does not require photorealism or human-like objects; developers should balance representational, interaction, and experiential fidelity.
  - Representational fidelity is how much a VR place conveys familiarity with an Earthly place, from photorealistic views to abstract worlds.
  - Interaction fidelity is how well virtual task actions correspond to real-world physical actions, from realistic motion to buttons.
  - Experiential fidelity is how closely the user's experience matches the creator's intended experience, with real-world constraints raising it.
  - VR developers should limit the uncanny valley by maintaining all three fidelities as high as possible.
  judge round 1: 2 of 6 failed
    1 FAIL supported,faithful  (Presence in VR does not require photorealism or human-like objects; developers should balance representational …)
      check: consider [2]
      reason: The point says developers should “balance” the three fidelities, but fact [2] says they should “consider” them and fact [9] says maintain them as high as possible; “balance” adds a trade-off idea not stated. A repaired version would replace “balance” with “consider” or “take into account”.
    2 pass  (Representational fidelity is how much a VR place conveys familiarity with an Earthly place …)
      check: none
      reason: Facts [3] and [4] support the definition and the high-to-low range from photorealistic real-world views to abstract unfamiliar worlds. The wording is a fair paraphrase.
    3 pass  (Interaction fidelity is how well virtual task actions correspond to real-world physical actions, from …)
      check: none
      reason: Facts [5] and [6] support the definition of interaction fidelity and the high-to-low range from realistic physical action to button-based interaction with no motion.
    4 pass  (Experiential fidelity is how closely the user's experience matches the creator's intended experience, with …)
      check: none
      reason: Facts [7] and [8] support that experiential fidelity is the match between user experience and creator intent, and that real-world constraints make the experience closer to the real world and therefore higher.
    5 pass  (VR developers should limit the uncanny valley by maintaining all three fidelities as high …)
      check: none
      reason: Fact [9] supports maintaining all three fidelities as high as possible so that the uncanny valley effect does not affect the virtual experience; “limit the uncanny valley” is an acceptable shorthand for preventing that effect.

9/A9  recap  9/S3  "Recap"  (7 facts, 15 concepts)
  Using Azuma's 1997 definition of augmented reality, the main AR challenges are technological rather than psychological. They concern display and interaction: suitable display technology must overlay virtual content on the real-world representation, and suitable input modalities must support real-time interaction. A third challenge is 3D registration, in which virtual content is anchored to the real world by determining the viewer's pose and updating it through registration and tracking.
  - Augmented reality challenges are mostly technological rather than psychological because immersion is less important than in virtual reality.
  - Azuma's 1997 definition of augmented reality is used to identify its main technological challenges.
  - Augmented reality display challenges involve overlaying virtual content on the device's real-world view, similar to virtual reality.
  - Augmented reality interaction requires suitable input devices and modalities for real-time interaction with overlaid digital content.
  - Augmented reality 3D registration anchors virtual content by determining the viewer's pose; registration sets it and tracking updates it.

9/A11  recap  9/S4  "Recap"  (4 facts, 11 concepts)
  Virtual reality and augmented reality face different major issues. In virtual reality, technological and psychological concerns lead to immersion and presence, while environments that are too familiar can cause an uncanny valley, which builders avoid by attending to representational, experiential, and interaction fidelity. In augmented reality, the main problems are mostly technological: display, input mechanisms, and pose tracking.
  - Virtual reality systems have technological and psychological concerns, tied respectively to immersion and presence.
  - In virtual reality, the uncanny valley effect is unease caused by environments that are too familiar.
  - Builders avoid the virtual reality uncanny valley by attending to representational, experiential, and interaction fidelity.
  - Major augmented reality issues are technological: display, input mechanisms, and pose tracking at the start and during use.
  judge round 1: 4 of 5 failed
    1 pass  (Virtual reality systems have technological and psychological concerns, tied respectively to immersion and presence.)
      check: none
      reason: Fact 1 states that VR systems have technological and psychological concerns connected to immersion and presence; the point is a shorter paraphrase of that idea.
    2 FAIL supported,faithful  (In virtual reality, the uncanny valley effect is unease caused by environments that are …)
      check: unease caused by environments that are too familiar (fact 2)
      reason: Fact 2 says the effect occurs when making environments as familiar as possible can cause uneasiness or creepiness. The point makes it deterministic and adds 'too familiar', so it goes beyond the fact. A repair should say the uncanny valley effect in VR can cause unease when environments are made as familiar as possible.
    3 FAIL supported,faithful  (Builders avoid the virtual reality uncanny valley by attending to representational, experiential, and interaction …)
      check: Builders avoid ... by attending to (fact 3)
      reason: Fact 3 says that to avoid the uncanny valley, one should be aware of the three fidelities; it does not state that builders avoid it by attending to them. A repair should preserve the recommendation, e.g. 'To avoid the VR uncanny valley, builders should attend to representational, experiential, and interaction fidelity.'
    4 FAIL faithful  (Major augmented reality issues are technological: display, input mechanisms, and pose tracking at the …)
      check: are technological (fact 4)
      reason: Fact 4 says major AR issues are mostly technological, not fully technological. The point drops the hedge 'mostly', making the claim stronger than the fact. A repair should say the major AR issues are mostly technological.
    0 FAIL supported,faithful  (Virtual reality and augmented reality face different major issues.)
      check: environments that are too familiar; builders avoid by attending to (facts 2, 3)
      reason: The text repeats the unsupported 'too familiar' wording from fact 2 and the stronger claim that builders avoid the uncanny valley by attending to the fidelities, whereas fact 3 only says one should be aware of them. 9/A14  match_pairs  lecture  "Match the terms"  (16 facts, 8 concepts)
  three-dimensional registration = The anchoring of virtual content in augmented reality at a suitable place in the real world so that it appears to be …
  presence = A subjective psychological state in which an experience generated by human-made technology is perceived as real, because the user fails to acknowledge …
  uncanny valley effect = A phenomenon in human perception in which almost realistic, subtly imperfect artificial or digital human-like figures, objects, or environments evoke unease or …
  representational fidelity = The degree to which a virtual reality experience conveys, matches, or exploits familiarity with a place that is or could be on …
  interaction fidelity = The degree to which physical actions for a virtual task correspond to physical actions for an equivalent real-world task, exploiting real-world experience …
  experiential fidelity = The degree to which a user's personal experience matches the virtual reality creator's intended experience, and it is higher when real-world constraints …
  pose = The position and orientation of a viewer or tracked object.
  pose estimation = The process of determining a viewer's position and orientation relative to a real-world anchor so that virtual content can be registered in …

9/A17  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (11 facts, 24 concepts)
  Q How does the ambiguity of reality in virtual reality create a design trade-off over realism?  [9/S0/F1, 9/S0/F2, 9/S0/F3, 9/S1/F0, 9/S1/F2; virtual reality system, reality, realism, uncanny valley effect]
    A The trade-off arises because some users want virtual reality to match reality, while others want it to surpass their everyday experience. A system that matches one conception may not satisfy another, and almost-real human-like figures can trigger the uncanny valley. Designers must therefore decide how much realism to include.
  Q How does the systemic definition of augmented reality point to its three main technological issues?  [5/S0/F1, 9/S3/F2, 9/S3/F3, 9/S3/F5, 9/S3/F6; augmented reality, display technology, input modality, three-dimensional registration]
    A The definition points to its issues by requiring combining real and virtual content, real-time interaction, and three-dimensional registration. Combining requires display technology to overlay virtual content on the representation of the real world. Interaction requires suitable input devices and modalities. Registration requires pose, where pose means position and orientation; the registration phase determines the initial pose, and the tracking phase updates it as the user moves.
  Q How are the registration and tracking phases of pose estimation needed for three-dimensional registration in augmented reality?  [9/S3/F4, 9/S3/F5, 9/S3/F6; three-dimensional registration, pose, registration phase, tracking phase]
    A Registration and tracking phases are needed because three-dimensional registration must keep virtual content anchored to the real world while the viewer moves. Pose means position and orientation relative to an anchor, and three-dimensional registration requires that pose to be estimated. The registration phase determines the initial pose at start, and the tracking phase updates it as the user moves, so the virtual content remains properly mixed.

===== lecture 10: Cybersickness

10/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (16 facts, 5 concepts)
  What is virtual reality (VR)? (lecture 4) -> Virtual reality (VR) is an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli provided by a computer, in which a person's actions partially determine what happens and which replaces the user's sense of reality without requiring the physical existence of objects or places.
  What is virtual reality system? (lecture 4) -> A virtual reality system is a system that presents a computer-generated artificial environment, provides computer-generated sensory stimuli for an immersive experience, and lets the user's actions partially determine what happens in it.
  What is head-mounted display (HMDs)? (lecture 6) -> A head-mounted display (HMD) is a wearable, mobile visual display that integrates electronic, optical, mechanical, and audio components and uses one or two small screens directly in front of the user's eyes to place images for monoscopic or stereoscopic viewing. It can be non-see-through, optical see-through, or video see-through.
  What is stereoscopic vision? (lecture 6) -> Stereoscopic vision is the perception of three-dimensional objects and space from left and right two-dimensional images processed simultaneously, aided by binocular vision.
  What is non-immersive virtual reality system? (lecture 2) -> A non-immersive virtual reality system is a limited class of computer application that provides a computer-generated environment in which a user controls characters or activities while retaining control of the physical environment. The user is psychologically engaged and remains physically attached to the real world, while the virtual environment does not directly interact with the user.

    - Sensory overload may be happening or going to happen

    - Motion sickness may be happening or going to happen
    * Cybersickness may be happening or going to happen
    because: Common symptoms such as nausea, dizziness, or dryness of mouth during VR can indicate that cybersickness is present or starting. Motion sickness may be related, but the indicated condition is cybersickness.

10/A2  recap  10/S0  "Recap"  (4 facts, 18 concepts)
  Cybersickness, also called visually induced motion sickness, is a condition that can affect people using VR. Recognizable symptoms can show that it is occurring or about to occur, and it can result from many factors rather than one. Reducing cybersickness is important for VR usability and acceptability because it improves the overall user experience and makes VR applications more appealing to a wider range of people.
  - Cybersickness, also called visually induced motion sickness, can occur during VR interaction and is primarily relevant to VR.
  - One or more symptoms, like nausea, dizziness, vomiting, fatigue, or disorientation, can signal cybersickness onset or occurrence in VR.
  - Cybersickness can be caused by many factors, not by a single factor.
  - Reducing cybersickness matters for VR usability and acceptability because it improves overall user experience and broadens appeal.
  judge round 1: 0 of 5 failed
    1 pass  (Cybersickness, also called visually induced motion sickness, can occur during VR interaction and is …)
      check: none
      reason: The point is fully carried by fact [1]: it names cybersickness/VIMS, says it can occur during VR interaction, and keeps the fact's limitation that it is primarily relevant to VR.
    2 pass  (One or more symptoms, like nausea, dizziness, vomiting, fatigue, or disorientation, can signal cybersickness …)
      check: none
      reason: Fact [2] supports the idea that one or more of the listed symptoms during VR can indicate onset or current cybersickness; the examples are presented non-exhaustively with "like".
    3 pass  (Cybersickness can be caused by many factors, not by a single factor.)
      check: none
      reason: This restates fact [3] exactly: cybersickness can be caused by many factors, not by a single factor.
    4 pass  (Reducing cybersickness matters for VR usability and acceptability because it improves overall user experience …)
      check: none
      reason: Fact [4] supports the point: reducing cybersickness is important for VR usability and acceptability because it enhances user experience and makes VR more appealing to more people.
    0 pass  (Cybersickness, also called visually induced motion sickness, is a condition that can affect people …)
      check: none
      reason: The text is supported by facts [1], [2], [3], and [4]; it explains what cybersickness is, how symptoms indicate onset or occurrence, its multifactorial causes, and why reducing it matters for VR usability.

10/A3  quiz  10/S1  "Quick quiz"  (7 facts, 24 concepts)
  Q Which of these is an internal factor in the causes of cybersickness?  [10/S1/F1, 10/S1/F2]
    - The design of the virtual reality content
    - The latency of the virtual display
    - The resolution of the head-mounted display
    * A user's susceptibility to motion sickness
    because: Cybersickness causes are divided into internal user-related factors and external factors; external factors include hardware and VR content, while motion-sickness susceptibility is an individual user characteristic.
  Q How can prior or repeated exposure to VR affect the link between motion sickness susceptibility and cybersickness?  [10/S1/F10, 10/S1/F11]
    - It can strengthen that link and increase cybersickness severity over time
    - It can mask that link by hiding the user's motion sickness susceptibility over time
    - It can shift that link from an internal factor to an external hardware factor over time
    * It can weaken that link and reduce cybersickness severity over time
    because: Motion sickness susceptibility and cybersickness risk are positively related, but prior or repeated VR exposure can reduce that effect and reduce severity over time, so the link may not hold once exposure is present.
  Q How does the relationship between age and cybersickness differ for general VR content compared with controllable VR content?  [10/S1/F3, 10/S1/F4]
    - Age may be equally clear for general content and controllable content
    - Age may be clearer for general content and less clear for controllable content
    * Age may be less clear for general content and clearer for controllable content
    - Age may be irrelevant for general content and decisive for controllable content
    because: Age can be independent of cybersickness when users view general VR content, but it can become a clearer factor when the content is controllable, making the age relationship more evident in that setting.

    - Confidence, relaxation, or enjoyment
    - Boredom, surprise, or curiosity
    * Anxiety, stress, or frustration
    - Hunger, thirst, or fatigue
    because: Negative emotional conditions at the time of use, such as anxiety, stress, and frustration, can increase the likelihood of cybersickness, while the other listed states are not given as typical risk factors.

10/A4  recap  10/S1  "Recap"  (17 facts, 37 concepts)
  Cyber sickness in VR can be understood by separating its causes into internal user factors and external hardware or content factors. Internal factors include age, gender, motion sickness susceptibility, physical condition, and emotional condition, which can all shape susceptibility. Age and gender effects are qualified by content type, evidence, and fit issues, while motion sickness, physical, and emotional factors may increase risk but repeated VR exposure can reduce it.
  - Cyber sickness is studied through causes, evaluation, and mitigation; causes are internal or external hardware and VR content.
  - Internal factors for cybersickness are age, gender, motion sickness susceptibility, physical condition, and emotional condition.
  - Age may affect cybersickness susceptibility, especially for controllable content, and it is highly unlikely from age 12 to 25.
  - Gender findings are inconclusive, but female HMD use may increase cybersickness, possibly due to poorer IPD fit.
  - Motion sickness susceptibility, physical conditions, and emotional conditions can increase cybersickness, but prior VR exposure may reduce it.

10/A5  quiz  10/S2  "Quick quiz"  (7 facts, 21 concepts)
  Q What does it show that cybersickness can persist in advanced VR systems?  [10/S2/F1]
    - that advanced hardware shifted the cause to user susceptibility
    - that advanced hardware shifted the cause to the virtual environment
    - that inferior hardware quality still explains the symptoms in advanced systems
    * that some aspects of the devices themselves induce it
    because: Cybersickness is not only a sign of poor hardware; some properties of VR devices can themselves induce it, so it can remain even in advanced systems.
  Q In VR display-resolution comparisons across 1K, 2K, 3K, and 4K, how does cybersickness induction change as resolution increases?  [10/S2/F2]
    * It drops substantially from 1K to 2K, then changes little afterward
    - It changes little from 1K to 2K, then drops substantially afterward
    - It rises from 1K to 2K, then drops substantially afterward
    - It drops gradually from 1K to 4K, then changes little afterward
    because: Higher resolution reduces cybersickness mainly up to a point: the large improvement is from 1K to 2K, with no significant further reduction from 2K to higher resolutions.
  Q How do latency and latency jitter differ in HMD-based VR?  [10/S2/F3, 10/S2/F5]
    - latency is resolution, while jitter is brightness
    * latency is a delay, while jitter is variability
    - latency is input method, while jitter is display type
    - latency is variability, while jitter is a delay
    because: Latency is the time gap between a physical movement and its virtual reflection; latency jitter is the variation in that time gap over time.
  Q How does display type relate to the severity of cybersickness when stereoscopic 3D content is viewed?  [10/S2/F7]

    - flat screens are associated with more cybersickness than HMD displays

    because: Display type matters: HMD or VR headset displays are associated with more cybersickness than conventional or non-immersive display types such as flat or panoramic screens.

    - gamepad controls can cause more cybersickness than hand controls
    - handlebar controls can cause less cybersickness than joystick controls
    - non-motion controls can cause more cybersickness than motion controls
    because: Input method can influence cybersickness: motion controls such as handlebars may cause more sickness than non-motion controls like joysticks, and a gamepad can cause less than a hand controller.

10/A6  recap  10/S2  "Recap"  (11 facts, 24 concepts)
  VR cybersickness can arise from external hardware factors, not only from poor hardware quality. Device characteristics matter: resolution helps only up to a point, while latency and its jitter can increase discomfort. The display and input method also influence severity, with headsets and motion controls sometimes increasing it, though higher-end HMDs and gamepads can reduce it.
  - Hardware is an external, not user-dependent VR cybersickness factor, and device aspects, rather than only poor quality, can induce it.
  - VR display resolution reduces cybersickness substantially from 1K to 2K, but little further from 2K onward.
  - VR latency is the delay between physical movement and virtual update, and higher latency increases cybersickness.
  - Latency jitter is changing latency; it disrupts timing and can cause discomfort, disorientation, and cybersickness.
  - Display type and input method affect cybersickness; headsets and motion controls can raise it, higher-end HMDs and gamepads lower it.
  judge round 1: 4 of 6 failed
    1 pass  (Hardware is an external, not user-dependent VR cybersickness factor, and device aspects, rather than …)
      check: none
      reason: Facts 1 and 2 support the point: hardware is one external category, and device aspects can induce cybersickness without reducing the claim to poor hardware quality.
    2 FAIL supported,faithful  (VR display resolution reduces cybersickness substantially from 1K to 2K, but little further from …)
      check: "no significant further reduction" [3]; "from 2K onward"
      reason: Fact 3 says there was no significant further reduction from 2K to 3K or 3K to 4K, not that resolution gives little further reduction from 2K onward. A repaired point should say the reduction is substantial from 1K to 2K but not significant between 2K, 3K, and 4K.
    3 FAIL supported,faithful  (VR latency is the delay between physical movement and virtual update, and higher latency …)
      check: "In head-mounted display (HMD)-based virtual reality (VR)" [5]
      reason: Fact 5 states the latency-cybersickness relationship specifically in HMD-based VR, while the point omits that condition and states it for VR generally. A repaired point should say that in HMD-based VR, higher latency increases cybersickness.
    4 pass  (Latency jitter is changing latency; it disrupts timing and can cause discomfort, disorientation, and …)

    5 FAIL faithful  (Display type and input method affect cybersickness; headsets and motion controls can raise it …)

10/A11  match_pairs  lecture  "Match the terms"  (16 facts, 8 concepts)
  virtual reality = An artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli provided by a computer, in which a person's actions partially determine what happens and which …
  cybersickness = A condition primarily relevant to virtual reality that may be caused by multiple internal and external factors and in which a user …
  internal factors = Individual characteristics and conditions inherent to users that can increase the likelihood of experiencing cybersickness.
  external factors = The hardware factors and virtual reality content factors that can induce cybersickness.
  motion sickness = A condition in which the brain receives conflicting signals from various sensory organs, causing symptoms like nausea and dizziness.
  body awareness = The user's ability to attend to and perceive bodily sensations, a physical condition related to cyber sickness.
  latency = The time delay, or time gap, in virtual reality between a user's movement in the physical world and the corresponding change in …
  latency jitter = The variability in latency in which the time gap between a physical-world action and its virtual-world reflection changes from time to time.

10/A14  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (8 facts, 22 concepts)
  Q Why might a wider inter-pupillary distance adjustable range in virtual reality displays be especially useful for female users of head-mounted displays?  [10/S1/F6, 10/S1/F7; head-mounted display, inter-pupillary distance, inter-pupillary distance fit, cybersickness]
    A A wider inter-pupillary distance adjustable range may be especially useful for female head-mounted display users because they are associated with increased cybersickness, and a possible reason is trouble finding a good inter-pupillary distance fit. Inter-pupillary distance determines stereoscopic vision. A wider adjustable range can therefore help female users achieve a better fit.
  Q Why can latency jitter be an additional cybersickness risk in head-mounted display virtual reality beyond the risk created by latency itself?  [10/S2/F3, 10/S2/F4, 10/S2/F5, 10/S2/F6; latency, latency jitter, head-mounted display, cybersickness]
    A Latency jitter can add risk on top of latency itself because it makes latency vary from time to time, causing irregularities in the timing of data delivery. In head-mounted display virtual reality, cybersickness increases with latency. Latency is the time gap between a user's movement and the corresponding change in the virtual world. Those irregularities can lead to inconsistencies, discomfort, disorientation, and cybersickness.
  Q Why can a high-end head-mounted display still produce more cybersickness than a conventional monitor, even though it produces less than a lower-end head-mounted display?  [10/S2/F7, 10/S2/F8; head-mounted display, conventional monitor, display type, cybersickness]
    A Display type significantly influences cybersickness severity, and head-mounted display users experience more cybersickness than users of conventional monitors or non-immersive virtual reality systems. Within head-mounted displays, higher-end models cause less cybersickness than lower-end models because of better resolution, brightness, clarity, and contrast. A high-end head-mounted display can therefore reduce some hardware-quality effects while still being a more sickness-inducing display type than a monitor.

===== lecture 11: Cybersickness

11/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (19 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is immersion? (lecture 2) -> Immersion is the objective, quantifiable degree to which a virtual reality system projects stimuli onto the sensory receptors of users in an extensive, matching, surrounding, vivid, interactive, and plot-informing way.
  What is virtual reality (VR)? (lecture 4) -> Virtual reality (VR) is an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli provided by a computer, in which a person's actions partially determine what happens and which replaces the user's sense of reality without requiring the physical existence of objects or places.
  What is presence? (lecture 8) -> Presence is a subjective psychological state in which an experience generated by human-made technology is perceived as real, because the user fails to acknowledge the technology's role and perceives computer-generated stimuli as coming from the real world.
  What is cybersickness (CS)? (lecture 10) -> Cybersickness (CS) is a condition primarily relevant to virtual reality that may be caused by multiple internal and external factors and in which a user may experience symptoms such as nausea, dizziness, headache, or disorientation.
  What is virtual environment? (lecture 4) -> Virtual environment is a non-real, computer-generated graphical representation of a real or imaginary world, populated with artificial objects, that is experienced through computer-generated sensory stimuli.
  What is head-mounted display (HMDs)? (lecture 6) -> A head-mounted display (HMD) is a wearable, mobile visual display that integrates electronic, optical, mechanical, and audio components and uses one or two small screens directly in front of the user's eyes to place images for monoscopic or stereoscopic viewing. It can be non-see-through, optical see-through, or video see-through.

11/A2  recap  11/S0  "Recap"  (8 facts, 22 concepts)
  Virtual environment design can shape the likelihood and severity of cybersickness through six VR-content factors. Visual motion is especially important because it is linked to vection, the self-motion sensation. The remaining motion conditions—height, speed, viewpoint, angular velocity, rotation axis, and exposure duration—help explain when cybersickness appears and how strong it becomes.
  - Virtual environment design significantly affects cybersickness through six content factors: visual motion, locomotion, field of view, content type, duration, complexity.
  - Higher visual motion, a primary cause of cybersickness, raises risk, and vection, the self-motion sensation, correlates with visual motion.
  - Cybersickness severity increases with greater height and faster speed; the viewpoint during virtual motion is also important.
  - Brief turbulent visual motion alone is not enough, but longer exposure to it can induce cybersickness.
  - Cybersickness increases with angular velocity and is more intense around the x and y axes than the z axis.

  Field of view and content type are two VR content factors that influence cybersickness. A wider field of view can increase immersion, but reducing it may reduce cybersickness, while excessive narrowing can make discomfort worse. Content with action, fast movement, abrupt changes, horror, bumpy terrain, or stormy weather tends to increase cybersickness, although some users are less affected by adventurous content.
  - VR field of view is how much of the user's vision the display captures and affects cybersickness.
  - A larger VR field of view generally increases immersion, but reducing it can reduce cybersickness; excessive narrowing can worsen it.
  - Action, fast movement, and abrupt changes tend to cause more cybersickness, though adventurous users may have less severe symptoms.
  - Horror virtual environments are likely to induce more cybersickness than pleasant general content.
  - Bumpy or irregular terrain and stormy weather are more likely to cause cybersickness than flat terrain or clear weather.

  Q Which set of components is needed when a technique measures cybersickness?  [11/S4/F0]
    - An input, a virtual scene, and a symptom list
    - A display, a user report, and a physiological reading
    - A questionnaire, a HMD setting, and a final diagnosis
    * An input, a measurement process, and an output
    because: Cybersickness measurement is framed as taking some input, applying a measurement or evaluation process, and producing an output. Virtual scenes, displays, or HMD settings are not the core components of the measurement framework.
  Q What kind of information does a questionnaire-based cybersickness measure collect?  [11/S4/F4]
    - The motion features present in the virtual content
    - The user's heart rate and other biometric signals
    - The user's observed movements inside a virtual environment
    * The user's own ratings of discomfort or disorientation
    because: Questionnaire-based cybersickness input relies on self-report ratings, usually asking users to rate discomfort or disorientation numerically. Biometric signals, observed behavior, and content features are different kinds of input.
  Q What is the most common timing for giving a cybersickness questionnaire?  [11/S4/F6]
    - After a physiological reading is taken
    - At a fixed point inside every virtual session
    * Before or after the experience
    - Mainly during the experience
    because: Questionnaires are most commonly administered before or after an experience, although they can sometimes be given during the experience. They are not chiefly timed to physiological readings or fixed points inside a session.

    * Understand causes and identify possible interventions
    - Classify virtual content by its visual complexity
    - Remove the subjectivity of self-report ratings
    - Record biometric changes while the user is immersed
    because: Questionnaire-based cybersickness scales help researchers and practitioners understand causes of cybersickness and identify potential interventions. They do not remove self-report subjectivity, and they are not primarily used to record biometrics or classify content.

    * They assess a user's tendency to experience cybersickness
    - They classify the motion features of the content

11/A14  recap  11/S6  "Recap"  (6 facts, 16 concepts)
  Behavioral and content-based inputs are two input types used to measure cybersickness. Behavioral inputs track observable user responses such as blinking, movement, and postural sway, and postural sway can indicate cybersickness severity. Content-based inputs include optical flow, depth cues, and exceptional motion velocity, with optical flow reflecting apparent motion from relative user-environment motion. These two types are among four input categories: subjective questionnaire-based, objective physiological/biometric, behavioral, and content-based.
  - Behavioral cybersickness inputs include blink rate, head and body movement, the manner of those movements, and postural sway.
  - Postural sway during VR exposure can be monitored using axial movements or center-of-pressure changes and can indicate cybersickness severity.
  - Content-based cybersickness inputs include optical flow, apparent motion from relative user-environment motion, depth cues, and exceptional motion velocity.
  - The four cybersickness input categories are subjective questionnaire-based, objective physiological/biometric, behavioral, and content-based.

  Respiration Signal | Galvanic Skin Response | Heart Rate | *Postural Sway  (Galvanic skin response, heart rate, and respiration signal are physiological inputs for detecting cybersickness, whereas postural sway is a behavioral input.)  [11/S5/F2, 11/S6/F0]

11/A22  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (7 facts, 16 concepts)
  Q Why might reducing a virtual reality headset's field of view help with cybersickness, while making it too narrow can worsen the problem?  [11/S2/F2, 11/S2/F3; field of view, cybersickness, head movement, immersion]
    A A smaller field of view can reduce cybersickness symptoms, but an excessively narrow one can create new problems that may increase cybersickness. Reducing the field of view can be an effective way to alleviate symptoms. If it is too narrow, however, it can decrease immersion and increase head movement as the user looks for things, and that head movement may exacerbate or increase cybersickness.
  Q Why does the perception of motion in peripheral stimuli matter for the onset and severity of cybersickness?  [11/S0/F2, 11/S0/F3; vection, peripheral stimulus, visual motion, cybersickness]
    A Vection is the sensation of self-motion, and it is highest when motion is sensed in peripheral stimuli. Vection is positively correlated with visual motion stimulus, and visual motion is one of the primary causes of cybersickness. This link shows that peripheral visual motion can contribute to the onset and severity of cybersickness.
  Q Why might a cybersickness measurement approach combine questionnaire-based input with physiological or biometric input?  [11/S4/F4, 11/S5/F0, 11/S6/F5; questionnaire-based input, physiological and biometric input, cybersickness]
    A Combining these inputs lets a cybersickness measurement capture users' reported experience while also using objective physiological evidence. Questionnaire-based input is common because it asks users to rate discomfort or disorientation on scales. It can be subjective, prone to inaccuracies, and not always reliable, so physiological or biometric input can complement it by detecting cybersickness.

===== lecture 12: Cybersickness

12/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (11 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is field of view (FOV)? (lecture 11) -> Field of view (FOV) is an angular measure of the region visible to the eye at a single point in time, and in virtual reality it is the amount of virtual environment visible.
  What is teleportation? (lecture 11) -> Teleportation is a virtual reality locomotion operation in which a user selects a virtual target location and the virtual viewpoint instantly changes from the current location to that target, without physical movement.
  What is questionnaire-based input? (lecture 11) -> Questionnaire-based input is a subjective input for measuring cybersickness that generally takes the form of ratings of users' discomfort or disorientation on a numerical scale.
  What is sickness score? (lecture 11) -> A sickness score is a numerical output of cybersickness measurement that quantifies the severity of the cybersickness experience and is generally produced by a regression model in machine learning-based evaluation.
  What is physiological input? (lecture 11) -> Physiological input is an input used to detect cybersickness, because questionnaire-based inputs can be subjective, inaccurate, and not always reliable.
  What is optical flow? (lecture 11) -> Optical flow is the apparent motion perceived by virtual reality users due to relative motion between the user and the environment.

Interpretable models prioritize transparency and flexible insight into input-output relationships, whereas black-box models are harder to explain and may deliver better accuracy at the cost of greater data and processing needs. Hybrid models attempt to join these advantages by providing good predictive accuracy with some interpretability.
  - Cybersickness evaluation strategies can be organized around input, process, and output aspects.
  - Interpretable cybersickness models are transparent, flexible, and give precise details about input-output relationships.
  - Black-box cybersickness models are hard to explain but can be more accurate than interpretable models, needing more data and processing.
  - Hybrid cybersickness models combine different machine-learning models to provide good accuracy and some interpretability.

  Q In cybersickness evaluation, which category uses measurements taken after a virtual reality experience to decide whether sickness has occurred?  [12/S1/F0]
    * Detection
    - Mitigation
    - Scoring
    - Prediction
    because: Detection is the event-based category that uses post-experience input to determine whether cybersickness has occurred. Prediction, by contrast, is made before the experience and is aimed at anticipating it.
  Q Why is prediction important in cybersickness evaluation?  [12/S1/F1]
    - It can identify the input type used by a model
    - It can confirm that sickness has already occurred
    - It can rate the severity from a self-report questionnaire
    * It can enable mitigation before sickness occurs
    because: Prediction is important because it can let countermeasures be started before cybersickness develops. Confirming that sickness has already occurred is the role of detection, not prediction.

    - A pre-immersion baseline measurement

12/A4  recap  12/S1  "Recap"  (7 facts, 21 concepts)
  Cybersickness evaluation is organized by when measurement occurs and by what output it produces. Detection uses information after an experience to decide whether sickness happened, while prediction tries to determine it beforehand; prediction is less common but may support mitigation. Limited prediction work uses physiological, video, or baseline data, and self-report questionnaires generally provide severity scores or ratings. Machine-learning evaluation can output class labels for likelihood or severity or a numerical sickness score, usually produced by regression.
  - Cybersickness evaluation distinguishes after-experience detection of sickness from before-experience prediction of sickness.
  - Most cybersickness evaluation focuses on detection, but prediction can enable mitigation before sickness occurs.
  - Limited cybersickness prediction research uses physiological or video data, baseline measurements, and machine-learning sickness predictions.
  - Self-report cybersickness questionnaires generally give scores or ratings that can assess severity.
  - Machine-learning cybersickness evaluation outputs class labels showing likelihood or severity, or a numerical sickness score usually from regression.

12/A6  recap  12/S2  "Recap"  (3 facts, 7 concepts)
  Cybersickness cannot usually be fully prevented, so mitigation focuses on reducing its effects or lessening its impact. The difficult choice is that reducing cybersickness can weaken presence and therefore user experience. For this reason, mitigation is planned from both the developer's and the user's perspectives, since even a strong developer solution can fail if the user does not use the system as expected.
  - Cybersickness mitigation aims to reduce or lessen cybersickness because complete prevention is generally not possible.
  - Cybersickness mitigation trades off reducing cybersickness against preserving presence, which affects user experience.
  - Cybersickness mitigation must consider both developer and user perspectives, because improper user use can defeat developer solutions.

12/A7  quiz  12/S3  "Quick quiz"  (8 facts, 28 concepts)
  Q Why can a narrowed field of view reduce the onset or severity of cybersickness?  [12/S3/F2]
    - It can strengthen the depth cues in the periphery
    - It can shorten the user's exposure to the virtual environment
    * It can lower the peripheral optical flow
    - It can keep the virtual scene stable relative to the user's head
    because: Restricting the field of view can reduce cybersickness because it reduces peripheral optical flow. Stabilizing the scene or shortening exposure are separate ideas, not the stated mechanism for field-of-view restriction.
  Q How does an asymmetric field-of-view restrictor reduce cybersickness differently from a symmetric mask?  [12/S3/F5, 12/S3/F6]
    - It keeps the ground plane visible while the rest of the periphery is obscured
    - It hides the central region while leaving the outer periphery visible
    - It hides the periphery in reaction to translational or angular velocity while keeping the center visible
    * It hides high-flow peripheral regions while leaving low-flow regions visible
    because: An asymmetric restriction adapts to optical flow by masking peripheral areas with higher optical flow and leaving lower-flow areas visible. A symmetric mask is based on velocity, while ground-visible restriction and central masking are different strategies.
  Q What distinguishes peripheral blur from depth-of-field blur in a dynamic visual blur strategy?  [12/S3/F9]
    - It blurs salient central regions
    - It blurs distant regions
    * It blurs non-salient regions
    - It blurs the entire display uniformly
    because: Peripheral blur, also called dynamic non-salient region blurring, targets non-salient regions. Depth-of-field blur is tied to depth cues, so blurring distant regions belongs to that sibling technique.
  Q What kind of feedback does the phantom legs method provide to reduce cybersickness?  [12/S3/F15, 12/S3/F16, 12/S3/F17, 12/S3/F18]
    - Whole-body vibrations matched to the virtual environment
    - Vibrotactile pulses behind the ears during walking
    * Alternating haptic cues synchronized to footsteps
    - Short bursts of rotational acceleration during forward motion
    because: Phantom legs applies alternating haptic cues synchronized to the user's footsteps. Whole-body vibration, rotational acceleration, and behind-the-ear pulses are different hardware-level alteration approaches.

12/A8  recap  12/S3  "Recap"  (20 facts, 47 concepts)
  Developer-side countermeasures for cybersickness include several technical controls. Field-of-view and visual-flow methods try to reduce the visual motion signals that contribute to discomfort, while hardware changes add or adjust physical and sensory cues. Locomotion techniques complete the developer-side toolkit by changing how virtual movement is controlled.
  - Developer-side cybersickness mitigation can use field-of-view adjustment, dynamic visual blur, rest frames, optical-flow manipulation, hardware-level alterations, and locomotion modifications.
  - Field-of-view adjustment, effective across genders, reduces cybersickness by limiting peripheral optical flow, though masks may reduce presence.
  - Dynamic visual blur, fixed rest frames, and optical-flow manipulation reduce cybersickness by changing visual cues or perceived motion.
  - Hardware-level alterations reduce or eliminate cybersickness by modifying or creating display, camera, haptic, vibration, or motion platforms.
  - Locomotion techniques can be modified or newly proposed to prevent or reduce cybersickness.

12/A9  quiz  12/S4  "Quick quiz"  (6 facts, 13 concepts)
  Q What does the variability of cybersickness susceptibility imply about user-side countermeasures?  [12/S4/F0]
    - They can work by changing the virtual display content before the virtual reality session starts
    - They can replace the need to keep a VR session within a moderate safe time range for every user
    * They can still be needed even when the system already includes sickness-reduction features
    - They can depend mainly on using one fixed approach for a large group of different XR users
    because: Cybersickness susceptibility differs between users, so system-side reductions may not be enough and users may need their own countermeasures. User-side measures do not replace time limits, fixed methods, or display changes.
  Q How can a user lower the risk of cybersickness by managing session length?  [12/S4/F1]
    * By avoiding continuous or long-duration exposure and keeping the session within a moderate range
    - By using one continuous virtual reality session long enough to build habituation before stopping
    - By ignoring the type of device or content once the session reaches a fixed safe time for all users
    - By repeating the same long virtual reality session immediately after the first symptoms start fading
    because: Longer continuous exposure increases risk, so session length should be kept within a moderate range. Habituation is built through repeated managed exposures, not one long session, and duration can depend on device and content.
  Q What is the two-stage approach for a user trying to build habituation to a virtual environment?  [12/S4/F2, 12/S4/F3]
    - Begin with repeated short-duration exposures after symptoms appear, then use repeated longer-duration exposures while symptoms are still present
    * Begin with repeated short-duration exposures until symptoms appear, then use repeated longer-duration exposures after full recovery
    - Begin with repeated long-duration exposures until symptoms appear, then use repeated shorter-duration exposures after full recovery
    - Begin with repeated short-duration exposures until full recovery, then use repeated longer-duration exposures without waiting for recovery
    because: Habituation develops through repeated exposure with a step-up in duration, and the longer exposures should follow full recovery from symptoms. Continuing while symptomatic or reversing the duration order does not match the described approach.
  Q What do controlled breathing, pleasant background music, and adequate airflow have in common as sickness-reduction strategies?  [12/S4/F4, 12/S4/F5]
    - They are content changes that remove virtual locomotion from the environment before the session starts
    - They are hardware changes that make the head-mounted display fit more tightly to the user's head
    * They are user-side measures that can reduce or delay cybersickness without changing the virtual display
    - They are developer-side techniques that restrict peripheral visual motion before a user enters the scene
    because: Breathing control, music, and airflow are actions or conditions managed by the user, not changes to the virtual display, hardware, or content. They help by calming or soothing the user and reducing sickness effects.

12/A10  recap  12/S4  "Recap"  (6 facts, 13 concepts)
  Cybersickness is subjective, so users may need their own countermeasures, because developer-side interventions alone may not be enough. Users can lower the risk by limiting continuous or long VR exposure, with generally safe sessions for most users likely between 55 and 70 minutes. Habituation can reduce cybersickness through repeated short-duration exposures until symptoms appear, then longer-duration exposures after full recovery. Slow diaphragmatic breathing, pleasant background music, and adequate external airflow are further user-side strategies that can calm the mind and reduce cybersickness.
  - Cybersickness varies between users, so users need their own countermeasures, since developer-side interventions alone may not suffice.
  - Limit continuous or long VR exposure to reduce risk; safe sessions for most users are likely 55 to 70 minutes.
  - Habituation is gradual cybersickness reduction; try repeated short-duration exposures until symptoms appear, then repeated longer-duration exposures after full recovery.
  - Slow diaphragmatic breathing can delay cybersickness onset, reduce severity, and largely reduce the possibility of cybersickness.
  - Pleasant background music and adequate external airflow can calm the mind and reduce cybersickness.
  judge round 1: 2 of 6 failed
    1 pass  (Cybersickness varies between users, so users need their own countermeasures, since developer-side interventions alone …)
      check: none
      reason: The point is supported by fact 1: cybersickness susceptibility varies, so users need their own countermeasures because developer-side interventions alone may not be sufficient. It is standalone, clear, and one idea.
    2 FAIL faithful  (Limit continuous or long VR exposure to reduce risk; safe sessions for most users …)
      check: generally safe maximum duration ... for the majority of users likely to suffer from cybersickness [2]
      reason: It fails faithful because it says “safe sessions for most users are likely 55 to 70 minutes,” whereas fact 2 says the “generally safe maximum duration” is “between 55 and 70 minutes” for the “majority of users likely to suffer from cybersickness.” A repaired version should say the safe maximum is up to 55–70 minutes for most users likely to be affected, varying by conditions.
    3 pass  (Habituation is gradual cybersickness reduction; try repeated short-duration exposures until symptoms appear, then repeated …)
      check: none
      reason: Facts 3 and 4 support the definition of habituation and the two-stage exposure method. The point is standalone, clear, and presents one connected habituation idea.
    4 pass  (Slow diaphragmatic breathing can delay cybersickness onset, reduce severity, and largely reduce the possibility …)
      check: none
      reason: Fact 5 supports that slow diaphragmatic breathing can delay onset, reduce severity, and largely reduce the possibility of cybersickness. The point is standalone, clear, and one idea.
    5 pass  (Pleasant background music and adequate external airflow can calm the mind and reduce cybersickness.)
      check: none
      reason: Fact 6 supports that pleasant background music and adequate external airflow can calm or soothe the mind and reduce cybersickness. The point is standalone, clear, and one connected user-side strategy idea.
    0 FAIL supported,faithful  (Cybersickness is subjective, so users may need their own countermeasures, because developer-side interventions alone …)
      check: generally safe maximum duration ... for the majority of users likely to suffer from cybersickness [2]; to delay the onset, reduce the severity, and ... reduce the possibility [5]; repeated longer-duration exposures [4]
      reason: The text fails supported/faithful in three places: it calls 55–70 minutes “generally safe sessions” rather than the “generally safe maximum duration” for users likely to suffer; it says breathing, music, and airflow can all “calm the mind,” although only music and airflow are said to calm or soothe the mind; and it omits that the longer-duration exposures after recovery should be repeated. A repaired text should specify maximum safe duration, separate breathing’s onset/severity effects from music/airflow calming, and say repeated longer exposures.
