12/A13  match_pairs  lecture  "Match the terms"  (16 facts, 8 concepts)
  field of view = An angular measure of the region visible to the eye at a single point in time, and in virtual reality it is …
  presence = A subjective psychological state in which an experience generated by human-made technology is perceived as real, because the user fails to acknowledge …
  sickness score = A numerical output of cybersickness measurement that quantifies the severity of the cybersickness experience and is generally produced by a regression model …
  interpretable model = A machine learning model used in cybersickness evaluation that reveals how or why its output is generated from its input and provides …
  black-box model = A model used in cybersickness evaluation that takes an input and produces an output without revealing how or why that output is …
  hybrid model = A combination of different machine learning models used to predict or classify cybersickness, designed to provide high accuracy and some transparency.
  classification based on the event of measurement = A category of cybersickness evaluation technique that distinguishes detection, which uses input generated after the experience to determine whether cybersickness has occurred …
  prediction = A cybersickness evaluation technique that occurs before an experience to determine whether cybersickness will occur, enabling mitigation measures before cybersickness occurs.

  Dynamic Visual Blur | Field of View Adjustment | Rest Frames | *Diaphragmatic Breathing  (Field of view adjustment, dynamic visual blur, and rest frames are developer-side cybersickness-reduction strategies, whereas diaphragmatic breathing is a user-side countermeasure.)  [12/S3/F0, 12/S4/F4]
  Linear Discriminant Analysis | *Convolutional Neural Network | Naive Bayes Classifier | K-nearest Neighbors  (Naive Bayes classifiers, linear discriminant analysis, and K-nearest neighbors are interpretable machine-learning algorithms for measuring cybersickness, whereas a convolutional neural network is a black-box model studied for that evaluation.)   *Peripheral Blur | Symmetric Mask | Asymmetric Mask | Side Restrictor  (Symmetric masks, asymmetric masks, and side restrictors are field-of-view adjustment strategies, while peripheral blur is a type of dynamic visual blur.)  [12/S3/F5, 12/S3/F6, 12/S3/F7, 12/S3/F9]

12/A16  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (7 facts, 18 concepts)
  Q Why can field-of-view adjustment reduce cybersickness while also degrading the user experience?  [12/S3/F2, 12/S3/F4, 12/S2/F1; field of view adjustment, peripheral optical flow, presence, user experience]
    A Field-of-view adjustment can, ideally, mitigate the onset or severity of cybersickness because restricting the field of view reduces peripheral optical flow. It can also degrade user experience because it can reduce presence and impair performance in visual tasks by restricting certain visual content. Since presence affects user experience, that potential reduction in presence can degrade the experience.
  Q Why is prediction of cybersickness important for mitigation, even though most cybersickness evaluation work focuses on detection?  [12/S1/F0, 12/S1/F1; detection, prediction, mitigation measures]
    A Detection uses input generated after the experience to determine whether cybersickness has occurred, whereas prediction occurs before the experience to determine whether it will occur. Prediction is important because it can enable mitigation measures before cybersickness occurs. Most evaluation work nevertheless focuses on detection rather than prediction.
  Q Why can hybrid machine-learning models be useful for cybersickness evaluation in application domains such as medical diagnosis?  [12/S0/F8, 12/S0/F10; hybrid model, transparent model, black-box model, prediction accuracy]
    A Hybrid models combine different machine-learning models and are designed to provide high accuracy and transparency in their decision-making process. They can combine the strengths of transparent and black-box models by providing good predictive accuracy and some interpretability. This makes them useful where both high accuracy and transparency are essential, such as medical diagnosis.

===== lecture 13: VR Hardware

13/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (15 facts, 5 concepts)
  What is virtual reality (VR)? (lecture 4) -> Virtual reality (VR) is an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli provided by a computer, in which a person's actions partially determine what happens and which replaces the user's sense of reality without requiring the physical existence of objects or places.
  What is presence? (lecture 8) -> Presence is a subjective psychological state in which an experience generated by human-made technology is perceived as real, because the user fails to acknowledge the technology's role and perceives computer-generated stimuli as coming from the real world.
  What is virtual environment? (lecture 4) -> Virtual environment is a non-real, computer-generated graphical representation of a real or imaginary world, populated with artificial objects, that is experienced through computer-generated sensory stimuli.
  What is virtual reality system? (lecture 4) -> A virtual reality system is a system that presents a computer-generated artificial environment, provides computer-generated sensory stimuli for an immersive experience, and lets the user's actions partially determine what happens in it.
  What is head-mounted display (HMDs)? (lecture 6) -> A head-mounted display (HMD) is a wearable, mobile visual display that integrates electronic, optical, mechanical, and audio components and uses one or two small screens directly in front of the user's eyes to place images for monoscopic or stereoscopic viewing. It can be non-see-through, optical see-through, or video see-through.

13/A2  recap  13/S0  "Recap"  (3 facts, 7 concepts)
  A complete VR system includes the organism, the VR hardware, and the surrounding physical world, not hardware alone. These parts are linked by data flows: tracking from the organism to VR hardware, stimulation from VR hardware to the organism, and bidirectional flows between the physical world and both the VR hardware and the organism. The organism is therefore an essential component to account for alongside the VR hardware.
  - A complete view of a VR system includes the organism, the VR hardware, and the surrounding physical world.
  - Tracking flows organism to VR hardware; stimulation flows VR hardware to organism; the physical world has bidirectional flows with both.
  - The organism, usually the human user, is as important as VR hardware and cannot be omitted; it is always present.

13/A4  recap  13/S1  "Recap"  (2 facts, 13 concepts)
  A VR system is described at the systems level by the way hardware and user are connected through data flows. One flow carries stimulation data that overrides the senses, while the other carries tracking data that lets the hardware adjust the stimuli. Tracking is commonly centered on the head, but it can also include button presses, controller movements, eye movements, and other body movements.
  - VR hardware and user exchange a stimulation data flow overriding senses and a tracking data flow adjusting stimuli from motion.
  - VR systems commonly track head most importantly, and can track button presses, controller movements, eye movements, and body movements.

13/A8  recap  13/S3  "Recap"  (4 facts, 6 concepts)
  VR hardware is organized into three functional parts: displays, sensors, and computers. These terms are used broadly: a display produces output that stimulates the user's sensory organs, a sensor tracks the user's movement and extracts information from the real world, and a computer processes inputs to produce outputs for the user to perceive the world. Together they describe how VR hardware produces output, captures user movement, and processes inputs for perception.
  - VR hardware has three major components: displays, sensors, and computers.
  - In VR hardware, a display is broadly any output device stimulating the user's sensory organs.
  - In VR hardware, a sensor is broadly any tracking device that tracks the user's movement and extracts real-world information.
  - In VR hardware, a computer is broadly any processing device that produces outputs from inputs for the user to perceive.

  Q Why can a non-tracked handheld controller cause a break-in presence?  [13/S4/F4]
    * The user's real hand movement may not produce a matching virtual hand movement
    - The user's real body movement may not produce a matching virtual body movement
    - The user's real eye movement may not produce a matching virtual gaze movement
    - The user's real head movement may not produce a matching virtual head movement

    - The hands are constrained to a fixed area, so direct touch is not fully possible

    - The hands are held in front of a sensor, so direct touch is not fully possible
    * The hands are occupied with the controller, so direct touch is not fully possible
    because: Tracked handheld controllers occupy the hands, so users cannot directly or fully touch passive virtual objects through tangible interaction.     - Bend-sensing gloves place sensors on the head, while pinch gloves place sensors on the hands
    - Bend-sensing gloves place sensors in a head-mounted display, while pinch gloves place sensors in a handheld controller
    because: Bend-sensing data gloves use sensors at many bend positions or joints, while pinch gloves place sensors at fingertip positions to detect a limited set of pinch gestures. The other options misplace the sensors or reverse the two glove types.

    - EMG electrodes can read muscle activity, a band can send the signals, and software can convert the signals into gestures
    * Infrared LEDs can illuminate the hands, cameras can capture the reflected light, and software can convert the signals into gestures
    - Buttons can send press events, a controller can send the events, and software can convert the events into gestures
    because: A bare-hand input device can use computer vision, such as infrared LEDs and cameras, to detect hand gestures and convert them into commands. EMG bands, buttons, and joysticks are other input approaches, not the mechanism described for bare-hand tracking.

13/A10  recap  13/S4  "Recap"  (13 facts, 36 concepts)
  Hand-based VR input devices are organized by how much they rely on tracked hardware, worn sensors, or the user's own hands. World-grounded and handheld controllers trade mobility, tracking accuracy, or direct touch, while hand-worn devices give richer gestures but bring calibration and comfort issues. Bare-hand tracking is the most natural option, though vision-based tracking still has line-of-sight and fatigue limits.
  - VR input devices are hand or non-hand; hand input devices have five broad categories.
  - World-grounded VR hand input devices are fixed in the real world, limiting the user's movement area.
  - Non-tracked handheld controllers can break presence, while tracked handheld controllers know position but can limit direct virtual touch.
  - Hand-worn VR input devices offer natural, rich gestures but may need learned gestures and can cause discomfort.
  - Bare-hand VR input, exemplified by Leap Motion, uses computer vision but needs line of sight and can cause fatigue.
  judge round 1: 4 of 6 failed

      reason: Facts 1 and 2 state that VR input devices divide into hand and non-hand devices and that hand input devices have five broad categories.
    2 pass  (World-grounded VR hand input devices are fixed in the real world, limiting the user's …)
      check: none
      reason: Fact 3 states that world-grounded devices are fixed in the real world and constrain the user to a specified movement area.
    3 FAIL faithful  (Non-tracked handheld controllers can break presence, while tracked handheld controllers know position but can …)
      check: break presence; know position; limit direct virtual touch
      reason: The point weakens and paraphrases the facts: fact 5 says non-tracked controllers can cause "break-in presence," not merely "break presence"; facts 4 and 6 contrast untracked devices whose exact position is unknown with tracked devices that can be tracked, not that tracked devices simply "know position"; and fact 7 says tracked controllers generally prevent directly or fully touching passive virtual objects, with force feedback only sometimes resolving this, which is stronger than "can limit direct virtual touch". A repaired version would say: "Non-tracked handheld controllers can cause break-in presence, while tracked handheld controllers can be tracked but generally prevent fully touching passive virtual objects."
    4 FAIL faithful  (Hand-worn VR input devices offer natural, rich gestures but may need learned gestures and …)
      check: natural, rich gestures
      reason: Fact 11 says hand-worn devices provide "natural input with potentially rich gesture interaction"; the point drops "potentially" and makes the rich gestures sound guaranteed. A repaired version would keep the hedge, e.g. "Hand-worn VR input devices can offer natural, potentially rich gestures but may require learned gestures and can cause discomfort."
    5 FAIL supported,faithful  (Bare-hand VR input, exemplified by Leap Motion, uses computer vision but needs line of …)

      reason: Facts 13, 14, and 16 support bare-hand input using computer vision and Leap Motion as an example, but facts 16’s line-of-sight and fatigue problems are specifically attributed to the Leap Motion device, not to bare-hand VR input as a whole. A repaired text would describe the categories and limitations without claiming an organizing principle or attributing Leap Motion’s specific problems to all bare-hand tracking.

13/A12  quiz  13/S5  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 16 concepts)
  Q In VR, which signal source characterizes a non-hand-based input device?  [13/S5/F0]
    - a handheld controller operated by the hand as input
    - a fixed joystick as input
    - a tracked trigger as input
    * body parts other than the hand as input
    because: A non-hand-based input device captures input from body parts other than the hand, such as the head, eyes, voice, or body. Handheld controllers, joysticks, and triggers are hand-based input sources.
  Q In what way can a head-mounted display also act as a head-tracking input device?  [13/S5/F1]
    * by detecting yaw, roll, and pitch with its sensors
    - by detecting hand gestures with its sensors
    - by detecting button and trigger presses with its sensors
    - by detecting controller shakes with its sensors
    because: An HMD can double as a head-tracking device when its sensors detect head motion, especially yaw, roll, and pitch, and use that motion to change the view. Button presses, hand gestures, and controller shakes are not the head-motion signal described.
  Q What signal does a headset-integrated sensor capture when it helps the system infer the action the user is taking?  [13/S5/F2]
    - the direction of the head and its movement
    * the direction of the eyes and their movement
    - the direction of the controllers and their movement
    - the direction of the hands and their movement
    because: Eye-tracking sensors track where the user is looking and how the eyes are moving, which helps the system infer the intended action. Head, hand, and controller movement are different input signals.
  Q Why can an eye-tracking-only input system accidentally perform an action?  [13/S5/F3]
    - because a background sound can be read as an intentional selection
    - because a head turn can be read as an intentional selection
    * because a blank gaze can be read as an intentional selection
    - because a quick eye blink can be read as an intentional selection
    because: The Midas touch problem occurs when eye tracking cannot tell an intentional selection gaze from a habitual blank gaze, so the system may select or act without the user's intent. Blinks, head turns, and background sounds are not the described cause.
  Q Why is multimodal input generally preferable over relying on a single channel for selection?  [13/S5/F4]
    - because hand-only input can cause accidental actions
    - because voice-only input can cause accidental actions
    * because eye-only input can cause accidental actions
    - because head-only input can cause accidental actions
    because: Multimodal input adds other input forms to eye tracking because eye tracking alone can select objects or perform actions from unintentional gazes. Accidental actions from hand, voice, or head-only input are not the stated reason.

13/A13  recap  13/S5  "Recap"  (5 facts, 16 concepts)
  Non-hand-based VR input captures input from body parts other than the hand, such as head, eyes, voice, or body movement. Head tracking uses a head-mounted display's yaw, roll, and pitch sensors to change the view, while eye tracking infers actions from eye movement. Eye tracking's Midas touch problem, confusing intentional and habitual blank gaze, makes multimodal input generally preferable.
  - Non-hand-based input devices capture input from body parts other than the hand, including head, eyes, voice, or body movement.
  - Head-tracking input devices typically use a head-mounted display's yaw, roll, and pitch sensors to change the view from head motion.
  - Eye-tracking devices integrated with headsets track where and how a user's eyes move to infer an action.
  - The Midas touch problem is eye tracking's confusion of intentional and habitual blank gaze, making multimodal input generally preferable.

13/A21  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (9 facts, 27 concepts)
  Q Why is the surrounding physical environment included in a complete view of a virtual reality system, rather than only the user and hardware?  [13/S0/F0, 13/S2/F1, 13/S2/F2, 13/S2/F4; complete view, surrounding physical environment, virtual reality hardware]
    A A complete view of a virtual reality system consists of the organism, the virtual reality hardware, and the surrounding physical environment. The surrounding physical environment is included because the user may still respond to real-world stimuli such as light, sound, and smell, so the environment can affect user behavior. The user's physical movement may change the environment, and virtual reality hardware may also change it, for example by using a robotic arm.
  Q Why can a tracked handheld controller help preserve presence better than a non-tracked handheld controller in a VR system?  [13/S4/F3, 13/S4/F4, 13/S4/F5; tracked handheld controller, non-tracked handheld controller, break-in presence]
    A A non-tracked handheld controller is not tracked in three-dimensional space, so the system does not know its exact position with respect to a reference frame. Therefore, the user's untracked hand movements may not produce corresponding changes in the virtual hands, which can cause break-in presence. A tracked handheld controller has six degrees of freedom tracking, so the system can track its movements and avoid that mismatch.
  Q Why is multimodal input generally preferable to relying only on eye tracking for selecting objects or performing actions in a VR system?  [13/S5/F3, 13/S5/F4; eye tracking, Midas touch problem, multimodal input]
    A Eye tracking alone can cause the Midas touch problem, where the system cannot differentiate an intentional gaze meant to select an object from a habitual blank gaze. As a result, objects may be selected or actions performed even though the user did not intend to. Multimodal input is generally preferable because it uses other forms of input in addition to eye tracking, rather than relying on eye tracking alone.
  judge round 1: 0 of 3 failed
    1 pass  (Why is the surrounding physical environment included in a complete view of a virtual …)
      check: The surrounding physical environment is included because the user may still respond to real-world stimuli, and both the user and VR hardware may change that environment.
      reason: Fact 1 establishes the complete view’s three components; facts 7, 8, and 10 explain why the environment belongs in that view by affecting the user and being changed by the user or hardware.
    2 pass  (Why can a tracked handheld controller help preserve presence better than a non-tracked handheld …)
      check: Tracked controllers help preserve presence because non-tracked controllers’ unknown positions can make hand movements mismatch virtual hands and cause break-in presence, while tracked controllers’ six degrees of freedom tracking lets the system track movements and break-in presence is avoided.
      reason: Facts 19 and 20 explain the non-tracked controller problem, and fact 21 supplies the tracked-controller contrast and the avoidance of break-in presence.
    3 pass  (Why is multimodal input generally preferable to relying only on eye tracking for selecting …)
      check: Multimodal input is preferable because eye tracking alone can cause the Midas touch problem, selecting objects or performing actions from unintentional gazes, whereas multimodal input adds other input forms.
      reason: Fact 35 states the Midas touch problem and its unintended-selection consequence; fact 36 directly states that multimodal input is generally preferable for this reason.
  judge kept: original

===== lecture 14: VR Hardware

14/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (19 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is augmented reality (AR)? (lecture 1) -> Augmented reality (AR) is an enhanced version of reality created by technology, in which computer-generated digital content is overlaid on the real world in real time and registered in 3D, so the user perceives and interacts with the enhanced environment.
  What is virtual reality (VR)? (lecture 4) -> Virtual reality (VR) is an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli provided by a computer, in which a person's actions partially determine what happens and which replaces the user's sense of reality without requiring the physical existence of objects or places.
  What is virtual reality system? (lecture 4) -> A virtual reality system is a system that presents a computer-generated artificial environment, provides computer-generated sensory stimuli for an immersive experience, and lets the user's actions partially determine what happens in it.
  What is visual motion? (lecture 11) -> Visual motion is the movement experienced by a user in a virtual reality environment, and it is a virtual reality content factor that can increase the risk and severity of cybersickness.
  What is computer? (lecture 13) -> A computer is one of the major components of virtual reality (VR) hardware, a device that processes data from input sensors and activates output devices so that a user can perceive the world.
  What is output device? (lecture 13) -> An output device is an XR hardware component that produces output to stimulate a user's sensory organs, not only a visual display; examples include visual displays, audio output, haptics, motion platforms, and treadmills.

14/A2  recap  14/S0  "Recap"  (7 facts, 25 concepts)
  Full-body and sound-based tracking are among the non-hand VR input methods alongside head and eye tracking. Full-body tracking goes beyond the head, hands, and eyes, and can strengthen the feeling of a fuller self and social presence in a virtual world. It is realized through motion capture suits or camera systems that read fiducial markers. Sound-based tracking is a separate input route that uses simple microphones or microphone arrays to capture speech and non-speech sound for interaction.
  - Non-hand VR input methods consist of head, eye, full-body, and sound-based tracking.
  - Full-body VR tracking tracks the whole body and can add to the illusion of self-embodiment and social presence.
  - Full-body VR tracking approaches are motion capture suits and camera-based fiducial-marker tracking.
  - Sound-based VR tracking captures voice, speech, and non-speech sound for interaction using simple microphones or microphone arrays.

    - Stores input-sensor data and displays the virtual scene
    because: The processing part works on data from input sensors and uses the result to actuate output devices. Storing, displaying, or merely sending measurements is not its stated role.

14/A4  recap  14/S1  "Recap"  (9 facts, 31 concepts)
  A VR system uses a computer to process sensor data and drive output devices, and that computer can be a PC, workstation, distributed system, or smartphone depending on the application, users, devices, and immersion. The GPU, CPU, and RAM determine performance: GPUs and multi-GPU systems support complex rendering, multicore CPUs increase processing capacity, and GPU support is preferable to CPU-only processing. An XR engine provides the middleware needed to support, develop, and render VR experiences, with at least 8 GB RAM typically preferable for a good user experience.
  - In a VR system, the computer processes input sensor data and activates output devices.
  - VR computer choices include PC, workstation, distributed system, or smartphone, based on application, users, device availability, and immersion.
  - A VR computer's major components are the GPU, CPU, and RAM.
  - In VR, GPUs and multi-GPU systems accelerate rendering, multicore CPUs increase capacity, and GPU support is preferable to CPU-only.
  - Each XR engine is middleware for VR experiences; at least 8 GB RAM is typically preferable for VR hardware.

  VR output devices include visual displays, audio, haptics, motion systems, and mostly specialized taste and smell outputs. Visual displays are divided into head-mounted, world-fixed, and regular displays. Head-mounted displays bring screens close to the eyes, world-fixed displays keep graphics on stationary surfaces while the user moves, and regular displays are ordinary mobile or stationary screens often used for augmented reality.
  - VR output devices include visual displays, audio, haptics, motion systems, and mostly specialized taste and smell outputs.
  - Visual displays stimulate the eyes and are head-mounted, world-fixed, or regular displays.
  - Head-mounted displays put screens directly before the eyes and can be non-see-through, optical, or video see-through.
  - World-fixed displays render graphics onto fixed screens, such as monitors or caves, while the user moves.
  - Regular displays are common tablets or smartphones, typically for non-immersive VR and mostly used for augmented reality.

14/A7  quiz  14/S3  "Quick quiz"  (6 facts, 18 concepts)
  Q Why are headphones preferred for a fully immersive VR audio setup?  [14/S3/F0]
    * They let the sound source change as the head moves
    - They make the sound source louder over distance
    - They keep the sound source fixed relative to the room
    - They keep the sound source fixed in the surrounding space
    because: Headphones support fully immersive audio because the sound source can shift as the user moves their head. Fixed speakers do not update the perceived sound position in the same way.
  Q What marks a haptic device as active rather than passive?  [14/S3/F2]
    * Computer-controlled physical feedback
    - Worn objects that move with the user
    - Attached objects that stay fixed in the room
    - Static objects that match virtual shapes
    because: Active haptic devices give physical feedback under computer control, while passive haptic devices are static real-world objects that are not computer-controlled.
  Q Which haptic type gives the sense of limb movement and muscular resistance?  [14/S3/F3, 14/S3/F4]
    - Shapes matched by static real objects
    - Vibrations applied to the skin surface
    * Forces applied to muscles and joints
    - Currents passed through the skin
    because: Proprioceptive force-based haptics work on muscles and joints to create a sense of limb movement and resistance. Tactile haptics instead stimulate the skin through vibration or electrical current.
  Q How can motion sickness caused by a VR motion platform be reduced?  [14/S3/F7]
    - By making the platform convey stronger acceleration and jerk
    - By choosing an active platform over a passive one
    - By increasing the conflict between visual motion and perceived real-world motion
    * By decreasing the conflict between visual motion and perceived real-world motion
    because: Motion sickness from a motion platform can be reduced by reducing the mismatch between what the user sees moving and what their body perceives. Increasing the mismatch or using more active control is not a stated way to reduce it.
  Q What does a treadmill provide in a VR output system?  [14/S3/F9]
    - The sense of touch while holding a virtual object
    - The sense of orientation while the body moves
    - The sense of gravity while moving through space
    * The sense of walking or running in place
    because: Treadmills give the feeling of walking or running in place by providing input to the feet or legs. Whole-body orientation and gravity are associated with motion platforms, and touch feedback comes from haptic devices.

14/A8  recap  14/S3  "Recap"  (11 facts, 29 concepts)
  Non-visual VR output devices add sound, touch, and physical movement to the visual display. Audio provides spatialized sound, while haptic systems create touch sensations through different control, sensation, and grounding approaches. Motion platforms and treadmills then give the user a sense of bodily motion, with passive designs often reducing motion sickness.
  - VR audio output can provide 3D audio, and headphones are preferred for fully immersive systems.
  - Haptic outputs activate touch sensation and are categorized as passive or active, tactile or proprioceptive, and self-grounded or world-grounded.
  - Motion platforms move the whole body, can cause motion sickness, and passive user-controlled ones likely reduce it.
  - Treadmills create the sense of walking or running in place; omnidirectional treadmills can be active or passive.
  judge round 1: 3 of 5 failed
    1 pass  (VR audio output can provide 3D audio, and headphones are preferred for fully immersive …)
      check: none
      reason: The point is supported by fact 1: VR audio output can provide 3D audio and headphones are preferred for fully immersive systems. It is concise, standalone, and has no source talk.
    2 FAIL faithful  (Haptic outputs activate touch sensation and are categorized as passive or active, tactile or …)
      check: "can be categorized" [2]
      reason: Fact 2 says haptic outputs "can be categorized" as these types, but the point says they "are categorized," dropping a hedge and making the classification sound stronger than the fact. A repaired version should say: "Haptic outputs activate touch sensation and can be categorized as passive or active, tactile or proprioceptive, or self-grounded or world-grounded."
    3 FAIL faithful  (Motion platforms move the whole body, can cause motion sickness, and passive user-controlled ones …)
      check: "than active platforms" [9]
      reason: Fact 9 says passive platforms are likely to result in less motion sickness than active platforms; the point says passive user-controlled ones "likely reduce it," losing the comparison with active platforms. A repaired version should keep the comparison, e.g., "Motion platforms move the whole body, may cause motion sickness, and passive user-controlled ones likely cause less than active ones."
    4 pass  (Treadmills create the sense of walking or running in place; omnidirectional treadmills can be …)
      check: none
      reason: The point is supported by facts 10 and 11: treadmills provide the sense of walking or running while staying in one place, and omnidirectional treadmills can be active or passive. It is standalone, concise, and contains one main idea about treadmills.
    0 FAIL supported,faithful  (Non-visual VR output devices add sound, touch, and physical movement to the visual display.)
      check: "to the visual display"; "provides" [1]; "often"; "passive designs" [9]
      reason: The text adds "to the visual display," which the facts do not state; it says audio "provides spatialized sound" instead of the fact's "can provide specialized 3D audio"; and it says passive designs "often reducing motion sickness," extending a claim supported only for passive motion platforms (fact 9) to treadmills as well and replacing "likely" with "often." A repaired text should avoid the unsupported visual-display claim, keep the "can" for audio, and limit the sickness reduction to passive motion platforms as less sickness than active platforms.
  judge kept: original; still failing: [2, 3, 0]

14/A14  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (8 facts, 31 concepts)
  Q Why can full-body tracking in virtual reality strengthen the sense of self-embodiment and social presence in a virtual world?  [14/S0/F1, 14/S0/F2; full-body tracking, self-embodiment, social presence]
    A Full-body tracking tracks full-body movement, more than the head, hands, and eyes. Its output can show the user a fuller representation of themselves. That fuller representation can add to the illusion of self-embodiment and social presence in a virtual world.
  Q Why is a graphics processing unit preferable for virtual reality processing even when modern central processing units are powerful?  [14/S1/F3, 14/S1/F6; graphics processing unit, central processing unit, rendering]
    A A graphics processing unit speeds up rendering because of its inherent parallel processing abilities and the inherent parallelism in the rendering process. Modern central processing units are powerful, but they have many other tasks to do. A CPU-only virtual reality processing system with minimal graphics processing unit support can therefore have performance issues.
  Q How do virtual reality and augmented reality differ in the head-mounted display type typically associated with each?  [14/S2/F8, 5/S1/F0; non-see-through head-mounted display, optical see-through head-mounted display]
    A Virtual reality is typically associated with non-see-through head-mounted displays, and augmented reality is typically associated with optical see-through head-mounted displays. Virtual reality completely replaces the user's sense of reality with a virtual environment, whereas augmented reality alters the ongoing perception of the real world.
  Q How do passive and active haptic devices differ?  [14/S3/F1, 14/S3/F2; passive haptic device, active haptic device, haptic output]
    A Haptic outputs can be categorized as passive versus active. Passive haptic devices are static real-world physical objects that match the shape of virtual objects and are not controlled by the computer, whereas active haptic devices are physical objects or physical feedback controlled by the computer that provide a sense of touch when interacting with virtual objects.

===== lecture 15: AR Hardware

15/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (15 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is head-mounted display (HMDs)? (lecture 6) -> A head-mounted display (HMD) is a wearable, mobile visual display that integrates electronic, optical, mechanical, and audio components and uses one or two small screens directly in front of the user's eyes to place images for monoscopic or stereoscopic viewing. It can be non-see-through, optical see-through, or video see-through.
  What is field of view (FOV)? (lecture 11) -> Field of view (FOV) is an angular measure of the region visible to the eye at a single point in time, and in virtual reality it is the amount of virtual environment visible.
  What is three-dimensional audio? (lecture 14) -> Three-dimensional audio is specialized audio that gives a sense of where sounds are coming from, with speakers fixed in space or moving with the head.
  What is augmented reality (AR)? (lecture 1) -> Augmented reality (AR) is an enhanced version of reality created by technology, in which computer-generated digital content is overlaid on the real world in real time and registered in 3D, so the user perceives and interacts with the enhanced environment.
  What is virtual reality (VR)? (lecture 4) -> Virtual reality (VR) is an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli provided by a computer, in which a person's actions partially determine what happens and which replaces the user's sense of reality without requiring the physical existence of objects or places.
  What is augmented reality system? (lecture 5) -> An augmented reality system is a system with four required characteristics: it enhances the real world with computer-generated digital content registered in 3D, that content is experienced through the user's sensory organs, and it supports real-time interaction with that content in the enhanced environment.

15/A4  recap  15/S1  "Recap"  (7 facts, 25 concepts)
  Augmented reality headsets are generally larger, more immersive, and have a wider field of view than virtual reality headsets, and they typically include built-in sensors such as cameras and depth sensors. The Microsoft HoloLens is an example of such AR hardware: it has more components than many VR headsets, projects digital content into the real-world view, and supports eye, voice, and hand-based interaction.
  - Generally, augmented reality headsets are larger, more immersive, and have a wider field of view.

15/A9  recap  15/S3  "Recap"  (14 facts, 27 concepts)
  Spatial AR is the projector-based, shared-space category of AR: virtual content is placed on physical objects in the real environment, so several users can interact with it at once. To make that content feel coexisting, systems must understand the environment's geometry and lighting, usually through depth sensors or computer vision. Representative examples include interactive projectors, air sandboxes, projection keyboards, and projection mapping, which differ in whether they project onto surfaces, sand, or 3D space. These systems are used in education, art, medicine, industry, museums, and entertainment.
  - Spatial AR devices are projector-based, room-scale systems that place virtual content on physical objects, not the user's view.
  - Their non-held displays can provide more natural interfaces and let multiple users interact with the same content.
  - Spatial AR is used in domains such as education, art, medicine, industry, museums, and entertainment.
  - Projection-based and spatial AR are generally similar ideas, needing geometry and lighting understanding via sensors or computer vision.
  - Examples include interactive projectors, air sandboxes, projection keyboards, and projection mapping, projecting interactive surfaces or 3D space.
  judge round 1: 6 of 6 failed

A repaired version could say “Spatial AR devices are room-scale systems that usually project virtual content onto physical objects, not the user's view.”

15/A11  recap  15/S4  "Recap"  (8 facts, 16 concepts)
  Head-up displays and AR contact lenses complete the AR display categories. Head-up displays project images onto transparent surfaces and are commonly used in cars and aircraft. AR contact lenses contrast with bulkier AR hardware as tiny future wearables that can place digital information directly on the eye and may include miniaturized electronic components. Their possible usefulness is set against the unresolved concern that constantly changing visual information may affect users or cause sickness.
  - A head-up display projects images onto a transparent surface; ideally only content is visible, though borders or shades may be.
  - Head-up displays are commonly used in cars and aircraft.
  - Some AR hardware is bulky or hard to hold, while AR contact lenses are tiny future wearables.
  - AR contact lenses superimpose digital information directly on the lens and may carry miniaturized display, imaging, wireless, and motion components.
  - AR contact lenses may show and let users change information, but their effects are not well known and may cause sickness.

15/A14  match_pairs  lecture  "Match the terms"  (19 facts, 8 concepts)
  augmented reality headset = A powerful wearable augmented reality device that presents real-world content with full 3D holograms, is generally larger, more immersive, and has a …
  smart glasses = Lightweight augmented reality wearable devices that resemble standard eyeglasses and provide heads-up display-type digital content overlays rather than full 3D holograms.
  spatial augmented reality system = An augmented reality system that typically projects digital content onto physical objects in the surrounding environment, so virtual content appears to coexist …
  head-up display = An augmented reality display category that projects images onto a transparent surface, usually a screen or visor; ideally the surface is invisible …
  augmented reality contact lens = A very small, emerging wearable display technology, still in the future, that can be placed directly on the eye, is not visible …
  Microsoft HoloLens = An augmented reality headset and a see-through display that integrates high-definition holograms or digital content with the real-world view obtained through special …
  projection keyboard = A spatial augmented reality system that projects a virtual keyboard onto a flat surface, converting the surface into an interactive keyboard, and …
  interactive projector = A spatial augmented reality system that projects images or interfaces onto any surface, turning that surface into an interactive display.

15/A17  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (12 facts, 29 concepts)
  Q Why can augmented reality headsets provide more immersive three-dimensional holographic content than augmented reality smart glasses?  [15/S1/F0, 15/S2/F0, 15/S2/F1; augmented reality headset, smart glasses, field of view, hologram]
    A Augmented reality headsets can provide more immersive three-dimensional holographic content because they generally have a wider field of view and contain more components, sensors, and projectors. They are generally larger and more immersive than smart glasses. Smart glasses are lighter, less powerful, and usually have a smaller field of view, so they provide simpler head-up-display-type overlays.
  Q Why can a virtual reality headset have fewer components than an augmented reality headset such as the Microsoft HoloLens?  [15/S1/F3, 15/S1/F4, 5/S1/F0; virtual reality headset, augmented reality headset, Microsoft HoloLens]
    A A virtual reality headset can have fewer components because it does not need to provide a real-world view. It replaces the user's sense of reality rather than altering perception of the real world. By contrast, the Microsoft HoloLens includes special glasses that project digital content onto the regular real-world view, along with a camera, depth cameras, and a projector.
  Q Why can a spatial augmented reality system let several users interact with the same digital content, while head-mounted displays, smart glasses, and handheld devices do not?  [15/S3/F0, 15/S3/F1, 15/S3/F2; spatial augmented reality system, head-mounted display, smart glasses, handheld device]
    A A spatial augmented reality system can let several users interact with the same digital content because its display is placed on shared physical objects in the real world, not tied to one user. These systems typically use projectors to augment physical objects, and the augmented content can therefore be used by multiple users at once. Headsets, glasses, and handheld devices instead show content only in the user's own view or on the user's own screen.
  Q Why might augmented reality contact lenses remain a future technology even though they can place digital information directly in the wearer's field of vision?  [15/S4/F3, 15/S4/F4, 15/S4/F8; augmented reality contact lens, wearable technology, field of vision]
    A Augmented reality contact lenses remain a future technology because their effect on users is not well known or researched. They are very small, can be placed on the eye like regular contact lenses, and can superimpose digital images or information directly onto the wearer's field of vision. However, a lot of changing information directly in front of the eyes may affect normal behavior or cause some sort of sickness.

===== lecture 16: Understanding Tracking I

16/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (17 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is augmented reality (AR)? (lecture 1) -> Augmented reality (AR) is an enhanced version of reality created by technology, in which computer-generated digital content is overlaid on the real world in real time and registered in 3D, so the user perceives and interacts with the enhanced environment.
  What is marker? (lecture 3) -> A marker is a real-world object or image placed in the environment that a system detects to identify its position or track a user's motion and to place digital content at that position.
  What is pose? (lecture 9) -> Pose is the position and orientation of a viewer or tracked object.
  What is Microsoft HoloLens? (lecture 15) -> The Microsoft HoloLens is an augmented reality headset and a see-through display that integrates high-definition holograms or digital content with the real-world view obtained through special glasses. Interaction takes place through eye movements, voice commands, and hand gestures.
  What is extended reality (XR)? (lecture 1) -> Extended reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR).
  What is augmented virtuality? (lecture 1) -> Augmented virtuality is the intermediate state on the reality-virtuality continuum, opposite augmented reality, in which a virtual environment is augmented with real-world images, videos, or live capture appearing in real time.

16/A1  quiz  16/S0  "Quick quiz"  (4 facts, 11 concepts)
  Q In an XR system, what kind of part is tracking?  [16/S0/F0]
    * An integral hardware component
    - A software tracking component
    - A display rendering component
    - An audio synchronization component
    because: Tracking is an integral hardware component of an XR system. It is not a software, display, or audio component.
  Q How does the main focus of tracking differ between virtual reality and augmented reality?  [16/S0/F2, 16/S0/F3]
    - VR tracks the physical environment to replace the real world, while AR tracks virtual motion to update the view
    - VR registers virtual content in real space, while AR translates user motion into virtual motion
    * VR translates user motion into virtual motion, while AR registers virtual content in real space
    - VR tracks the user's virtual motion, while AR tracks the user's real motion
    because: VR tracking is primarily about turning the user's physical motion or input into motion in the virtual world. AR tracking is primarily about registering virtual content in 3D space relative to real-world anchors.
  Q In XR, how is tracking related to sensing?  [16/S0/F4]
    - Tracking names the software side, while sensing names the hardware side
    - Sensing is a display task, while tracking is a rendering task
    - They name different activities, and sensing is the more common term
    * They name the same activity, and tracking is the more common term
    because: Tracking is also commonly called sensing, but tracking is the more popular term for the activity. The devices that enable it are more often called sensors.

16/A2  recap  16/S0  "Recap"  (5 facts, 11 concepts)
  Tracking is an integral hardware component of XR systems, and keeping track of physical motion is crucial there, especially in VR. In VR, this tracking translates the user's physical motion or input into motion in the virtual world. In AR, the purpose shifts to registering virtual 3D content against a real-world anchor while also tracking the user's pose, position, orientation, and moving real-world objects in the field of view. The same capability is also called sensing, although the enabling devices are more often called sensors than trackers.
  - Tracking is an integral XR hardware component and is crucial for keeping track of physical motion, especially in VR.
  - In VR, tracking captures the user's physical motion or input and translates it into motion in the virtual world.
  - In AR, tracking registers virtual content in 3D space with respect to an anchor in the real world.
  - AR tracking also tracks the user's pose, position, and orientation, plus moving real-world objects in the field of view.
  - Tracking, the more popular term, is also called sensing; its devices are more often called sensors than trackers.
  judge round 1: 2 of 6 failed
    1 pass  (Tracking is an integral XR hardware component and is crucial for keeping track of …)
      check: none
      reason: Facts 1 and 2 support that tracking is an integral XR hardware component and that keeping track of physical motion is crucial, more importantly in VR; the paraphrase does not add a new claim.
    2 FAIL supported,faithful  (In VR, tracking captures the user's physical motion or input and translates it into …)
      check: fact 3: 'primarily about'; 'so that it can be translated'
      reason: It changes fact 3 by dropping the hedges 'primarily' and 'can be', making tracking assertively 'captures' and 'translates' rather than being primarily about motion that can be translated. A repaired version would say: 'In VR, tracking is primarily about capturing the user's physical motion or input so that it can be translated into virtual motion.'
    3 pass  (In AR, tracking registers virtual content in 3D space with respect to an anchor …)
      check: none
      reason: Fact 4 supports that AR tracking involves registering virtual content in 3D space with respect to a real-world anchor; the point leaves out the additional tracking requirements, which are covered separately.
    4 pass  (AR tracking also tracks the user's pose, position, and orientation, plus moving real-world objects …)
      check: none
      reason: Fact 4 states that AR tracking requires tracking the user's pose, position, orientation, and moving real-world objects in the field of view, which the point faithfully summarizes.
    5 pass  (Tracking, the more popular term, is also called sensing; its devices are more often …)
      check: none

16/A3  quiz  16/S1  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 26 concepts)
  Q Why does an XR system need to track the position and orientation of the user's sense organs?  [16/S1/F1]
    - so virtual audio can be raised when the ears turn toward a sound source
    - so the headset can replace external cameras used for outside-in tracking
    * so a display attached to them is perceived as attached to the surrounding world
    - so the user's walking speed can be used to adjust rendering resolution
    because: Sense organs such as eyes and ears have body-controlled degrees of freedom, so their position and orientation must be tracked to keep an attached display perceived as tied to the world. Tracking them is not primarily about replacing sensors, adjusting rendering from speed, or changing audio volume.
  Q In VR, for what reason may eye tracking be needed?  [16/S1/F3]
    - to register digital content with a moved object in an augmented reality view
    - to replace head tracking for the visual and aural components
    - to identify the position of external room sensors in an outside-in tracking setup
    * to compensate for eye movements required by the rendering or display technology
    because: Eye tracking may be needed when the rendering or display technology requires compensation for eye movements. Head tracking already serves the usual visual and aural components in VR, while locating room sensors or registering AR content are different tracking needs.
  Q Why is exact, perfect matching not required when a user's hands or face are tracked for a virtual representation?  [16/S1/F5, 16/S1/F6]
    - because the virtual world already contains a permanent model of the user
    * because an approximate movement can still reproduce the body-part motion well enough
    - because external room sensors can replace body-part tracking in a virtual reality setup
    - because a button press can directly set a fixed grasp or pose
    because: Tracking other body parts does not require perfect matching; an approximate virtual reproduction of the movement can still give a good experience. A button press is a limiting case for setting a fixed configuration, not the general reason approximate tracking is acceptable.
  Q In VR, why must a physical wall around the user be tracked rather than relying on the user's pose?  [16/S1/F9]
    - because the user's head pose alone can show where the virtual room boundary ends
    - because the user's eye movements must be matched to the wall for sound
    * because the wall must be detected as a physical object missing from the virtual world
    - because the wall must serve as an anchor for digital content in an augmented reality view
    because: A wall not represented in the virtual world must itself be tracked so the user can be alerted to it and reduce harm. Tracking the user's pose alone does not reveal that physical object, and anchoring digital content is an AR concern.

16/A4  recap  16/S1  "Recap"  (12 facts, 40 concepts)
  Tracking in extended reality is divided by what is tracked: the user's sense organs, other body parts, and the surrounding environment. Sense-organ tracking keeps the virtual world aligned with the user's eyes and ears, while other-body-part tracking gives a usable virtual representation of the user. Environment tracking connects the virtual or digital experience to real objects, supporting augmented reality placement, virtual reality safety or touch, and telepresence.
  - Tracking in extended reality is categorized by what is tracked: sense organs, other body parts, and the environment.
  - Sense-organ tracking updates the virtual world because displays move with the user; virtual reality mostly tracks the head, sometimes eyes.
  - Other-body-part tracking adds avatars or gestures to the virtual world; approximate matching or simple input can suffice.
  - Environment tracking aligns augmented reality content, alerts or gives touch feedback in virtual reality, and supports telepresence live capture.
  judge round 1: 1 of 5 failed
    1 pass  (Tracking in extended reality is categorized by what is tracked: sense organs, other body …)
      check: none
      reason: Fact 1 supports the three categories of tracking by what is tracked; the brief names are a faithful, standalone paraphrase.
    2 FAIL faithful  (Sense-organ tracking updates the virtual world because displays move with the user; virtual reality …)
      check: 4: may be required if rendering and display technology require compensating for eye movements
      reason: The point says VR “sometimes” tracks eyes, dropping the fact’s condition that eye tracking may be required only when rendering/display technology needs compensation. A repaired point should say eye tracking is used in VR when such compensation is required, not that it is an occasional general feature.
    3 pass  (Other-body-part tracking adds avatars or gestures to the virtual world; approximate matching or simple …)
      check: none
      reason: Facts 5, 6, and 7 support that other-body-part tracking can create avatars or gestures, that approximate matching can work, and that simple input can be a limiting case.
    4 pass  (Environment tracking aligns augmented reality content, alerts or gives touch feedback in virtual reality …)
      check: none
      reason: Facts 8 through 12 support the listed roles: AR registration, VR alerts and touch feedback, and telepresence live capture as environment tracking.
    0 pass  (Tracking in extended reality is divided by what is tracked: the user's sense organs …)

    - To merge many readings from different sources into one estimate
    - To find where the sensor is before any movement begins
    * To make imperfect sensor output approximate the real value
    - To switch from external trackers to trackers on the user

    - The difference between the unknown starting pose and the known initial orientation

    because: Drift correction compensates for the gap between estimated and actual position and orientation. The other options describe raw sensor error, initial pose setup, and sensor fusion, not drift correction.

16/A8  recap  16/S3  "Recap"  (6 facts, 13 concepts)
  Tracking obtains input by either inside-out or outside-in methods. The tracking process then consists of calibration, registration, integration, and drift correction. Calibration and registration prepare movement tracking by reducing sensor error and determining the sensor’s starting position and orientation, while integration combines measurements from multiple sources and drift correction reduces the difference between estimated and actual position and orientation.
  - Tracking input can be obtained in two broad ways: inside-out and outside-in.
  - The tracking process consists of calibration, registration, integration, and drift correction.
  - Before movement tracking, calibration reduces sensor error, and registration determines the sensor’s starting position and orientation.
  - Integration aggregates measurements from multiple sources at discrete time points to track sense organs, body parts, or the environment.
  - Drift correction compensates for differences between estimated and actual position and orientation, reducing estimation error.
  judge round 1: 2 of 6 failed
    1 pass  (Tracking input can be obtained in two broad ways: inside-out and outside-in.)

16/A14  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (7 facts, 25 concepts)
  Q How does the main purpose of tracking differ between virtual reality and augmented reality?  [16/S0/F2, 16/S0/F3; tracking, virtual reality, augmented reality]
    A In virtual reality, tracking is primarily about translating the user's physical motion or input into virtual motion in the virtual world. In augmented reality, tracking registers virtual content in three-dimensional space with respect to a real-world anchor. It therefore also requires the user's pose, position, and orientation and tracking of moving real-world objects in the field of view.
  Q How does the placement of sensors in outside-in tracking explain its range limitation compared with inside-out tracking?  [16/S2/F2, 16/S2/F4, 16/S2/F5; outside-in tracking, inside-out tracking, sensor range, head-mounted display]
    A Outside-in tracking relies on external sensors or markers in the real world, not on sensors inside the user's experience device. Because those external sensors are placed in a specific area, the system works only when the user is within their sensor range. Inside-out tracking puts the needed cameras or other sensors within the experience device, such as a head-mounted display, so the user wears the sensors and does not have that placement restriction.
  Q Why is tracking the environment itself, rather than only the user, needed in virtual reality when a physical wall is not represented in the virtual world?  [16/S1/F9, 16/S1/F10; environment tracking, user tracking, physical object, touch feedback]
    A Tracking the user is not useful for alerting the user to a physical object that is not represented in the virtual world. Tracking the environment itself can detect that physical object, such as a wall, and alert the user, reducing harm. In addition, the tracked physical object may be matched in the virtual world so the user receives touch feedback while interacting with it.
  judge round 1: 0 of 3 failed
    1 pass  (How does the main purpose of tracking differ between virtual reality and augmented reality?)
      check: In virtual reality tracking primarily translates the user's physical motion or input into virtual motion, whereas in augmented reality tracking registers virtual content in 3D space relative to a real-world anchor and also tracks the user's pose and moving real-world objects.
      reason: Facts 3 and 4 directly give the VR purpose and the AR purpose, including the AR tracking requirements, so the reference answer states the requested comparison without adding outside material.
    2 pass  (How does the placement of sensors in outside-in tracking explain its range limitation compared …)
      check: Outside-in tracking uses external real-world sensors fixed in a limited area, so it works only within their sensor range, while inside-out tracking places the sensors in the experience device that the user wears, avoiding that placement restriction.
      reason: Facts 20, 22, and 23 jointly explain why external sensor placement limits outside-in tracking and why inside-out tracking does not have that limitation.
    3 pass  (Why is tracking the environment itself, rather than only the user, needed in virtual …)
      check: Tracking the environment is needed because user tracking alone is not useful for alerting the user to unrepresented physical objects such as walls, while environment tracking can alert the user to them and reduce harm.

===== lecture 17: Understanding Tracking - I

17/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (16 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is sensor? (lecture 13) -> Sensor is a device that converts an energy source into electrical signals, or, in the human body, an organ that converts a stimulus into neural impulses; in XR hardware it is a tracking device that tracks a user's movements and extracts information from the real world.
  What is tracking? (lecture 13) -> Tracking is the integral XR hardware component that keeps track of physical-world motion, translating user pose, position, and orientation—or real objects—into virtual motion or 3D content registered to a real-world anchor.
  What is registration? (lecture 16) -> Registration is the step in the tracking process that estimates the initial position and orientation of the sensor or user, so the starting point is known before movement is tracked, and sets the initial alignment between the real and virtual worlds. It may be aided by fiducial markers, reflectors, or tags, or performed without them using computer vision.
  What is calibration? (lecture 16) -> Calibration is the step in the tracking process that transforms the output of imperfect sensors so that it behaves as closely as possible to the natural or real value, reducing sensor error.
  What is integration? (lecture 16) -> Integration is a stage of the tracking process that aggregates sensory measurements from multiple sensors or input data sources at discrete time points to combine the values and track sense organs, body parts, or the environment, and computes the current sensor orientation from the initial orientation estimated during registration and calibrated angular velocity samples.
  What is drift correction? (lecture 16) -> Drift correction is a step in the tracking process that compensates for the difference between estimated and actual position and orientation of the user, sense organs, body parts, or objects in the environment, reducing estimation error. It is usually done by blending values from at least two sensors, such as a gyroscope and camera, to estimate and correct drift.

17/A3  quiz  17/S1  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 11 concepts)
  Q What is the purpose of comparing an IMU gyro reading with a more accurate benchmark sensor during calibration?  [17/S1/F0, 17/S1/F1]
    - To choose the sampling interval used later when the angular velocity samples are integrated
    * To reduce the error between the measured angular velocity and the actual angular velocity
    - To estimate the user's position from visual landmarks and use that estimate for tracking
    - To detect drift by blending two independently computed orientations during the session
    because: Calibration aims to make the measured angular velocity as close as possible to the actual angular velocity, thereby reducing the measurement error. It is not a drift-correction step, nor a pose estimation or sampling choice.
  Q Why does the calibration procedure collect readings from both a cheap IMU and a more accurate benchmark sensor?  [17/S1/F3]
    - To compare the IMU's gyro output with its accelerometer output for drift detection
    - To establish the initial orientation of the headset before any tracking begins
    - To average the two sensors' raw outputs into a single reading that is used for later tracking
    * To create paired samples in which the accurate readings provide the angular velocity values to be matched
    because: The calibration needs many paired samples so that cheap sensor readings can be compared with much more accurate benchmark readings. It does not produce a single averaged sensor, use the accelerometer for drift detection here, or set the initial orientation.
  Q What quantity is minimized when the calibration constants are estimated from many paired samples?  [17/S1/F4]
    - The sum of squared differences between C1 plus C2 times omega_a and omega_g
    - The difference between the calibrated value and the measured value
    * The sum of squared differences between C1 plus C2 times omega_g and omega_a
    - The sum of absolute differences between the measured angular velocity and the benchmark angular velocity
    because: The simple method chooses C1 and C2 to minimize the total squared error between the transformed cheap reading and the benchmark reading. It uses squared differences, not absolute differences, and the target is the benchmark value rather than the original cheap reading.
  Q Once the calibration constants are determined, how is a new cheap IMU angular velocity reading converted into the calibrated angular velocity?  [17/S1/F5]

    * By computing C1 plus C2 times the new reading
    - By computing the stored benchmark reading as the calibrated value
    - By computing the difference between the new reading and the stored benchmark reading
    because: After the constants are found, the calibrated value is the linear transform C1 + C2 times the cheap sensor's reading. The benchmark reading is not used directly, averaged in, or subtracted from the new reading.

17/A4  recap  17/S1  "Recap"  (6 facts, 13 concepts)
  IMU calibration makes an inaccurate angular velocity reading closer to an actual value. Paired samples from a cheap IMU and a more accurate benchmark sensor are used to find a simple mapping with least-squares regression. The resulting constants transform each cheap reading into a calibrated value that approximates the actual angular velocity.
  - IMU calibration aims to reduce the error between measured and actual angular velocity.
  - One simple calibration model assumes a linear, non-ideal relation between measured and actual angular velocity.
  - Least squares fits C1+C2ωg to actual ωa using many cheap and benchmark paired samples.
  - Calibration maps cheap measured ωg to calibrated ωcal using C1 and C2, matching actual ωa closely.

17/A12  match_pairs  lecture  "Match the terms"  (15 facts, 8 concepts)
  registration = The step in the tracking process that estimates the initial position and orientation of the sensor or user, so the starting point …
  inertial measurement unit = A self-contained composite hardware unit that mainly contains a gyroscope, accelerometer, and magnetometer to measure changes in orientation, translation velocity, or acceleration …
  gyroscope = An inertial sensor that captures angular velocity.
  accelerometer = An inertial sensor that captures linear acceleration along the x, y, and z axes, and in an inertial measurement unit its readings …
  magnetometer = A sensor that captures magnetic field strength along the x, y, and z axes and can be used to detect drift errors …
  calibration = The step in the tracking process that transforms the output of imperfect sensors so that it behaves as closely as possible to …
  integration = A stage of the tracking process that aggregates sensory measurements from multiple sensors or input data sources at discrete time points to …
  drift correction = A step in the tracking process that compensates for the difference between estimated and actual position and orientation of the user, sense …

17/A16  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (12 facts, 34 concepts)
  Q How does an IMU calibration process use many paired samples from a cheap IMU and a more accurate benchmark sensor to produce a calibrated angular velocity?  [17/S1/F3, 17/S1/F4, 17/S1/F5; calibration, benchmark sensor, measured angular velocity, calibrated value]
    A The calibration collects many paired samples in which the cheap IMU produces measured angular velocity omega_g and the benchmark sensor produces a close estimate of the actual angular velocity omega_a. It finds constants C1 and C2 by linear least squares regression, minimizing the sum of squared differences between C1 + C2 omega_g and omega_a. The resulting calibrated value is omega_cal = C1 + C2 omega_g, which maps the cheap reading to the closest match with the actual value.
  Q Why is registration required before integration can compute a sensor's current orientation in an XR tracking system?  [17/S2/F0, 17/S2/F3, 17/S2/F4, 16/S3/F3; registration, integration, initial orientation, calibrated angular velocity sample]
    A Registration is required because integration needs the initial orientation, theta_0, as the starting point before movement is accumulated. Registration finds this initial orientation and sets the initial alignment between the real and virtual worlds. Integration then computes the current sensor orientation at k delta_t by adding theta_0 to the sum of calibrated angular velocity samples W_cal_i times delta_t, where each sample indicates that orientation change.
  Q Why are accelerometer and magnetometer readings useful in an IMU even though IMU-based tracking mainly uses gyroscope readings?  [17/S0/F1, 17/S0/F2, 17/S3/F1; accelerometer, magnetometer, gyroscope, drift error]
    A Accelerometer and magnetometer readings are useful because, although they do not directly contribute to IMU tracking, they can detect drift error. IMU tracking relies mainly on gyroscope angular velocity readings, while the accelerometer captures linear acceleration and the magnetometer captures magnetic field strength. Drift correction can use those accelerometer and magnetometer readings in addition to gyroscope values.
  Q How does a classic drift-correction approach combine orientations from a gyroscope and a camera to obtain a drift-corrected orientation?  [17/S3/F0, 17/S3/F1, 17/S3/F2; drift correction, gyroscope, camera, drift-corrected orientation]
    A Drift correction usually uses at least two sensors whose values are blended to estimate and correct drift. In this classic approach, the gyroscope provides an integrated orientation theta_gk and the camera provides orientation theta_ck at the same instant. The method computes theta_dk = alpha theta_gk + (1 - alpha) theta_ck, where alpha is a normalized gain parameter between 0 and 1.
  judge round 1: 1 of 4 failed
    1 pass  (How does an IMU calibration process use many paired samples from a cheap IMU …)
      check: The facts say that calibration uses paired measured and benchmark angular velocities, fits C1 and C2 by minimizing squared differences with least squares, and then defines omega_cal = C1 + C2 omega_g.
      reason: The cited facts 7, 8, and 9 carry the full link from paired samples to regression constants to the calibrated value, and the reference answer follows those facts without adding unsupported claims.
    2 pass  (Why is registration required before integration can compute a sensor's current orientation in an …)
      check: The facts say registration provides the initial orientation needed by integration, and integration adds that initial orientation to accumulated calibrated angular-velocity changes.
      reason: Facts 10, 13, and 23 directly support the causal link that registration must establish the starting orientation before integration can compute the current orientation; fact 14 supports the role of each sample.
    3 FAIL clear  (Why are accelerometer and magnetometer readings useful in an IMU even though IMU-based tracking …)
      check: The facts say the accelerometer and magnetometer do not directly drive tracking but can detect drift and be used in drift correction alongside the gyroscope.
      reason: Facts 2, 3, and 16 together explain why the non-gyroscope readings are still useful: they do not directly estimate tracking orientation, but they support drift detection/correction. The main repair needed is to put that direct reason first in the reference answer rather than beginning with background about the gyroscope.

===== lecture 18: Understanding Tracking II

18/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (12 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is registration? (lecture 16) -> Registration is the step in the tracking process that estimates the initial position and orientation of the sensor or user, so the starting point is known before movement is tracked, and sets the initial alignment between the real and virtual worlds. It may be aided by fiducial markers, reflectors, or tags, or performed without them using computer vision.
  What is inertial measurement unit (IMU)? (lecture 17) -> An inertial measurement unit (IMU) is a self-contained composite hardware unit that mainly contains a gyroscope, accelerometer, and magnetometer to measure changes in orientation, translation velocity, or acceleration rather than absolute values.
  What is gyroscope? (lecture 17) -> A gyroscope is an inertial sensor that captures angular velocity. In an inertial measurement unit, it is a main component, and sensor tracking relies mainly on its readings.
  What is accelerometer? (lecture 17) -> An accelerometer is an inertial sensor that captures linear acceleration along the x, y, and z axes, and in an inertial measurement unit its readings can be used to detect drift errors.
  What is magnetometer? (lecture 17) -> A magnetometer is a sensor that captures magnetic field strength along the x, y, and z axes and can be used to detect drift errors in tracking.
  What is augmented reality (AR)? (lecture 1) -> Augmented reality (AR) is an enhanced version of reality created by technology, in which computer-generated digital content is overlaid on the real world in real time and registered in 3D, so the user perceives and interacts with the enhanced environment.

  Electromagnetic and acoustic or ultrasonic trackers estimate a head’s real-time position using signals between transmitters and receivers. Electromagnetic tracking uses magnetic fields, while acoustic or ultrasonic tracking uses ultrasonic signals. Although both use stationary transmitters and receivers that move with the head or body, acoustic tracking needs line of sight and electromagnetic tracking does not.
  - Non-contact electromagnetic trackers estimate head position from magnetic fields, generally using three orthogonal fields that induce AC or DC currents.
  - Acoustic or ultrasonic tracking determines real-time head position using ultrasonic signals from transmitters to HMD microphones.
  - Electromagnetic and acoustic or ultrasonic trackers both use stationary transmitters and receivers that move with the head or body.
  - Acoustic or ultrasonic tracking requires line of sight, whereas electromagnetic tracking does not require this line of sight.

    - It uses a pre-existing map to localize the object within it

18/A15  recap  18/S6  "Recap"  (8 facts, 14 concepts)
  Model-based tracking is the third category of visible light-based sensing. SLAM, originally developed for robot navigation and later adapted for augmented reality, creates and updates a map while localizing changing positions, enabling drift-free real-time tracking of unknown environments. PTAM is a further SLAM optimization designed for augmented reality; it separates tracking and mapping, improving tracking accuracy and overall performance, though it is more suitable for smaller environments because larger environments have quite high computational requirements.
  - Model-based tracking is the third category of visible light-based sensing.
  - SLAM simultaneously creates and updates a map while localizing changing positions, enabling real-time tracking.
  - Originally developed for robot navigation and adapted for augmented reality, SLAM allows drift-free tracking of unknown environments.
  - PTAM is a further SLAM optimization designed for augmented reality, separating tracking and mapping, improving tracking accuracy and overall performance.
  - PTAM is more suitable for smaller environments because larger environments have quite high computational requirements.

  Q What do inertial trackers report?  [18/S8/F0]
    - Absolute-distance readings from a fixed base station
    - Absolute-value readings for orientation, velocity, or acceleration
    - Absolute-position readings for the surrounding room
    * Rate-of-change readings for orientation, velocity, or acceleration
    because: Inertial trackers measure changes such as orientation, translation velocity, or acceleration, rather than absolute values. They do not by themselves provide absolute position or distance from a fixed reference.
  Q Why are inertial trackers readily usable on smartphones and head-mounted displays?  [18/S8/F1]
    - They are built into the device but have a short range limitation
    - They rely on external beacons and have a room-scale limitation
    * They are built into the device and have no range limitation
    - They rely on GPS satellites and have an outdoor coverage limitation
    because: Inertial trackers are typically MEMS-based sensors inside the user's device, so they can be used readily without an external tracking range. They do not depend on beacons or GPS for basic tracking.
  Q Why might GPS be used in a hybrid XR tracking system?  [18/S8/F5, 18/S8/F6, 18/S8/F8]
    - It can provide full body pose when precise position is not needed
    - It can provide precise indoor position when precise position is needed
    * It can provide approximate outdoor position when precise position is not needed
    - It can provide head orientation when precise position is not needed
    because: GPS is useful outdoors and is appropriate when an approximation is enough or as part of a hybrid system. It is generally less accurate indoors and provides only positional tracking, not orientation or full pose.

    - Magnetometer measurements that improve outdoor accuracy
    - Camera-feature measurements that improve tracking accuracy
    - Acoustic-ranging measurements that improve indoor accuracy
    because: RTK improves basic global positioning system positioning by using signal carrier waves for measurement, giving better accuracy. It is not based on acoustic-ranging, magnetometer, or camera-feature measurements.
