18/A19  recap  18/S8  "Recap"  (9 facts, 18 concepts)
  Built-in inertial tracking and positional GPS provide different kinds of tracking data. Inertial sensors measure changes and can be combined in software into hybrid sensors, while GPS works outdoors but is position-only and often inaccurate indoors. RTK can improve GPS accuracy, and GPS is typically used when approximation suffices or it is part of a hybrid tracking system.
  - Inertial trackers are MEMS-based, self-contained device sensors that measure changes, not absolute values, without range limits.
  - Hybrid software-level sensors can be part of devices using gyroscope, accelerometer, and magnetometer.
  - Basic tracking sensors include electromechanical, electromagnetic, inertial, 3D structure, and light-based sensing, unlike acoustic or GPS.
  - GPS is useful outdoors, gives only position, and generally has low accuracy, especially indoors.
  - RTK improves basic GPS accuracy using GPS carrier waves, while GPS fits approximate or hybrid tracking needs.

18/A21  recap  18/S9  "Recap"  (8 facts, 24 concepts)
  Motion capture and eye tracking track movement and gaze, while hybrid tracking combines basic tracking methods. Motion capture records real-world movement, typically through wearable suits, and can be real-time or non-real-time. Eye tracking observes the gaze point or area using optical, infrared lighting, EOG, or VOG methods, with systems head-mounted, display-attached, or part of other trackers. Hybrid trackers combine two or more basic tracking methods and typically outperform single-technology trackers.
  - Motion capture is not a fundamentally new tracking method; it can be based on any tracking method.
  - Motion capture is typically packaged as wearable suits with tracking sensors and need not be real-time.
  - Eye-tracking systems can be head-mounted, display-attached, or built into other trackers, using optical, infrared lighting, EOG, or VOG methods.
  - Eye-tracking systems typically track the user's gaze point or gaze area.
  - Hybrid trackers combine two or more basic tracking methods and typically outperform single-technology trackers.
  judge round 1: 4 of 6 failed
    1 pass  (Motion capture is not a fundamentally new tracking method; it can be based on …)
      check: none
      reason: The point is directly carried by fact 1: motion capture can be based on any tracking method, so it is not a fundamentally new tracking method.
    2 FAIL supported,faithful,one_idea  (Motion capture is typically packaged as wearable suits with tracking sensors and need not …)
      check: typically [2]
      reason: It fails supported/faithful because “typically packaged” adds a hedge not attached to packaging in fact 2, which says motion capture “is packaged as wearable suits.” It also packs two separable ideas into one point: the wearable-suit packaging from fact 2 and the non-real-time option from fact 3. A repaired version would split these into two points and avoid “typically” unless tied to the details in fact 2.
    3 FAIL one_idea  (Eye-tracking systems can be head-mounted, display-attached, or built into other trackers, using optical, infrared …)
      check: none
      reason: The point is supported by facts 4 and 5, but it packs two separable ideas into one point: the possible placements of eye-tracking systems from fact 4 and the sensing methods from fact 5. A repaired version would split placement and methods into separate points.
    4 pass  (Eye-tracking systems typically track the user's gaze point or gaze area.)
      check: none
      reason: The point is directly carried by fact 6, which says eye-tracking systems typically track the user's gaze point or area of gaze.
    5 FAIL one_idea  (Hybrid trackers combine two or more basic tracking methods and typically outperform single-technology trackers.)
      check: none
      reason: The point is supported by facts 7 and 8, but it packs two separable ideas into one point: what a hybrid tracker is from fact 7 and its typical performance advantage from fact 8. A repaired version would split definition and performance into separate points.
    0 FAIL faithful  (Motion capture and eye tracking track movement and gaze, while hybrid tracking combines basic …)
      check: typically [2], typically [6]
      reason: The text fails faithful in two places: it says motion capture is “typically through wearable suits,” but fact 2 says motion capture “is packaged as wearable suits” without making the packaging typical; and it says eye tracking “observes the gaze point or area” without the fact 6 hedge “typically.” A repaired text would make the motion-capture packaging categorical or avoid the unsupported hedge, and would restore “typically” for gaze tracking. The text otherwise reads as a coherent summary of the segment.
  judge kept: original; still failing: [2, 3, 5, 0]

18/A24  match_pairs  lecture  "Match the terms"  (19 facts, 8 concepts)
  global positioning system = A positional tracking device, particularly useful outdoors, that generally offers low accuracy, particularly indoors, and allows only positional tracking.
  pose = The position and orientation of a viewer or tracked object.
  eye tracking = A non-hand-based input technique that tracks a user's gaze point or area, using optical, camera-based or other tracking techniques in systems that …
  inertial measurement unit = A self-contained composite hardware unit that mainly contains a gyroscope, accelerometer, and magnetometer to measure changes in orientation, translation velocity, or acceleration …
  inside-out = A way to obtain input for tracking in which a camera mounted with the user detects external targets and estimates poses from …
  outside-in = An infrared tracking input method that uses cameras placed in the environment rather than on the tracked object to detect targets attached …
  electromechanical tracker = A serial or parallel kinematic structure composed of links interconnected by joints with sensors, in world-fixed or wearable forms, with wearable forms …
  kinematic structure = A serial or parallel structure composed of links that are interconnected using joints with sensors.

18/A27  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (12 facts, 30 concepts)
  Q Why can an electromagnetic tracker estimate a receiver's position when obstacles block the transmitter-receiver path, while an acoustic tracker cannot?  [18/S2/F0, 18/S2/F2, 18/S2/F3, 18/S2/F4; electromagnetic tracking, acoustic tracking, line of sight]
    A Electromagnetic tracking does not require line of sight between transmitter and receiver, whereas acoustic tracking does. Both rely on stationary transmitters and receivers that move with the head or body. Electromagnetic trackers obtain the receiver's real-time position from the direction of the magnetic field, while acoustic tracking uses ultrasonic signals to determine the receiver's position, so an obstacle blocks the acoustic measurement.
  Q Why is parallel tracking and mapping considered an optimization of simultaneous localization and mapping that is more suitable for smaller than larger environments?  [18/S6/F1, 18/S6/F4, 18/S6/F6, 18/S6/F7; simultaneous localization and mapping, parallel tracking and mapping, tracking accuracy, computational requirement]
    A PTAM is an SLAM optimization because it separates camera tracking from environment mapping. SLAM creates and updates a map while localizing, but PTAM's separate activities improve tracking accuracy and performance. It is more suitable for smaller environments because its computational requirements for larger ones are quite high.
  Q Why is the global positioning system more useful as part of a hybrid tracking system than as the only tracking method for an XR system?  [18/S8/F6, 18/S8/F8, 18/S9/F6, 18/S9/F7; global positioning system, hybrid tracking, positional tracking, tracking accuracy]
    A The global positioning system is more useful in a hybrid tracking system because GPS generally offers low accuracy and allows only positional tracking, while a hybrid tracker uses two or more basic tracking systems and typically performs better than single-technology-based tracking. GPS is typically used when accurate position registration is not important, when an approximation is good enough, or as part of a hybrid system.
  judge round 1: 3 of 3 failed

===== lecture 19: VR Software

19/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (18 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM)? (lecture 18) -> Simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) is a technique that simultaneously creates and updates a map of a real environment while localizing positions within it, enabling real-time, drift-free tracking of unknown environments.
  What is virtual reality (VR)? (lecture 4) -> Virtual reality (VR) is an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli provided by a computer, in which a person's actions partially determine what happens and which replaces the user's sense of reality without requiring the physical existence of objects or places.
  What is virtual environment? (lecture 4) -> Virtual environment is a non-real, computer-generated graphical representation of a real or imaginary world, populated with artificial objects, that is experienced through computer-generated sensory stimuli.
  What is virtual reality system? (lecture 4) -> A virtual reality system is a system that presents a computer-generated artificial environment, provides computer-generated sensory stimuli for an immersive experience, and lets the user's actions partially determine what happens in it.
  What is head-mounted display (HMDs)? (lecture 6) -> A head-mounted display (HMD) is a wearable, mobile visual display that integrates electronic, optical, mechanical, and audio components and uses one or two small screens directly in front of the user's eyes to place images for monoscopic or stereoscopic viewing. It can be non-see-through, optical see-through, or video see-through.
  What is cybersickness (CS)? (lecture 10) -> Cybersickness (CS) is a condition primarily relevant to virtual reality that may be caused by multiple internal and external factors and in which a user may experience symptoms such as nausea, dizziness, headache, or disorientation.

    - To make it build a model of the surrounding physical environment

    - head tracking, stereoscopic output rendering, and interaction incorporation
    - environment modeling, visual display rendering, and interaction incorporation

    because: Creating a VR experience involves building the environment, rendering the stereoscopic output view, and incorporating interactions that use tracking hardware.   - Creating a VR experience involves environment modeling, stereoscopic output rendering in a broad sense, and interactions.

  - In practice, VR developers may build from scratch and must understand a platform-dependent SDK for lowest-level operations.
  - A game engine can be VR middleware, but can be cumbersome and less flexible for ideas outside standard video games.

    because: The virtual world generator abstraction treats the entire VR software system as a black box, so its internal operation is not considered. A head tracker, renderer, or recorded-world component is only one part that may interact with that abstraction.

    - eye distance and focus

    because: A head tracker estimates the user's head position and orientation. It does not provide hand tracking, body dimensions, or eye-focus data in this abstraction.
  Q Which two operations in the virtual world generator preserve the relationship between user actions and what the display shows?  [19/S3/F2]
    - defining triangular meshes and maintaining surface properties
    - capturing physical worlds and applying SLAM techniques
    * converting input to output and synchronizing output devices
    - mapping camera images onto objects and applying textures
    because: Converting input into output and synchronizing output devices with input data are the two operations that keep the display tied to user input. Defining meshes, capturing worlds, or mapping textures create world content rather than maintain that relationship.

    - by triangular-mesh definition and surface-property maintenance
    because: A virtual world can be a recorded physical world made realistic by capturing the real world with cameras and using computer-vision or SLAM techniques. Triangular meshes describe completely synthetic worlds, texture mapping places real images on synthetic objects, and input queuing handles event processing.

19/A9  recap  19/S3  "Recap"  (8 facts, 36 concepts)
  The virtual world generator is treated as a black box that queues input, maintains an internal virtual reality, and keeps output synchronized with input. It can drive visual, aural, haptic, and other renderers. The needed software support depends on how the world is created: synthetic worlds require computer graphics, while worlds based on real captured images may use SLAM, computer vision, or texture mapping.
  - The virtual world generator is a black-box abstraction of the whole virtual reality software system.
  - The virtual world generator queues input, maintains an internal reality, and keeps output synchronized with input.
  - The virtual world generator can drive visual, aural, haptic, and other output renderers.
  - Synthetic virtual worlds require computer graphics operations for triangular meshes and surface properties.
  - Virtual reality software may support SLAM, computer vision, and texture mapping of real images onto synthetic objects.

19/A10  quiz  19/S4  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 10 concepts)
  Q What is matched motion in a VR experience?  [19/S4/F0]
    * the correspondence between real-world user motion and virtual user motion
    - the restriction of real-world user motion to a safe physical region
    - the alignment of real-world obstacle motion and virtual obstacle motion
    - the conversion of controller input into virtual avatar motion
    because: Matched motion keeps the user's real-world motions and the corresponding virtual motions aligned. Restricting motion to a safe region describes the matched zone, while controller-driven avatar movement is a form of locomotion.
  Q What is the matched zone in a VR setup?  [19/S4/F1]
    * a safe real-world region that allows extended virtual movement
    - a seated controller input that produces avatar movement
    - a safe virtual region that allows extended real-world movement
    - a tracked body part that requires matched movement
    because: The matched zone is the real-world area where physical movement is limited, while movement there can be translated into movement in other parts of the virtual world. It is not a virtual region, a body part, or a controller input.
  Q What is an obstacle mismatch in VR?  [19/S4/F2]
    - a missing correspondence between a controller command and an avatar action in the matched zone
    * a missing correspondence between a virtual obstacle and a physical obstacle in the matched zone
    - a missing correspondence between a user's head motion and the rendered viewpoint in the matched zone
    - a missing correspondence between a physical location and a virtual location outside the matched zone
    because: An obstacle mismatch occurs when a virtual obstacle and a physical obstacle do not correspond in the matched zone. Head-motion matching, controller-driven avatar action, and general location mapping are different VR concerns.
  Q Why is it useful for VR software to provide several user-locomotion operations?  [19/S4/F9, 19/S4/F8]
    * to address cyber sickness
    - to resolve an obstacle mismatch
    - to maintain a correct visual viewpoint
    - to track a user's hand motion
    because: Different locomotion options are part of VR software because avoiding physical movement can cause cyber sickness, and multiple choices help address it. Correct viewpoint, obstacle matching, and hand tracking are separate matched-motion or rendering needs.

19/A11  recap  19/S4  "Recap"  (10 facts, 19 concepts)
  VR software must keep the user's real movements corresponding to the virtual experience, especially inside the safe matched zone. This includes deciding which body motions to match and preventing physical and virtual obstacles from disagreeing. It must also support user locomotion, where virtual movement does not depend on matched physical movement, while offering choices that may reduce cyber sickness.
  - VR matched motion aligns real and virtual movement, using the safe matched zone as the physical area.
  - VR obstacle mismatch can occur when physical and virtual obstacles in the matched zone do not correspond.
  - VR software should support matching head and needed body motions and mapping zone motion to virtual motion.
  - User locomotion in VR moves the user without matched physical motion, using teleportation, inputs, or vehicles.
  - Unmatched VR locomotion may increase cyber sickness, so VR software should offer multiple locomotion options.

19/A17  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (8 facts, 34 concepts)
  Q Why is virtual reality software needed between a user and virtual reality hardware, rather than the user simply operating the hardware directly?  [19/S0/F0, 19/S1/F1; virtual reality software, virtual reality hardware, input device, output device]
    A Virtual reality software is needed because it processes data generated when the user operates input devices. It then sends processed data to output devices, which generate stimuli that are appropriately received by the user's sense organs. This lets the software drive the hardware to create the sensory virtual reality experience.
  Q Why must a virtual world generator keep output synchronized with incoming input?  [19/S3/F1, 19/S3/F2; virtual world generator, input-output match, synchronization, renderer]
    A A virtual world generator keeps output synchronized with input to maintain the input-output match that supports an internal reality appearing real to the user. It receives input events from devices such as a head tracker and converts them into outputs for renderers. The renderers then calculate outputs for displays, so the user's actions and the sensory output remain aligned.
  Q Why can teleportation and a vehicle metaphor both be useful for user locomotion in virtual reality?  [19/S4/F5, 19/S4/F6, 19/S4/F7, 19/S4/F8; teleportation, vehicle metaphor, user locomotion, cybersickness]
    A They are useful because user locomotion lets the user move in the virtual world while physical motion in the real world is not matched. Teleportation sends the user to a selected virtual location without any physical movement. A vehicle metaphor lets the user operate a game controller, mouse, or keyboard so the avatar can move while the user remains seated. Such operations may lead to cybersickness.
  judge round 1: 1 of 3 failed
    1 pass  (Why is virtual reality software needed between a user and virtual reality hardware, rather …)
      check: Virtual reality software is needed because it processes data generated by the user's operation of input devices and sends processed data to output devices, thereby driving the hardware to generate stimuli that create the sensory virtual reality experience.
      reason: The cited facts carry the link: fact 3 states that software processes input-device data and sends processed data to output devices, and fact 1 states that this drives hardware to generate appropriately received stimuli and create the VR experience.
    2 FAIL answerable  (Why must a virtual world generator keep output synchronized with incoming input?)
      check: A virtual world generator must keep output synchronized with incoming input to maintain an input-output match while it receives input events and converts them into outputs for renderers.
      reason: The reference says the input-output match “supports an internal reality appearing real to the user,” but facts 15 and 16 only state that the VWG must maintain an internal reality and, separately, keep output synchronized with input “to maintain an input-output match”; they do not state that the match supports the internal reality. A repaired reference would remove the unsupported “that supports...” phrase or make the question ask only for the stated purpose of synchronization.

===== lecture 20: VR Software

20/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (14 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is software development kit (SDK)? (lecture 19) -> Software development kit (SDK) is a platform-dependent installable package of software development tools for a specific hardware and operating system combination that provides fundamental tools to design, build, and test virtual or augmented reality experiences.
  What is rendering? (lecture 19) -> Rendering is the multi-stage computational process that creates a scene's visual output as a two-dimensional image that can be displayed, and, in a broad sense, output for other senses.
  What is middleware? (lecture 19) -> Middleware is software that sits between hardware and higher-level application software, abstracts hardware functionalities for developers, and supports the development and rendering of extended reality (XR) experiences.
  What is matched zone? (lecture 19) -> A matched zone is the safe real-world region in a virtual reality application where the real and virtual worlds perfectly align, so the user's restricted physical movement within it is translated into movement in other parts of the virtual world.
  What is game engine? (lecture 19) -> A game engine is a software development environment and middleware that sits between hardware and higher-level application software, abstracting hardware for developers to build games or extended reality (XR) experiences. It typically provides rendering, physics, audio, scripting, and low-level platform-specific support.
  What is platform? (lecture 19) -> A platform is the combination of hardware and an operating system.

20/A1  quiz  20/S0  "Quick quiz"  (4 facts, 16 concepts)
  Q What is the basic purpose of physics support in a virtual world generator?  [20/S0/F2]
    - To make user locomotion match the user's real body movements
    - To make shared virtual worlds consistent across networked users
    * To make virtual events resemble their real-world counterparts
    - To make rendering depend on computer graphics and computer vision
    because: Physics support exists so that real-world events have similar events in the virtual world. Matching user movement, rendering, and network consistency are separate support areas.
  Q How should a virtual world generator treat basic and advanced mechanical support for object motion?  [20/S0/F3]
    - Basic support should cover collisions, and advanced support can add realism when desired
    - Basic support should be limited to rendering, and advanced support can add realism when desired
    - Basic support should cover locomotion, and advanced support can add realism when desired
    * Basic support should be good enough, and advanced support can add realism when desired
    because: Object motion is usually governed by basic mechanical laws, with advanced laws sometimes making motion more realistic. Rendering, collision handling, and locomotion are not the basic mechanical laws being described.
  Q What should collision support in a virtual world generator ideally include?  [20/S0/F5]
    * Detecting whether bodies intersect and deciding how they behave after a collision
    - Detecting whether sounds overlap and deciding how they mix after a reflection
    - Detecting whether bodies are visible and deciding how they render after an occlusion
    - Detecting whether avatars move and deciding how they align after a gesture
    because: Collision support consists of collision detection, which finds intersecting bodies, and collision response, which determines post-collision behavior. Visibility, sound mixing, and gesture alignment are different concerns.
  Q Besides motion and collisions, what physical-world behavior should a virtual world generator's physics support replicate?  [20/S0/F6]
    * How light, sound, and smell propagate and how light interacts with surfaces
    - How meshes, materials, and terrain are rendered and how avatars animate
    - How assets, scenes, and state are loaded and how servers synchronize users
    - How avatars, users, and inputs are tracked and how zones align with movement
    because: Physics support should also reproduce physical phenomena such as the propagation of light, sound, and smell and the interaction of light with surfaces. Tracking, synchronization, and rendering are not part of that physical replication.

Because users may be nearby or far apart, the system must handle both physical proximity and virtual interactions safely. It manages virtual collisions in the shared world regardless of real distance. For social interaction, the virtual world generator also supports expressive cues, with matched-motion demands rising as users encounter each other.

  - The VR system must manage user interactions, including collisions, in the shared virtual world whether users are close or remote.
  - Virtual world generators should support eye movements, facial expressions, and body language; matched-motion burden may rise as users meet.

20/A5  quiz  20/S2  "Quick quiz"  (6 facts, 22 concepts)
  Q When building a virtual world generator directly from a basic SDK, what advantage does the developer gain?  [20/S2/F3]
    - Lower implementation burden from packaged hardware and tracking support
    * Maximum control over the algorithms used for physics support
    - Easier customization through packaged menu and scripting support
    - Reduced effort from packaged collision and physics support
    because: Starting from a basic SDK lets the developer choose and implement physics algorithms according to performance, giving maximum control. Packaged collision, menu, scripting, hardware, or tracking support are not the advantage of this lower-level route.
  Q When a developer uses a basic SDK to build a virtual world generator, which major support is still typically not fully provided and must be implemented by the developer?  [20/S2/F1, 20/S2/F2]
    - Basic drivers needed to run the headset hardware
    - Menu-based configuration and high-level scripting support
    - Interfaces for reading tracking data from sensors
    * Physics support such as collision detection and response
    because: A basic SDK may provide drivers, tracking access, and rendering-library calls, but the developer must still build physics support, including collision detection and response. The other listed items are either provided by the SDK or belong to a ready-made virtual world generator.
  Q What is a main downside of building a virtual world generator from a basic SDK?  [20/S2/F4]
    - The developer must avoid writing high-level scripts for the experience
    - The developer must build basic drivers and tracking APIs from scratch
    * The developer must understand and implement the overall system from scratch
    - The developer must rely on the package's fixed physics algorithms
    because: Building from a basic SDK imposes a difficult implementation burden because the overall system must be understood and implemented from scratch. Reliance on fixed package algorithms describes a ready-made generator, not the SDK route, and basic drivers or tracking APIs are typically already provided.
  Q Why is a ready-made virtual world generator often faster to use for a VR experience?  [20/S2/F6]
    - It requires the developer to build collision support from scratch
    - It removes the need for high-level scripting and menu choices
    * It comes with built-in collision and physics support
    - It gives the developer direct control over the engine's internal algorithms
    because: A ready-made virtual world generator speeds up development because it already includes supports such as collisions and physics. It does not require building collision support from scratch, and it does not give direct control over internal engine algorithms or eliminate scripting and menu-based customization.
  Q What can make a ready-made virtual world generator difficult to use for a highly original experience?  [20/S2/F7]
    - It requires building the whole virtual world from basic drivers
    - It lacks supports for collisions and physics
    * It comes with its own function supports and algorithm implementations
    - It gives the developer maximum control over physics algorithms
    because: A ready-made generator can restrict highly original experiences because the developer must work with the engine's own function supports and algorithm implementations. It is not difficult because it lacks physics support, gives maximum control, or requires building everything from basic drivers.

20/A6  recap  20/S2  "Recap"  (7 facts, 22 concepts)
  Building a virtual reality experience can mean either creating a virtual world generator from a basic software development kit or customizing a ready-made virtual world generator. A basic software development kit typically supplies drivers, tracking access, and rendering interfaces, while leaving physics, audio, lighting, and sometimes collaborative support to the developer. The from-scratch route gives control and performance tuning; ready-made generators provide built-in supports and faster creation, but limit highly original experiences.
  - A developer can either build a virtual world generator from a basic software development kit or customize a ready-made one.
  - Basic software development kits typically give drivers, tracking and rendering interfaces, so developers build physics, audio, lighting, or sometimes collaboration.
  - Building from a basic software development kit gives maximum control and performance optimization but requires heavy implementation effort.
  - Ready-made virtual world generators provide physics and collision supports, enabling quick creation but restricting highly original experiences.

20/A8  recap  20/S3  "Recap"  (6 facts, 22 concepts)
  A game engine is the software layer for building VR applications. It acts as middleware that abstracts hardware and also serves as a development environment on top of which applications are built. Its authoring tool exposes the engine's components and settings, while the engine typically provides rendering, physics, audio, scripting, multiplayer collaborative VR networking, and low-level platform support.
  - A game engine is XR middleware that abstracts hardware and is a development environment for building XR applications.
  - An authoring tool lets developers access a game engine's loading, feature-setting, and logic-setting options, sometimes through scripting.
  - A game engine typically includes rendering, physics, audio, scripting, multiplayer collaborative VR networking, user interfaces, and low-level platform support.

20/A10  recap  20/S4  "Recap"  (10 facts, 27 concepts)
  Game engines for VR support experiences through internal rendering, audio, and physics engines. Rendering engines produce 3D graphics through rasterization or ray tracing, often using APIs that abstract GPUs, while audio engines handle sound without requiring GPUs. Physics engines make objects respond to forces and collisions realistically, though not every game engine includes every engine type. Unity 3D and Unreal Engine dominate the game-engine market, with different licensing models.
  - A rendering engine generates 3D graphics by rasterization or ray tracing, using APIs abstracting GPUs; rasterization is less intensive.
  - An audio engine loads, modifies, and generates sound, may use audio APIs, and runs without needing a GPU.
  - A physics engine simulates forces and collisions at runtime, but not every game engine includes all such components.
  - Unity 3D and Unreal Engine are the most popular game engines, with Unity 3D at almost 51%.
  - Unreal Engine’s major features are freely available, whereas Unity 3D is proprietary, with a limited free version.

      reason: The point drops “helps,” “animated,” “such as,” and “typically,” making the rendering engine’s role, method list, and use of APIs sound more complete and universal than the facts state. A repair could say: “A rendering engine helps generate animated 3D graphics using methods such as rasterization or ray tracing, often via GPU APIs; rasterization is less computationally intensive.”

20/A14  recap  20/S6  "Recap"  (8 facts, 33 concepts)
  Web deployment tools for VR applications are grouped according to what they provide. Cloud tools mainly host and render remote scenes, while libraries and complete tools support building and deploying web-based VR experiences. These categories show where web deployment sits between simple cloud rendering and full application development.
  - Web deployment tools fall into cloud hosting and rendering, web libraries, complete tools, generic editors, and SDK support.
  - Cloud hosting and rendering web tools, like Azure Remote Rendering, only provide hosting and rendering over networks.
  - Web development libraries include WebXR, Three.js, and WaveXR; WebXR uses WebGL, Three.js makes WebGL easier, and WaveXR builds on Three.js.
  - Complete web development and deployment tools include ZappAir, 8thWall, MyWebAR, VRDirect, GmetriXR, InstaVR, PlugXR, and Amazon Sumerian.

20/A17  match_pairs  lecture  "Match the terms"  (17 facts, 8 concepts)
  software development kit = A platform-dependent installable package of software development tools for a specific hardware and operating system combination that provides fundamental tools to design …
  graphics processing unit = A parallel hardware component of a graphics card, with its own memory, that speeds up the rendering process by exploiting the inherent …
  middleware = Software that sits between hardware and higher-level application software, abstracts hardware functionalities for developers, and supports the development and rendering of extended …
  game engine = A software development environment and middleware that sits between hardware and higher-level application software, abstracting hardware for developers to build games or …
  platform = The combination of hardware and an operating system.
  physics support = A required key support in a virtual world generator that makes the virtual world appear to behave like the real world, for …
  collision support = A virtual world generator component that ideally includes collision detection, which determines whether two or more bodies intersect, and collision response, which …
  collision detection = A part of collision support in a virtual world generator that determines whether two or more bodies intersect.

20/A21  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (14 facts, 50 concepts)
  Q Why can building a virtual world generator from a basic headset software development kit give a developer more performance control than using a ready-made virtual world generator, even though the basic kit leaves many supports to be built?  [20/S2/F1, 20/S2/F2, 20/S2/F3, 20/S2/F7; virtual world generator, software development kit, physics support, performance]
    A Building from a basic headset software development kit can give more performance control because the developer chooses and implements physics algorithms according to performance. The kit provides drivers, tracking, and rendering-library interfaces, but not every aspect of physics, matched motion, locomotion, or collaboration, so the developer must build physics support, collisions, lighting, and audio. A ready-made virtual world generator supplies its own function supports and algorithm implementations, reducing effort but restricting highly original experiences.
  Q Why must a networked collaborative virtual reality system manage virtual collisions even when users' real-world matched zones are far apart?  [20/S1/F0, 20/S1/F1, 20/S1/F2; networked collaborative virtual reality experience, matched zone, shared virtual world, collision]
    A A networked collaborative virtual reality system must manage virtual collisions because all user interactions in the shared virtual world must be managed by the virtual reality system, whether users are close or spread around the world. The experience maintains a shared virtual world over a network, although each user has a distinct matched zone. Those zones are often disjoint and distributed around the Earth, so physical collision is possible only when users are close.
  Q Why is a graphics processing unit central to a rendering engine but not required for an audio engine in a game engine?  [20/S4/F2, 20/S4/F3, 20/S4/F5, 20/S4/F6; rendering engine, graphics processing unit, audio engine, central processing unit]
    A A rendering engine is typically built on rendering application programming interfaces that provide software abstractions of the graphics processing unit, which speeds up rendering. An audio engine generates sound through a speaker system and can perform calculations on a central processing unit or a dedicated application-specific integrated circuit. Therefore it does not require a graphics processing unit.
  Q How do native application deployment and web application deployment differ in the software resources required to make a virtual reality experience available to users?  [20/S5/F0, 20/S5/F2, 20/S6/F0; native application deployment, web application deployment, software development kit, web deployment tool]
    A Native application deployment requires software development kits tailored to the platform and hardware, and an SDK is a collection of development tools specific to a hardware and operating system combination. Web application deployment allows the experience to be obtained remotely without a specific device. Web deployment tools can instead include cloud hosting and rendering services, development libraries, complete web development and deployment tools, generic editors, or SDK support.
  judge round 1: 0 of 4 failed
    1 pass  (Why can building a virtual world generator from a basic headset software development kit …)
      check: It can because a basic SDK lets the developer choose and implement physics algorithms according to performance, while a ready-made generator supplies its own algorithms and supports.
      reason: Facts 15 and 19 carry the performance-control comparison, and facts 13/14 support the burden side; the answer is direct, comparative, and one-threaded.
    2 pass  (Why must a networked collaborative virtual reality system manage virtual collisions even when users' …)
      check: It must manage them because, in the shared virtual world, user interactions including collisions must be managed by the VR system whether users are close or spread around the world.
      reason: Fact 10 directly answers the question, while facts 8 and 9 explain the shared-world and matched-zone context; the reference states the required link without source talk.
    3 pass  (Why is a graphics processing unit central to a rendering engine but not required …)
      check: A rendering engine is built on rendering APIs that abstract a GPU used to speed up rendering, whereas an audio engine can run on a CPU or dedicated ASIC and therefore does not require a GPU.
      reason: Facts 29 and 30 support the GPU role in rendering, and facts 32 and 33 support the audio engine not requiring a GPU; the answer compares the two roles directly.
    4 pass  (How do native application deployment and web application deployment differ in the software resources …)
      check: Native deployment requires platform- and hardware-tailored SDKs, while web deployment allows remote access without a specific device and may use web deployment tools such as hosting/rendering tools, libraries, complete tools, editors, or SDK support.
      reason: Facts 40 and 42 give the native side, and fact 40 plus fact 47 give the web side; the reference compares the two deployment paths using only the cited facts.
  judge kept: original

===== lecture 21: AR Software

21/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (17 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is platform? (lecture 19) -> A platform is the combination of hardware and an operating system.
  What is authoring tool? (lecture 20) -> An authoring tool is a tool that lets a developer create software or content by accessing underlying system functionalities, with options for loading, feature-setting, and logic-setting; for augmented reality, it can be standalone or an existing tool extended by a plugin.
  What is augmented reality (AR)? (lecture 1) -> Augmented reality (AR) is an enhanced version of reality created by technology, in which computer-generated digital content is overlaid on the real world in real time and registered in 3D, so the user perceives and interacts with the enhanced environment.
  What is marker? (lecture 3) -> A marker is a real-world object or image placed in the environment that a system detects to identify its position or track a user's motion and to place digital content at that position.
  What is virtual reality (VR)? (lecture 4) -> Virtual reality (VR) is an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli provided by a computer, in which a person's actions partially determine what happens and which replaces the user's sense of reality without requiring the physical existence of objects or places.
  What is three-dimensional registration? (lecture 7) -> Three-dimensional registration is the anchoring of virtual content in augmented reality at a suitable place in the real world so that it appears to be part of the physical environment and mixes seamlessly with real-world objects.

21/A4  quiz  21/S1  "Quick quiz"  (6 facts, 20 concepts)
  Q Which characteristic makes low-level AR libraries and frameworks the most skill-demanding software category?  [21/S1/F0]
    - They hide tracking behind a ready-made authoring tool
    - They limit development to a single platform and tracker
    - They provide finished interaction and realistic graphics
    * They give access to core tracking and display functions
    because: Low-level AR software gives developers direct access to the core tracking and display functionality needed to build an AR application, so they must manage those functions directly. The other options describe higher-level or restrictive tools rather than the low-level category.
  Q Why is a complete realistic AR application difficult to build with ARToolKit alone?  [21/S1/F3, 21/S1/F4]
    - It provides interaction but not tracking or display
    - It provides natural-feature tracking but not marker tracking or display
    - It provides realistic rendering but not tracking or interaction
    * It provides tracking but not interaction or realistic rendering
    because: ARToolKit is primarily a tracking-support library, and its rendering is low-level and primitive, so interaction and complex realistic graphics must be added separately. Options that credit ARToolKit with interaction or realistic rendering reverse its actual role.
  Q When ARToolKit is paired with a scene-graph library, which task does the scene-graph library mainly perform?  [21/S1/F9, 21/S1/F14]
    - Reading the motion sensors
    - Tracking the physical marker
    * Rendering the virtual object
    - Detecting the natural features
    because: The scene-graph library handles low-level rendering of the virtual content, while ARToolKit handles tracking and 3D registration. Marker tracking and sensor reading belong to the tracking side.
  Q Which tracking capability is available in ARToolKit's commercial version but not in its open-source version?  [21/S1/F2]
    - Sensor-based tracking from phone motion
    - GPS-based tracking for outdoor mobile use
    * Natural-feature tracking on an arbitrary image
    - Marker-based tracking on printed patterns
    because: The commercial ARToolKit version adds computer-vision tracking of natural features on an arbitrary image, while the open-source version is marker-based. GPS and phone-motion tracking are not the added capability of the commercial version.

21/A5  recap  21/S1  "Recap"  (19 facts, 57 concepts)
  Low-level AR software gives developers direct access to core tracking and display, but ARToolKit is mainly a tracking-support library with primitive rendering and little interaction support. Scene graph libraries such as Open Scene Graph and Vulkan Scene Graph manage rendering and interaction, so combining them with ARToolKit allows tracking and rendered virtual content to work together in AR frameworks and mobile tools.
  - Low-level AR libraries and frameworks expose core tracking and display functionality, so they demand the most developer skill.
  - ARToolKit is a widely used C library that mainly provides tracking, marker-based openly and natural-feature commercially.
  - ARToolKit and many tracking-focused toolkits provide primitive rendering and no interaction support, making complete realistic AR apps difficult and time-consuming.
  - Scene graphs such as OSG or VSG are C++ OpenGL libraries that manage complex 3D rendering and interaction.
  - Combining ARToolKit tracking with OSG or VSG rendering supports AR scenes, including example frameworks and mobile frameworks.
  judge round 1: 3 of 6 failed
    1 pass  (Low-level AR libraries and frameworks expose core tracking and display functionality, so they demand …)
      check: none
      reason: Fact 1 states that low-level AR libraries/frameworks require maximum developer skill because they give access to core tracking and display functionality, which the point paraphrases without adding or changing meaning.
    2 FAIL clear  (ARToolKit is a widely used C library that mainly provides tracking, marker-based openly and …)
      check: none
      reason: The point is supported by facts 2, 3, and 4, but “marker-based openly and natural-feature commercially” is not plain or fully grammatical; a repaired version would say “marker-based in its open-source version and natural-feature in its commercial version.”
    3 FAIL supported,faithful  (ARToolKit and many tracking-focused toolkits provide primitive rendering and no interaction support, making complete …)
      check: 5, 6
      reason: Fact 5 says “using it alone” is difficult and time-consuming, and fact 6 only says many toolkits “lack features needed” for realistic rendering and interaction; the point wrongly extends “primitive rendering” and “difficult and time-consuming” to many tracking-focused toolkits. A repair would separate ARToolKit’s specific limitation from the broader lack of realistic rendering/interaction support.
    4 pass  (Scene graphs such as OSG or VSG are C++ OpenGL libraries that manage complex …)
      check: none
      reason: Facts 8, 9, 11, and 12 support the point: OSG and VSG are widely used scene-graph libraries written in C++ on top of OpenGL, and scene-graph representations manage graphics-pipeline operations and interaction. “Scene graphs” here is a reasonable shorthand for “scene-graph libraries” given the named examples.
    5 FAIL supported,faithful,clear,one_idea  (Combining ARToolKit tracking with OSG or VSG rendering supports AR scenes, including example frameworks …)
      check: 15, 17, 18, 19
      reason: Fact 15 supports combining ARToolKit with OSG or VSG for an example, but facts 17 and 18 do not say that all named example or mobile frameworks combine ARToolKit with OSG/VSG; the point therefore overgeneralizes. It also packs the combination, example frameworks, and mobile frameworks into one unclear sentence, so a repair should state only that ARToolKit can be combined with OSG/VSG for tracking plus rendered AR scenes, with examples/mobile tools separate if needed.
    0 pass  (Low-level AR software gives developers direct access to core tracking and display, but ARToolKit …)
      check: none
      reason: The text is supported by facts 1, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10, 11, 12, 15, 17, 18, and 19: it gives the main segment idea—low-level AR software, ARToolKit’s tracking focus, scene-graph rendering/interaction, and combining them into AR frameworks/mobile tools—without source talk or unsupported causation.

21/A6  quiz  21/S2  "Quick quiz"  (6 facts, 25 concepts)
  Q What is the main purpose of rapid prototyping and development tools in augmented-reality projects?  [21/S2/F1]
    - To replace a low-level library for clients before major development
    * To show a simple visualization for end users before major development
    - To provide maximum flexibility for developers before major development
    - To remove camera tracking for clients before major development
    because: Rapid prototyping and development tools let an AR idea be visualized with simple means and shown to end users or clients before major development, so an unsuitable idea does not need further coding. They are not primarily for low-level flexibility, replacing libraries, or removing camera tracking.
  Q Why can implementing an augmented-reality application directly with low-level AR libraries be time-consuming?  [21/S2/F0]
    * Because it requires significant programming skill
    - Because it requires markerless tracking support
    - Because it requires a Flash-enabled web browser
    - Because it requires a Flash AR Manager framework
    because: Low-level AR libraries give maximum flexibility, but using them requires knowing the library or framework and writing programs, so implementation takes time and significant programming skill. Flash-based tools or markerless tracking are not requirements of low-level AR libraries in general.
  Q What allows FLAR Toolkit to let a user develop an augmented-reality experience with minimal effort?  [21/S2/F4, 21/S2/F5]
    * Its marker tracking and content overlay are possible with a few lines of code
    - Its markerless tracking and content placement are possible with a few lines of code
    - Its library combination and graphics rendering are possible with a few lines of code
    - Its low-level coding and manual rendering are possible with a few lines of code
    because: FLAR Toolkit lets a user activate a camera, track AR markers, and overlay virtual content using only a few lines of code, so little programming is needed. Combining libraries is the role of FLAR Manager, and FLAR Toolkit is marker-based rather than markerless.
  Q What is Flash AR Manager designed to combine AR tracking and graphics libraries for?  [21/S2/F6, 21/S2/F7]
    * For prototyping rather than full-fledged development
    - For low-level library authoring rather than full-fledged development
    - For non-Flash prototyping rather than full-fledged development
    - For deployment rather than full-fledged development
    because: Flash AR Manager is a framework that combines AR tracking libraries with 3D graphics libraries, and such combinations are used primarily for prototyping rather than full-fledged development. It is not aimed at deployment, low-level library authoring, or non-Flash workflows.

21/A7  recap  21/S2  "Recap"  (8 facts, 28 concepts)
  Low-level AR libraries are contrasted with rapid prototyping tools, showing why prototyping is useful before major development. Flash-based prototyping uses Adobe Flash with AR plugins to create desktop or mobile AR experiences. FLAR Toolkit makes browser-based marker tracking and 3D overlay simple, while Flash AR Manager combines tracking libraries with 3D graphics libraries mainly for prototypes.
  - Low-level AR libraries offer maximum flexibility but require substantial programming and are time-consuming.
  - Rapid prototyping tools visualize an AR idea for users or clients before major development.
  - Adobe Flash can be used with AR plugins to prototype desktop and mobile AR experiences.
  - FLAR Toolkit runs Flash AR in a browser, with few lines of code tracking markers and overlaying 3D content.
  - Flash AR Manager combines AR tracking libraries with 3D graphics libraries, mainly for prototyping rather than full development.
  judge round 1: 1 of 6 failed
    1 pass  (Low-level AR libraries offer maximum flexibility but require substantial programming and are time-consuming.)
      check: none
      reason: Fact 1 supports the flexibility-versus-effort contrast: low-level AR libraries/frameworks provide maximum development flexibility, but implementation requires knowing the library/framework, writing programs, significant programming skill, and is time-consuming.
    2 pass  (Rapid prototyping tools visualize an AR idea for users or clients before major development.)
      check: none
      reason: Fact 2 supports that rapid prototyping tools are used to visualize an AR idea before major development and show it to end users or clients; the point is a shortened but faithful version of that idea.
    3 pass  (Adobe Flash can be used with AR plugins to prototype desktop and mobile AR …)
      check: none
      reason: Fact 3 states that Adobe Flash can be used through AR plugins to prototype desktop and mobile AR experiences, which is exactly what the point says.
    4 pass  (FLAR Toolkit runs Flash AR in a browser, with few lines of code tracking …)
      check: none
      reason: Facts 4, 5, and 6 support that FLAR Toolkit allows a Flash-based AR experience to run in a browser and, with a few lines of code, track markers and overlay virtual content for 3D registering; the point is a compact paraphrase.
    5 pass  (Flash AR Manager combines AR tracking libraries with 3D graphics libraries, mainly for prototyping …)
      check: none
      reason: Facts 7 and 8 support that Flash AR Manager is a framework combining AR tracking libraries with 3D graphics libraries, primarily for prototyping rather than full-fledged development.
    0 FAIL coverage  (Low-level AR libraries are contrasted with rapid prototyping tools, showing why prototyping is useful …)
      check: fact 2: 'so an unsuitable idea does not require further coding'; fact 9: 'Non-Flash-based authoring tools for augmented reality prototyping exist'
      reason: The text is mostly supported, but it fails coverage because it does not give the central reason rapid prototyping is useful from fact 2, namely that showing the idea to users or clients means an unsuitable idea does not require further coding, and it omits fact 9's note that non-Flash-based authoring tools exist, which the segment explicitly notes. A repaired text would say rapid prototyping lets an AR idea be shown to users or clients before major development so a weak idea need not be fully coded, and that non-Flash tools also exist.

21/A13  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (11 facts, 47 concepts)
  Q Why does a skill-based classification place low-level augmented reality software libraries or frameworks at the highest programming-skill end and standalone augmented reality authoring tools at the no-programming end?  [21/S0/F1, 21/S0/F2, 21/S1/F0; low-level software library or framework, standalone augmented reality authoring tool, skill-based hierarchy, programming skill]
    A The skill-based hierarchy orders tools by decreasing programming skill. Low-level libraries or frameworks sit highest because they require strong programming, require knowing how to call library functions, and give access to core tracking and display functionality. Standalone authoring tools sit lowest because they assume no programming ability and can be used without any knowledge.
  Q How does combining ARToolKit with a scene graph library make it easier to build a complete realistic augmented reality application than using ARToolKit alone?  [21/S1/F4, 21/S1/F6, 21/S1/F9; augmented reality toolkit, scene graph, tracking, interaction]
    A ARToolKit alone provides only primitive OpenGL-based rendering and no built-in interaction support, so interaction must be written from scratch and a complete realistic application is difficult. A framework can combine tracking-focused libraries with libraries that provide interaction and realistic graphics. With a scene graph library, low-level object rendering is handled while ARToolKit remains responsible for tracking, letting the developer focus on interaction.
  Q Why might a developer choose a Flash-based rapid prototyping tool to test an augmented reality idea before major development?  [21/S2/F1, 21/S2/F2, 21/S2/F8; rapid prototyping tool, Adobe Flash, prototype, flash-based tool]
    A Rapid prototyping tools let an augmented reality idea be visualized with simple means and shown to end users or clients, so an unsuitable idea does not require further coding. Flash-based tools may be chosen because they have greater market penetration, and Adobe Flash can be used with augmented reality plugins to prototype desktop and mobile experiences.
  Q How does the desktop-versus-mobile categorization of augmented reality software tools correspond to the deployment meaning of a platform as operating system plus hardware?  [21/S0/F0, 20/S5/F1; application platform, platform, desktop augmented reality application, mobile augmented reality application]
    A In augmented reality software categorization, the target application platform can be a desktop or a mobile augmented reality application. In deployment, a platform means the operating system plus hardware, with Windows or Mac OS representing desktop platforms and Android or iOS representing mobile platforms, so the categories name the target operating-system and hardware environment.

===== lecture 22: AR Software

22/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (16 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is three-dimensional registration? (lecture 7) -> Three-dimensional registration is the anchoring of virtual content in augmented reality at a suitable place in the real world so that it appears to be part of the physical environment and mixes seamlessly with real-world objects.
  What is augmented reality toolkit? (lecture 7) -> An augmented reality toolkit (ARToolKit) is a low-level, open-source software library for developing augmented reality applications that primarily provides real-time, marker-based tracking of a user’s viewpoint, with only primitive rendering support and no built-in interaction support.
  What is tracking? (lecture 13) -> Tracking is the integral XR hardware component that keeps track of physical-world motion, translating user pose, position, and orientation—or real objects—into virtual motion or 3D content registered to a real-world anchor.
  What is rapid prototyping tool? (lecture 21) -> Rapid prototyping tool is an augmented reality software tool that requires some programming ability and may require design prototyping skills, and is used to visualize an augmented reality idea with simple means before major development and show it to end users or clients, so an unsuitable idea does not require further coding.
  What is plugin to existing tools? (lecture 21) -> A plugin to existing tools is a category of augmented reality (AR) software in which a plugin is added to an existing interactive 2D or 3D content authoring tool that may not support AR content, adding AR-specific functions such as tracking, visualization, and 3D registration, while relying on that tool for content authoring.
  What is standalone augmented reality authoring tool? (lecture 21) -> A standalone augmented reality authoring tool is an application that lets users create augmented reality experiences without programming experience, and it is a complete package that includes content authoring and augmented reality support without depending on any other tool.

  Q How can a non-flash browser-based rapid AR prototype avoid third-party browser plugins?  [22/S0/F0]
    - By adding an AR plugin to an existing interactive 3D authoring tool
    - By connecting a mobile device to a backend server for rendering
    - By using a complete drag-and-drop package that includes AR support
    * By writing code in HTML, WebGL, or similar web components
    because: A non-flash browser-based AR prototype can avoid third-party browser plugins when the developer writes the prototype code directly in web component technologies such as HTML or WebGL. Plugins, standalone packages, and backend rendering are different AR software approaches.
  Q What kind of authoring tool is Open Frameworks?  [22/S0/F1]
    - A drag-and-drop package that supports non-programmer scene construction
    * An open-source C++ middleware framework for desktop and mobile platforms
    - A plugin that adds AR functions to an existing 3D authoring tool
    - A browser-based application for mobile augmented-reality prototyping
    because: Open Frameworks is an open-source C++ middleware framework and library for desktop and mobile platforms, not a browser app, a plugin, or a drag-and-drop authoring package. Its role is to combine lower-level libraries rather than to replace an entire authoring environment.
  Q What does Open Frameworks enable in AR application development?  [22/S0/F2]

    because: Open Frameworks supports AR development by combining libraries that provide tracking, rendering, and interaction. Backend content, default content, and dependence on a host authoring tool describe other AR software patterns, not Open Frameworks.

22/A4  recap  22/S1  "Recap"  (7 facts, 32 concepts)
  Plugins to existing tools let an AR application be built inside a familiar 2D or 3D authoring tool, with the plugin supplying AR-specific capabilities. This is mainly useful for developers already skilled in the host tool, and Unity is a central example because it has many AR plugin options. The trade-off is that the underlying tool can constrain design, configuration, and software dependence, while low-level libraries offer a from-scratch alternative.
  - Plugins to existing tools add AR tracking, visualization, and 3D registration to an existing 2D/3D authoring tool.
  - Plugins to existing authoring tools offer a quick start only when the developer already knows the host authoring tool.
  - Unity has the widest range of AR plugins, including AR Toolkit and Vuforia for mobile AR.
  - Plugins can limit interface and interaction design, configuration, and usually leave content dependent on proprietary player software.
  - To resolve such limitations, use low-level software libraries and build the system from scratch instead of third-party tools.

22/A6  recap  22/S2  "Recap"  (6 facts, 13 concepts)
  Standalone AR authoring tools are complete, independent packages, setting them apart from plugins that require a base tool. They let non-programmers build AR experiences through drag-and-drop interfaces, while capability can range from simple scenes to complex interactive behavior. Optional scripting support gives advanced developers more flexibility, with Wikitude Studio as a web-based example.
  - Standalone AR authoring tools let non-programmers create AR experiences, often using drag-and-drop graphical user interfaces.
  - Unlike plugins, standalone AR authoring tools are complete packages that do not depend on any other tool.
  - Standalone AR authoring tools typically support scene construction, animation, and interactive behavior, ranging from scenes only to complex interactive behavior.
  - Standalone AR authoring tools can offer scripting support, while zero-coding apps have limited utility versus more flexible scripted systems.
  - Wikitude Studio is a web-based standalone AR authoring package for creating mobile AR content, including 3D models and animations.
  judge round 1: 1 of 6 failed

      reason: Facts 1 and 4 support that standalone AR authoring tools allow users without programming experience to create AR experiences, and most provide drag-and-drop GUIs usable by non-programmers; “often” is a softer but not contradictory paraphrase of “most”.
    2 pass  (Unlike plugins, standalone AR authoring tools are complete packages that do not depend on …)
      check: none
      reason: Fact 2 states that standalone AR authoring tools are complete packages that do not require or depend on any other tool, unlike plugins that require a base software or authoring tool.
    3 pass  (Standalone AR authoring tools typically support scene construction, animation, and interactive behavior, ranging from …)

    4 pass  (Standalone AR authoring tools can offer scripting support, while zero-coding apps have limited utility …)
      check: none
      reason: Fact 5 supports that standalone AR authoring tools can provide scripting support and that zero-coding applications have limited utility compared with systems using scripting support for more flexibility.
    5 pass  (Wikitude Studio is a web-based standalone AR authoring package for creating mobile AR content …)
      check: none

    0 FAIL supported,faithful  (Standalone AR authoring tools are complete, independent packages, setting them apart from plugins that …)

22/A11  match_pairs  lecture  "Match the terms"  (17 facts, 8 concepts)
  standalone augmented reality authoring tool = An application that lets users create augmented reality experiences without programming experience, and it is a complete package that includes content authoring …
  OpenFrameworks = An open-source C++ middleware framework and library that is a non-web-based authoring and rapid prototyping tool for desktop and mobile augmented reality …
  Vuforia = A cross-platform augmented reality (AR) software development kit (SDK) that uses computer vision to recognize and track images and objects in the …
  Wikitude augmented reality browser app = A free augmented reality browser application for mobile prototyping that treats the device mainly as a rendering device and retrieves content and …
  non-flash-based browser tool = An augmented reality rapid prototyping browser tool that can avoid third-party browser plugins by letting a developer with mastery of HyperText Markup …
  AR Toolkit for Unity = An AR plugin for Unity that provides marker-based tracking, image-based or computer-vision-based tracking, and AR visualization support.
  augmented reality = An enhanced version of reality created by technology, in which computer-generated digital content is overlaid on the real world in real time …
  augmented reality application = An application that emphasizes augmenting digital content onto the real-world view rather than being immersive.

22/A14  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (9 facts, 31 concepts)
  Q Why are plugins to existing tools useful mainly when the developer already knows the host authoring tool, while standalone augmented reality authoring tools can be used by developers without that prior knowledge?  [22/S1/F0, 22/S1/F1, 22/S2/F1, 22/S2/F3; plugin to existing tools, standalone augmented reality authoring tool, authoring tool, programming skill]
    A A plugin adds augmented reality support to an existing authoring tool and relies on it for content authoring, so it is easy and quick only if the developer already knows that host tool. A standalone augmented reality authoring tool is a complete package that includes content authoring and augmented reality support; most provide drag-and-drop graphical user interfaces, so it does not require prior knowledge of another tool or programming.
  Q How does the Wikitude augmented reality browser app support mobile prototyping when the mobile device is mainly treated as a rendering device?  [22/S0/F3, 22/S0/F4, 22/S0/F5; Wikitude augmented reality browser app, mobile device, backend server, mobile prototyping tool]
    A The Wikitude augmented reality browser app runs on mobile devices as a browser application for augmented reality mobile prototyping. It treats the device mainly as a client or rendering device and connects to a backend server for content and specification of user interface elements, so computation may take place on that server. This makes prototyping easier or faster when developers have their own content; without content, default tool content is still usable but less flexible.
  Q Why can low-level software development tools address the limitations of using plugins to add augmented reality support to existing content authoring tools?  [22/S1/F5, 22/S1/F6; plugin to existing tools, low-level software development tool, authoring tool, third-party tool]
    A Plugins can limit user interface and interaction design to what the underlying authoring tool provides, can make software and hardware configuration depend on that tool, and usually make content dependent on proprietary player software. Low-level software development tools such as software libraries provide a way to resolve these limitations by letting developers build the system from scratch rather than depending on a third-party tool.
  judge round 1: 0 of 3 failed
    1 pass  (Why are plugins to existing tools useful mainly when the developer already knows the …)
      check: Plugins rely on a host authoring tool for content authoring, so they are easy and quick mainly for developers already knowing that tool, whereas standalone tools are complete, non-dependent packages with drag-and-drop interfaces that non-programmers can use.
      reason: Facts 7 and 8 state that plugins depend on an existing authoring tool and are easy only when that host tool is already known. Facts 15 and 17 state that standalone tools are complete packages that do not depend on another tool and often let non-programmers create AR experiences by drag-and-drop.
    2 pass  (How does the Wikitude augmented reality browser app support mobile prototyping when the mobile …)
      check: It supports mobile prototyping by running as a mobile AR browser app while the phone acts mainly as client/renderer, connecting to backend servers for content and UI specification and possibly computation, making prototyping easier or faster with own content and still usable with default content.
      reason: Fact 4 identifies Wikitude as a mobile AR browser prototyping tool, and fact 5 explains the client/renderer role with backend servers for content, UI specification, and possible computation. Fact 6 supplies the prototyping benefit and the own-content versus default-content condition.
    3 pass  (Why can low-level software development tools address the limitations of using plugins to add …)
      check: Low-level tools such as software libraries can resolve plugin limitations because they let developers build the system from scratch instead of depending on a third-party authoring tool that constrains UI, interaction, configuration, and proprietary player content.
      reason: Fact 12 gives the limitations of plugin-based AR support: constrained UI/interaction, dependence of software/hardware configuration on the authoring tool, and usual dependence on proprietary player software. Fact 13 gives the resolving link: low-level software development tools let developers build from scratch rather than depend on a third-party tool.

===== lecture 23: XR as Interactive Systems

23/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (3 facts, 1 concepts)
  What is presence? (lecture 8) -> Presence is a subjective psychological state in which an experience generated by human-made technology is perceived as real, because the user fails to acknowledge the technology's role and perceives computer-generated stimuli as coming from the real world.

23/A1  quiz  23/S0  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 13 concepts)
  Q Which broader category includes extended reality systems?  [23/S0/F0]
    - Augmented reality systems
    * Interactive systems
    - Virtual reality systems
    - Non-immersive virtual reality systems
    because: Extended reality systems are treated as part of the broad class of interactive systems. Virtual reality and augmented reality are areas within extended reality, not broader containers for it.
  Q What outcome does the disappearing-technology ideal aim for in an extended reality system?  [23/S0/F2, 23/S0/F3]
    - The user feels like dealing with technical system state
    - The user feels like dealing with a specialized technological item
    * The user feels like dealing with an ordinary item
    - The user feels like dealing with a fully rendered virtual environment
    because: The ideal is that the technological aspect should not be apparent, so the user should feel as if using an ordinary item rather than a specialized product. Feeling that one is dealing with a specialized technological item is the opposite of the ideal.
  Q In the development trend for popular computing products, what is true of the computers around the user?  [23/S0/F4, 23/S0/F5]
    - They are room-sized machines accessible to a few select people
    - They are operated one at a time by the user
    * They communicate without separate user operation
    - They are programmed by the user reconnecting wires
    because: Modern popular computing products represent a trend in which users are surrounded by connected computers that can communicate without being separately operated. The wire-reconnecting, one-at-a-time, and room-sized machine descriptions belong to earlier computing, not the current trend.

23/A2  recap  23/S0  "Recap"  (6 facts, 13 concepts)
  Extended reality systems are a kind of interactive system, and the goal is that the user should not notice a specialized technological product. Mark Weiser's claim that the most profound technologies disappear expresses this goal, and it is equated with presence. Computing history points the same way, moving from large specialist machines to IoT or ubiquitous computing, where connected devices can communicate without separate user operation.
  - Extended reality systems are a kind of interactive system.
  - Mark Weiser's claim that the most profound technologies disappear, equated with presence, means technology should not seem specialized.
  - Computer systems have moved from large specialist machines to IoT or ubiquitous computing, moving toward disappearing technology.

23/A3  quiz  23/S1  "Quick quiz"  (4 facts, 8 concepts)
  Q What best describes an interactive computing system?  [23/S1/F0]
    - A system in which the computer performs tasks by itself
    * A system in which the computer and user exchange actions
    - A system in which the user reads the source code
    - A system in which the hardware processes data internally
    because: An interactive system is defined by interaction between the system and the user. Options without user-system interaction describe one-sided or non-interactive processes.
  Q What characterizes a typical lay user of an interactive system?  [23/S1/F1]
    - A person who wants to maintain it rather than understand how it works
    - A person who wants to design it rather than understand how it works
    - A person who wants to program it rather than understand how it works
    * A person who wants to use it rather than understand how it works
    because: A lay user is not necessarily a technology expert and wants to use the system rather than understand how it works. Maintaining, designing, or programming the system are not the defining aims of a lay user.
  Q With a hexadecimal status code in an error message, what is a lay end user generally not expected to do?  [23/S1/F2]
    - Copy it or send it
    - Read it aloud or memorize it
    * Understand it or act on it
    - Change it or hide it
    because: A hexadecimal status code is generally incomprehensible to a layperson, so the user should not be expected to understand it or act on it. Copying, reading aloud, changing, or hiding a code are actions a layperson could still perform; the problem is comprehension and taking informed action.
  Q What design rule follows for interactive systems intended to be used by laypersons?  [23/S1/F4]
    - Do not force users to maintain the underlying technology
    - Do not force users to pay for the underlying technology
    - Do not force users to install the underlying technology
    * Do not force users to learn the underlying technology
    because: Designers should not require lay users to learn the underlying technology or understand technical terms. Installation, maintenance, and payment are different practical concerns, not the learning burden the rule targets.

23/A4  recap  23/S1  "Recap"  (5 facts, 8 concepts)
  Interactive systems place a non-expert in direct interaction with the system, and that user wants results rather than technical understanding. When error messages use technical terms or codes, the user may not grasp the problem and may become anxious or stop using the system. This makes it a design requirement to keep the system usable without making the user learn its underlying technology.
  - Interactive systems are systems in which interaction takes place between the system and the user.
  - In interactive systems, the user is a lay user who wants to use the system rather than understand it.
  - Technical terms and hexadecimal status codes in error messages are generally incomprehensible to laypersons.
  - Incomprehensible technical error messages can make lay users anxious, unsure, and less willing to use the system further.
  - Designers of interactive systems for laypersons should not force users to learn the underlying technology or technical terms.

23/A6  recap  23/S2  "Recap"  (2 facts, 9 concepts)
  User-centric design, generally recommended for interactive computer systems, starts with users' characteristics, needs, and expectations. That understanding guides acceptable interface elements, layouts, the user's view of system state, and interactions that help users move from one state to a goal state.
  - The user-centric approach starts by understanding users' characteristics, needs, and expectations before designing computer systems.
  - User-centric systems use acceptable elements, expected layouts, states from users' viewpoints, and interactions that move users to goal states.
