23/A7  quiz  23/S3  "Quick quiz"  (2 facts, 2 concepts)
  Q What is the scope of HCI for interactive computing systems?  [23/S3/F0]
    - Their design, evaluation, and implementation as hardware products
    - Their design, evaluation, and implementation as display interfaces
    * Their design, evaluation, and implementation for human use
    - Their design, evaluation, and implementation as software components
    because: HCI is concerned with interactive computing systems as systems for human use, not merely with their hardware, display, or software parts. The tempting option about display interfaces is too narrow because the definition covers the whole system's design, evaluation, and implementation.
  Q What does HCI study, beyond design, evaluation, and implementation?  [23/S3/F0]
    - Major users around interactive computing systems
    * Major phenomena surrounding interactive computing systems
    - Major interfaces around interactive computing systems
    - Major hardware around interactive computing systems
    because: The definition of HCI includes studying the major phenomena that surround interactive computing systems. Users and interfaces are relevant to the field, but the stated scope is phenomena surrounding the systems, not the systems' users, interfaces, or hardware as separate objects of study.
  Q What sequence does the core concern of HCI require?  [23/S3/F2]
    - Testing hardware first, then incorporating hardware characteristics
    * Understanding users first, then incorporating user characteristics
    - Evaluating systems first, then incorporating system characteristics
    - Implementing software first, then incorporating software characteristics
    because: The core concern of HCI is incorporating humans into design, which means designers must first understand users and then bring user characteristics into the design. Options that start with evaluating, implementing, or testing put the system or technology before the users.

23/A16  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (11 facts, 17 concepts)
  Q Why should an extended reality system be designed so that the technological aspect surrounding the user disappears from the user's perception?  [23/S0/F0, 23/S0/F3, 23/S1/F1, 23/S1/F4, 8/S2/F1; extended reality system, disappearing technology, presence, lay person]
    A This design realizes presence, in which part or all of the individual's perception fails to accurately acknowledge the role of the technology. Disappearing technology is the same thing: the technological aspect surrounding the user should not be apparent. Since extended reality systems are interactive systems used by lay persons who want to use the system rather than understand it, designers should not force users to learn the underlying technology.
  Q Why can a traveler and a database administrator who both obtain railway ticket information need different interfaces in an interactive system?  [23/S2/F0, 23/S4/F0; user-centric approach, user characteristic, human factors, interface]
    A A user-centric approach begins by understanding user characteristics, what users need and expect, and then designing from that. Human factors in system design requires knowing those characteristics because users performing the same broad task can have different expectations, needs, and query-language skills. Those differences mean they require different interfaces for providing input, seeing the outcome, and acting on the outcome.
  Q Why can an error message containing an event log term or a hexadecimal status code reduce a lay person's motivation to keep using an interactive system?  [23/S1/F1, 23/S1/F2, 23/S1/F3; interactive system, lay person, error message]
    A In an interactive system, the user is a lay person who wants to use the system rather than understand it. An event log term is not expected to be understood by such a user, and a hexadecimal status code is generally incomprehensible. A jargon error message can make the user anxious, leave the user not knowing how to get out, and may lead the user to refrain from further use and lose motivation.
  Q Why is human-computer interaction a discipline concerned with extended reality systems?  [23/S0/F0, 23/S1/F0, 23/S3/F0; extended reality system, interactive system, human-computer interaction]
    A Extended reality systems are interactive systems because interaction takes place between the system and the user. Human-computer interaction is a discipline concerned with the design, evaluation, and implementation of interactive computing systems for human use, and with the study of major phenomena surrounding interactive computing systems. Therefore HCI covers extended reality systems.

===== lecture 24: XR as Interactive Systems

24/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (15 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is middleware? (lecture 19) -> Middleware is software that sits between hardware and higher-level application software, abstracts hardware functionalities for developers, and supports the development and rendering of extended reality (XR) experiences.
  What is human factors? (lecture 23) -> Human factors is the system-design consideration that requires knowing users’ differing expectations, needs, skills, and how they perceive stimuli, so that suitable input and output can be designed.
  What is interactive system? (lecture 23) -> Interactive system is a system in which interaction takes place between the computer or system and the user, a lay person who is not necessarily a technology expert and who wants to use the system rather than understand how it works.
  What is user-centric approach? (lecture 23) -> A user-centric approach is the process of designing computer systems in which users' needs and expectations are taken care of by considering user characteristics, starting with understanding those characteristics, needs, and expectations, then designing the system on that basis.
  What is augmented reality (AR)? (lecture 1) -> Augmented reality (AR) is an enhanced version of reality created by technology, in which computer-generated digital content is overlaid on the real world in real time and registered in 3D, so the user perceives and interacts with the enhanced environment.
  What is virtual reality (VR)? (lecture 4) -> Virtual reality (VR) is an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli provided by a computer, in which a person's actions partially determine what happens and which replaces the user's sense of reality without requiring the physical existence of objects or places.

24/A1  quiz  24/S0  "Quick quiz"  (7 facts, 12 concepts)
  Q In what way does the novice, intermittent, and expert categorization reduce reliance on initial field studies?  [24/S0/F0, 24/S0/F3, 24/S0/F6]
    * It gives designers a broad starting point for design decisions
    - It gives designers an exact, fine-grained user profile for design decisions
    - It gives designers a final, permanent user specification for design decisions
    - It gives designers a complete set of empirical findings for design decisions
    because: The three user classes are a broad early basis for design decisions. They are useful when design starts, but they are not an exact or final replacement for empirical user studies.
  Q What does the expert user class refer to in the novice, intermittent, and expert classification?  [24/S0/F2]
    - A person who is expert in testing that system
    * A person who is expert in using that system
    - A person who is expert in building that system
    - A person who is expert in the technology behind that system
    because: An expert user is expert in using the system efficiently. The term does not mean that the person is a technology expert or that they build or test the system.
  Q In the three-class user model, what distinguishes an intermittent user from an expert user?  [24/S0/F1]
    - First-time use versus occasional use
    * Occasional use versus regular long-term use
    - Occasional use versus regular short-term use
    - First-time use versus regular long-term use
    because: An intermittent user uses the system occasionally, while an expert user uses it regularly over a long period. First-time use describes a novice user.
  Q For a novice user saving a file, what makes a menu option more suitable than a hotkey option?  [24/S0/F4, 24/S0/F5]
    * Difficulty remembering the hotkey option
    - Easier recall of the hotkey option
    - Faster execution of the menu option
    - Greater familiarity with the hotkey option
    because: A menu option can be more suitable for first-time users because remembering hotkey combinations is generally difficult for them. The menu option is not faster than the hotkey option.
  judge round 1: 0 of 4 failed

24/A2  recap  24/S0  "Recap"  (7 facts, 12 concepts)
  Interactive-system design can use a practical shortcut for understanding users: a broad novice, intermittent, and expert classification. Because field studies are costly, designers can begin from that classification. It helps make early design decisions by recognizing likely differences in user behavior, for example in choosing menu or hotkey support. It remains a starting point, not a replacement for more detailed empirical studies.
  - Field studies are time-consuming and laborious, so designers can use the novice, intermittent, and expert categorization.
  - The classes are novice first-time users, intermittent occasional users, and expert long-term, efficient system users, not technology experts.
  - Because user classes behave differently, these classes give designers a starting point for broad interactive-system design decisions.
  - Applications can offer slower menu and faster hotkey options, matching menu to novices and hotkeys to intermittent and expert users.
  - This categorization is broad and useful at design start, though finer empirical studies can produce better user categorizations.

24/A6  recap  24/S2  "Recap"  (4 facts, 6 concepts)
  Usability gives an explicit user-based way to judge how good a system is. The ISO definition bounds that judgment by specifying the users, the goals, and the context of use. Within those bounds, effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction measure whether users can achieve what they want, how fast they can do it, and how satisfied they are.
  - Usability is an explicit measure of how good a system is from the user's point of view.
  - ISO usability is the extent specified users can use a product to achieve specified goals in a specified context.
  - Usability is measured by effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction: whether users succeed, how fast, and how satisfied.

24/A8  recap  24/S3  "Recap"  (5 facts, 12 concepts)
  User-centered design is a user-centric approach that involves users in a design or development lifecycle used to build usable software. Ben Shneiderman coined the term in 1986 for graphical user interfaces, and its objective is to create usable systems that meet lay users’ needs and expectations. Cooperative, participatory, contextual, and human-centered design are related terms for taking users into design, with ISO preferring human-centered design.
  - User-centered design applies a user-centric approach and involves users in a design or development lifecycle to build usable software.
  - Ben Shneiderman coined user-centered design in 1986 for graphical user interfaces.
  - User-centered design aims to design usable systems that meet lay users’ needs and expectations.
  - Cooperative, participatory, contextual, and human-centered design are related terms for taking users into design; ISO prefers human-centered over user-centered design.

24/A11  recap  24/S4  "Recap"  (7 facts, 25 concepts)
  XR is treated as an interactive system because users act on and receive feedback from a virtual environment. Hardware, the XR engine, and the application layer track user actions, render the environment, and stimulate the senses, so software and hardware together shape the user–environment relationship. Because this relationship depends on how users give input and perceive output, user-centered design is needed for both interaction and perception.
  - User-centered software development involves users actively or passively in the chosen software development lifecycle.
  - XR systems are highly interactive, making human factors important for how easily users provide input and perceive output.
  - XR software’s core concern is creating a relationship between the user and virtual environment, with software and hardware both important.
  - XR system components (hardware, XR engine, application) track user input, render the environment, and stimulate the senses through output devices.
  - User-centered design shapes XR input interaction and output perception so users can provide input and perceive output easily.
  judge round 1: 3 of 6 failed

      reason: The point is a shortened paraphrase of fact [1]: user-centered software development involves users, actively or passively, in the chosen development lifecycle.
    2 FAIL supported,faithful  (XR systems are highly interactive, making human factors important for how easily users provide …)
      check: consideration of human factors is important to understand [2]
      reason: The point adds a causal link with “making” and shifts the claim from “consideration of human factors is important to understand how easily” to “human factors important for how easily users provide input and perceive output.” A repaired version would say: XR systems are highly interactive, and considering human factors is important to understand how easily users provide input and perceive output.
    3 pass  (XR software’s core concern is creating a relationship between the user and virtual environment …)
      check: none
      reason: The point faithfully paraphrases fact [3]: the core concern of XR software is creating a user–virtual environment relationship, and both software and hardware are important in building it.
    4 FAIL supported,faithful  (XR system components (hardware, XR engine, application) track user input, render the environment, and …)
      check: hardware, the middleware that is the XR engine, and the application layer [4]; the user's actions and positions are tracked by input devices and sent as input data; the input data is processed and the environment is rendered; output devices stimulate the user's senses [5]
      reason: The point makes all listed components jointly “track user input, render the environment, and stimulate the senses,” but the facts assign tracking to input devices, rendering to the processing of input data, and sense stimulation to output devices; it also says “track user input” rather than tracking the user’s actions and positions and sending input data. 24/A17  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (9 facts, 22 concepts)
  Q Why can interactive-system designers start from the novice, intermittent, and expert user categorization rather than always conducting field studies?  [24/S0/F0, 24/S0/F3, 24/S0/F6; field study, novice, intermittent, and expert user categorization, interactive-system design]
    A Field studies are typically needed to understand users, but they are time-consuming, laborious, and require elaborate setup and planning, so designers can rely on the categorization as a starting point. Users in the novice, intermittent, and expert classes are likely to behave differently, which lets designers make broad interactive-system design decisions. The categorization is broad, but it is useful when the design process starts, while finer empirical categorizations are possible.
  Q How does user-centered design guide both input and output design in an extended reality system?  [24/S4/F1, 24/S4/F5, 24/S4/F6; user-centered design, extended reality system, interaction design, perceptual design]
    A Because an extended reality system is highly interactive, human factors are important for understanding how easily a user can provide input and perceive output. User-centered interaction design and user input modeling let the user provide input data seamlessly, effectively, and easily. Perceptual design and output modeling also require a user-centered approach because output stimuli must match the user's perception, so the user can perceive and understand the output.
  Q How does the International Standards Organization 9241-210-2009 definition connect a product's specified users, goals, and context of use with its usability measures?  [24/S2/F1, 24/S2/F2, 24/S2/F3; usability, context of use, effectiveness, efficiency]
    A It defines usability as the extent to which specified users achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction in a specified context of use. A usable product is therefore intended for a specified group of users, supports a specified set of goals, and is designed for a specified context of use. Effectiveness is whether the user can do what they want, efficiency is how fast, and satisfaction is how satisfied the user is.
  judge round 1: 1 of 3 failed

      reason: The reference answer's first sentence says “Because an extended reality system is highly interactive, human factors are important,” but fact 20 only states that XR systems “are highly interactive … and consideration of human factors is important,” without the causal “because.” A repaired reference answer should omit the causal or restate fact 20 without asserting that high interactivity is the reason human factors matter.
    3 pass  (How does the International Standards Organization 9241-210-2009 definition connect a product's specified users, goals …)

===== lecture 25: Human Factors in XR

25/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (15 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is usability? (lecture 24) -> Usability is an explicit measure of how good a system is from the point of view of the user: the extent to which a product can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction in a specified context of use.
  What is extended reality system? (lecture 24) -> An extended reality system is an interactive system that comprises hardware, an XR engine as middleware, and the application layer, in which input devices track the user's actions and positions, send them as input data, the data is processed to render an environment, and output devices stimulate the user's senses.
  What is extended reality (XR)? (lecture 1) -> Extended reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR).
  What is augmented reality (AR)? (lecture 1) -> Augmented reality (AR) is an enhanced version of reality created by technology, in which computer-generated digital content is overlaid on the real world in real time and registered in 3D, so the user perceives and interacts with the enhanced environment.
  What is mixed reality (MR)? (lecture 1) -> Mixed reality (MR) is an immersive technology that is the same as augmented reality, in which digital content is overlaid on the view of reality and can be interacted with.
  What is immersion? (lecture 2) -> Immersion is the objective, quantifiable degree to which a virtual reality system projects stimuli onto the sensory receptors of users in an extensive, matching, surrounding, vivid, interactive, and plot-informing way.

25/A3  quiz  25/S1  "Quick quiz"  (4 facts, 9 concepts)
  Q What must a VR system do for the user to feel strongly present?  [25/S1/F0]
    - Present sensory signals that are usually consistent with the user's real-life behavior
    - Keep the virtual environment visually simple so the brain can rest
    * Fool the user's perceptual system into accepting the virtual world as real
    - Reduce the user's awareness of the physical display hardware
    because: Presence in VR depends on making the user's perceptual system accept the virtual system as the familiar real world. Consistency with real-life behavior is not the basis of presence, because VR generally provides inconsistent signals.
  Q What can happen to a user's awareness of system flaws after successful adaptation to inconsistent VR stimulation?  [25/S1/F4]
    - The user may report the flaws to a developer
    - The user may see the flaws as harmless
    * The user may become unaware of the flaws
    - The user may become more aware of the flaws
    because: Successful adaptation to inconsistent VR stimulation can make the user unaware of flaws in the system. Noticing flaws more clearly or reporting them is not the adaptation outcome.
  Q What can happen when a user's body does not adapt to generally inconsistent VR stimulation?  [25/S1/F5]
    - The user may stop noticing flaws and may take the virtual system for the real world
    - The user may feel more relaxed and may become unaware of the display hardware
    * The user may feel increased fatigue or headaches, and may develop cyber sickness
    - The user may remember the virtual environment better and may report less presence
    because: When the body cannot adapt to inconsistent VR stimulation, the result can be increased fatigue or headaches, and this non-adaptation may lead to cyber sickness such as dizziness or nausea. Taking the virtual system for the real world is an effect of adaptation, not of non-adaptation.

25/A4  recap  25/S1  "Recap"  (7 facts, 13 concepts)
  VR aims to create presence by fooling the user's perceptual system into accepting the virtual world as real. Human perception is formed from evolved physiology and stored experience, while VR generally supplies sensory signals inconsistent with real-life experience and behavior. That inconsistency can lead either to adaptation, where the user accepts the virtual system as real, or to non-adaptation, which may cause cybersickness. These risks motivate studying human perception to design better VR systems and resolve flaws in existing ones.
  - VR creates presence by fooling perceptual mechanisms that evolved for the real world through artificial stimulation.
  - Human perception is formed from physiology and experience stored in long-term memory.
  - Virtual reality generally provides sensory signals inconsistent with the user's real-life experiences and behavior.
  - Inconsistent VR stimulation can lead to accepting the virtual as real or to non-adaptation, causing cybersickness.
  - Understanding human perception is needed to design better VR systems or identify and resolve flaws in them.

  - Perceptual psychology requires knowledge of human physiology, theories from experimental perceptual psychology, and XR interference with common perceptual processes.

25/A8  recap  25/S3  "Recap"  (3 facts, 32 concepts)
  The term sensor connects machine systems and the human body by separating device sensors from human bodily sensors. Stimulus, receptor, and sense organ form the common scheme for organizing the six human senses. This scheme marks balance as unusual, because it has no specific organ, even though vestibular organs act as sense organs for it.
  - A device sensor converts energy into electrical signals; a human bodily sensor converts stimuli into neural impulses.
  - Vision, auditory, touch, balance, taste, and smell are classified by stimulus, receptor, and sense organ.
  - Balance has no specific organ unlike the other five senses, though vestibular organs act as sense organs.

25/A10  recap  25/S4  "Recap"  (6 facts, 23 concepts)
  Sensory system selectivity means that receptors in a sense organ respond only to a particular type of stimulus. Different senses are therefore built from different receptors: photoreceptors detect visible light, mechanoreceptors detect motion, vibration, or gravitational force, thermoreceptors detect temperature, and chemoreceptors detect chemical composition. This organizes the senses by the stimulus each receptor responds to.
  - Sensory system selectivity means sense-organ receptors target particular stimuli and activate only to a specific stimulus.
  - The eyes contain photoreceptors, which activate only to electromagnetic energy in the visible-light frequency range.
  - Auditory, touch, and balance use mechanoreceptors for motion, vibration, or gravitational force; touch adds thermoreceptors, balance: head and upward direction.
  - Taste and smell rely on chemoreceptors that signal based on chemical composition, in the tongue and nasal passage.
  judge round 1: 2 of 5 failed
    1 pass  (Sensory system selectivity means sense-organ receptors target particular stimuli and activate only to a …)
      check: none
      reason: The point paraphrases the definition in fact 1: sensory selectivity means receptors in a sense organ target particular stimuli and are activated only for a specific stimulus type.
    2 pass  (The eyes contain photoreceptors, which activate only to electromagnetic energy in the visible-light frequency …)
      check: none
      reason: Fact 2 carries the point: the eyes contain photoreceptors tied to electromagnetic energy in the visible-light frequency range, so they target only visible light.
    3 FAIL faithful,stands_alone,clear,one_idea  (Auditory, touch, and balance use mechanoreceptors for motion, vibration, or gravitational force; touch adds …)
      check: balance: head and upward direction [5]
      reason: The point is not standalone or grammatical because “Auditory” is not named as a sense, and “balance: head and upward direction” drops fact 5’s meaning that balance helps know which way the head is oriented. It also packs three separate ideas into one point: mechanoreceptors for three senses, touch’s thermoreceptors, and balance orientation. A repaired version should be one full sentence about one idea, for example: “The auditory, touch, and balance senses use mechanoreceptors that sense motion, vibration, or gravitational force.”
    4 pass  (Taste and smell rely on chemoreceptors that signal based on chemical composition, in the …)
      check: none
      reason: Fact 6 carries the point: taste and smell rely on chemoreceptors whose signals depend on chemical composition, associated with the tongue and nasal passage.
    0 FAIL faithful  (Sensory system selectivity means that receptors in a sense organ respond only to a …)
      check: thermoreceptors detect temperature [4]
      reason: The text changes fact 4 by saying “thermoreceptors detect temperature,” while the fact says they “detect changes in temperature”; the repaired text should say “thermoreceptors detect changes in temperature.” Its second sentence also uses a causal “therefore” that the facts do not state, but the main repair is to make the receptor list faithful and avoid adding that cause.
  judge kept: original; still failing: [3, 0]

25/A11  quiz  25/S5  "Quick quiz"  (3 facts, 6 concepts)
  Q What part of perceptual psychology deals with the body's sensing mechanisms?  [25/S5/F1]
    - the psychology of presence
    * the physiology of the senses
    - the perception of sensory signals
    - the study of user characteristics
    because: The physiology of the senses is the part of perceptual psychology concerned with the body's sensing mechanisms. Perception, presence, and user characteristics are related human-factor topics, but they are not the physiological part of perceptual psychology.
  Q For each of the six senses, what are receptors part of?  [25/S5/F3]
    - the perceptual process
    - the sensory stimuli
    * the sensory organs
    - the neural impulses
    because: For each sense, receptors are part of the sensory organ that receives the relevant stimuli. The perceptual process, stimuli, and neural impulses are related to sensing, but receptors are not part of them.
  Q In the human body, what are sensory organs considered to be?  [25/S5/F5]
    * the hardware of sensing
    - the perception of sensing
    - the output of sensing
    - the software of sensing
    because: Sensory organs are the hardware of sensing in the human body. The other options invert the hardware metaphor or confuse sensing with later perceptual or system output.

25/A12  recap  25/S5  "Recap"  (6 facts, 17 concepts)
  Perceptual psychology provides the needed background for human factors in XR systems, with sensory physiology as one of its parts. The six senses are considered, and each sense is linked to sensory organs whose receptors receive stimuli depending on the organ. Those sensory organs form the human body’s hardware of sensing, and their receptor types include photoreceptors, chemoreceptors, and mechanoreceptors.
  - Some knowledge of perceptual psychology, including sensory physiology, is needed to understand human factors in XR systems.
  - The six senses are vision, auditory, balance, taste, smell, and touch.
  - For each sense, receptors in its sensory organs receive stimuli depending on that sensory organ.
  - Different types of receptors include photoreceptors, chemoreceptors, and mechanoreceptors.
  - In the human body, sensory organs are the hardware of sensing.

      check: none

      check: none

25/A18  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (8 facts, 24 concepts)
  Q How do interaction design and perceptual design together support usability in an extended reality system?  [25/S0/F0, 24/S2/F1; interaction design, perceptual design, usability]
    A Interaction design supports usability by making the user's input easier to perform, while perceptual design supports it by making the system's output appropriately sensed and understood. Together they help specified users achieve their goals with effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction.
  Q How can generally inconsistent sensory stimulation in virtual reality lead to presence in one case and cybersickness in another?  [25/S1/F0, 25/S1/F3, 25/S1/F4, 25/S1/F5; virtual reality, sensory input, presence, cybersickness]
    A Virtual reality often supplies the brain with sensory signals that do not match real-life experience, and the body may either adapt or not. If it adapts, the user can stop noticing flaws and may believe the virtual system is real, supporting presence. If it does not adapt, the mismatch can cause fatigue, headaches, dizziness, nausea, or other cybersickness symptoms.
  Q Why is creating a convincing illusion of reality more crucial for virtual reality than for augmented or mixed reality?  [25/S0/F1, 25/S0/F2, 25/S1/F0; virtual reality, augmented reality, mixed reality, illusion of reality]
    A Virtual reality needs the illusion more because it aims for total immersion in a virtual environment, while augmented and mixed reality leave the real world available and are only partly immersive. XR interaction and output are designed to create such an illusion to enhance presence. Therefore, presence in virtual reality depends on fooling the perceptual system into accepting the virtual system as real.
  judge round 1: 0 of 3 failed
    1 pass  (How do interaction design and perceptual design together support usability in an extended reality …)
      check: In an XR system, interaction design supports usability by making input easier to interact with, and perceptual design supports it by making output appropriately sensed and understood, where usability means specified users can achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction.
      reason: Fact 1 supplies the input/output roles of interaction and perceptual design, and fact 31 supplies the usability components used in the final sentence.
    2 pass  (How can generally inconsistent sensory stimulation in virtual reality lead to presence in one …)
      check: Generally inconsistent VR sensory stimulation can lead to presence when the body adapts and the user comes to believe the virtual system is real, and it can lead to cybersickness when the body does not adapt, causing fatigue, headaches, dizziness, nausea, or other symptoms.
      reason: Fact 7 states the inconsistent stimulation, fact 8 links adaptation to belief in reality, fact 4 links that belief to presence, and fact 9 links non-adaptation to cybersickness symptoms.
    3 pass  (Why is creating a convincing illusion of reality more crucial for virtual reality than …)
      check: The illusion is more crucial for VR because VR aims for total immersion in a virtual environment, whereas AR and MR have only partial immersion and leave the real world viewable or experienced; XR interaction and output create the illusion to enhance presence, and VR presence depends on fooling the perceptual system into accepting the virtual system as real.
      reason: Fact 3 gives the comparison between VR and AR/MR, fact 2 gives the purpose of the illusion, and fact 4 explains the dependence of VR presence on perceptual belief.

===== lecture 26: Human Factors in XR

26/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (20 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is presence? (lecture 8) -> Presence is a subjective psychological state in which an experience generated by human-made technology is perceived as real, because the user fails to acknowledge the technology's role and perceives computer-generated stimuli as coming from the real world.
  What is cybersickness (CS)? (lecture 10) -> Cybersickness (CS) is a condition primarily relevant to virtual reality that may be caused by multiple internal and external factors and in which a user may experience symptoms such as nausea, dizziness, headache, or disorientation.
  What is point of interest (POIs)? (lecture 21) -> Point of interest (POI) is a significant spot in a virtual tour, modeled as a graph node or vertex with importance and a maximum waiting time, that need not be a physical object and is visited to inspect or interact with objects.
  What is sensory organ? (lecture 25) -> A sensory organ is hardware of sensing in the human body that contains receptors that receive stimuli and is designed to perceive the real world rather than a virtual world.
  What is smell? (lecture 25) -> Smell is a human chemical sense in which chemoreceptors in the nasal passage work by chemical reaction with specific molecules or chemical stimuli at appropriate concentrations.
  What is receptor? (lecture 25) -> A receptor is a bodily sensor that is part of a sense organ, targets particular stimuli, and is activated only when a specific type of stimulus arrives. Types include photoreceptors, chemoreceptors, mechanoreceptors, and thermoreceptors.

    - The axon terminals
    - The dendrites
    - The neuron cell bodies
    * The cerebral cortex
    because: The cerebral cortex is the part of the brain responsible for perception and other functions such as attention, memory, language, and consciousness. Neuron cell bodies, dendrites, and axon terminals are parts of individual neurons rather than that named brain region.
  Q Why is the cerebral cortex heavily folded?  [26/S0/F2]
    * To fit into the skull
    - To combine sensory input with long-term memory
    - To convert stimuli into neural impulses
    - To generate virtual stimuli for the user
    because: The cerebral cortex is a heavily folded sheet of neurons so that it can fit into the skull. Its folding is not the means by which it converts stimuli, combines sensory input with memory, or generates virtual stimuli.

26/A3  quiz  26/S1  "Quick quiz"  (3 facts, 17 concepts)
  Q In the directed-graph analogy for neuron interconnection, how are the cell body, dendrites, and axons represented?  [26/S1/F2]
    * Cell bodies are nodes, dendrites are input edges, and axons are output edges
    - Dendrites are nodes, cell bodies are input edges, and axons are output edges
    - Cell bodies are nodes, dendrites are output edges, and axons are input edges
    - Axons are nodes, cell bodies are output edges, and dendrites are input edges
    because: The cell body is the node that processes input, dendrites carry impulses toward it, and axons carry impulses away from it. Reversing input and output edges misreads the direction of signaling.
  Q How does a signal pass from the axon of one neuron to the dendrite of the next neuron?  [26/S1/F4]
    - Across a direct junction with physical contact
    - Across a continuous fiber with electrical contact
    * Across a synapse without physical contact
    - Across a shared terminal with physical contact
    because: An axon of one neuron is paired with a dendrite of the next, but they are not physically connected; the synapse is the gap across which electrical or chemical signals pass.
  Q What does a neuron do with information it receives from other neurons in the brain's network?  [26/S1/F3]
    - It can aggregate information from other neurons and pass the same information to other neurons
    - It can aggregate raw sensory information and pass unchanged information to other neurons
    - It can receive already aggregated information and pass lower-level information to other neurons
    * It can aggregate already aggregated information and pass processed information to other neurons
    because: A neuron can receive information that has already been aggregated by other neurons, process it in the cell body, and transmit that processing to other neurons. It is not merely a relay of unchanged or lower-level signals.

26/A4  recap  26/S1  "Recap"  (6 facts, 24 concepts)
  The biological basis of perception rests on how neurons are connected. Each neuron receives information through dendrites, processes it in its cell body, and passes it onward through axons, while synapses transmit signals between neurons. The large number of synaptic connections in the human brain shows the scale of the network that supports perception and cognition.
  - Perception and overall cognitive ability depend on the interconnection of neurons.
  - A neuron has a nucleus or cell body, dendrites, an axon, axon branches, and axon terminals.
  - Neuron interconnections form a directed network: dendrites carry aggregated inputs to the cell body, and axons send processed outputs onward.
  - An axon and a dendrite are paired but not connected; signals cross the synapse gap electrically or chemically.
  - The human brain's neuron graph has about 10^15 edges because each neuron averages about 7,000 synapses.

26/A7  quiz  26/S3  "Quick quiz"  (3 facts, 11 concepts)
  Q When interpreting a stimulus, what does the cerebral cortex combine with real-time sensory input?  [26/S3/F0]
    - Aggregation performed by hierarchical processing
    - A efference copy from the motor cortex
    - Selectivity of the relevant sense organ
    * Stored life experience from long-term memory
    because: Interpretation is not produced by sensory input alone; it uses real-time sensory input together with life experience stored in long-term memory. Sense-organ selectivity and hierarchical aggregation operate on incoming signals, while efference copies relate to body-motion information rather than general stimulus interpretation.

    - The type of receptor selectivity
    * The amount of long-term experience
    - The number of activated sense organs
    - The amount of proprioceptive feedback
    because: A person's interpretation of a stimulus depends on their long-term experience, so a person with little experience and a person with much experience can interpret the same stimulus very differently. The number of activated sense organs, receptor selectivity, and proprioceptive feedback are not the reason given for this difference.

    - Neuron aggregation and transmission of neural signals across synapses in the cortex
    - Receptor selectivity and activation of the particular sense organs involved
    because: Overall perceptual processing results from hierarchical neural processing and from combining real-time sensory input with long-term knowledge or experience. The other options name earlier sensing steps, general neural transmission, or body-motion signals, not the two components identified for overall perceptual processing.

26/A8  recap  26/S3  "Recap"  (3 facts, 11 concepts)
  Perception is formed after sensory signals reach the cerebral cortex. The brain does not rely on sensory input alone; it combines that input with long-term memory or experience. Because this combination depends on each person's experience, different people can interpret the same stimulus differently, and overall perceptual processing is hierarchical as it produces interpretation.
  - In the cerebral cortex, perceptual interpretation combines real-time sensory input with long-term memory, not input alone.
  - Interpretation depends on the interpreter's long-term experience, so people with different experience can interpret a stimulus differently.
  - Overall perceptual processing is an outcome of hierarchical processing and combining real-time input with long-term knowledge.

26/A10  recap  26/S4  "Recap"  (2 facts, 13 concepts)
  Proprioception is introduced as a sixth sense that detects relative body-part positions and the muscular effort used to move them, without a direct sensory organ. This ability is supported by motor-cortex signals called efference copies. Those copies report executed motions to other brain areas, where processing yields a sense of relative body position and muscular effort.
  - Proprioception is the ability to sense relative body-part positions and muscular effort, without a direct sensory organ.
  - The motor cortex sends efference copies of executed motions that are processed to sense relative body positions and muscular effort.

26/A11  quiz  26/S5  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 13 concepts)
  Q Why can a new immersive VR input conflict with familiar perception?  [26/S5/F1]
    * The brain cannot retune its learned sensory processing in a short time
    - The user cannot align the headset with the room in a short time
    - The visual display cannot keep the rendered image stable in a short time
    - The balance sense cannot detect the virtual movement in a short time
    because: Perception relies on long-learned sensory patterns, and an immersive VR input can create a mismatch because the brain cannot quickly retune that learned processing.
  Q Which signal pattern creates the vection illusion of self-motion?  [26/S5/F4]
    - Auditory input reports movement while the balance sense reports no motion
    * Visual input reports movement while the balance sense reports no motion
    - Visual input reports stillness while the balance sense reports no motion
    - Proprioception reports movement while the balance sense reports no motion
    because: Vection occurs when visual cues indicate motion or acceleration while the balance sense or proprioception indicates that the body is stationary. The other patterns either remove the visual motion cue or put the motion report in a different sense.
  Q What physical response can follow a sensory mismatch in VR for a user who does not adapt?  [26/S5/F2]
    - Conscious recognition that the scene is artificial appearing in the user
    - Automatic retuning of learned sensory processing appearing in the user
    - Stabilization of the balance sense against the visual flow appearing in the user
    * Fatigue, dizziness, or nausea appearing in the user
    because: When a VR mismatch is not adapted away, it can produce cybersickness symptoms such as fatigue, headache, dizziness, and nausea. Conscious recognition of artificiality is a presence-related effect, not the described physical cybersickness response.
  Q How can a sensory mismatch weaken a user's sense of presence in VR?  [26/S5/F3]
    - It makes the user's attention move away from the virtual scene
    - It makes the user's visual system ignore the virtual details for a time
    - It makes the user's balance system stop reporting any body position
    * It makes the user consciously aware that the experience is artificial
    because: A mismatch can reduce presence by making the user consciously aware that the sensory inputs are not in the familiar, natural relationship, so the experience is recognized as artificial.
  Q What design response follows from the need to manage sensory conflict in XR?  [26/S5/F5]
    * Balance the experiences offered by the different senses so the brain processes them as intended
    - Reduce the number of active channels until one sense dominates the experience
    - Amplify the strongest channel until the brain stops noticing the others
    - Give the visual channel priority over the balance sense until the conflict disappears
    because: XR design should balance the experiences presented through the various senses so the brain processes the information in the intended way, rather than prioritizing, reducing, or amplifying a single channel.
  judge round 1: 0 of 5 failed
    1 pass  (Why can a new immersive VR input conflict with familiar perception?)
      check: A
      reason: Fact 2 states that an immersive VR mismatch can occur because “the brain cannot be retuned to process the new inputs in a short span of time,” which directly supports option A. The other options introduce headset alignment, display stability, or balance detection issues not stated by the cited fact.
    2 pass  (Which signal pattern creates the vection illusion of self-motion?)

The other options replace the visual motion cue or assign the motion report to a different sense.
    3 pass  (What physical response can follow a sensory mismatch in VR for a user who …)
      check: D
      reason: Fact 3 says that when a VR mismatch is not insignificant, it “can cause cybersickness, with symptoms such as fatigue, headache, dizziness, and nausea,” so option D is a correct physical response. 26/A12  recap  26/S5  "Recap"  (6 facts, 14 concepts)
  Perception works by combining sensory and proprioceptive signals with long-learned expectations. Immersive VR can create a sensory mismatch because the brain cannot retune quickly, and this mismatch may cause cybersickness or weaken presence by making the experience seem artificial. Vection shows the conflict through visual self-motion while the body remains stationary, so XR design should balance the senses to keep the brain processing the experience as intended.

  - A VR sensory mismatch can compromise presence by exposing the experience as artificial.
  - Vection is an illusion of self-motion caused by visual motion without a matching proprioceptive signal.
  - XR design should balance the senses so the brain processes the experience as intended.

26/A19  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (8 facts, 27 concepts)
  Q Why can a newborn and an aged person interpret the same stimulus differently?  [26/S3/F0, 26/S3/F1; perception, interpretation of a stimulus, long-term memory, sensory input]
    A A newborn and an aged person can interpret the same stimulus differently because perception combines real-time sensory input with long-term memory. In the cerebral cortex, interpretation is not produced by sensory input alone; it is produced by combining sensory input with life experience or knowledge stored in long-term memory. Since the interpreter's long-term experience differs, a person with less experience and a person with long experience can interpret the stimulus very differently.
  Q Why can a sensory mismatch in a virtual reality system cause cybersickness for some users?  [26/S5/F1, 26/S5/F2; virtual reality system, sensory mismatch, cybersickness, sensory processing]
    A A sensory mismatch can cause cybersickness when a user's brain cannot adapt to the new, conflicting inputs. In a virtual reality system, interference with the brain's long-term learned sensory processing can create a mismatch because the brain cannot be retuned quickly. For users who cannot adapt, the resulting conflict can produce symptoms such as fatigue, headache, dizziness, and nausea.
  Q Why does moving in a virtual environment while physically stationary create a sensory conflict?  [26/S5/F4, 26/S4/F0; vection, proprioception, sensory mismatch, visual input]
    A Moving in a virtual environment while physically stationary creates a sensory conflict because visual input and proprioception disagree. Vection is the illusion of self-motion: visual input reports movement or acceleration while the person is physically stationary. Proprioception is the ability to sense the relative positions of body parts and the amount of muscular effort involved in moving them, and in this situation it reports no motion, so the brain receives conflicting reports.
  Q How can a sensory mismatch compromise presence?  [26/S5/F3, 8/S2/F1; presence, sensory mismatch]
    A A sensory mismatch can compromise presence by making the user consciously aware that the experience is artificial. Presence is a subjective state in which part of the experience is generated by technology, but the user does not accurately acknowledge that technology's role. When the senses conflict, the user understands that the experience is artificial rather than natural or real, so the technology's role is acknowledged.

===== lecture 27: Visual Perception & Displays I

27/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (17 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is virtual reality (VR)? (lecture 4) -> Virtual reality (VR) is an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli provided by a computer, in which a person's actions partially determine what happens and which replaces the user's sense of reality without requiring the physical existence of objects or places.
  What is sensor? (lecture 13) -> Sensor is a device that converts an energy source into electrical signals, or, in the human body, an organ that converts a stimulus into neural impulses; in XR hardware it is a tracking device that tracks a user's movements and extracts information from the real world.
  What is tracking? (lecture 13) -> Tracking is the integral XR hardware component that keeps track of physical-world motion, translating user pose, position, and orientation—or real objects—into virtual motion or 3D content registered to a real-world anchor.
  What is receptor? (lecture 25) -> A receptor is a bodily sensor that is part of a sense organ, targets particular stimuli, and is activated only when a specific type of stimulus arrives. Types include photoreceptors, chemoreceptors, mechanoreceptors, and thermoreceptors.
  What is visual sense? (lecture 25) -> Visual sense is a human sense that has electromagnetic energy as its stimulus, photoreceptors as its receptors, and the eye as its sense organ.
  What is photoreceptor? (lecture 25) -> Photoreceptor is a bodily sensor in the eye's retina that is activated only by visible light and converts visible light into neural pulses for visual perception.

27/A3  quiz  27/S1  "Quick quiz"  (3 facts, 14 concepts)
  Q Which description of light is useful when calculating how much light reaches a sensor or receptor?  [27/S1/F1]
    * Light as a large number of tiny energy particles
    - Light as energy that stops inside a material body
    - Light as ripples that explain a color spectrum
    - Light as paths that show what can be seen
    because: The photon view treats light as many tiny energy particles, which makes it useful for estimating how much light a sensor or receptor receives. The wave and ray views are better tied to color spectrum and visibility or lens behavior, not to received amount.
  Q Which light-related explanation is especially supported by the wave view of light?  [27/S1/F2]
    - The amount of light received by a receptor
    * The spectrum of color
    - The way a surface reflects or absorbs light
    - The path of a single hypothetical photon
    because: The wave view describes light as ripples through space and is especially useful for explaining the spectrum of color. The amount received by a receptor belongs to the photon view, while paths and visibility belong to the ray view.
  Q What does the ray view of light describe in order to explain lenses and visibility?  [27/S1/F3]
    - Many tiny energy particles moving through space
    - Ripples through space that form a color spectrum
    - Light beams that terminate inside a material surface
    * Paths that trace a single hypothetical photon
    because: The ray view models light as rays, which are assumed trajectories of a single hypothetical photon, and this helps explain how lenses work and what is visible. The other options describe the photon view, the wave view, or absorption at a surface.

27/A6  recap  27/S2  "Recap"  (4 facts, 5 concepts)
  Light's interaction with a material surface is described through three basic optical processes. Transmission lets some rays pass through the material, absorption stops some rays inside it, and reflection sends a ray away without entering the material. These processes can occur separately or all together, so a surface's optical behavior combines them.
  - When light strikes a material surface, one of transmission, absorption, or reflection can occur, or all three can occur.
  - In transmission, some light rays pass through the material and come out of it.
  - In absorption, some light rays terminate inside the material and do not propagate further outside.
  - In reflection, a light ray is reflected from the surface without entering or penetrating it.

  - Peripheral rods share optic fibers for low light, while foveal cones mostly use individual fibers for acuity.
  - Photopic vision uses only cones for central color sight; scotopic vision uses only rods for peripheral grayscale sight.

27/A15  recap  27/S6  "Recap"  (7 facts, 19 concepts)
  Human vision depends on how photoreceptors are distributed across the retina. The fovea packs the most photoreceptors, especially cones, so central vision is sharp and colorful when the eyes are focused and pointed at an object; the peripheral retina has fewer photoreceptors and favors movement detection over color. The retina's inside-out anatomy and optic nerve create a blind spot, an area with no photoreceptors and therefore no visual perception.
  - Human eyes support central and peripheral vision because photoreceptor density across the retina varies greatly.
  - The fovea is the retina's central region with the greatest photoreceptor concentration, especially cones in its innermost part.
  - Central vision requires the eyes to be focused and pointed straight at an object for a sharp color image.
  - Peripheral retina has fewer photoreceptors, mainly rods and few cones; it detects movement better than central vision, with weak color.
  - The blind spot has no photoreceptors because the retina's inside-out anatomy and optic nerve make light there imperceptible.

27/A18  match_pairs  lecture  "Match the terms"  (17 facts, 8 concepts)
  virtual reality headset = A wearable display that places a screen close to the eyes and uses a lens to focus the screen's light on the …
  human eye = The sense organ for vision that contains a cornea, iris, pupil, and natural lens and focuses visible light on the retina, where …
  photoreceptor = A bodily sensor in the eye's retina that is activated only by visible light and converts visible light into neural pulses for …
  visible light = A spectrum of frequencies of electromagnetic light waves, ranging from red light to violet light, that can excite the cones in the …
  retina = The non-planar image surface at the back of the eye where light falls and is converted by photoreceptors into neural pulses transmitted …
  lens = An engineered part of a virtual reality headset or a natural part of the human eye that guides and refracts light so …
  photon view = One of the views of light that describes light as a large number of photons, tiny energy particles moving through space at …
  wave view = One of three views of light that describes light as waves, ripples through space, and is helpful for explaining the spectrum of …

27/A21  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (14 facts, 47 concepts)
  Q Why is color perception much stronger in central vision than in peripheral vision?  [27/S4/F4, 27/S4/F7, 27/S6/F1, 27/S6/F2, 27/S6/F4; color perception, central vision, peripheral vision, cone, fovea]
    A Color perception is much stronger in central vision because the fovea, the small central part of the retina, contains almost entirely cones in its innermost region and has the greatest photoreceptor concentration. Cones support photopic vision, which gives a sense of color. Peripheral vision is supported by the peripheral retina, where cone density is very low, so it does not provide effective color perception.
  Q How does the wave view of light explain the color spectrum in ways the photon and ray views do not?  [27/S1/F1, 27/S1/F2, 27/S1/F3; wave view, photon view, ray view, color spectrum]
    A The wave view describes light as waves and is helpful for explaining the spectrum of color. The photon view is instead helpful for calculating the amount of light received by a sensor or receptor. The ray view is helpful for explaining how lenses work and the concept of visibility.
  Q Why can visible light waves produce color perception while electromagnetic light waves outside the visible spectrum cannot?  [27/S4/F7, 27/S5/F0, 27/S5/F1; visible light, electromagnetic light wave, cone, color perception]
    A Visible light is a spectrum of electromagnetic light waves ranging from red light at 4.3 times 10 to the power 14 hertz to violet light at 7.5 times 10 to the power 14 hertz. These visible waves can excite cones, producing photopic vision, which gives a sense of color. Electromagnetic waves outside the visible spectrum cannot excite cones, so they do not produce color perception.
  Q How do engineered lenses in a virtual reality headset and the natural lenses of the human eye work together to produce visual perception?  [27/S0/F0, 27/S4/F0, 27/S4/F1, 27/S4/F3; virtual reality headset, lens, human eye, retina, visual perception]
    A In a virtual reality headset, light from the display is guided by engineered headset lenses and by the natural lenses of the eye. In the human eye, light passes through the cornea, pupil, and lens, and the cornea and lens refract the light so that images are focused on the retina. The photoreceptors in the retina then support visual perception.
  judge round 1: 1 of 4 failed
    1 pass  (Why is color perception much stronger in central vision than in peripheral vision?)
      check: Color perception is stronger in central vision because the fovea contains especially many cones, cones support color-perceiving photopic vision, and the peripheral retina has very low cone density and ineffective color perception.
      reason: Facts 27 and 28 give the fovea’s high cone concentration, fact 23 gives cones/photopic vision as the basis of color perception, and fact 30 gives the peripheral retina’s low cone density and lack of effective color perception. These facts carry the requested central-versus-peripheral link.
    2 FAIL answers_question  (How does the wave view of light explain the color spectrum in ways the …)
      check: The facts say the wave view is helpful for the color spectrum, the photon view for calculating received light, and the ray view for lenses and visibility, but they do not directly state that the photon and ray views do not explain the color spectrum.
      reason: The reference answer lists the different helpful uses of the three views (facts 7, 8, 9) but does not directly state that the photon and ray views do not explain the color spectrum, which is what the question asks. A repaired reference answer should explicitly contrast the wave view’s use for the color spectrum with the other views’ stated uses.
    3 pass  (Why can visible light waves produce color perception while electromagnetic light waves outside the …)

===== lecture 28: Visual Perception & Displays II

28/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (13 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is photoreceptor? (lecture 25) -> Photoreceptor is a bodily sensor in the eye's retina that is activated only by visible light and converts visible light into neural pulses for visual perception.
  What is virtual reality headset (VR)? (lecture 27) -> Virtual reality headset is a wearable display that places a screen close to the eyes and uses a lens to focus the screen's light on the retina, making the screen appear as a virtual image.
  What is human eye? (lecture 27) -> The human eye is the sense organ for vision that contains a cornea, iris, pupil, and natural lens and focuses visible light on the retina, where photoreceptors convert it into neural pulses sent to the brain.
  What is retina? (lecture 27) -> Retina is the non-planar image surface at the back of the eye where light falls and is converted by photoreceptors into neural pulses transmitted to the brain by optic nerve fibers.
  What is lens? (lecture 27) -> A lens is an engineered part of a virtual reality headset or a natural part of the human eye that guides and refracts light so that images are focused on the retina.
  What is cornea? (lecture 27) -> The cornea is a refracting medium in the human eye that acts as a powerful lens with fixed focal depth, helping focus incoming light onto the retina.

28/A1  quiz  28/S0  "Quick quiz"  (7 facts, 19 concepts)
  Q Why is the human eye not described as having a separate focal plane like an artificial lens setup?  [28/S0/F0, 28/S0/F1]
    * Its curved retina replaces the focal plane as the image surface
    - Its natural lens replaces the focal plane as the image surface
    - Its optical nerves replace the focal plane as the image surface
    - Its liquid interior replaces the focal plane as the image surface
    because: The eye’s spherically curved retina is the surface where light lands and is converted into neural signals, so it replaces the focal plane. The liquid, natural lens, or nerves do not act as that image surface.
  Q Compared with an artificial lens setup, what does light in the human eye pass through after the natural lens?  [28/S0/F2]
    - A second glass lens before the retina
    * Liquid inside the eye
    - Air inside the eye
    - A flat focal plane behind the lens
    because: Light in the eye travels through the liquid interior after passing through the natural lens, whereas light in an artificial lens setup travels through air after the lens. A second glass lens or flat plane is not the medium it passes through.
  Q What explains the need for high optical power in the human eye?  [28/S0/F4, 28/S0/F5]
    - The wide field of view of the human eye
    - The curved retinal surface of the human eye
    * The small outer diameter of the human eye
    - The liquid-filled interior of the human eye
    because: The eye's short outer diameter means parallel rays must be converged onto the retina with high optical power. Field of view, liquid interior, and retinal curvature are not the reason for that need.
  Q Why does a VR headset place its screen at the focal length of its engineered lens?  [28/S0/F6, 28/S0/F7]
    - So the screen appears as a flat picture on the headset's front surface
    - So the screen appears as a real image on the engineered lens
    - So the screen appears as a small virtual image at a close distance
    * So the screen appears as an enormous virtual image at infinity
    because: Placing the screen at the engineered lens’s focal length makes the small nearby display appear to the user as a large image at an infinite distance. It does not make the screen appear small and close, nor does it place a visible real image on the lens or headset.

28/A4  quiz  28/S1  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 13 concepts)
  Q What is field of view in human vision?  [28/S1/F0]
    - the size of the screen visible to the eye
    - the number of objects visible to the eye
    - the distance to the boundary visible to the eye
    * the angular region visible to the eye
    because: Field of view is the angular region of the scene visible from one point in time. It is not a count of objects, a screen size, or a distance to a boundary.
  Q What does the region seen by both eyes contribute to depth perception?  [28/S1/F2, 28/S1/F3]
    - A separate image that links objects in 3D space
    * A common image that links objects in 3D space
    - A peripheral image that links objects in 3D space
    - A monocular image that links objects in 3D space
    because: In binocular vision, both eyes see the same image over their common viewing region, and this shared view helps a person understand relationships between objects in 3D space. Areas seen by only one eye are not the shared depth cue.
  Q How does stereoscopic viewing produce a three-dimensional view?  [28/S1/F4, 28/S1/F5]
    - Simultaneous processing of one 2D image generates a 3D view
    - Simultaneous processing of two 3D images generates a 3D view
    - Sequential processing of two 2D images generates a 3D view
    * Simultaneous processing of two 2D images generates a 3D view
    because: Stereoscopy works because the left and right eyes process their two 2D images at the same time, and that simultaneous processing produces a 3D view. One image, sequential processing, or already-3D source images are not the described mechanism.

  - Field of view is the angular region visible to the eye at one point in time.

  - Binocular vision enhances depth perception and helps understand relationships between 3D objects.
  - Stereoscopy presents left and right 2D images to the eyes simultaneously, and processing generates a 3D view of objects.

  Q In an XR display, which property describes the rate at which pixels change so that movement appears smooth?  [28/S3/F1]
    - Color resolution
    * Temporal resolution
    - Spatial resolution
    - Intensity resolution
    because: Temporal resolution refers to the frame rate or speed at which display pixels change, which is what allows motion to be perceived smoothly. Spatial resolution concerns pixel count per area, and intensity resolution concerns the range of intensity values.
  Q What condition makes a sharp diagonal line look jagged?  [28/S3/F2]

28/A9  recap  28/S3  "Recap"  (9 facts, 30 concepts)
  Human visual physiology sets the goals for XR displays, because a VR display should match the visual system without exceeding receptor limits. To do that, displays need adequate spatial resolution, intensity range, and frame rate. Spatial resolution is visible as aliasing or a screen-door effect when pixels can be seen; close-to-eye XR displays need much more resolution than distant ones, and rendering or field-of-view changes can reduce the artifacts. Temporal resolution is especially demanding for immersive motion, requiring frame rates well above ordinary television or movie standards.
  - Human visual physiology sets XR display requirements: spatial, intensity, and temporal resolution must match perceptual limits.
  - Visible individual display lights can cause jagged lines or a screen-like overlay, known as aliasing or screen door effect.
  - The 326 ppi retina criterion may suit distant AR displays, but close-to-eye XR displays need roughly 7–8 times more.
  - VR headsets can reduce aliasing or screen door effects with higher resolution, field-of-view changes, or foveated rendering.
  - Immersive VR motion needs frame rates much higher than ordinary 24 or 60 fps, with higher preferred.
  judge round 1: 2 of 6 failed
    1 pass  (Human visual physiology sets XR display requirements: spatial, intensity, and temporal resolution must match …)
      check: none
      reason: Facts [1] and [2] carry the point: human visual properties affect display requirements, and the relevant display factors are spatial resolution, intensity resolution/range, and temporal resolution.
    2 FAIL supported,faithful  (Visible individual display lights can cause jagged lines or a screen-like overlay, known as …)
      check: in which an image appears to have a screen on top of it [4]
      reason: The point says visible individual display lights can cause both jagged lines and a screen-like overlay, but fact [3] links visible lights only to aliasing, while fact [4] describes the screen door effect without saying it is caused by visible lights. A repaired version would keep the two effects separate and avoid attributing the screen door effect to visible lights.
    3 pass  (The 326 ppi retina criterion may suit distant AR displays, but close-to-eye XR displays …)
      check: none
      reason: Facts [5], [6], and [7] support the comparison: 326 ppi is a retina criterion that may be considered for distant AR displays, while close-to-eye displays require roughly 7–8 times higher ppi.
    4 pass  (VR headsets can reduce aliasing or screen door effects with higher resolution, field-of-view changes …)

    5 pass  (Immersive VR motion needs frame rates much higher than ordinary 24 or 60 fps …)

28/A12  match_pairs  lecture  "Match the terms"  (17 facts, 8 concepts)
  virtual reality headset = A wearable display that places a screen close to the eyes and uses a lens to focus the screen's light on the …
  stereoscopic vision = The perception of three-dimensional objects and space from left and right two-dimensional images processed simultaneously, aided by binocular vision.
  field of view = An angular measure of the region visible to the eye at a single point in time, and in virtual reality it is …
  stereoscopy = The process in which two eyes view two images simultaneously, the left eye processing the left image and the right eye processing …
  human eye = The sense organ for vision that contains a cornea, iris, pupil, and natural lens and focuses visible light on the retina, where …
  retina = The non-planar image surface at the back of the eye where light falls and is converted by photoreceptors into neural pulses transmitted …
  cornea = A refracting medium in the human eye that acts as a powerful lens with fixed focal depth, helping focus incoming light onto …
  view frustum = The region visible to the human eye.

  4 across: Minimum and maximum producible light values a display handles with perceptual quality (9,5) = INTENSITYRANGE
  6 across: Visual screen defined by at least 326 pixels per linear inch (6,7) = RETINADISPLAY

  11 across: Two-eyed seeing form using a shared region and 2D inputs for depth (9,6) = BINOCULARVISION
  12 across: Back-of-eye surface that turns light into nerve pulses (6) = RETINA
  1 down: Convex part inside the human eye with variable focal depth (7,4) = NATURALLENS
  2 down: Angular size an eye sees at one instant (5,2,4) = FIELDOFVIEW
  3 down: Independent movement ways an object has in 3D space (6,2,7) = DEGREEOFFREEDOM
  5 down: Scan-conversion distortion from placing pixels near, not on, shape points (8) = ALIASING
  7 down: Organ holding cornea, iris, pupil, and variable focusing element (5,3) = HUMANEYE
  10 down: Refracting medium with fixed focal depth that helps focus incoming light (6) = CORNEA
  judge round 1: 1 of 12 failed
    1 pass  (intensity range: Minimum and maximum producible light values a display handles with perceptual quality)
      check: none
      reason: The clue paraphrases the answer text’s “minimum and maximum of the producible intensity values” and “perceptual quality” without naming intensity range. “Light values” is a fair visual-perception paraphrase of intensity values.
    2 pass  (retina display: Visual screen defined by at least 326 pixels per linear inch)
      check: none
      reason: The clue restates the definition’s “display with a minimum resolution of 326 pixels per linear inch” as “visual screen” and “at least 326 pixels per linear inch,” identifying Retina display uniquely.
    3 pass  (view frustum: Visible region perceived by one human eye)
      check: none
      reason: The clue matches “the region visible to the human eye,” while field of view is explicitly an angular measure rather than the visible region itself.
    4 FAIL from_text  (stereoscopy: Process that sends left image to left eye and right image to right …)
      check: binocular vision

28/A15  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (12 facts, 38 concepts)
  Q How does placing a screen in a virtual reality headset at the focal length of its engineered lens allow the screen to appear distant while still enabling perception on the retina?  [28/S0/F6, 28/S0/F7, 28/S0/F8; virtual reality headset, engineered lens, virtual image, real image, retina]
    A It makes the close screen appear as an enormous virtual image at an infinite distance. The headset's convex lens focuses the screen's light on the retina, forming a real image. A real image on the retina is required for perception.
  Q Why is the 326 pixels per linear inch retina display criterion suitable for distant augmented reality displays but not very suitable for head-mounted displays, virtual reality headsets, or wearable displays?  [28/S3/F4, 28/S3/F5, 28/S3/F6; augmented reality, virtual reality, retina display criterion, pixels per linear inch]
    A The 326 pixels per linear inch criterion can be considered for augmented reality displays at a distance, such as televisions, laptops, and smartphones. For head-mounted displays, virtual reality headsets, or wearable displays close to the eye, a magnifying lens brings the display close to the eye. Therefore, the required pixels per linear inch is probably 7 to 8 times higher than a retina display.
  Q How does binocular vision enable stereoscopy to produce a three-dimensional view from left and right two-dimensional images?  [28/S1/F2, 28/S1/F3, 28/S1/F4, 28/S1/F5; binocular vision, stereoscopy, depth perception, three-dimensional view]
    A Binocular vision gives both eyes a common region of about 120 degrees when they focus on infinity. Stereoscopy then uses the left eye to process the left two-dimensional image and the right eye to process the right one. Processing these images simultaneously generates a three-dimensional view, and binocular vision enhances depth perception of object relationships in three-dimensional space.
  Q Why must a virtual reality headset have a temporal resolution higher than ordinary television or movie frame rates for motion perception?  [28/S3/F1, 28/S3/F8; temporal resolution, frame rate, motion perception, virtual reality headset]
    A It must allow motion to be perceived smoothly without jitter. Temporal resolution is the frame rate, that is, the speed at which display pixels change, and in an immersive environment a virtual reality headset requires frame rates much higher than ordinary television or movie standards such as 24 or 60 frames per second. Higher frame rates are preferred.

===== lecture 29: Auditory Sense & Immersive Experience

29/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (11 facts, 5 concepts)
  What is virtual reality (VR)? (lecture 4) -> Virtual reality (VR) is an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli provided by a computer, in which a person's actions partially determine what happens and which replaces the user's sense of reality without requiring the physical existence of objects or places.
  What is presence? (lecture 8) -> Presence is a subjective psychological state in which an experience generated by human-made technology is perceived as real, because the user fails to acknowledge the technology's role and perceives computer-generated stimuli as coming from the real world.
  What is visual sense? (lecture 25) -> Visual sense is a human sense that has electromagnetic energy as its stimulus, photoreceptors as its receptors, and the eye as its sense organ.
  What is virtual environment? (lecture 4) -> Virtual environment is a non-real, computer-generated graphical representation of a real or imaginary world, populated with artificial objects, that is experienced through computer-generated sensory stimuli.
  What is immersive experience? (lecture 1) -> An immersive experience is a perceived experience through sensory organs that appears real, because a person cannot distinguish the experienced environment from their real environment and perceives it as that real environment.

29/A1  quiz  29/S0  "Quick quiz"  (4 facts, 21 concepts)
  Q Why is audio combined with vision in an immersive XR experience?  [29/S0/F1]
    - To replace visual information with a separate audio-only experience
    - To reduce the number of senses needed for a believable experience
    - To turn a virtual environment into a physical surround environment
    * To add sensory information that vision alone may not fully provide
    because: Vision alone may not give a full picture of the surroundings, so adding audio helps create a more complete immersive experience. It is not meant to replace vision or to reduce the number of senses involved.
  Q What does combining audio with visual effects do in a virtual environment?  [29/S0/F3]
    - It can reduce the perceived size, volume, material, intensity, and distance of the environment
    - It can alter the actual size, volume, material, intensity, and distance of the environment
    - It can replace the visual cues for size, volume, material, intensity, and distance of the environment
    * It can reinforce the perceived size, volume, material, intensity, and distance of the environment
    because: Looking alone gives some idea of these properties, but adding audio reinforces their perception. It does not change the actual scene properties or simply replace visual cues.
  Q What does presence in a virtual environment require?  [29/S0/F5]
    - A head-mounted display and a surround-sound experience
    - A cave-like display and a wearable display experience
    - A high-fidelity audio track and a photorealistic visual experience
    * A believable experience and an attachment to that experience
    because: Presence depends on the virtual experience feeling believable and on the user developing attachment to it. Specific displays or high-fidelity hardware may help, but they are not the stated requirements for presence.
  Q How can audio recording and reproduction count as a VR experience?  [29/S0/F2]
    - It can provide a tactile experience even when other senses are missing
    * It can provide an immersive experience even when other senses are missing
    - It can provide a scent experience even when other senses are missing
    - It can provide a visual experience even when other senses are missing
    because: Audio recording and reproduction can themselves form a VR experience because an immersive effect can still arise without the other senses. It is an auditory, not visual, tactile, or scent-based, experience.
