35/A18  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (12 facts, 32 concepts)
  Q Why are decisions to use a mobile platform and a programming language such as Java or JavaScript not considered end-user usability requirements in requirement gathering for the calendar application?  [35/S0/F0, 35/S2/F0, 35/S2/F1; requirement gathering, user requirement, feasibility stage]
    A Because requirement gathering focuses on end-user requirements that ensure usability, not on technical feasibility choices. In the calendar application, choosing a mobile platform and a programming language such as Java or JavaScript is related to the feasibility stage. These choices may be considered during requirement gathering, but they are not end-user usability requirements.
  Q Why are usability requirements classified as non-functional requirements instead of functional requirements in the specification of an interactive system?  [35/S3/F1, 35/S3/F2, 35/S3/F3; usability requirement, functional requirement, non-functional requirement, user interface]
    A Functional requirements are system features or abilities to carry out tasks, treated as black boxes that produce an output from an input. Non-functional requirements are system characteristics that cannot be expressed as functions and typically concern software quality attributes. Usability requirements are such non-functional requirements because they concern the design and qualities of the user interface that make it usable.
  Q Why must the users and their work context be specified before end-user usability requirements can be gathered?  [35/S4/F0, 35/S4/F1, 35/S4/F2; user requirement, context of use, usability, user behavior]
    A End-user requirements cannot be gathered without specified users. The ISO definition of usability requires a usable product to have a specified context of use. Knowing how users behave in that specific work context is essential because usability is defined with respect to it.
  Q Why does contextual inquiry in a natural work setting help designers derive usable features for the calendar application?  [35/S4/F6, 35/S4/F9, 35/S5/F1; contextual inquiry, user behavior, user activities, feature]
    A Contextual inquiry observes users performing tasks in their natural work setting to gather insight about user behavior and end-user requirements. It also reveals the task domain, work culture, and physical or social constraints that support design decisions. The user activities observed, such as setting meeting dates and reminders, must then be supported as features for the app to be usable for that user group.

===== lecture 36: Usability requirement gathering and specification

36/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (4 facts, 1 concepts)
  What is contextual inquiry (CI)? (lecture 35) -> Contextual inquiry (CI) is a usability requirement-gathering method, often described as a semi-structured interview process, that observes users performing tasks in their natural work setting and asks users questions to clarify behavior.

36/A1  quiz  36/S0  "Quick quiz"  (3 facts, 4 concepts)
  Q What does contextual inquiry primarily involve?  [36/S0/F0]
    * Observing targeted users in their natural work setting
    - Testing targeted users in a controlled work setting
    - Observing targeted users in a controlled work setting
    - Interviewing targeted users in their natural work setting
    because: Contextual inquiry is a requirement-gathering method based on observing users in their natural work setting. Interviewing, controlled settings, and testing are not the defining activity of contextual inquiry.
  Q What is true of the active mode of contextual inquiry?  [36/S0/F1]
    - An observer is absent while the users work
    - An observer tests users while the users work
    - An observer advises users while the users work
    * An observer is present while the users work
    because: In active mode, the observer is physically present while users do their tasks. The observer is not absent, and advising or testing users is not what defines the active mode.

    * To learn how users behave rather than to advise them
    - To teach how tasks should be done rather than to advise them
    - To direct how tasks should be done rather than to advise them
    because: The observer acts as an apprentice by learning from the users, who are treated as masters. Advising, teaching, directing, or merely assessing performance does not match the apprentice role.

36/A2  recap  36/S0  "Recap"  (3 facts, 4 concepts)
  Contextual inquiry gathers usability requirements by observing users in their natural work setting. It can be carried out actively with an observer present, or passively by reviewing recorded user activities and clarifying issues with users. In either case, the observer should remain an apprentice, learning from users as teachers rather than advising how they should behave.
  - Contextual inquiry gathers usability requirements by observing specified user groups in their natural work setting.
  - Active contextual inquiry has an observer present, while passive reviews recorded user activities and clarifies issues with users.
  - The contextual inquiry observer must act as an apprentice, treating users as teachers and not giving advice.

36/A4  recap  36/S1  "Recap"  (7 facts, 12 concepts)
  Contextual inquiry is carried out through five ordered stages that make usability observation systematic. Planning and initiating prepare the observation, then executing records it and closing finishes it politely. Reflection then organizes the collected data with affinity diagrams, revealing patterns that lead to design goals.
  - The five stages of contextual inquiry systematically run in this order: plan, initiate, execute, close, reflect.
  - The plan stage sets goals, gathers domain knowledge, and arranges recording, users, time, place, and rehearsal.
  - The initiate stage obtains permissions and reduces user anxiety so users behave naturally.
  - The execute stage records observations, and the close stage ideally thanks users and authorities for possible future testing.
  - The reflect stage uses affinity diagrams to arrange execute-stage data, find patterns, and specify design goals.
  judge round 1: 5 of 6 failed
    1 pass  (The five stages of contextual inquiry systematically run in this order: plan, initiate, execute …)
      check: none
      reason: Fact 1 states the five stages in this order and says they provide a systematic way of carrying out the inquiry process.
    2 FAIL supported,faithful,stands_alone  (The plan stage sets goals, gathers domain knowledge, and arranges recording, users, time, place …)
      check: identifying the goals of observation (2); planning arrangements for recording observations, identifying the users and the date, time, and place (2); scripting and rehearsing the procedure (2)
      reason: It says the plan stage "sets goals" and "arranges ... users," whereas fact 2 says it identifies observation goals and identifies users, date, time, and place; it also leaves out date and scripting. A repair should say: "The plan stage of contextual inquiry identifies goals, gathers task-domain knowledge, plans recording and logistics, and may script/rehearse the observation."
    3 FAIL faithful,stands_alone  (The initiate stage obtains permissions and reduces user anxiety so users behave naturally.)
      check: remove anxieties that the observation may lead to something bad for them (3); so that they behave naturally (3)
      reason: "Reduces user anxiety" is weaker and broader than fact 3's "remove anxieties that the observation may lead to something bad for them," and the point's subject is not named in full. A repair should say: "The initiate stage of contextual inquiry obtains necessary permissions and opens communication to remove users' anxieties so they behave naturally."

36/A7  recap  36/S2  "Recap"  (7 facts, 9 concepts)
  The affinity diagram method organizes contextual inquiry notes by generating, displaying, sorting, and naming them, then drawing the resulting groups. Reflection on the finished diagram turns those grouped patterns into design recommendations. These recommendations are informed by inquiry data, unlike uninformed guidelines made without it, and they state what must be done for usability rather than how to implement it.
  - The affinity diagram method generates and displays contextual inquiry notes, then sorts, names, and diagrams the groups.
  - Sorting similar notes into groups and adding a header names a pattern not present in the initial ideas.
  - Reflection on the finished diagram yields design recommendations, informed by inquiry data, unlike uninformed design choices made without it.

36/A12  match_pairs  lecture  "Match the terms"  (11 facts, 8 concepts)
  contextual inquiry = A usability requirement-gathering method, often described as a semi-structured interview process, that observes users performing tasks in their natural work setting and …
  active mode = A mode of contextual inquiry in which the observer is physically present in the environment where users are doing their tasks.
  passive mode = A mode of contextual inquiry in which no observer is present while users perform tasks, and their activities are recorded or videotaped …
  master-apprentice model = A model for genuine contextual inquiry in which the observer acts as an apprentice or learner, treats users as masters or teachers …
  plan stage = The first stage of contextual inquiry that involves identifying observation goals, gathering task-domain knowledge, planning recording arrangements, identifying the users and date …
  initiate stage = A stage of contextual inquiry that involves obtaining all necessary permissions from relevant authorities before observing employees in their workplace and opening …
  execute stage = A stage of contextual inquiry in which the actual inquiry takes place through performing observations and recording data.
  close stage = The fourth stage of contextual inquiry, in which the inquiry is formally closed, ideally by sending thank-you notes or a message of …

36/A15  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (9 facts, 21 concepts)
  Q Why is the observer's role in genuine contextual inquiry described by the master-apprentice model?  [36/S0/F2, 35/S4/F6; master-apprentice model, observation]
    A In genuine contextual inquiry, the observer acts as an apprentice or learner while users are masters or teachers. This role requires learning how users behave instead of advising or teaching them, and advice is prohibited. It supports the objective of watching users perform tasks in their natural work setting to gather insight about behavior and requirements.
  Q How does affinity diagram analysis connect contextual inquiry observations to design recommendations?  [36/S1/F3, 36/S1/F5, 36/S1/F6, 36/S2/F5; reflect stage, affinity diagram method, design guideline]
    A The execute stage of contextual inquiry performs observations and records data. In the reflect stage, the team analyzes that data and identifies design goals, using affinity diagram analysis to arrange the notes so patterns can be found. The finished affinity diagram leads to a design specification, and reflection then formulates design recommendations from the data.
  Q Why are design guidelines formulated after an affinity diagram considered informed design choices, while guidelines created without contextual inquiry are not?  [36/S2/F5, 36/S2/F6; design guideline, informed design choice, uninformed design choice, affinity diagram method]
    A Design guidelines are formulated after the finished affinity diagram, so they reflect analysis of collected inquiry data. Guidelines derived from contextual inquiry are informed design choices because they are produced by analyzing that data, ensuring users' needs and expectations are taken into account. Guidelines created without contextual inquiry are uninformed design choices because they do not ensure that users' needs and expectations are taken into account.
  Q How does the calendar app affinity diagram example show that there is no unique way to group contextual inquiry observations?  [36/S3/F1, 36/S3/F2; calendar app, affinity diagram method, work scheduling, overall scheduling]
    A In the calendar app example, five observations not related to reminder setting were first grouped under the header work scheduling. These were then refined into the headers overall scheduling and day-wise scheduling, producing a finished diagram with reminder setting, overall scheduling, and day-wise scheduling. This illustrates that different groupings are possible, because an affinity diagram has no unique way to group observations.

===== lecture 37: Usability requirement gathering and specification

37/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (22 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is presence? (lecture 8) -> Presence is a subjective psychological state in which an experience generated by human-made technology is perceived as real, because the user fails to acknowledge the technology's role and perceives computer-generated stimuli as coming from the real world.
  What is virtual reality tour? (lecture 33) -> A virtual reality tour is a virtual reality experience for visiting a recreated place without physically going there, in which movement from one point to another is either user-controlled or system-controlled.
  What is contextual inquiry (CI)? (lecture 35) -> Contextual inquiry (CI) is a usability requirement-gathering method, often described as a semi-structured interview process, that observes users performing tasks in their natural work setting and asks users questions to clarify behavior.
  What is requirement? (lecture 36) -> A requirement is an end-user requirement that states what must be done to make a system usable, without specifying how to implement it; it can be functional or non-functional.
  What is design guideline? (lecture 36) -> Design guideline is a statement about an interactive system that says what should or should not be done to make it usable, without saying how to implement it; it can be generic or particular to a system, and is only a starting point to be implemented and tested.
  What is virtual reality (VR)? (lecture 4) -> Virtual reality (VR) is an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli provided by a computer, in which a person's actions partially determine what happens and which replaces the user's sense of reality without requiring the physical existence of objects or places.

37/A1  quiz  37/S0  "Quick quiz"  (2 facts, 12 concepts)
  Q In addition to being framed as design guidelines, design recommendations, or design principles, which form can the outcome of contextual inquiry take?  [37/S0/F0]
    * functional requirements
    - interaction design requirements
    - human factors requirements
    - perceptual design requirements
    because: Contextual inquiry outcomes can be turned into functional requirements, not merely interaction, perceptual, or human-factor labels. The usable forms are guideline-like statements and functional requirements.
  Q What specification form makes a requirement easy to convert into code?  [37/S0/F1]
    - A requirement with a well-defined goal and a well-defined output
    - A function with a well-defined purpose and a well-defined output
    * A function with a well-defined input and a well-defined output
    - A prototype with a well-defined design and a well-defined output
    because: A function with a well-defined input and output can be translated directly into code. A purpose, goal, or design description does not fix the input side needed for implementation.

37/A2  recap  37/S0  "Recap"  (2 facts, 12 concepts)
  Contextual inquiry outcomes can be documented as usability requirements in two linked forms. They can guide the work as design guidelines, design recommendations, or design principles. They can also be expressed as functional requirements, which define functions with clear inputs and outputs and make the transition to code design easier.
  - Contextual inquiry outcomes can be used as design guidelines, design recommendations, design principles, or functional requirements.
  - Functional requirements specify functions with well-defined input and output, making their transition to code design easier.

  Q What do the guidelines framed from contextual inquiry observations do in the note-taking application example?  [37/S1/F0]
    - They state how each observed behavior must be implemented for the application
    - They state the exact order in which supported tasks should be run for the application
    - They state which observed behaviors should be excluded from use for the application
    * They state what should or should not be done, not how, for the application
    because: The framed guidelines are generic: they specify what the application should or should not do, without specifying how that should be implemented.
  Q What kind of support do the observation-based guidelines specify for academic information in the note-taking application?  [37/S1/F1]
    * Supporting viewing of deadlines, meetings, timetables, and lecture schedules
    - Supporting sharing of deadlines, meetings, timetables, and lecture schedules
    - Supporting reminders for deadlines, meetings, timetables, and lecture schedules
    - Supporting printing of deadlines, meetings, timetables, and lecture schedules
    because: The guidelines call for viewing features: upcoming assignment deadlines, current scheduled meetings, the timetable on a given day, and lecture schedules on a given day. They do not specify reminders, printing, or sharing.
  Q How are behaviors observed in the context of use used in the note-taking application guidelines?  [37/S1/F2]
    * They are included in the overall system so the user is involved in the design
    - They are converted into code before any interaction is modeled in the design
    - They are treated as developer preferences so the user is not involved in the design
    - They are recorded as evidence but do not influence the overall system in the design
    because: Observed context-of-use behaviors are used to include those behaviors in the overall system, which keeps the user involved in design through observation and feedback.

37/A5  quiz  37/S2  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 11 concepts)
  Q What allows usability requirements to be incorporated directly into an app's code?  [37/S2/F1]
    - Keeping them as non-functional requirements
    - Organizing them under SRS identifiers
    - Recording them in contextual inquiry notes
    * Converting them into functional requirements
    because: Usability requirements are non-functional, but they can be converted into functional requirements, which specify codeable system features. Merely keeping them as non-functional notes, listing them, or recording observations does not put them into the system through code.
  Q Which property makes a requirement easy to convert into code as a functional requirement?  [37/S2/F0]
    - It describes a usability property with a clear target and test
    - It describes a usage scenario with a clear user and device
    - It describes a set of observations with a clear user group and task
    * It describes a black-box function with a clear input and output
    because: A functional requirement is specifiable as a black-box function with a well-defined input and output, which is what makes it easy to convert into code. Usage scenarios, usability properties, and observation sets are not themselves codeable functions.
  Q In an SRS hierarchy, what does a sub-requirement identifier such as R1.1 represent?  [37/S2/F3]
    - A contextual inquiry observation grouped by user
    - A usability note kept as a non-functional requirement
    - A design guideline for future development
    * A function with a defined input and output
    because: In an SRS hierarchy, each requirement identifier stands for a function with a clearly defined input and output. A sub-identifier like R1.1 therefore names a more specific function, not a note, observation, or guideline by itself.
  Q What does contextual inquiry produce as its output?  [37/S2/F4]
    * A group-wise organization of observation notes
    - A single user group for the system
    - A complete SRS with formal function specs
    - A list of code-ready functional requirements
    because: Contextual inquiry yields observation notes organized by user group. Those notes can later inform design guidelines or, for some items, be converted into functional requirements, but the inquiry output itself is not a finished SRS, a list of code-ready functions, or a single user group.
  Q In the college calendar example, why are R1.1, R1.2, and R1.3 subrequirements under R1 views?  [37/S2/F5]
    - They each record a usability issue from observation
    * They each turn a date input into a different view
    - They each describe the same view in more detail
    - They each take a different input for the same output
    because: R1 views takes a date and produces one of several views, while each subrequirement specifies a different output view for that date input. They are not separate input types, repetitions of the same view, or usability issues.
  judge round 1: 0 of 5 failed
    1 pass  (What allows usability requirements to be incorporated directly into an app's code?)
      check: D
      reason: Fact 2 says usability requirements “can be converted into functional requirements (FRs) … so that usability requirements are directly incorporated into the system through code.”
    2 pass  (Which property makes a requirement easy to convert into code as a functional requirement?)
      check: D
      reason: Fact 1 says a functional requirement is “easy to convert into code because it specifies a system feature as a black-box function with a well-defined input, a well-defined output.”
    3 pass  (In an SRS hierarchy, what does a sub-requirement identifier such as R1.1 represent?)
      check: D
      reason: Fact 4 says in an SRS hierarchy “each requirement identifier represents a function with a clearly defined input, a clearly defined output.”
    4 pass  (What does contextual inquiry produce as its output?)
      check: A
      reason: Fact 5 states “The output of contextual inquiry is a group-wise organization of the notes taken during observation.”
    5 pass  (In the college calendar example, why are R1.1, R1.2, and R1.3 subrequirements under R1 …)
      check: B
      reason: Fact 6 says R1.1, R1.2, and R1.3 each have “date input” and produce different output views: “day timetable”, “submission deadlines”, and “list of meetings scheduled on the day”.
  judge kept: original

37/A6  recap  37/S2  "Recap"  (5 facts, 11 concepts)
  Contextual inquiry notes are organized into group-wise findings that first serve as design guidelines. Some of these usability findings can be restated as functional requirements, where each requirement has a clear input and output. The SRS then records these requirements in a hierarchy, as shown by the calendar app's R1 views with date input and subrequirements for timetable, deadline, and meeting views.
  - A functional requirement is a black-box function with a defined input and output, easy to convert into code.
  - Usability requirements, as non-functional requirements, can be converted into functional requirements and incorporated into code.
  - An SRS documents all requirements and organizes functional requirements in an identifier hierarchy, each with input and output.
  - Group-wise contextual inquiry notes can guide design and, for some items, become functional requirements implemented in code.
  judge round 1: 2 of 5 failed
    1 pass  (A functional requirement is a black-box function with a defined input and output, easy …)
      check: none
      reason: The point is a faithful compression of fact 1: a functional requirement is a black-box function with defined input and output that is easy to convert into code.
    2 pass  (Usability requirements, as non-functional requirements, can be converted into functional requirements and incorporated into …)
      check: none
      reason: Fact 2 supports that usability requirements are non-functional requirements that can be converted into functional requirements and thereby incorporated through code.
    3 FAIL faithful  (An SRS documents all requirements and organizes functional requirements in an identifier hierarchy, each …)
      check: generally (4)
      reason: It drops the hedge in fact 4 by saying an SRS "organizes" requirements in an identifier hierarchy, whereas fact 4 says requirements are "generally organized" that way. A repaired version would keep the generalization, for example: "An SRS documents all requirements and generally organizes requirements in an identifier hierarchy, each with input and output."
    4 pass  (Group-wise contextual inquiry notes can guide design and, for some items, become functional requirements …)
      check: none
      reason: Fact 5 supports that group-wise contextual inquiry notes can serve as design guidelines and that some, if not all, can become functional requirements implemented in code.
    0 FAIL faithful  (Contextual inquiry notes are organized into group-wise findings that first serve as design guidelines.)
      check: generally (4)
      reason: The sentence "The SRS then records these requirements in a hierarchy" states the hierarchy as a definite fact, while fact 4 says requirements are "generally organized" in a hierarchy. The rest is supported, including the calendar example from fact 6.

37/A7  quiz  37/S3  "Quick quiz"  (6 facts, 20 concepts)
  Q Why is the usability of the Majuli VR Tour claimed only for students or learners, tourists, and pilgrims?  [37/S3/F3]
    - because each group was given a subset of the collected data to avoid confusion in a large space
    * because those are the identified user groups and usability is not claimed for any person in any work context or task
    - because field trips and interviews were done with samples from those groups to learn their needs
    - because the virtual tour was intended for people who do not reside on Majuli rather than for residents who are already on the island
    because: The usability claim is limited to the three user groups identified in the case study, not to every possible person or task context. The other options introduce technical, exclusion, or implementation reasons that are not the stated basis for the claim.
  Q Why was contextual inquiry in the Majuli VR Tour carried out after the user groups had been identified?  [37/S3/F4]
    - to choose the three user groups from possible island visitors before the field visits in Majuli
    * to study samples from those groups and learn their needs, expectations, and design issues
    - to identify residents as a fourth user group after collecting observations on the island
    - to make sure that sampled people could receive a tailored subset of the collected tour data
    because: Contextual inquiry was done on samples from the already identified groups, not to choose the groups or to give everyone the full data set. Its purpose was to learn the sampled groups’ needs and issues related to the system’s broad design challenges.
  Q Why did the Majuli VR Tour give each user group only a subset of the collected data?  [37/S3/F6, 37/S3/F7]
    - to make the complete island view available to every group for a short session
    - to remove the need for accurate location information in a large virtual space
    - to separate tangible heritage from intangible heritage so that each group could explore one type only
    * to reduce the information each group had to explore and to lower the chance of cybersickness
    because: Restricting each group to a relevant subset reduced the expanse of information and the need to explore everything, which lowered the possibility of cybersickness and increased interest. Making the whole data set available could instead confuse users, reduce interest, and lead to cybersickness.
  Q Why was location awareness treated as a usability issue for users exploring a large virtual space in the Majuli VR Tour?  [37/S3/F8, 37/S3/F9]
    * because accurate location information prevents disorientation and gives users confidence and purpose
    - because accurate location information reduces the amount of multimodal data that must be streamed
    - because accurate location information turns every usability requirement into a functional requirement
    - because accurate location information replaces the need for navigation support in a large geography
    because: Location awareness matters in a large VR geography because it tells users where they are, preventing disorientation and supporting confidence and purpose. It is not a way to reduce data streaming, replace navigation support, or convert all usability requirements into functional requirements.

37/A8  recap  37/S3  "Recap"  (12 facts, 33 concepts)
  Contextual inquiry shaped usability requirements for the Majuli VR Tour. Fieldwork first defined the intended non-resident user groups, and CI then clarified their needs, supported features, and usability challenges. Those challenges motivate targeted design decisions, such as group-specific data subsets, location awareness, heritage presentation, and interaction support.
  - Majuli VR Tour usability requirements were gathered through field trips, interviews, natural work-setting observations, and notes.
  - Majuli VR Tour usability is claimed only for non-resident student, tourist, and pilgrim groups.
  - For large geographies, each user group accesses a CI-identified subset of Majuli data, reducing exploration and cybersickness risk.
  - CI then studied user-group samples to identify needs, features, and location, heritage, and interaction challenges.
  judge round 1: 2 of 5 failed
    1 pass  (Majuli VR Tour usability requirements were gathered through field trips, interviews, natural work-setting observations …)
      check: none
      reason: The point accurately condenses fact 1: the Majuli VR Tour usability requirements were gathered by field trips, interviews, natural work-setting observations, and notes as collected data.
    2 pass  (Majuli VR Tour usability is claimed only for non-resident student, tourist, and pilgrim groups.)
      check: none
      reason: Facts 2, 3, and 4 together support the claim that the tour is intended for non-residents and that usability is claimed only for the identified student, tourist, and pilgrim groups.
    3 FAIL supported,faithful  (For large geographies, each user group accesses a CI-identified subset of Majuli data, reducing …)
      check: large geographical area [6]
      reason: Fails because “For large geographies” generalizes beyond the facts, which describe the large geographical area challenge specifically in the Majuli VR Tour case. A repaired version would say “In the Majuli VR Tour, each user group accessed a CI-identified subset of data, reducing exploration and cybersickness risk.”
    4 FAIL faithful,one_idea  (CI then studied user-group samples to identify needs, features, and location, heritage, and interaction …)
      check: system features [5]; broad design challenges [5]
      reason: Fails because it packs several distinct outputs of CI into one point and turns specific challenge examples—location, heritage, and interaction—into the list of CI outcomes, while facts 11 and 12 do not explicitly say CI identified those heritage and interaction challenges. A repaired version would focus on CI’s stated purpose: “CI on Majuli user-group samples identified their needs, expected features, and usability issues such as location awareness.”
    0 pass  (Contextual inquiry shaped usability requirements for the Majuli VR Tour.)
      check: none
      reason: The text is a coherent summary of how fieldwork identified the intended non-resident user groups and how CI then clarified needs, supported features, and usability challenges, connecting them to design responses such as data subsets, location awareness, heritage presentation, and interaction support.

37/A13  match_pairs  lecture  "Match the terms"  (17 facts, 8 concepts)
  contextual inquiry = A usability requirement-gathering method, often described as a semi-structured interview process, that observes users performing tasks in their natural work setting and …
  functional requirement = A formally specifiable requirement that specifies a system feature as a black-box function with a well-defined input and output, optionally its purpose …
  design guideline = A statement about an interactive system that says what should or should not be done to make it usable, without saying how …
  software requirements specification = A textual document that specifies all of a system's requirements, both functional and non-functional, including the formal specification of its functional requirements.
  requirement hierarchy = A hierarchy in which requirements are generally organized in a software requirements specification, with identifiers distinguishing top-level requirements from sub-requirements, each representing …
  requirement identifier = An identifier in a software requirements specification hierarchy that represents a function with a clearly defined input, a clearly defined output, and …
  location awareness = A wayfinding feature for ascertaining a path through the environment to a desired destination and transferring spatial knowledge to the real world.
  interaction aid = A virtual reality design aid that enhances user experience by providing navigation support, user-friendly interfaces, and natural interactions that increase presence.

37/A16  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (7 facts, 26 concepts)
  Q How can a usability requirement gathered through contextual inquiry become part of the code design of an XR system?  [37/S0/F0, 37/S2/F1, 37/S0/F1; contextual inquiry, usability requirement, functional requirement, code design]
    A The outcome of contextual inquiry can be used as a functional requirement. Usability requirements are non-functional requirements, and they can be converted into functional requirements that are added to the system's requirements. A functional requirement specifies a function with a well-defined input and output, making it easy to convert into code, so usability is incorporated through code design.
  Q Why did the Majuli virtual reality tour address the large geography challenge by giving each user group only a subset of the collected data?  [37/S3/F6, 37/S3/F7; cybersickness, data subset restriction, user group]
    A The tour used group-specific subsets because that reduced the expanse of information and the need to explore everything in detail, reduced the possibility of cybersickness, and increased interest for each group. Contextual inquiry identified what each user group typically does, so each group was allowed to access only that subset instead of the entire data set. Making the entire data set accessible to all users could confuse users, reduce their interest, and lead to cybersickness.
  Q How does a location awareness feature address the challenge of exploring a large geographical area in the Majuli virtual reality tour?  [37/S3/F8, 37/S3/F9; location awareness, large geographical area, geographical space]
    A Accurate location information is crucial in any virtual reality tour, especially for a large geographical area, because it prevents disorientation and gives users confidence and purpose by telling them where they are in geographical space. Contextual inquiry in the Majuli virtual reality tour identified location awareness as an issue for users exploring a large space, and a possible resolution was to add a location awareness feature later converted into functional requirements.

===== lecture 38: System Design

38/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (14 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is design guideline? (lecture 36) -> Design guideline is a statement about an interactive system that says what should or should not be done to make it usable, without saying how to implement it; it can be generic or particular to a system, and is only a starting point to be implemented and tested.
  What is extended reality (XR)? (lecture 1) -> Extended reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR).
  What is augmented reality (AR)? (lecture 1) -> Augmented reality (AR) is an enhanced version of reality created by technology, in which computer-generated digital content is overlaid on the real world in real time and registered in 3D, so the user perceives and interacts with the enhanced environment.
  What is mixed reality (MR)? (lecture 1) -> Mixed reality (MR) is an immersive technology that is the same as augmented reality, in which digital content is overlaid on the view of reality and can be interacted with.
  What is immersive experience? (lecture 1) -> An immersive experience is a perceived experience through sensory organs that appears real, because a person cannot distinguish the experienced environment from their real environment and perceives it as that real environment.
  What is immersion? (lecture 2) -> Immersion is the objective, quantifiable degree to which a virtual reality system projects stimuli onto the sensory receptors of users in an extensive, matching, surrounding, vivid, interactive, and plot-informing way.

    * the design stage in the design-prototype-evaluate cycle and the code design stage
    - the implementation stage and the empirical usability evaluation stage
    - the requirement-gathering stage and the interface and interaction design stage
    - the prototyping stage and the early evaluation stage
    because: The interactive system development lifecycle has two design stages: the design stage within the design-prototype-evaluate cycle and code design. The other pairs either name non-design stages or mix a design activity with a stage that is not itself a design stage.
  Q How is code design characterized in the interactive system development lifecycle?  [38/S0/F1]
    - a new design language created for immersive system development
    - a later implementation step performed after coded development
    * the same code design used in non-interactive software development
    - a special code design introduced by interactive system development
    because: Code design in interactive system development is the same as code design in any other non-interactive software development, so it is not a special interactive-system design activity. A design language is a separate way of expressing design, not the code design itself.

38/A3  quiz  38/S1  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 11 concepts)
  Q In interface and interaction design, what are the two central issues?  [38/S1/F1]
    - How to gather and how to approve a design
    * Where to start and how to express a design
    - Where to place and how to style a design
    - How to test and how to refine a design
    because: Interface and interaction design centers on where or how to begin the design process and on having a way to express the design so it can be developed further. Placement, styling, approval, and testing are related activities but not the two central design issues.
  Q Which pair can serve as starting points for interface and interaction design?  [38/S1/F2]
    - Code design and release checks as starting points

38/A10  recap  38/S4  "Recap"  (4 facts, 7 concepts)
  Usable interface design depends on two related rules: informative feedback and task closure. Informative feedback responds to user actions, helping the user understand what the system is doing and whether an action succeeded. Task closure complements this by organizing tasks into beginning, middle, and end, with feedback at each group’s end, so the user experiences the task as started, executed, and completed.
  - The third usable-design rule is to provide informative feedback for every user action, showing progress or successful completion.
  - The fourth usable-design rule is to design dialogues to yield closure by organizing tasks into groups and giving feedback after each.

38/A13  quiz  38/S6  "Quick quiz"  (4 facts, 15 concepts)
  Q What does feedback about a user's action mainly protect against under the keeping-users-in-control rule?  [38/S6/F0]
    - the user missing the end of a task sequence
    * the user feeling at a loss about the system's response
    - the user accidentally selecting a nearby wrong control
    - the user being unable to reverse an incorrect choice
    because: Under the control rule, feedback lets a lay user see that their interaction changed the system state and produced a result; without it, the user can feel at a loss. The other options describe error prevention, reversal, or task closure rather than the control problem.
  Q What does the short-term memory usability rule require a designer to do with the information a user must remember to operate an interface?  [38/S6/F2, 38/S6/F3]
    - storing it in long-term memory before the task begins
    * keeping it within the five-to-nine chunk limit
    - reducing it to one fixed-size unit for every application
    - showing it as a progress indicator during the interaction
    because: The rule keeps required interaction information within the short-term memory range of five to nine chunks. Long-term memory is a different store, chunk size is not fixed, and a progress indicator is a feedback device rather than a memory-load control.
  Q Why can the eight generic usability rules be applied to an extended reality system?  [38/S6/F5]

    - because they define the correct input modality for VR
    - because they measure a user's physiological comfort during use
    because: The rules are generic enough to be analyzed for applicability to broad classes of interactive systems, including XR. They do not substitute for hardware, prescribe a single input modality, or measure comfort.

38/A14  recap  38/S6  "Recap"  (6 facts, 17 concepts)
  Two usability rules are examined: keeping users in control and reducing short-term memory load. The control rule concerns user feedback and awareness of system change, while the memory rule is grounded in short-term memory's five-to-nine-chunk limit and in what counts as a chunk. The eight generic rules are not tied to one product, so they can be assessed for broad interactive systems, including extended reality.
  - The keeping-users-in-control rule helps lay users feel in control, perceive state changes, and receive feedback, reducing loss and poor usability.
  - Human short-term memory is a non-permanent store that brings long-term information to aid day-to-day activities.
  - George Miller's 1956 seven-plus-or-minus-two rule says short-term memory holds five to nine chunks, so fewer underuses and more harms it.
  - The reducing-short-term-memory-load rule keeps interaction information between five and nine chunks, a chunk being a letter, word, sentence, or concept.
  - The eight generic usability rules are not product-specific; they can be assessed for broad interactive systems, including extended reality.
  judge round 1: 4 of 6 failed

    - Lower memory load
    - Simplified setup
    - Standardized actions
    * Enhanced presence

    * System control
    - Navigation

38/A16  recap  38/S7  "Recap"  (3 facts, 14 concepts)
  XR interaction differs between non-immersive and immersive settings: non-immersive AR uses familiar touch and gesture-like interactions, while immersive VR or MR uses specialized techniques. Those immersive techniques are organized into object interaction, navigation, and interaction for system control. This organization helps design the experience properly and enhance presence.
  - AR interaction in non-immersive settings is similar to familiar touch and gesture interactions.
  - Immersive VR or MR experiences require specialized, suitable interaction techniques to design properly and enhance presence.
  - Immersive interaction is categorized into object interaction, navigation, and interaction for system control, with selection, movement, and setting changes.
  judge round 1: 2 of 4 failed

      reason: The point says immersive VR or MR experiences "require specialized, suitable interaction techniques," but fact 2 only says specialized techniques and setups are used and suitable interaction techniques should be known and used. A repaired version should say something like: "For immersive VR or MR experiences, suitable specialized interaction techniques should be known and used to design the experience properly and enhance presence."
    3 pass  (Immersive interaction is categorized into object interaction, navigation, and interaction for system control, with …)
      check: none
      reason: Fact 3 supports that immersive interaction is broadly categorized into object interaction, navigation, and interaction for system control, and the brief phrases selection, movement, and setting changes are supported as shortened descriptions of those categories.
    0 FAIL supported,faithful  (XR interaction differs between non-immersive and immersive settings: non-immersive AR uses familiar touch and …)

38/A23  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (8 facts, 20 concepts)
  Q Why might design guidelines for avoiding cybersickness in virtual reality not transfer directly to an augmented reality system?  [38/S2/F0, 8/S3/F0; cybersickness, virtual reality, augmented reality, immersion]
    A Such guidelines are specific to virtual reality or immersive systems where immersion is very important. An augmented reality system's immersion differs from that of a virtual reality system, and immersion is an objective, quantifiable description of what a particular system can provide. Therefore a guideline based on virtual reality immersion may not be specifically applicable to augmented reality.
  Q Why can Shneiderman's Eight Golden Rules help in designing an extended reality system although they were originally developed mainly for graphical user interfaces?  [38/S2/F1, 38/S2/F2, 38/S6/F5; Ben Shneiderman's Eight Golden Rules, extended reality system, interactive system, graphical user interface]
    A They are generic design rules applicable to any interactive system, and an extended reality system is a kind of interactive system. The rules are not specific to a particular product or system, so they can be analyzed for applicability to a broad class of interactive systems. Because they can be partly or fully applicable to other interfaces, they remain useful for extended reality despite their graphical user interface origin.
  Q How do internal consistency and external consistency differ as aspects of consistency in system design?  [38/S3/F1, 38/S3/F2, 38/S3/F3; consistency, internal consistency, external consistency, system design]
    A Internal consistency means using the same elements and interactions for the same task across different parts of a design and different usage instances, rather than separate objects, elements, or interactions. External consistency means that elements and interactions in a virtual world should closely match the user's real-world experience and knowledge. The first is uniformity within the design; the second is alignment with the user's real-world knowledge so it can transfer to the virtual world.

===== lecture 39: System Design

39/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (12 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is interaction? (lecture 23) -> Interaction is the activity that takes place between a user and a system, often by manipulating an image or parts of it with input devices. In immersive environments it is broadly categorized into object interaction, navigation, and system control.
  What is degree of freedom? (lecture 28) -> Degree of freedom is an indication of the different ways an object can move in space; in 3D space, an object can have six degrees of freedom: three translational degrees of freedom along the x, y, and z axes, and three rotational degrees of freedom called yaw, roll, and pitch.
  What is six degrees of freedom? (lecture 28) -> Six degrees of freedom is the total of six freedoms an object can have in three-dimensional space, consisting of three rotational freedoms called yaw, roll, and pitch, and three translational freedoms along the x, y, and z axes.
  What is object interaction? (lecture 38) -> Object interaction is a kind of interaction in immersive virtual environments that involves selecting one or more virtual objects in the environment and manipulating a selected object to change its properties.
  What is navigation? (lecture 38) -> Navigation is an interaction in an immersive virtual world that moves the user from one point to another by changing the user's viewpoint, mostly without object interaction, and has two components: locomotion and wayfinding.
  What is augmented reality system? (lecture 5) -> An augmented reality system is a system with four required characteristics: it enhances the real world with computer-generated digital content registered in 3D, that content is experienced through the user's sensory organs, and it supports real-time interaction with that content in the enhanced environment.

39/A2  recap  39/S0  "Recap"  (1 facts, 9 concepts)
  Interaction in immersive experience design is grouped into three broad categories. Object interaction involves interacting with virtual objects, while navigation moves from one point to another with a corresponding change in viewpoint; it mostly does not involve object interaction, though some navigation techniques may require it. System control is set apart from object manipulation, object interaction, and navigation; it is a mostly regular type of interaction used to set up the system, initialize parameters, provide initial information, and set options or menus.
  - Interaction in immersive experience design is broadly divided into object interaction, navigation, and system control.

39/A5  quiz  39/S2  "Quick quiz"  (7 facts, 10 concepts)
  Q Why can the virtual hand technique become annoying when the selected object is far away?  [39/S2/F2, 39/S2/F3]
    - The physical hand must stop for a long time before the virtual grab occurs
    - The virtual arm must lengthen for a long time before the virtual grab occurs
    * The physical hand must move for a long time before the virtual grab occurs
    - The proximity sphere must shrink for a long time before the virtual grab occurs
    because: The virtual hand follows the physical hand closely, so reaching a distant object can require a long real hand movement. The other options describe effects of other techniques, not the basic virtual hand.
  Q How does the go-go technique make a distant virtual object easier to reach?  [39/S2/F4]
    - It maps smaller physical hand movements to the same virtual hand movements as distance grows
    - It maps smaller physical hand movements to slower virtual hand movements as distance grows
    - It maps smaller physical hand movements to stopped virtual hand movements as distance grows
    * It maps smaller physical hand movements to faster virtual hand movements as distance grows
    because: Go-go increases virtual hand movement for smaller physical hand movements as the target gets farther, reducing the real movement needed to reach it. A one-to-one or reduced mapping would not provide that reaching benefit.
  Q What control does the prism technique add for a distant target that go-go does not have?  [39/S2/F6, 39/S2/F7]
    - Stopping the physical hand can enlarge the proximity sphere
    - Stopping the physical hand can shorten the virtual arm
    * Stopping the physical hand can stop the virtual hand
    - Stopping the physical hand can lengthen the virtual arm
    because: Prism can keep the virtual hand still when the physical hand is still, which helps with precise distant selection. Go-go lacks that stop control, and stopping does not change arm length or the proximity sphere.

39/A6  recap  39/S2  "Recap"  (12 facts, 15 concepts)
  Hand-based object selection uses the physical hand to virtually touch and grab objects. Its techniques differ in reach: virtual hand keeps a one-to-one avatar of the physical hand but can make distant reaches tiring, while go-go and prism adjust speed for distant objects and introduce precision, stopping, and alignment trade-offs. Intent-driven selection refines a target through finger posture and shrinking proximity spheres, and it can be combined with the go-go or prism travel techniques.
  - Hand selection uses one physical hand to virtually touch and grab objects, with virtual hand, go-go, prism, and intent-driven techniques.
  - Virtual hand maps the physical hand one-to-one to a visible hand, but distant objects require tiring reaches.
  - Go-go speeds distant reaches but loses precision, while prism improves go-go by slowing or stopping the hand, but mismatches positions.
  - Intent-driven selection uses finger posture and shrinking proximity spheres to indicate confidence and refine the chosen object.
  - Go-go and prism are travel techniques, while intent-driven selection is a grabbing technique that can combine with them.
  judge round 1: 5 of 6 failed
    1 FAIL faithful  (Hand selection uses one physical hand to virtually touch and grab objects, with virtual …)

39/A10  recap  39/S4  "Recap"  (14 facts, 23 concepts)
  Image-plane and volumetric selection form the third category of object selection. Image-plane methods select on a two-dimensional view plane by occlusion or framing, while volumetric methods select objects inside a three-dimensional region using cone, sphere, or two-handed box methods. Volumetric methods can pick multiple objects, and they are most useful for small, well-defined isolated objects in less complex virtual environments.
  - The third object selection category is image-plane or volumetric selection.
  - Image-plane selection is 2D occlusion/framing: the user aligns a hand or finger with an object and signals.
  - Image-plane techniques include head crusher, sticky finger, lifting palm, and framing hands, with framing hands being more common.
  - Volumetric selection selects objects inside a 3D region using cone, sphere, or two-handed box methods; cones can select multiple objects.
  - Volumetric selection is most useful for small, well-defined isolated objects in less complex virtual environments.

  - Object manipulation modifies an object's properties and usually comes after selecting that object.

  - Hand manipulation may need somewhat more computational power or specialized devices that may be relatively costly.

39/A14  recap  39/S6  "Recap"  (7 facts, 12 concepts)
  Indirect manipulation controls virtual objects through other mapped objects rather than by moving the virtual object with the physical hand. One simple form uses 3D widgets placed in the scene, although each usually handles only a small set of degrees of freedom. Proxy-based techniques let a user move a local proxy to move a linked virtual object, and world-in-miniature uses a handheld miniature model to reach objects both nearby and distant, though building that model is hard for large complex environments.
  - Indirect manipulation controls virtual objects by manipulating mapped objects, not by manipulating the virtual objects with the physical hand.
  - 3D widgets are scene controls; each typically handles a small set of degrees of freedom, so several may be used.
  - Indirect proxies offer more natural grasping by letting users move a local proxy that moves a linked virtual object.
  - World-in-miniature is a miniature proxy model, where manipulating a model object moves the corresponding virtual object, both nearby and distant.
  - World-in-miniature is not very practical for large, complex virtual environments because making its miniature model is very difficult.

  - A bimanual manipulation technique uses both hands, with synchronous or asynchronous hand movement.

  - In the spindle technique, unison hand movement can move and also simultaneously rotate a virtual world object.
  - The spindle technique is not easy because synchronous hand movement in a virtual world requires practice to use efficiently.
  - Spindle plus wheel is an asymmetric synchronous extension of the spindle technique, requiring both hands moved together but not symmetrically.

39/A18  recap  39/S8  "Recap"  (5 facts, 12 concepts)
  Integrated hybrid manipulation describes techniques that automatically move from selection to manipulation and back without an explicit user signal. HOMER applies this idea by combining ray-casting selection with hand manipulation. When the ray selects an object, HOMER attaches the user's virtual hand to the object, enables hand manipulation of its position and orientation, and ends with a trigger or specific gesture that returns the hand to its original position.
  - Integrated hybrid manipulation techniques automatically switch from selection to manipulation and back without an explicit user signal.
  - HOMER is an integrated hybrid technique that combines ray-casting selection with hand manipulation, so they are not separate.
  - In HOMER, when the ray hits the desired object, the virtual hand automatically attaches, not the ray.
  - After the virtual hand attaches, HOMER switches to manipulation mode, enabling hand manipulation of the object's position and orientation.
  - In HOMER, a trigger or specific hand gesture ends manipulation and returns the virtual hand to its original position.

  interaction = The activity that takes place between a user and a system, often by manipulating an image or parts of it with input …

  immersive environment = An environment that, in the ideal case, blocks the user's senses and cuts the user off from the real world.
  object interaction = A kind of interaction in immersive virtual environments that involves selecting one or more virtual objects in the environment and manipulating a …
  navigation = An interaction in an immersive virtual world that moves the user from one point to another by changing the user's viewpoint, mostly …
  object manipulation = An interaction technique in immersive environments that, typically after selection, modifies a virtual object's properties such as position, orientation, scale, shape, color …
  navigation technique = An interaction technique for moving from one point to another in a virtual world with a change in viewpoint, mostly without object …
  system control = A mostly regular type of interaction in immersive experiences that uses familiar computer-system techniques to set up the system, initialize parameters, provide …

39/A27  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (14 facts, 28 concepts)
  Q Why might the prism technique be easier to control than the go-go technique when selecting a small distant virtual object?  [39/S2/F4, 39/S2/F5, 39/S2/F6, 39/S2/F7; prism technique, go-go technique, hand velocity]
    A The prism technique is easier to control because slowing or stopping the physical hand slows or stops the virtual hand, which go-go cannot do. Go-go maps smaller physical movements to larger, faster virtual movements as distance increases, so a distant small target can be missed or bypassed. Prism scales down virtual motion when the hand is slow and keeps the virtual hand still below a minimum speed.
  Q Why might depth ray be more reliable than bend cast when several objects are close to the path of a virtual ray?  [39/S3/F6, 39/S3/F7, 39/S3/F8; bend cast, depth ray, depth marker, virtual ray]
    A Depth ray is more reliable in that case because the user can choose depth explicitly, while bend cast relies on closeness to the ray. Bend cast bends toward the closest selectable object by point-line distance, so several nearby objects of similar distances can make the intended object not the closest. Depth ray uses a user-controlled depth marker to disambiguate multiple intersected objects and select the one closest to the marker.
  Q How does Hand-Centered Object Manipulation Extending Ray Casting combine selection and manipulation into one continuous interaction?  [39/S1/F0, 39/S8/F0, 39/S8/F1, 39/S8/F2; Hand-Centered Object Manipulation Extending Ray Casting, ray casting, hand manipulation, integrated hybrid manipulation]
    A It reduces separate actions by automatically moving from selection to manipulation once a ray selects the object. Selection and manipulation mostly use separate techniques. HOMER mixes ray casting with hand manipulation and switches automatically without an explicit signal; when the ray intersects the object, the virtual hand moves to and attaches to it.
  Q Why is world in miniature less practical for large and complex virtual environments even though it can manipulate distant virtual objects?  [39/S6/F4, 39/S6/F5, 39/S6/F6; world in miniature, miniature model, virtual environment, virtual object]
    A World in miniature becomes less practical for large and complex virtual environments because creating the miniature model is very difficult. The technique provides a miniature handheld model that represents all objects in the virtual environment. Manipulating an object in that model manipulates the corresponding actual object, even outside the user's reach, but that complete model is hard to create when the environment is large and complex.

===== lecture 40: System Design

40/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (15 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is tangible user interface? (lecture 31) -> Tangible user interface is a real-world object whose virtual avatar appears in a virtual world and that, by aligning the real world and the virtual world, provides feedback to the user's somatosensory system in place of computer-controlled haptic devices.
  What is navigation? (lecture 38) -> Navigation is an interaction in an immersive virtual world that moves the user from one point to another by changing the user's viewpoint, mostly without object interaction, and has two components: locomotion and wayfinding.
  What is object manipulation? (lecture 39) -> Object manipulation is an interaction technique in immersive environments that, typically after selection, modifies a virtual object's properties such as position, orientation, scale, shape, color, texture, or behavior.
  What is go-go technique? (lecture 39) -> The go-go technique is a virtual hand selection technique for distant virtual objects that uses one-to-one mapping when the target is close, allows the user to change virtual arm and hand length interactively, and, as distance increases, maps smaller physical hand movements to larger and faster virtual hand movements, possibly exponentially, so distant objects can be reached quickly.
  What is three-dimensional widget? (lecture 39) -> A three-dimensional widget is a simple indirect manipulation technique that places controls directly in a 3D scene with virtual objects, so manipulating a widget manipulates its associated object; each widget is typically responsible for only a small set of manipulation degrees of freedom.
  What is world in miniature (WIM)? (lecture 39) -> World in miniature (WIM) is an indirect proxy that provides a miniature handheld model of a virtual environment, representing all objects in the virtual world. Manipulating a model object manipulates the corresponding virtual object, even if it is outside the user's reach; moving certain model objects can also change the virtual viewpoint.

40/A4  recap  40/S1  "Recap"  (5 facts, 12 concepts)
  Navigation’s travel side, called locomotion, is the actual motor movement between places, and locomotion techniques make that movement happen and perceptible in virtual worlds. That travel can serve open exploration, targeted search, or short precise maneuvering, and the techniques fall into walking-based, steering-based, selection-based, and manipulation-based families. Object manipulation is mostly absent across these families except for manipulation-based locomotion, though it is not entirely avoided in immersive implementations.
  - The travel part of navigation, also called locomotion, is its motor component, the actual movement between locations.
  - Locomotion techniques, also travel techniques, let users travel between virtual places and perceive that travel occurred.
  - Navigation travel can be exploration with no target, search for a target, or short precise maneuvering.
  - Four broad locomotion technique types are walking-based, steering-based, selection-based, and manipulation-based.
  - Walking, steering, and selection may not involve object manipulation; manipulation-based uses it, though it is mostly avoided in immersive travel.

40/A10  recap  40/S4  "Recap"  (8 facts, 14 concepts)
  Selection-based and manipulation-based locomotion are two families of travel techniques. Selection-based locomotion has the user choose a target or route; target selection moves the viewpoint to a chosen place, while route planning follows a selected path and gives more control and slightly more natural movement than target teleportation. Manipulation-based locomotion instead changes position, orientation, or scale through gestures and miniature-world object changes.
  - Selection-based locomotion lets the user choose where to go rather than steer or look continuously.
  - Selection-based locomotion has two types: target selection and route planning.
  - Target selection-based locomotion can change the viewpoint to a chosen destination, using teleportation, map dragging, or the cave-system jumper.
  - Route planning-based locomotion lets the user select a route, giving more control and slightly more natural movement than target teleportation.
  - Manipulation-based locomotion can use gestures to manipulate position, orientation, or scale, combining go-go, homer, and miniature-world metaphors.

40/A12  recap  40/S5  "Recap"  (12 facts, 33 concepts)
  Wayfinding is the mental part of navigation: it involves knowing where one is, choosing a path, and retaining usable spatial knowledge. Because this mental model is what allows users to move toward destinations, environment design should help users form it. In complex virtual environments, locomotion alone is insufficient, so designers can add supports such as landmarks, maps, paths, breadcrumbs, and direction indicators to strengthen wayfinding.
  - Navigation has locomotion and wayfinding; wayfinding is location awareness, finding destination paths, and transferring spatial knowledge to the real world.
  - Wayfinding builds a mental model of the environment, so design should support it or user experience deteriorates.
  - Wayfinding spatial knowledge includes landmark, procedural, and topological knowledge, built through maps, real-space exploration, or model exploration.
  - In complex virtual environments, wayfinding support is essential; without it, travel techniques are not used efficiently or effectively.
  - Wayfinding supports include visible landmarks, maps, colored paths, breadcrumbs, and direction indicators.

40/A17  match_pairs  lecture  "Match the terms"  (15 facts, 8 concepts)
  locomotion = The motor component of navigation in a virtual world, the actual movement between two locations, carried out by techniques that let a …
  teleportation = A virtual reality locomotion operation in which a user selects a virtual target location and the virtual viewpoint instantly changes from the …
  locomotion technique = A technique that lets a user travel in a virtual world from one place to another and perceive that travel has taken …
  navigation = An interaction in an immersive virtual world that moves the user from one point to another by changing the user's viewpoint, mostly …
  interaction for system control = An interaction technique in immersive environments that issues commands to change system state, mode, or system-related settings.
  world in miniature = An indirect proxy that provides a miniature handheld model of a virtual environment, representing all objects in the virtual world.
  wayfinding = The component of navigation, other than locomotion or travel, that provides location awareness, ascertains a path to a destination, transfers spatial knowledge …
  exploration = A kind of travel in navigation that has no explicit goal or target point, where the user moves around to see, learn …

40/A20  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (14 facts, 47 concepts)
  Q How does navigation differ from object manipulation and interaction for system control in terms of what each changes in a virtual experience?  [40/S0/F0, 40/S1/F4, 40/S6/F0, 39/S5/F0; navigation, object manipulation, interaction for system control]
    A Navigation changes the user's location by changing the virtual viewpoint, and it mostly does not involve object manipulation. Object manipulation changes the properties of a selected virtual object, such as its position, orientation, or scale. Interaction for system control issues commands that change the system's state or mode, such as settings or applications.
  Q Why is wayfinding support essential in a complex virtual environment even when a system provides many locomotion techniques?  [40/S5/F2, 40/S5/F3, 40/S5/F6; wayfinding, mental model, user experience]
    A Wayfinding aims to build a mental model of the surroundings and of the path to a destination, so that the user can locate themselves and choose a suitable path. Environment design should support this mental map. Without wayfinding support, travel techniques cannot be used efficiently or effectively, and the overall user experience deteriorates.
  Q How does route planning-based locomotion create movement differently from target selection-based locomotion?  [40/S4/F2, 40/S4/F3, 40/S4/F4; target selection-based locomotion, route planning-based locomotion, viewpoint]
    A In target selection-based locomotion, the user selects a destination and the viewpoint changes to make the user feel moved there, as in teleportation or map dragging. In route planning-based locomotion, the user selects a route to the target, and different viewpoint changes along that route make the user feel movement along a path. This gives more granular control and slightly more natural movement than teleportation.
  Q How do spatial steering-based navigation and physical steering-based navigation differ in how the user controls direction and speed?  [40/S3/F0, 40/S3/F1, 40/S3/F2, 40/S3/F3; steering-based navigation, spatial steering-based navigation, physical steering-based navigation]
    A Both types continuously control direction and speed while the user moves. Spatial steering uses body-based signals, such as gaze, hand gestures, or body lean, to determine travel. Physical steering uses separate hardware or setups, such as bike locomotion platforms or VR simulators, where moving the controls changes virtual travel.
  judge round 1: 0 of 4 failed
    1 pass  (How does navigation differ from object manipulation and interaction for system control in terms …)
      check: The cited facts say navigation changes the user’s viewpoint or location and mostly does not involve object manipulation, while object manipulation changes an object’s properties and system control issues commands that change system state or mode.
      reason: Facts 1 and 7 carry navigation’s viewpoint/location change and its mostly non-manipulative nature; fact 46 carries object manipulation’s property changes; fact 40 carries system control’s state/mode-changing commands.
    2 pass  (Why is wayfinding support essential in a complex virtual environment even when a system …)

      reason: Fact 30 links wayfinding to a mental model for location and path identification; fact 34 says many locomotion techniques are not useful or effective without wayfinding support; fact 31 adds that unsupported mental mapping worsens user experience.

      reason: Facts 22 and 23 state target selection’s direct viewpoint change to a destination, including teleportation and map dragging; fact 24 states route planning’s selected route, multiple viewpoint changes, and its advantage over teleportation.

      check: The cited facts say both steering types continuously control direction and speed, with spatial steering using body-based signals such as gaze, hand, or body lean and physical steering using hardware or setups such as bike platforms or VR simulators.

===== lecture 41: System Design

41/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (14 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is teleportation? (lecture 11) -> Teleportation is a virtual reality locomotion operation in which a user selects a virtual target location and the virtual viewpoint instantly changes from the current location to that target, without physical movement.
  What is navigation? (lecture 38) -> Navigation is an interaction in an immersive virtual world that moves the user from one point to another by changing the user's viewpoint, mostly without object interaction, and has two components: locomotion and wayfinding.
  What is locomotion technique? (lecture 40) -> Locomotion technique is a technique that lets a user travel in a virtual world from one place to another and perceive that travel has taken place.
  What is wayfinding? (lecture 40) -> Wayfinding is the component of navigation, other than locomotion or travel, that provides location awareness, ascertains a path to a destination, transfers spatial knowledge to the real world, and builds a mental model of the environment.
  What is virtual reality (VR)? (lecture 4) -> Virtual reality (VR) is an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli provided by a computer, in which a person's actions partially determine what happens and which replaces the user's sense of reality without requiring the physical existence of objects or places.
  What is virtual environment? (lecture 4) -> Virtual environment is a non-real, computer-generated graphical representation of a real or imaginary world, populated with artificial objects, that is experienced through computer-generated sensory stimuli.

41/A23  match_pairs  lecture  "Match the terms"  (20 facts, 8 concepts)
  interactive system development lifecycle = A staged development method that is similar to regular software development but distinctive in its end-user requirement gathering, iterative design-prototype-evaluate cycle, and …
  textual description = Descriptive text that provides additional context about locations, significant spots, artifacts, objects, or elements in a virtual tour or multimodal archive.
  minimap = A local world-in-miniature map of a specific place, distinct from a global map, that shows the arrangement of 360-degree images as white …
  tutorial video = A video that explains to users how to control and use a system.
  boat ride experience = The opening part of a virtual tour that uses a 360-degree boat ride video to give the user the feeling of being …
  preprocessing = A process for collected images and videos that improves their visual appearance and the user's quality of experience by using high-resolution content …
  tablet interface = A virtual interface that serves as the main interface in a virtual tour system, providing navigation tools, a video player, and access …
  navigation tool = A tool provided by a virtual tablet interface, such as a left-side island map presented as a world in miniature and buttons …

41/A26  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (9 facts, 33 concepts)
  Q How do the global island map and the local minimap in the Majuli VR tour work together to support a user's location awareness and wayfinding?  [41/S5/F5, 41/S5/F6, 41/S5/F0; dual maps, island map, minimap, location awareness]
    A The global island map and the local minimap form dual maps: the island map shows the whole island as a world in miniature on the tablet, while the minimap shows a specific place on the local interface. This separation reduces clutter and gives clear navigation support. The minimap also gives local orientation and indicates direction, helping the user build a mental model and wayfind.
  Q Why did the Majuli VR tour use a virtual vehicle travel technique for long-distance movement rather than walking-based navigation across the island?  [41/S6/F4, 41/S6/F5, 41/S6/F6; virtual vehicle travel technique, walking-based technique, cybersickness, selection-based locomotion technique]
    A Exploring the entire island with walking-based navigation would take a lot of time and may lead to cybersickness, so a different travel technique was required. The virtual vehicle gives the user a seated viewpoint inside the vehicle and changes the surrounding scenes as it moves to create motion. The user selects a destination by ray casting, and because the route is pre-planned, this is selection-based route selection rather than target selection or instantaneous movement.
  Q Why does the Majuli VR tour ask a user to choose pilgrim, student, or tourist before the virtual tour begins?  [41/S1/F1, 41/S2/F2, 41/S7/F1; user group, user type, virtual reality tour, tablet interface]
    A The choice is needed because the tour distinguishes pilgrims, students, and tourists as distinct user groups, and each group has its own preferences for exploring the island. The user chooses one of these icons before the tour so the experience can be tailored to that user type. At each spot, the tablet interface adds and lists videos whose relevance is determined by the current location and the user type.
  judge round 1: 0 of 3 failed
    1 pass  (How do the global island map and the local minimap in the Majuli VR …)
      check: They form dual maps: the tablet’s global island map gives whole-island orientation, while the local minimap gives local orientation and direction, reducing clutter and supporting navigation and wayfinding.
      reason: Facts 27 and 28 carry the dual-map link, clutter reduction, and wayfinding support, and fact 22 adds the minimap’s specific-place local orientation.
    2 pass  (Why did the Majuli VR tour use a virtual vehicle travel technique for long-distance …)
      check: Walking across the whole island would take too long and could cause cybersickness, so the tour uses a virtual vehicle that gives a seated moving viewpoint and lets the user select a pre-planned destination route.
      reason: Fact 33 gives the problem with walking-based island exploration, and facts 34 and 35 describe the virtual vehicle’s seated motion, ray-cast destination selection, and pre-planned route selection.
    3 pass  (Why does the Majuli VR tour ask a user to choose pilgrim, student, or …)
