===== lecture 42: System Implementation

42/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (17 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is interactive system development lifecycle (ISDLC)? (lecture 32) -> Interactive system development lifecycle (ISDLC) is a staged development method that is similar to regular software development but distinctive in its end-user requirement gathering, iterative design-prototype-evaluate cycle, and empirical usability evaluation.
  What is design? (lecture 41) -> Design is the interface and interaction design part of the design-prototype-evaluate cycle in interactive system development, not code design, that may be based on intuition, design guidelines, or team brainstorming, and is refined through prototyping and quick evaluation until stable.
  What is extended reality (XR)? (lecture 1) -> Extended reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR).
  What is augmented reality (AR)? (lecture 1) -> Augmented reality (AR) is an enhanced version of reality created by technology, in which computer-generated digital content is overlaid on the real world in real time and registered in 3D, so the user perceives and interacts with the enhanced environment.
  What is virtual reality (VR)? (lecture 4) -> Virtual reality (VR) is an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli provided by a computer, in which a person's actions partially determine what happens and which replaces the user's sense of reality without requiring the physical existence of objects or places.
  What is virtual environment? (lecture 4) -> Virtual environment is a non-real, computer-generated graphical representation of a real or imaginary world, populated with artificial objects, that is experienced through computer-generated sensory stimuli.

42/A1  quiz  42/S0  "Quick quiz"  (6 facts, 21 concepts)
  Q At what point is the final usability evaluation of the whole system performed in an interactive system lifecycle?  [42/S0/F0, 42/S0/F2]
    - After the feasibility study approves the idea
    - After the final prototype is accepted as usable
    * After code testing shows the system runs smoothly
    - After the requirements are signed off by the client
    because: The whole system is empirically evaluated for usability after implementation and code testing have made it run smoothly. Prototype acceptance or early requirement sign-off does not make the full system ready for final usability evaluation.
  Q What signals that the prototype and evaluation loop can stop?  [42/S0/F3]
    * When the design has stabilized
    - When the bugs have been removed
    - When the code has compiled
    - When the final evaluation is finished
    because: The loop is repeated as evaluation results refine the design, and it ends when that design stabilizes. Compilation, bug removal, or final evaluation belong to later stages, not the design refinement cycle.
  Q Which part of an XR project can be handled like ordinary software development?  [42/S0/F4]
    - Prototyping and quick evaluation are standard SDLC stages
    * Coding and code testing are standard SDLC stages
    - Usability evaluation and prototyping are standard SDLC stages
    - Interface design and prototyping are standard SDLC stages
    because: Code design, coding and implementation, code testing, and system evaluation follow standard software development practice, so they are not treated as XR-specific techniques. Prototyping and quick evaluation support design decisions, but they do not replace code testing or fix the final interface by themselves.

    - The feasibility and coding cycle

42/A2  recap  42/S0  "Recap"  (7 facts, 23 concepts)
  System implementation sits in the interactive system development lifecycle, which also applies to XR systems. That lifecycle moves from feasibility and requirements through a design-prototype-quick-evaluation cycle, then standard coding and testing, and finally whole-system usability evaluation. The design-prototype-evaluate cycle can repeat until the design stabilizes, while other cycles are kept generally infrequent to avoid cost and time overrun.
  - Usability evaluation is the empirical evaluation of the whole system from the usability point of view in interactive system development.
  - The interactive system development lifecycle applies to XR systems and includes feasibility, requirements, a design-prototype-evaluate cycle, coding, testing, and usability evaluation.
  - The design, prototype, and quick evaluation stages form a cycle that repeats until the design stabilizes.
  - Code design, coding, implementation, and code testing are standard software development lifecycle stages with nothing VR or AR specific.
  - Other cycles can connect coding, testing, evaluation, and requirements, but should generally be infrequent to avoid cost and time overrun.

    - Gathering, analyzing, and approving requirements
    - Specifying, budgeting, and procuring hardware
    because: The cycle repeatedly builds a quick prototype of the design, evaluates it, finds problems, and refines the design until it stabilizes. Coding, requirements approval, and hardware procurement are separate parts of the wider development process.

    - Interface and code design
    * Interface and interaction design
    - Code and implementation design
    - Interaction and requirement design
    because: In this cycle, design means the interface and interaction design, not the design of the code or implementation. Code design and implementation belong to later, standard software development stages.
  Q Why is a quick usability evaluation technique required in the design-prototype-evaluate cycle?  [42/S1/F2]
    - To fit code design into the prototype before any user testing
    - To fit each prototype into the final product without further evaluation
    * To fit many cycles into a reasonable timeframe without cost overrun
    - To fit requirement gathering into the design before any prototype
    because: Quick usability evaluation lets the many design-prototype-evaluate cycles stay within a reasonable timeframe and avoids cost overrun. A prototype is not automatically the final product, and the cycle is not a substitute for code design or requirement gathering.

    - A fully implemented system and a quick evaluation method
    because: Quick evaluation needs both a prototype that can be built fast and an evaluation method that is also quick. A full implementation is too heavy for fast cycling, a final report is not an evaluation method, and design guidelines alone do not test a design idea.

42/A5  recap  42/S1  "Recap"  (4 facts, 10 concepts)
  The design-prototype-evaluate cycle in experience design repeatedly designs, quickly prototypes, evaluates, finds problems, and refines until the design stabilizes, with design meaning interface and interaction design, not code design. Many iterations make speed important, so quick usability evaluation is required to keep the work within reasonable time and cost and to make implemented ideas usable. For that evaluation to be quick, a quickly built design prototype and a quick evaluation method are both needed and equally important.
  - The design-prototype-evaluate cycle in experience design repeats designing, quickly prototyping, evaluating, finding problems, and refining until stabilized.
  - In the design-prototype-evaluate cycle, design means interface and interaction design, not code design.
  - Quick usability evaluation keeps cycles within reasonable time and cost, prevents cost overrun, and makes implemented ideas usable.
  - Quick evaluation of design ideas needs a quickly built design prototype and a quick evaluation method, both equally important.

42/A7  recap  42/S2  "Recap"  (5 facts, 8 concepts)
  Design guidelines are only a starting point, so a design must be implemented and tested to determine whether it works. A prototype gives a quick, lightweight way to test a design idea with far fewer resources, skilled manpower, and cost than a full implementation, whose failure wastes money and time. After testing, a prototype can be discarded, or in the best case it can be incrementally evolved into the final product.
  - Prototyping techniques support quick prototype building and evaluation to collect usability feedback on design ideas.
  - Design guidelines are only a starting point, so designs need implementation and testing to determine whether they work.
  - A prototype is a lightweight implementation for testing design ideas needing fewer resources, skilled manpower, and cost than full implementation.
  - A full software implementation needs skilled programmers, resources, and cost, so a bad idea wastes money and time.
  - A prototype can be discarded after testing, or in the best case incrementally evolved into the final product.

  Q What kind of user feedback is a horizontal prototype suitable for collecting?  [42/S3/F1, 42/S3/F2]
    - feedback on the performance and reliability of commonly used features
    - feedback on the interactions and screen changes in a selected task
    * feedback on the look, feel, and appearance of the whole interface
    - feedback on the sequence of screens and states in a complete workflow
    because: A horizontal prototype presents the interface’s appearance without real functionality or interaction, so it is used to discuss and elicit feedback about how the interface looks, feels, and appears.     because: A vertical prototype implements selected features in depth, but not all features, because covering every feature would already be the full system. Cost, display requirements, or hiding interactions are not the reason for this scope limit.

    because: In this context, “screen” is generic: it can mean a two-dimensional computer screen or a scene in a virtual or immersive environment. Paper storyboards, physical models, and three-dimensional prints are not what the term “screen” refers to here.

42/A9  recap  42/S3  "Recap"  (6 facts, 14 concepts)
  Horizontal and vertical prototypes are distinguished by the aspect of the interface they represent. A horizontal prototype presents the whole interface at a surface level, without functionality, so it can be used to gather feedback on its appearance. A vertical prototype instead implements selected common features in depth, from first to last screen, and therefore supports analysis of interactions and features. In this vertical prototype context, the terms implemented and screen are used generically.
  - Prototypes can be broadly considered in two categories: horizontal prototypes and vertical prototypes.
  - A horizontal prototype depicts the entire interface at surface level, with no functionality, for user feedback on appearance.
  - A vertical prototype implements a few selected likely common features in depth, not all, from first to last screen.
  - Vertical prototypes are suitable for analysis of interactions and features because they implement interactions.
  - In vertical prototypes, implemented need not mean code, and screen can be a 2D computer screen or an immersive scene.

42/A10  quiz  42/S4  "Quick quiz"  (6 facts, 13 concepts)
  Q What distinguishes a low-fidelity prototype from a coded prototype?  [42/S4/F0]
    - a simple animation tool without real software for the prototype
    - a reduced-scale program with limited functionality for the prototype
    - a computer without programming code for the prototype
    * non-digital materials such as paper or cardboard for the prototype
    because: A low-fidelity prototype is made without a computer, code, or programming, using non-digital materials such as paper, cardboard, or wood. Digital mockups, reduced-scale programs, and animation tools are not low-fidelity in this sense.
  Q Why is low-fidelity prototyping useful early in interface design?  [42/S4/F1]
    - It is a quick and inexpensive way to render a virtual environment for review
    * It is a quick and inexpensive way to compare interface ideas and collect usability feedback
    - It is a quick and inexpensive way to test coded interactions under load
    - It is a quick and inexpensive way to verify every feature of the final system
    because: Low-fidelity prototyping is mainly used for fast, cheap brainstorming and user feedback on usability, not for testing coded interaction, full final functionality, or rendered virtual environments.
  Q What can a storyboard show that a single interface sketch cannot?  [42/S4/F4, 42/S4/F5, 42/S4/F6]
    * the order of user actions and the screen changes needed to complete a task
    - the complete working functionality of every feature in the system from the first action to the last
    - the final polished appearance of each interface element in detail
    - the full virtual environment with all objects in their final positions and scale
    because: A single sketch gives a static view of one interface, while a storyboard uses a series of keyframes to capture the sequence of actions and corresponding screens for a task. It does not imply complete working functionality, a full virtual environment, or final polished detail.
  Q What does evaluation of an early interface sketch allow the design to do?  [42/S4/F7]
    * change elements, appearance, position, or layout after feedback
    - keep the elements, appearance, position, or layout after feedback
    - repeat the elements, appearance, position, or layout after feedback
    - copy the elements, appearance, position, or layout after feedback
    because: Prototypes are made to be evaluated and revised, so an early sketch is not a fixed final design. Feedback can change interface elements, their appearance, position, or layout.

    - low-fidelity approaches are primarily meant for vertical prototypes
    because: High-fidelity prototyping is primarily meant for vertical prototypes, so using it mainly to produce a horizontal prototype is usually not a good fit. Low-fidelity work is primarily horizontal, and medium-fidelity work is meant for both horizontal and vertical prototypes.

42/A13  recap  42/S5  "Recap"  (5 facts, 20 concepts)
  Medium- and high-fidelity prototyping are contrasted by how much real software is involved. Medium-fidelity uses computers without coding and can support horizontal or vertical prototypes, while high-fidelity uses programming and is effectively reduced-scale software development. The higher effort and programming requirement make high-fidelity less suitable for horizontal prototypes, which are mainly the domain of lower-fidelity approaches.
  - Medium-fidelity prototyping uses a computer to make simple prototypes without coding; low-fidelity does not use computers or digital media.
  - High-fidelity prototyping uses computer programs or programming, so it is actual software development, perhaps on a reduced scale.
  - High-fidelity prototyping is more sophisticated and needs much more effort than low- or medium-fidelity, requiring skilled programmers.
  - Medium-fidelity prototypes can be horizontal as static interface sketches or vertical with simple keypress or timer simulations.
  - Low-fidelity prototyping is primarily horizontal, high-fidelity prototyping is primarily vertical, so high-fidelity horizontal prototypes may not make much sense.

  - IBM used Wizard of Oz in 1984 to test a speech-recognition idea before speech recognizer technology was available.

42/A18  match_pairs  lecture  "Match the terms"  (25 facts, 8 concepts)
  prototype = A lightweight implementation, with much lower requirements for resources, skilled manpower, and cost than a full implementation, that can be built quickly …
  design-prototype-evaluate cycle = A cycle in the iterative software development lifecycle for interactive system development that quickly prototypes, evaluates, and refines interface and interaction design …
  empirical study = A usability-testing stage in interactive system development, performed after code testing, that systematically tests a fully implemented system with end users through …
  interactive system development lifecycle = A staged development method that is similar to regular software development but distinctive in its end-user requirement gathering, iterative design-prototype-evaluate cycle, and …
  design guideline = A statement about an interactive system that says what should or should not be done to make it usable, without saying how …
  full implementation = A complete implementation of a software idea that involves highly skilled programmers and many cost components, including setting up or procuring resources …
  horizontal prototype = A prototype that depicts the entire interface at a surface level, showing its look, feel, and appearance without functionality or interaction, so …
  vertical prototype = A type of prototype that implements a few selected features likely to be most commonly used in depth, from the first screen …

42/A21  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (10 facts, 25 concepts)
  Q Why does the design-prototype-evaluate cycle in interface and interaction design need both a quickly built prototype and a quick usability evaluation method?  [42/S1/F0, 42/S1/F2, 42/S1/F3; design-prototype-evaluate cycle, prototype, usability, quick evaluation]
    A The cycle can require many rounds of design, prototyping, evaluation, and refinement before the design stabilizes. Quick usability evaluation keeps the turnaround time short so those many cycles can be done without cost overrun. A quickly built prototype is also needed to model the design idea, because both are required for fast execution of the cycle.
  Q How does a vertical prototype differ from a horizontal prototype in the usability aspects it can test?  [42/S3/F1, 42/S3/F2, 42/S3/F3, 42/S3/F4; horizontal prototype, vertical prototype, functionality, interaction]
    A A horizontal prototype shows the entire interface at a surface level, without functionality or interaction, so it is suited to feedback on look, feel, and appearance. A vertical prototype implements a few selected features in depth from the first screen to the last screen, so it is suited to analyzing interactions and features.
  Q Why can a series of interface sketches represent a vertical prototype while a single interface sketch represents only a horizontal prototype?  [42/S4/F4, 42/S4/F5, 42/S4/F6; interface sketch, storyboard, keyframe, vertical prototype]
    A A single interface sketch gives only a horizontal prototype because it does not show the sequence of user actions and interface changes needed to execute a task. A series of sketches forms a storyboard, where each sketch is a keyframe, a snapshot of the interaction at a particular point. The keyframes capture the sequence of user actions and screen appearances from the beginning of the task to its end, so the series can depict interaction as a vertical prototype.

===== lecture 43: System Implementation

43/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (13 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is prototype? (lecture 42) -> A prototype is a lightweight implementation, with much lower requirements for resources, skilled manpower, and cost than a full implementation, that can be built quickly to model or demonstrate a design idea and to test whether it will work in practice. It can be discarded after testing or refined into the final product.
  What is horizontal prototype? (lecture 42) -> Horizontal prototype is a prototype that depicts the entire interface at a surface level, showing its look, feel, and appearance without functionality or interaction, so it is used to discuss, brainstorm, and elicit feedback about whether the interface is understandable, intuitive, and usable.
  What is vertical prototype? (lecture 42) -> A vertical prototype is a type of prototype that implements a few selected features likely to be most commonly used in depth, from the first screen to the last, to represent interactions rather than all system functionalities.
  What is low-fidelity prototype? (lecture 42) -> A low-fidelity prototype is a prototype of an interface made without technological intervention, programming, code, or a computer, using non-digital materials such as paper, cardboard, or wood, and to represent interaction it needs a series of interface sketches, often called a storyboard, rather than a single sketch.
  What is storyboard? (lecture 42) -> A storyboard is a low-fidelity prototype consisting of a series of interface sketches, each a keyframe, that captures the sequence of user actions and screen changes for a specific task from beginning to end.
  What is interactive system? (lecture 23) -> Interactive system is a system in which interaction takes place between the computer or system and the user, a lay person who is not necessarily a technology expert and who wants to use the system rather than understand how it works.

43/A2  recap  43/S0  "Recap"  (5 facts, 8 concepts)
  Prototyping in system implementation takes three different forms. Throwaway prototypes give cheap, disposable evaluation, while incremental prototypes build the system module by module. Evolutionary prototypes instead refine a whole-system version from a simple start until it becomes the final product.
  - In system implementation, prototypes can be used as throwaway, incremental, or evolutionary prototypes.
  - Throwaway prototypes are used for quick evaluation, mainly with easy low-fidelity mockups, and then discarded.
  - Incremental prototypes are created when the design divides the system into modules, each separately prototyped, tested, and integrated.
  - Evolutionary prototypes begin simple, then are tested, refined, and expanded into a final whole system, not modules.

    3 pass  (Incremental prototypes are created when the design divides the system into modules, each separately …)
      check: none
      reason: This faithfully compresses fact [4]: design division into modules, separate prototyping and testing, then integration.
    4 pass  (Evolutionary prototypes begin simple, then are tested, refined, and expanded into a final whole …)

      reason: This captures fact [5]: a whole-system prototype begins simpler, is tested/refined/expanded, and becomes the final product rather than assembled from modules.

43/A4  recap  43/S1  "Recap"  (6 facts, 14 concepts)
  Expert evaluation is a fast, low-cost way to check a prototype early in design, requiring at least a low-fidelity prototype and an evaluator team. It differs from full usability testing because the team is usually designers or domain experts, sometimes with a few end users, since their feedback is quicker and cheaper to obtain. With three to five evaluators, each independently reports perceived usability issues, and the design team or lead combines those reports into a final issue list.
  - Expert evaluation is a quick, cheap early-stage prototype evaluation, unlike robust evaluation.
  - Expert evaluation needs at least a low-fidelity prototype, ideally higher-quality, and an evaluator team.
  - Although a usability test, expert evaluation mainly uses design-team or domain experts, optionally a few end users.
  - Experts can replace end users because they are assumed user-like, quicker, and cheaper to engage.
  - Three to five evaluators are sufficient, and each independently reports usability issues, which the lead combines.

    - To record user satisfaction after public release
    * To inspect a prototype for usability problems
    - To validate a finished product with end users
    - To test implementation code for performance faults

    * A low-fidelity vertical prototype that supports several tasks

  Q How do evaluators use a task scenario in a cognitive walkthrough?  [43/S2/F3]
    - They rate how realistic the task description sounds
    - They compare the task with a general usability checklist
    - They select the screens they expect the user to visit
    * They perform the interface-level actions for the task
    because: The task scenario is converted into interface-level actions, and evaluators perform those actions with the prototype. Merely predicting screens, judging realism, or checking a general list does not capture the task-based evaluation.
  Q What do usability questions guide evaluators to do in a cognitive walkthrough?  [43/S2/F4, 43/S2/F5]
    * To report where and why they found difficulty
    - To justify a simple affirm-or-deny verdict
    - To choose the evaluator whose findings seem most serious
    - To confirm that the interface looks aesthetically pleasing
    because: Usability questions serve as guidelines for identifying likely user problems, and each should lead to a detailed explanation of where and why the interface caused difficulty. A simple yes-or-no verdict, aesthetic judgment, or ranking of evaluators does not serve that purpose.

The evaluators work from a task scenario converted into interface-level actions and apply pre-framed usability questions as guidelines.   - Evaluators answer pre-framed usability questions with detailed reports explaining where and why the interface or interaction is difficult.
  - The evaluators' reports are collected, combined, and analyzed at the end to identify broader usability issues.

43/A8  recap  43/S3  "Recap"  (7 facts, 30 concepts)
  Heuristic evaluation is an expert-based way to review a prototype comprehensively by comparing it against usability checklists. Nielsen's 10 heuristics provide a general, 1994 checklist that can be used early on low-fidelity prototypes, especially horizontal ones. In practice, a small team of evaluators independently checks each heuristic, explains violations, and combines their reports to reveal the major usability issues.
  - Heuristic evaluation checks a whole prototype without tasks, using system-specific or broader, shorter heuristics checklists.
  - Nielsen's 10 heuristics are a general 1994 interactive set: status, match, control, consistency, error prevention, recognition, flexibility, minimalism, recovery, help.
  - Nielsen's heuristics can spot problems early on low-fidelity prototypes, mainly horizontal, with vertical optional, unlike cognitive walkthrough.
  - Heuristic evaluation uses at least three to five evaluators, who may be design-team or expert designers.
  - Each evaluator reports heuristic violations with reasons, and combined reports identify major usability issues.

A repaired version would say 'using detailed system-specific checklists or broader checklists with fewer heuristics'.
    2 FAIL supported,faithful  (Nielsen's 10 heuristics are a general 1994 interactive set: status, match, control, consistency, error …)
      check: interactive (3); control (4); flexibility (4); minimalism (4); recovery (4)
      reason: 'interactive set' omits that the heuristics are primarily GUI-related, and the labels 'control', 'flexibility', 'minimalism', and 'recovery' drop stated parts of the heuristics (freedom, efficiency, aesthetic, and recognize/diagnose).     3 FAIL supported,faithful  (Nielsen's heuristics can spot problems early on low-fidelity prototypes, mainly horizontal, with vertical optional …)

  error prevention = A system design rule in which the design helps users prevent errors by aiming to keep error rates low, because user errors …
  storyboard = A low-fidelity prototype consisting of a series of interface sketches, each a keyframe, that captures the sequence of user actions and screen …
  throwaway prototype = A prototype that is easy and fast to create, is used for quick evaluation, and is then discarded.
  incremental prototype = A kind of prototype that is created by dividing a system into units or modules, separately prototyping and testing each module, and …
  evolutionary prototype = A prototype created by prototyping and testing the whole system, starting with a simpler version, refining it, adding more functionalities, and altering …
  expert evaluation = A quick, cheap usability test of a prototype at an early design stage, in which design-team members or domain experts independently report …
  evaluation team = A group, mainly the design team or domain experts and optionally a few end users, used to assess a prototype in quick …
  cognitive walkthrough = A quick expert usability inspection method in which evaluators identify problems by performing interface-level tasks converted from a scenario on at least …

43/A15  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (10 facts, 31 concepts)
  Q Why are low-fidelity cardboard mockups and paper sketches particularly suitable for throwaway prototypes?  [43/S0/F1, 43/S0/F2; throwaway prototype, low-fidelity cardboard mockup, paper sketch]
    A Throwaway prototypes are made for quick evaluation and then discarded. Low-fidelity cardboard mockups and paper sketches are suitable because they are less costly, so discarding them does not incur significant cost. Throwaway prototypes should be easy and fast to create, because otherwise working with them becomes expensive.
  Q How do incremental and evolutionary prototypes differ in the way a system is built from prototypes?  [43/S0/F3, 43/S0/F4; incremental prototype, evolutionary prototype, module]
    A Incremental prototyping is used when system design divides the system into units or modules; each module is separately prototyped and tested, then integrated. Evolutionary prototyping instead builds the whole system from the beginning. It starts with a simpler version, refines it, adds more functionalities, and alters it based on testing until it becomes the final product.
  Q Why can expert evaluation be carried out mainly by design-team members or domain experts, even though usability testing primarily involves users?  [43/S1/F2, 43/S1/F3; expert evaluation, usability testing, design team, domain expert]
    A Design-team members or domain experts are assumed to have user-like experience in the problem domain, so their feedback likely reflects users. Engaging them is less complicated, quicker, and cheaper than engaging a full evaluation team with end users.
  Q Why does a cognitive walkthrough need a vertical prototype, while heuristic evaluation can mainly use a horizontal low-fidelity prototype?  [43/S2/F1, 43/S2/F3, 43/S3/F0, 43/S3/F4; cognitive walkthrough, heuristic evaluation, vertical prototype, horizontal prototype]
    A Cognitive walkthrough requires a vertical prototype because its low-fidelity prototype must support several tasks, and evaluators then perform the interface-level actions from a scenario. Therefore it can be based on simple low-fidelity, primarily horizontal prototypes, with vertical prototypes optional.

===== lecture 44: System Implementation

44/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (23 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is expert evaluation? (lecture 43) -> Expert evaluation is a quick, cheap usability test of a prototype at an early design stage, in which design-team members or domain experts independently report usability issues, and a few end users may be included optionally.
  What is virtual reality (VR)? (lecture 4) -> Virtual reality (VR) is an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli provided by a computer, in which a person's actions partially determine what happens and which replaces the user's sense of reality without requiring the physical existence of objects or places.
  What is head-mounted display (HMDs)? (lecture 6) -> A head-mounted display (HMD) is a wearable, mobile visual display that integrates electronic, optical, mechanical, and audio components and uses one or two small screens directly in front of the user's eyes to place images for monoscopic or stereoscopic viewing. It can be non-see-through, optical see-through, or video see-through.
  What is cybersickness (CS)? (lecture 10) -> Cybersickness (CS) is a condition primarily relevant to virtual reality that may be caused by multiple internal and external factors and in which a user may experience symptoms such as nausea, dizziness, headache, or disorientation.
  What is teleportation? (lecture 11) -> Teleportation is a virtual reality locomotion operation in which a user selects a virtual target location and the virtual viewpoint instantly changes from the current location to that target, without physical movement.
  What is simulator sickness questionnaire (SSQ)? (lecture 11) -> The simulator sickness questionnaire (SSQ) is a widely used questionnaire for measuring cybersickness in immersive experiences. It contains 16 items in oculomotor, disorientation, and nausea subscales, rated from 0 to 3, with subscale and total sickness scores.

44/A2  recap  44/S0  "Recap"  (8 facts, 13 concepts)
  User evaluation is a self-report technique that asks users directly to answer rating scales, producing subjective or preference data and making feedback easier to collect than with more rigorous methods. The rating items are questions or statements, commonly called questionnaires, and suitable questionnaires are challenging to identify. Feedback can be collected after each task, after the session, or both when feasible, with questionnaires matched to the point; standard post-task instruments include ASQ and EM, while standard post-session instruments include SUS, CSUQ, QUIS, and USE.
  - User evaluation is a self-report technique requiring users to directly answer rating scales, yielding subjective or preference data.
  - Collecting rating-scale feedback in user evaluation is easier than more rigorous evaluation techniques.
  - User-evaluation questionnaires are questions or statements for users to rate, and choosing suitable ones is challenging.
  - User feedback may be collected after each task, after the session, or both if feasible, with matching questionnaires.
  - Well-known post-task questionnaires include ASQ and EM; well-known post-session questionnaires include SUS, CSUQ, QUIS, and USE.

44/A4  recap  44/S1  "Recap"  (4 facts, 9 concepts)
  The After Scenario Questionnaire is a post-task instrument that captures how satisfied users are with task ease, task time, and support information. By rating those three statements on a seven-point agreement scale, the questionnaire produces usability feedback that aligns with ISO measures: ease as effectiveness, time as efficiency, and the combined statements as satisfaction. Those ratings can then be reduced to averages either for each statement across users or for all statements together.
  - The After Scenario Questionnaire is a post-task questionnaire with three statements about task ease, task time, and support information.
  - In the After Scenario Questionnaire, users rate each statement from 1, strongly disagree, to 7, strongly agree.
  - Per ISO usability, the After Scenario Questionnaire roughly maps ease to effectiveness, time to efficiency, and statements together to satisfaction.
  - The After Scenario Questionnaire can be summarised by averaging each statement across users or all statements together.

44/A6  recap  44/S2  "Recap"  (6 facts, 10 concepts)
  The System Usability Scale evaluates a system after a completed session by asking users to rate ten short statements. The statements alternate in wording, and their 5-point ratings are combined by a fixed formula into a single score. That score is interpreted as a percentage, with 70% or higher typically indicating a usable system and lower scores suggesting problems. SUS provides a quick user-based signal of usability problems, but it does not explain the causes, so designers must investigate the issues separately.
  - The System Usability Scale is a post-session questionnaire using statements rather than questions after all tasks.
  - The System Usability Scale has ten statements, with each even-numbered statement as the negative counterpart of the preceding odd statement.
  - System Usability Scale ratings are 1–5; score = 2.5 × (sum odd rating−1 plus sum 5−even rating).
  - System Usability Scale scores are read as percentages; 70% or higher is typically desirable, below may need design review.
  - Unlike expert evaluation, System Usability Scale ratings quickly signal usability problems but not reasons, so designers must identify specific problems.
  judge round 1: 2 of 6 failed

    2 pass  (The System Usability Scale has ten statements, with each even-numbered statement as the negative …)
      check: none
      reason: Fact 2 states that SUS has 10 numbered statements and that each even-numbered statement is the negatively worded counterpart of the preceding odd-numbered statement; the point faithfully compresses that structure without adding unsupported claims.
    3 FAIL faithful,clear  (System Usability Scale ratings are 1–5; score = 2.5 × (sum odd rating−1 plus …)

44/A8  recap  44/S3  "Recap"  (7 facts, 18 concepts)
  Questionnaires for general interactive systems are separated from questionnaires designed for XR discomfort. The XR-specific instruments are organized around what they assess: cybersickness, specific conditions, susceptibility to cyber sickness, and overall discomfort. This arrangement makes it clearer which questionnaire matches which XR evaluation target.
  - ASQ and SUS are generic questionnaires for interactive systems, not specifically for XR.
  - SSQ, VRSQ, and CSQ address XR cybersickness; SSQ is most extensively used and CSQ fits HMD VR.
  - MIS and FMS are shorter, more precise, more concise questionnaires assessing specific XR conditions.

44/A10  recap  44/S4  "Recap"  (7 facts, 29 concepts)
  The Majuli VR Tour was implemented in Unity for Oculus Quest 2 and Android, using the XR toolkit for Quest and the Google VR SDK for Cardboard, with 3D models created in Autodesk Maya. Its full geographic content made the initial package 9.85 GB, so the Quest version loaded clicked videos from the cloud and reduced the app to 5.1 GB. The Google Cardboard version was smaller at 0.7 GB because it compressed images and removed most video playback, keeping one initial 360-degree video.
  - The Majuli VR Tour used Unity 2021.3.22f1 for Oculus Quest 2 and Android smartphones requiring Android 6.0.
  - The Majuli VR Tour used the XR toolkit for Oculus Quest and the Google VR SDK for Google Cardboard.
  - Autodesk Maya created the Majuli VR Tour’s 3D models using real images as references and textures.
  - Loading clicked Oculus Quest videos from the cloud reduced the Majuli VR Tour from 9.85 GB to 5.1 GB.
  - Compressing images and removing most video support made the Google Cardboard Majuli VR Tour 0.7 GB.
  judge round 1: 1 of 6 failed

      check: requiring Android 6.0 [1]
      reason: The point says “Android smartphones requiring Android 6.0,” but fact [1] states the Android 6.0 requirement is for both versions. A learner could therefore believe the requirement applied only to the smartphone version. A repaired version should say the Majuli VR Tour used Unity 2021.3.22f1 for Oculus Quest 2 and Android smartphones, and both versions required Android 6.0.
    2 pass  (The Majuli VR Tour used the XR toolkit for Oculus Quest and the Google …)
      check: none
      reason: Fact [2] directly supports that the Majuli VR Tour used the XR toolkit for its Oculus Quest version and the Google VR SDK for its Google Cardboard version.
    3 pass  (Autodesk Maya created the Majuli VR Tour’s 3D models using real images as references …)
      check: none
      reason: Fact [3] states that Autodesk Maya was used to create the 3D models using real images as references and textures, which the point accurately summarizes.
    4 pass  (Loading clicked Oculus Quest videos from the cloud reduced the Majuli VR Tour from …)
      check: none

    5 pass  (Compressing images and removing most video support made the Google Cardboard Majuli VR Tour …)

44/A13  recap  44/S5  "Recap"  (16 facts, 31 concepts)
  Three Majuli VR Tour implementations adapt the tour to different hardware. The Oculus Quest 360-degree-image tour uses media and a guided flow: introduction, boat ride, tablet map, local movement, and fixed-route teleportation between 360-degree views. The 3D-model Quest tour replaces that media-based approach with textured models of the island, while the smartphone-based Google Cardboard version reduces features and videos but keeps the main navigation, boat ride, and minimap.
  - The Majuli VR Tour has three implementations: 360-degree-image and 3D-model Oculus Quest tours and a Google Cardboard mobile tour.
  - The 360-degree-image Quest tour uses images, videos, sound, ray-cast selection, a boat ride and tablet map selection.
  - Inside 360-degree locations, users move with arrow keys, see icons and cultural videos, and travel via minimap vehicle-metaphor teleportation.
  - The 3D-model Quest tour replaces images or videos with textured models of Kamalabadi Satra, campus roads, villages and dwellings.
  - The smartphone-based Google Cardboard tour is a reduced Quest version: fewer videos, but similar controls, boat ride and minimaps.
  judge round 1: 2 of 6 failed

44/A16  match_pairs  lecture  "Match the terms"  (20 facts, 8 concepts)
  simulator sickness questionnaire = A widely used questionnaire for measuring cybersickness in immersive experiences.
  Cyber Sickness Questionnaire = A questionnaire relevant to cyber sickness in extended reality that is good for evaluating virtual reality experiences with head-mounted displays.
  Google Cardboard = A head-mounted display in which a smartphone is inserted to provide a 360-degree virtual reality experience.
  user evaluation = A quick evaluation technique that obtains feedback by asking users directly using rating scales, and it requires user involvement.
  questionnaire = A set of questions or statements provided to users to rate in user evaluation, although it need not contain questions.
  after scenario questionnaire = A post-task questionnaire in which users rate three statements about satisfaction with ease of completing tasks, time taken to complete tasks, and …
  system usability scale = A post-session questionnaire containing ten statements, not questions, that users rate on a five-point agreement scale after completing all tasks, giving a …
  seven-point rating scale = A rating scale for statements that ranges from 1 to 7, with 1 indicating strong disagreement and 7 indicating strong agreement.

44/A19  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (14 facts, 45 concepts)
  Q How did the heavy content of the Majuli virtual reality system shape the size-reduction strategy used for its Oculus Quest and Google Cardboard versions?  [44/S4/F3, 44/S4/F4, 44/S4/F5; Majuli virtual reality system, application size, video, Google Cardboard]
    A The initial system was 9.85 GB because its content covered the entire geographic spread. Moving videos to the cloud and loading them on demand reduced the client application to 5.1 GB. Because that size was not suitable for mobile deployment, the Google Cardboard version compressed high-resolution 360-degree and 2D images and removed most video playback, reaching 0.7 GB.
  Q Why can the After Scenario Questionnaire and the System Usability Scale both be used in user evaluation, even though they are administered at different stages?  [44/S0/F5, 44/S0/F6, 44/S0/F7, 44/S1/F2, 44/S2/F0, 44/S2/F5; after scenario questionnaire, system usability scale, post-task data collection, post-session data collection]
    A User evaluation can collect feedback after each task and at the end of a session, and using both points is desirable if feasible. The After Scenario Questionnaire is a post-task questionnaire whose statements relate to effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction. The System Usability Scale is a post-session questionnaire that gives a quick general indication of whether usability problems exist after all tasks are completed.
  Q Why is the Simulator Sickness Questionnaire a suitable complement to generic usability questionnaires for evaluating the Majuli virtual reality tour?  [44/S3/F0, 44/S3/F1, 10/S0/F0; simulator sickness questionnaire, cybersickness, usability]
    A The After Scenario Questionnaire and System Usability Scale are generic questionnaires applicable to any interactive system, not specifically meant for extended reality. The Simulator Sickness Questionnaire is the most extensively used questionnaire specifically designed for cybersickness in extended reality. Cybersickness is primarily relevant to virtual reality, so it addresses a problem that generic usability questionnaires do not specifically target.
  Q How does the 360-degree-image Majuli virtual reality tour use teleportation to support travel between locations?  [44/S5/F8, 19/S4/F6; teleportation, 360-degree image tour, navigation]
    A It uses teleportation, a virtual reality locomotion operation in which a user points to a desired virtual location and is sent there without physical movement. In this tour, travel from one point to another combines that instant change of viewpoint with a vehicle-metaphor route-planning method. The road route is fixed, and the user experiences motion as if riding a vehicle along the road.

===== lecture 45: System Implementation

45/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (20 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is empirical study? (lecture 32) -> Empirical study is a usability-testing stage in interactive system development, performed after code testing, that systematically tests a fully implemented system with end users through a controlled experiment to collect and analyze data for assessing overall usability.
  What is interactive system development lifecycle (ISDLC)? (lecture 32) -> Interactive system development lifecycle (ISDLC) is a staged development method that is similar to regular software development but distinctive in its end-user requirement gathering, iterative design-prototype-evaluate cycle, and empirical usability evaluation.
  What is prototype? (lecture 42) -> A prototype is a lightweight implementation, with much lower requirements for resources, skilled manpower, and cost than a full implementation, that can be built quickly to model or demonstrate a design idea and to test whether it will work in practice. It can be discarded after testing or refined into the final product.
  What is usability? (lecture 24) -> Usability is an explicit measure of how good a system is from the point of view of the user: the extent to which a product can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction in a specified context of use.
  What is user feedback? (lecture 32) -> User feedback is the involvement of users in different ways, not only through feedback, that iterations between stages in an interactive system development lifecycle account for.
  What is code testing? (lecture 32) -> Code testing is a standard software development stage in interactive system development that evaluates code as part of coding and implementation by ensuring it is bug-free and executes properly, but does not establish whether the system is usable.

45/A1  quiz  45/S0  "Quick quiz"  (2 facts, 5 concepts)

    - Requirement collection by analysts for a developed system
    - Interface completion by designers for a developed system
    - Function verification by developers for a developed system
    * Usability judgment by end users for a developed system
    because: Empirical evaluation is the stage where end users judge the usability of the developed system. It is distinct from developer testing, requirement collection, or interface completion.
  Q Why is empirical evaluation placed after code testing in interactive system development?  [45/S0/F1]
    - Code testing checks the functional requirements and thereby confirms that the system is usable
    - Code testing compares the finished system with earlier prototypes and selects the better design
    - Code testing asks end users to try the finished system and report their problems
    * Code testing produces an executable system but does not establish that it is usable
    because: Code testing can show that the software runs, but it does not show that users can use it effectively, so a separate usability evaluation with users is needed after it.

45/A4  recap  45/S1  "Recap"  (3 facts, 7 concepts)
  Quick prototype evaluations can surface some major usability problems early, but their small scale means they cannot decide the overall usability of the finished system. A conclusive assessment therefore evaluates the fully implemented system, preferably with more users, in a controlled experiment that collects and analyzes behavioral data. This controlled experiment is generally referred to as empirical research, an empirical study, a user study, or a usability study.
  - Quick prototype evaluations are limited early tests that can find some major issues but cannot conclusively assess overall end-system usability.
  - Conclusive usability assessment requires the fully implemented system, preferably more users, and a controlled experiment collecting and analyzing behavioral data.
  - A controlled experiment for usability evaluation is generally called empirical research, an empirical study, a user study, or usability study.

    - It has users complete a text input task and compare the two interfaces on features
    - It has users complete a text input task and compare the two interfaces on preference
    because: Asking about speed frames the comparison around completing a text input task and comparing performance on speed. Comparing features, comfort, or preference would leave the judgment tied to users' broader quality ideas.

    - Users' subjective speed answers can be made definitive by asking each user twice, whereas logged characters per minute can be compared directly
    * Users' subjective speed answers can split, whereas logged characters per minute can be compared directly
    - Users' subjective speed answers can be made definitive by using a familiar text, whereas logged characters per minute can be compared directly
    because: Even a clear faster-than question can receive split subjective responses, so the experiment logs each user's characters per minute and compares those values directly. Repeating the question, choosing a familiar text, or comparing features does not remove that uncertainty.

45/A11  quiz  45/S5  "Quick quiz"  (4 facts, 12 concepts)
  Q What makes a research question testable?  [45/S5/F0]
    - It allows a broad term such as good to cover several aspects of the system at once
    - It allows users' opinions to be collected and conclusions to be drawn after subjective interpretation
    - It avoids collecting data by relying on a single researcher's judgment of the interface
    * It allows objective data to be collected and conclusions to be drawn without subjective interpretation
    because: A testable research question supports a study that yields objective data and conclusions independent of users' subjective interpretation. The other options describe reliance on opinion, broad framing, or no data collection, which do not make a question testable.
  Q Why can a question about whether an interface is good not be directly tested objectively?  [45/S5/F1]
    - because it depends on comparing the interface with an existing alternative
    - because it depends on assigning fixed levels to the interface factor
    * because it depends on users' subjective interpretation and feedback
    - because it depends on logging text entry speed in characters per minute
    because: A generalized question about whether something is good cannot be directly tested objectively because it rests on users' subjective interpretation and feedback. The other options describe steps that can appear in an objective experiment, not the reason this broad question is untestable.
  Q Why may the answer to "Does interface A let users enter text faster than interface B?" not answer "Is A better than B?"?  [45/S5/F4]
    - because a faster interface is by definition a better interface
    - because speed and overall goodness refer to the same concept
    - because the broader question becomes testable once the interfaces are compared
    * because speed addresses one aspect rather than overall goodness
    because: Faster performance is one specific, measurable aspect, while better is a broader judgment that can include other aspects. Comparing two interfaces does not make the broader question testable by itself.
  Q How can a broader untestable usability question be addressed in stage 1 of an empirical study?  [45/S5/F5]
    - by applying a set of generic usability rules and treating them as the main questions
    * by framing multiple testable questions covering different aspects and combining their conclusions
    - by selecting one testable aspect and using its single result as the broader judgment
    - by framing one generalized question that is expected to cover the whole system in one pass
    because: To balance testability and generalization, an empirical study can frame several testable questions about different aspects and combine their conclusions toward a broader untestable usability question. A single broad question, a single narrow result, or generic design rules do not provide that structure.

45/A12  recap  45/S5  "Recap"  (6 facts, 14 concepts)
  Testable research questions, or hypotheses, allow studies to collect objective data and draw objective conclusions, while non-testable questions depend on subjective interpretation. Broad concepts such as “good” are ambiguous, so studies prefer specific testable questions instead. Stage 1 of an empirical study frames several testable questions about different aspects and combines their conclusions to answer a broader untestable usability question.
  - A testable research question, or hypothesis, permits collecting objective data and drawing conclusions independent of users' subjective interpretation.
  - A non-testable research question, also untestable, depends on subjective interpretation, so controlled experiments generally cannot draw reliable conclusions.
  - Research questions should avoid generalized concepts like “good” because they create untestable questions; testable questions support reliable, definite conclusions.
  - A specific testable question, such as whether an interface is faster, may not answer the broader question whether it is better.
  - Stage 1 of an empirical study frames multiple testable questions about system aspects and combines conclusions for a broader untestable question.

45/A13  quiz  45/S6  "Quick quiz"  (4 facts, 7 concepts)
  Q In an empirical usability experiment, what is an independent variable?  [45/S6/F0]
    - A value that an interface factor can take in the experiment
    - A variable whose measured value depends on an interface factor in the experiment
    - A user characteristic that varies between participants in the experiment
    * A variable whose values are assigned and controlled in the experiment
    because: An independent variable, also called a factor, is the one whose values are assigned and controlled. A dependent variable is measured as an outcome, and a level is a value taken by a factor.
  Q How do factors and levels determine the test conditions in an experiment?  [45/S6/F1, 45/S6/F2]
    - Each level of a dependent variable gives one test condition in the experiment
    - Each user characteristic gives one test condition in the experiment
    - Each factor gives one test condition without using its levels in the experiment
    * Each level of a factor gives one test condition in the experiment
    because: A factor’s levels are its assigned values, and each level becomes one test condition in which the dependent variable is observed. A dependent variable or a user characteristic does not supply the factor’s test conditions.
  Q Why is text entry rate called a dependent variable in the text-entry research question?  [45/S6/F3]
    - Because it is a condition used to observe interface performance in the experiment
    * Because its value depends on the interface levels in the experiment
    - Because it is a value assigned to the interface factor in the experiment
    - Because it is a user characteristic compared between participants in the experiment
    because: A dependent variable is one whose measured value depends on an independent variable’s levels. Here, text entry rate depends on which interface level is being tested.
  judge round 1: 0 of 3 failed
    1 pass  (In an empirical usability experiment, what is an independent variable?)

      check: D
      reason: Facts 2 and 3 state that a factor's assigned values are its levels and that, in the example, "these two levels give two test conditions," supporting the idea that each level of a factor gives a test condition.
    3 pass  (Why is text entry rate called a dependent variable in the text-entry research question?)

45/A14  recap  45/S6  "Recap"  (4 facts, 7 concepts)
  For an empirical usability experiment, an independent variable, also called a factor, has values that are assigned and controlled, and those values are the factor's levels. A factor combined with its levels defines the test conditions. A dependent variable is the outcome whose value depends on those levels, such as text entry rate depending on interface levels.
  - An independent variable, also called a factor, has values that are assigned and controlled.
  - The values assigned to an independent variable or factor are called its levels.
  - Factors combined with their levels define an experiment's test conditions.
  - A dependent variable's value depends on an independent variable's levels, as text entry rate depends on interface levels.

    - Specification of a context of use in the real world

  Q How does research question framing handle a broad, untestable question about an interface?  [45/S7/F3]
    * Framing multiple testable questions and combining their conclusions
    - Choosing a single testable question and reporting its conclusions
    - Collecting subjective feedback and forming general conclusions
    - Asking one untestable question and accepting users' conclusions
    because: A broad untestable question is addressed by deriving several testable questions, collecting objective data for each, and combining the definite conclusions. A single untestable question or subjective feedback alone cannot support a reliable general conclusion.
  Q In an empirical study, how do independent variables differ from dependent variables?  [45/S7/F4]

    - Independent variables are user judgments, and dependent variables are assigned levels
    because: Independent variables, also called factors, are the conditions that can take levels, while dependent variables depend on those levels. Reversing the roles, or treating the dependent variable as something that is set, is incorrect.

45/A16  recap  45/S7  "Recap"  (5 facts, 11 concepts)
  An empirical usability evaluation observes real users in the real world after the system is fully implemented, giving an overall picture of usability. Its empirical research process has four stages, with research question framing and variables as the first two. Research question framing turns untestable broad questions into testable questions, collects objective data, and combines definite conclusions, while the variables stage identifies independent variables, or factors, and dependent variables that depend on those factors and levels to design an experiment.
  - Empirical evaluation, or usability research, observes real users in the real world after full implementation to judge overall usability.
  - Empirical research has four stages, starting with research question framing and then variables.
  - Research question framing converts untestable broad questions into testable ones, uses objective data, and combines definite conclusions.
  - The variables stage identifies independent variables, or factors, and dependent variables that depend on factors and levels for an experiment.

A repaired version should say it is done after full implementation to get an overall idea of usability.
    2 pass  (Empirical research has four stages, starting with research question framing and then variables.)
      check: none
      reason: Fact 3 directly states that the empirical research process has four stages, with research question framing first and variables second.
    3 FAIL supported,faithful  (Research question framing converts untestable broad questions into testable ones, uses objective data, and …)

    4 FAIL supported,faithful  (The variables stage identifies independent variables, or factors, and dependent variables that depend on …)

45/A19  match_pairs  lecture  "Match the terms"  (16 facts, 8 concepts)
  empirical study = A usability-testing stage in interactive system development, performed after code testing, that systematically tests a fully implemented system with end users through …
  quick prototype evaluation = A limited-scale early evaluation that uses a limited number of evaluators to evaluate prototypes, so it can quickly identify some major usability …
  experiment = The designed and executed part of an empirical study that collects and compares objective data to answer a research question and measure …
  testable research question = A research question that allows a study to collect objective data and draw reliable conclusions independent of users' subjective interpretation.
  non-testable research question = A broader, generalized research question that cannot be directly tested objectively because it depends on users' subjective interpretation and feedback, so a …
  independent variable = A variable whose values are assigned and controlled; these values are called levels and are used to design an experiment.
  level = A value assigned to an independent variable or factor in an experiment.
  test condition = A combination of factor levels that is used to design an experiment.

45/A23  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (14 facts, 26 concepts)
  Q Why must code testing be followed by an empirical study rather than serving as the final check of an interactive system?  [45/S0/F0, 45/S0/F1, 32/S4/F3; code testing, empirical study, usability, interactive system development lifecycle]
    A Code testing only checks that code is bug-free and executes, so it does not establish whether end users find the system usable. An empirical study follows it as a separate stage in which end users evaluate the developed system. Thus the system can be executable while still needing this user-based usability assessment.
  Q Why are quick prototype evaluations insufficient for a conclusive judgment about the overall usability of a fully implemented system?  [45/S1/F0, 45/S1/F1, 45/S7/F1; quick prototype evaluation, fully implemented system, usability, user behavioral data]
    A Quick prototype evaluations use a limited number of evaluators and prototypes, so they can identify some major usability issues but cannot give a conclusive result about the end system. A conclusive assessment requires evaluating the whole fully implemented system, preferably with a larger number of users, through a controlled experiment collecting and analyzing user behavioral data. The empirical study is carried out at the end, when the system is fully implemented, to obtain an idea of the overall usability.
  Q Why can a testable research question support a definite scientific conclusion when a non-testable research question generally cannot?  [45/S5/F0, 45/S5/F1, 45/S5/F3; testable research question, non-testable research question, objective data, subjective interpretation]
    A A non-testable question depends on users' subjective interpretation and feedback, so a controlled experiment cannot be set up to collect objective data and generally no reliable conclusion can be drawn. A testable question allows a study to collect objective data and draw conclusions independently of subjective interpretation. Therefore testable questions should be used because they support reliable, definite scientific conclusions.
  Q In the variables stage of an empirical study, how do independent variables and dependent variables define the experiment for a text entry research question?  [45/S6/F0, 45/S6/F1, 45/S6/F2, 45/S6/F3, 45/S7/F4; independent variable, level, test condition, dependent variable]
    A The variables stage identifies the variables in the testable question to design the experiment. The independent variable, interface, has levels such as the course's design and MS Word, and these levels give the test conditions. The dependent variable, text entry rate, depends on those interface levels.

===== lecture 46: System Implementation

46/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (15 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is empirical study? (lecture 32) -> Empirical study is a usability-testing stage in interactive system development, performed after code testing, that systematically tests a fully implemented system with end users through a controlled experiment to collect and analyze data for assessing overall usability.
  What is experiment? (lecture 45) -> An experiment is the designed and executed part of an empirical study that collects and compares objective data to answer a research question and measure the usability of an implemented interface.
  What is independent variable? (lecture 45) -> An independent variable is a variable whose values are assigned and controlled; these values are called levels and are used to design an experiment.
  What is level? (lecture 45) -> A level is a value assigned to an independent variable or factor in an experiment.
  What is test condition? (lecture 45) -> A test condition is a combination of factor levels that is used to design an experiment.
  What is usability? (lecture 24) -> Usability is an explicit measure of how good a system is from the point of view of the user: the extent to which a product can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction in a specified context of use.

46/A1  quiz  46/S0  "Quick quiz"  (4 facts, 16 concepts)
  Q In an experiment, why should the selected participants be chosen carefully?  [46/S0/F0]
    - to simplify the whole user group
    - to recruit the whole user group
    - to define the whole user group
    * to represent the whole user group
    because: The participant subset stands for the full user group, so conclusions remain valid and reliable only when the subset represents that group. A subset does not define the group; the user profile does.
  Q When is a homogeneous participant subset acceptable in an experiment?  [46/S0/F1]
    - when the participants are from a homogeneous user group
    * when the system is for a homogeneous user group
    - when the system is for a heterogeneous user group
    - when the experiment is for a homogeneous user group
    because: A homogeneous subset can support conclusions for a system aimed at a homogeneous group, but it cannot reliably support conclusions for a heterogeneous user group. The acceptable case depends on the system's target group, not merely on the experiment or the participants' background.
  Q What should be used first when choosing participants for an experiment?  [46/S0/F2, 46/S0/F3]
    - a software stack with well-defined characteristics
    - a device set with well-defined characteristics
    * a user profile with well-defined characteristics
    - a task list with well-defined characteristics
    because: Participants are selected on the basis of a user profile, which specifies relevant user characteristics. User characteristics such as age or computer-use frequency belong to that profile, not to the tasks, devices, or software being evaluated.
  judge round 1: 0 of 3 failed
    1 pass  (In an experiment, why should the selected participants be chosen carefully?)

46/A2  recap  46/S0  "Recap"  (4 facts, 16 concepts)
  Experiment participants are a sample of all potential users, so their representative selection is what makes conclusions valid. A user profile gives the well-defined characteristics used to define and choose those participants. A homogeneous group can be used when the system targets that group, but broader heterogeneous groups require profile characteristics such as age and computer-use frequency.
  - Experiment participants are a sample of potential users; without representativeness, conclusions are not valid or reliable.
  - A homogeneous user group is acceptable only when the system is for that group, not for heterogeneous user groups.
  - A user profile is a set of well-defined characteristics used to define the user and select experiment participants.
  - Experiment participant selection using user profiles must consider age and computer-use frequency, which can affect typing behavior and speed.

46/A3  quiz  46/S1  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 15 concepts)
  Q Why is a participant set below the commonly used range treated as a problem in a controlled empirical experiment?  [46/S1/F0]
    - because tasks may not be representative and may not cover the interface's full use
    - because data may mostly be subjective and may not support interface claims
    - because task order may add practice noise and may hide interface effects
    * because conclusions may not be reliable and may change if participants are added

  A controlled empirical study of an XR interface relies on objective task-performance data, so the participant count and the selected tasks shape whether conclusions about the interface are reliable. The participant number is generally kept between 12 and 25, and the small tested task subset should represent tasks potential users commonly use in practice. These choices together help the experiment avoid unreliable conclusions about the interface.

46/A5  quiz  46/S2  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 9 concepts)
  Q In an experimental interface study, what does a within-subject design require of participants?  [46/S2/F0]
    - Every participant does the tasks for one test condition
    * Every participant does the tasks for all test conditions
    - Every participant does the tasks for alternate test conditions
    - Every participant does the tasks for a share of test conditions
    because: A within-subject, or repeated-measures, design has every participant perform the tasks associated with all test conditions. A between-subjects design instead divides the conditions among different participants.
  Q Why might a between-subjects design be chosen even though a within-subject design is easier to manage?  [46/S2/F0, 46/S2/F1]
    - Limited participant or resource availability may make using the same numbered task sequence for each participant necessary
    * Limited participant or resource availability may make dividing the tasks among different participant groups necessary
    - Limited participant or resource availability may make repeating the same tasks for each participant necessary
    - Limited participant or resource availability may make assigning a single task to each participant necessary
    because: A within-subject design is easier to manage, but limited participants or resources can make a between-subjects arrangement necessary, in which tasks are split among different participant groups. Repeating tasks or task orders for each participant, or assigning a single task to each participant, is not the reason stated.
  Q Why can a practice effect confound the analysis of a within-subject study?  [46/S2/F2]
    * Performance gains may come from practice rather than the interface
    - Performance gains may come from chance rather than the interface
    - Performance gains may come from the interface rather than practice
    - Performance gains may come from the task list rather than practice
    because: Practice effect is an improvement in task performance caused by repeated practice, so it can add noise by making it unclear whether gains come from the interface or from practice. Reversing the cause or blaming chance or the task list does not describe this confound.
  Q How does a Latin square design reduce the practice effect in a within-subject study?  [46/S2/F3, 46/S2/F4]
    * By shifting a numbered task sequence for each successive participant
    - By repeating the same task sequence for each successive participant
    - By randomizing the task sequence for each successive participant
    - By reversing the task sequence for each successive participant
    because: A Latin square design systematically varies the task sequence, for example by shifting a numbered sequence one position for each successive participant, so the practice effect is spread across conditions. Randomization can also reduce practice effects, but a Latin square is specifically a systematic variation.

46/A6  recap  46/S2  "Recap"  (5 facts, 9 concepts)
  Task assignment in an XR user experiment contrasts within-subject and between-subjects designs, depending on participant and resource availability. Within-subject designs are easier to manage, but repeated practice can confound the data because performance gains may reflect practice rather than the interface. Randomizing or systematically varying task sequences, such as using a Latin square, is intended to statistically nullify that practice effect.
  - Task assignment can be within-subject, where every participant does all test conditions, or between-subjects, where conditions are divided among participants.
  - Within-subject designs are easier to manage, but participant or resource limits may force a between-subjects design.
  - A practice effect confounds within-subject analysis by adding noise, since gains may reflect practice rather than the interface.
  - Within-subject task sequences can be randomized or systematically varied, such as with Latin squares, to statistically nullify the practice effect.

    - The data come from a sample, while the conclusions concern the selected participants

    - It is due to chance and reflects the tested conditions

    * It is not due to chance and reflects the tested conditions
    - It is not due to chance and reflects participant preferences
    because: A significance test is used to decide whether an observed difference is likely to be reliable rather than a chance outcome. Statistical significance concerns the role of chance and the tested conditions, not merely the size of the difference.

    - A repeated test with the same participants
    because: A higher mean speed alone may occur by chance, so the difference between the group means must be statistically significant before one interface can be judged faster. Absolute mean size or repeating the test with the same participants is not the stated requirement.

46/A8  recap  46/S3  "Recap"  (6 facts, 18 concepts)
  Data analysis in system implementation checks whether empirical results are reliable before design claims are made. Interface studies use user samples to support population-level claims, so an observed advantage may only reflect chance. A statistical significance test therefore distinguishes chance differences from condition-related differences, and text-entry comparisons require a significant relative difference between group mean speeds.
  - In system implementation, stage 4, data analysis, tests empirical data for statistical significance before drawing conclusions about design efficacy.
  - Empirical interface studies collect data from a sample of users, but conclusions concern a larger population.
  - Straightforward conclusions may be chance, so a statistical significance test checks whether a difference is due to chance or conditions.
  - Comparing text-entry interfaces requires a statistically significant relative difference between mean text-entry speeds, not absolute values or a higher mean.

46/A9  quiz  46/S4  "Quick quiz"  (4 facts, 18 concepts)
  Q Which non-parametric significance test is indicated for a within-subject design with a nominal or categorical scale of measurement and one factor having two levels?  [46/S4/F4]
    - Mann-Whitney U test
    - Wilcoxon signed-rank test
    - Chi-square test
    * McNemar's test
    because: For a nominal or categorical outcome with one factor at two levels, the non-parametric test is chi-square for a between-subject design and McNemar's test for a within-subject design. Wilcoxon signed-rank and Mann-Whitney U are used for one-factor two-level designs without the nominal or categorical condition, and Mann-Whitney U is a between-subject test.
  Q Which non-parametric test can also be used for a between-subject design with one factor having more than two levels?  [46/S4/F6]
    - Mann-Whitney U test
    - Friedman test
    * Kruskal-Wallis test
    - Wilcoxon signed-rank test
    because: A between-subject design with one factor having more than two levels can use the non-parametric Kruskal-Wallis test. The Friedman test is for within-subject designs, while Mann-Whitney U and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests apply to one-factor two-level designs.
  Q In a statistical significance test, what does a lower p-value indicate?  [46/S4/F2]
    - The observed difference is less likely to have been obtained by chance
    - The observed data are more likely to have been obtained by chance
    - The observed effect is less likely to have been obtained by chance
    * The observed data are less likely to have been obtained by chance
    because: A p-value is the probability of obtaining the data by chance, so a lower p-value means the data are less likely to have arisen by chance. It describes the probability of obtaining the data, not merely the observed difference or effect.
  Q What determines the method for performing a statistical significance test?  [46/S4/F0]
    - The task sequence in the experiment and the nature of the input data
    - The number of participants in the experiment and the nature of the input data
    * The design of the experiment and the nature of the input data
    - The number of conditions in the experiment and the nature of the input data
    because: The appropriate significance test depends on the experiment's design and the nature of the input data. Participant count, task sequence, and condition count are not the factors given as determining the test method.

46/A10  recap  46/S4  "Recap"  (8 facts, 28 concepts)
  Choosing a statistical test to check whether differences in empirical XR experiment data are significant depends on the experiment design and input data. Statistical significance tests are divided into parametric and non-parametric tests. The choice then differs for two-level designs and for designs with more levels or factors, since different between-subject and within-subject tests apply in each case.
  - The statistical significance test used depends on the experiment design and the nature of the input data.
  - Significance-test results can include group-means difference, p-value, T value, degrees of freedom, and significance; lower p-values mean less likely.
  - Statistical significance tests fall into two groups: parametric tests and non-parametric tests.
  - For one-factor two-level designs, choose between- or within-subject tests according to measurement scale and design type.
  - For more levels or factors, choose between-subject one-way or factorial ANOVA or within-subject repeated-measures ANOVA.
