46/A13  match_pairs  lecture  "Match the terms"  (9 facts, 8 concepts)
  data analysis = The fourth stage of the system implementation process in which empirical data from an experiment are processed and tested for statistical significance …
  homogeneous user group = A user group whose members have similarities such as the same age group and similar educational, socio-economic, and/or cultural backgrounds.
  user profile = A set of well-defined user characteristics or entries that, in experiment design, defines a user and is the only basis for selecting …
  representative task set = A small, well-defined subset of the tasks that potential users most frequently or commonly use when an interface is deployed in practice …
  within-subject design = An experimental design in which every participant performs tasks corresponding to all test conditions; because repeated practice can confound the analysis, the …
  between-subjects design = An experimental design in which the tasks for all test conditions are divided and distributed among subsets of participants.
  practice effect = ___ is, in a within-subject design, an improvement in task performance from repeated practice that is a confounding variable and adds noise …
  Latin square design = A design that systematically varies the task sequence allocated to each participant.

46/A16  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (11 facts, 37 concepts)
  Q Why does using a homogeneous participant sample limit the user group to whom conclusions about an interface can be generalized?  [46/S0/F0, 46/S0/F1; participant, sample, homogeneous user group, heterogeneous user group]
    A A sample must be representative of the whole user group for its conclusions to be valid or reliable. A homogeneous group has members with the same or similar age, educational, socio-economic, and cultural backgrounds, so it can represent a homogeneous target group. It does not represent a heterogeneous group, so conclusions from such a sample are not reliable for that broader group.
  Q Why does choosing a random piece of text weaken conclusions about the overall usability of a typing interface?  [46/S1/F2, 46/S1/F3, 46/S1/F4; representative task set, typing task, usability, typing interface]
    A An empirical study can use only a small subset of all supported tasks, so that subset must be chosen carefully. A random piece of text is not a representative task, because representative tasks are commonly used strings chosen by metrics and measures that indirectly encompass the whole interface and users' typing skills. Data from a non-representative task may not support a reliable conclusion about overall usability.
  Q How does a Latin square design reduce the practice effect in a within-subject experiment?  [46/S2/F2, 46/S2/F3, 46/S2/F4; practice effect, within-subject design, Latin square design, confounding variable]
    A In a within-subject design, repeated practice can improve performance and confound the analysis. A Latin square design systematically varies the task sequence, for example by shifting it one position for each successive participant. These variations are supposed to nullify the practice effect, so gains are less likely to be mistaken for an interface effect.
  Q Why is a higher mean text-entry speed by itself insufficient for concluding that one text-entry interface is better?  [46/S3/F3, 46/S3/F4, 46/S3/F5; mean text-entry speed, statistical significance test, text input interface]
    A The analysis compares the relative difference between the mean text-entry speeds of the two groups rather than the absolute values. A higher mean alone may be due to chance, because an observed difference may appear even when the conditions do not cause it. A statistical significance test is needed to show that the difference is not due to chance; only a statistically significant difference supports concluding that one design is better in speed or efficiency.
  judge round 1: 0 of 4 failed
    1 pass  (Why does using a homogeneous participant sample limit the user group to whom conclusions …)
      check: The facts say a homogeneous sample is acceptable for a homogeneous target group but is not reliable for drawing conclusions for a heterogeneous group because a sample must be representative.
      reason: Facts 1 and 2 carry the link: a sample must be representative for valid conclusions, and a homogeneous subset is acceptable for a homogeneous group but not reliable for a heterogeneous group. The reference answer stays within those facts and directly answers the generalization limit.
    2 pass  (Why does choosing a random piece of text weaken conclusions about the overall usability …)
      check: The facts say a random piece of text is not a representative typing task, and tasks not chosen carefully may make the observed data unusable for a reliable conclusion about overall usability.
      reason: Facts 7, 8, and 9 support the answer: the task subset must be chosen carefully, representative tasks are commonly used and chosen by metrics and measures, and a random text is not representative. The reference answer explains the weakening link without adding unsupported claims.
    3 pass  (How does a Latin square design reduce the practice effect in a within-subject experiment?)
      check: The facts say a Latin square systematically varies the task sequence across participants, and such systematic variation is supposed to nullify the practice effect that can confound within-subject comparisons.
      reason: Facts 12, 13, and 14 carry the link: the practice effect can confound within-subject data, systematic variation of task sequence is supposed to nullify it, and a Latin square is an example of that systematic variation. The reference answer directly answers how the design reduces the effect.
    4 pass  (Why is a higher mean text-entry speed by itself insufficient for concluding that one …)
      check: The facts say a higher mean may be due to chance, so a statistically significant relative difference between the means is required before concluding that one interface is better.
      reason: Facts 18, 19, and 20 support the answer: the comparison concerns the relative difference between means, a higher mean alone may be due to chance, and a statistically significant difference is required for a conclusion about better speed or efficiency.

===== lecture 47: System Implementation

47/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (15 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is simulator sickness questionnaire (SSQ)? (lecture 11) -> The simulator sickness questionnaire (SSQ) is a widely used questionnaire for measuring cybersickness in immersive experiences. It contains 16 items in oculomotor, disorientation, and nausea subscales, rated from 0 to 3, with subscale and total sickness scores.
  What is questionnaire? (lecture 44) -> A questionnaire is a set of questions or statements provided to users to rate in user evaluation, although it need not contain questions.
  What is seven-point rating scale? (lecture 44) -> A seven-point rating scale is a rating scale for statements that ranges from 1 to 7, with 1 indicating strong disagreement and 7 indicating strong agreement.
  What is statistically significant difference? (lecture 46) -> A statistically significant difference is an observed difference in data that a statistical significance test indicates is not due to chance.
  What is virtual reality (VR)? (lecture 4) -> Virtual reality (VR) is an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli provided by a computer, in which a person's actions partially determine what happens and which replaces the user's sense of reality without requiring the physical existence of objects or places.
  What is virtual environment? (lecture 4) -> Virtual environment is a non-real, computer-generated graphical representation of a real or imaginary world, populated with artificial objects, that is experienced through computer-generated sensory stimuli.

47/A8  recap  47/S3  "Recap"  (5 facts, 15 concepts)
  The controlled VR tour evaluation follows standard experimental stages: defining and identifying users, preparing hardware, software, questionnaires and logistics, and setting a bias-eliminating procedure. Brief pre-experiment training helps make unfamiliar users comparable with familiar users by reducing prior-experience bias. Participants then complete the simulator sickness questionnaire before and after exposure and the presence questionnaire after exploration. Finally, each participant individually explores the whole tour for 45 to 50 minutes, a time estimated to provide heritage access while limiting exposure-linked cybersickness.
  - A controlled experiment defines users, identifies participants, prepares hardware, software, questionnaires and logistics, with a procedure that eliminates bias.
  - Brief pre-experiment training can equalize users by demonstrating the VR system's features and use, reducing familiarity or prior-experience bias.
  - Participants complete the simulator sickness questionnaire before and after exposure and the presence questionnaire after VR exploration.
  - The 45 to 50 minute individual, controlled VR tour exploration was estimated to allow heritage access and limit exposure-linked cybersickness.

47/A12  recap  47/S5  "Recap"  (4 facts, 11 concepts)
  The Majuli VR tour cyber sickness evaluation compared pre- and post-exposure SSQ scores for nausea, disorientation, oculomotor, and total severity. The results showed little change in nausea and disorientation, so the tour did not generally induce cyber sickness, while the oculomotor and total sickness outcomes changed. A Wilcoxon signed-rank test then showed those oculomotor and total sickness changes were statistically significant, indicating the tour design had some effect on total sickness.
  - The Majuli VR tour cyber sickness evaluation collected pre- and post-exposure SSQ scores for nausea, disorientation, oculomotor, and total severity.
  - Majuli VR tour evaluation showed little nausea and disorientation change, suggesting it did not generally induce cyber sickness.
  - A Wilcoxon signed-rank test found statistically significant pre-to-post changes for oculomotor and total sickness, showing the design affected total sickness.

  virtual reality = An artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli provided by a computer, in which a person's actions partially determine what happens and which …
  head-mounted display = A wearable, mobile visual display that integrates electronic, optical, mechanical, and audio components and uses one or two small screens directly in …
  virtual environment = A non-real, computer-generated graphical representation of a real or imaginary world, populated with artificial objects, that is experienced through computer-generated sensory stimuli.

47/A20  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (9 facts, 34 concepts)
  Q What does the Wilcoxon signed-rank test result tell us about the cybersickness changes observed in the Majuli virtual reality tour evaluation?  [47/S5/F1, 47/S5/F2, 47/S5/F3, 46/S3/F3; Wilcoxon signed-rank test, cybersickness, total sickness, statistically significant difference]
    A The Wilcoxon signed-rank test showed that the pre- and post-exposure differences for the oculomotor item and total sickness were not due to chance. Thus, although box plots showed little change in nausea and disorientation and the tour did not generally induce cybersickness, the tour design had some effect on total sickness.
  Q How does the additional reconstruction-fidelity rating for previous visitors help interpret the presence results for the Majuli virtual reality tour?  [47/S2/F4, 47/S4/F2, 47/S4/F4; questionnaire for environmental presence, presence, tangible and intangible reconstruction fidelity, digital avatar]
    A The questionnaire for environmental presence was tailored with items asking previous visitors whether the virtual tour matched their real visit. Their ratings were more favorable on all presence factors, including tangible and intangible reconstruction fidelity. This suggests that the tour's design elements, interaction, implementation and digital avatar reasonably mimicked the physical island, even with higher expectations.
  Q Why was the Majuli virtual reality tour exploration limited to about 45 to 50 minutes?  [47/S3/F2, 47/S3/F3; exploration time, cybersickness, exposure]
    A The 45 to 50 minute exploration time was estimated from pilot studies, trials, and literature to give users sufficient time to explore the large island and obtain heritage information. It was also chosen to minimize the possibility of cybersickness, which depends on exposure.

===== lecture 48: System Implementation

48/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (20 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is empirical study? (lecture 32) -> Empirical study is a usability-testing stage in interactive system development, performed after code testing, that systematically tests a fully implemented system with end users through a controlled experiment to collect and analyze data for assessing overall usability.
  What is cognitive walkthrough? (lecture 43) -> Cognitive walkthrough is a quick expert usability inspection method in which evaluators identify problems by performing interface-level tasks converted from a scenario on at least a low-fidelity vertical prototype, guided by usability questions framed in advance.
  What is heuristic evaluation? (lecture 43) -> Heuristic evaluation is an evaluation technique in which evaluators assess a prototype by ticking items on a checklist of heuristics, without a task scenario or task performance, to identify usability problems across the whole system at an early design stage.
  What is integration? (lecture 16) -> Integration is a stage of the tracking process that aggregates sensory measurements from multiple sensors or input data sources at discrete time points to combine the values and track sense organs, body parts, or the environment, and computes the current sensor orientation from the initial orientation estimated during registration and calibrated angular velocity samples.
  What is interaction design? (lecture 25) -> Interaction design is the activity of designing user input in an XR system from the user's point of view to make the user's interaction easy, effective, and seamless.
  What is iteration? (lecture 32) -> Iteration is a cycle that returns to a previous stage of interactive system development to account for user feedback, in which a design is prototyped, evaluated, and refined until it is stabilized.

48/A1  quiz  48/S0  "Quick quiz"  (7 facts, 33 concepts)
  Q During requirement gathering for an interactive system, which group is the primary source of usability requirements?  [48/S0/F0]
    - Design teams
    - Clients
    - Testers
    * End users
    because: Usability requirements are collected mainly from end users, while functional requirements may come from both end users and clients and other non-functional requirements may come from clients.
  Q Which observation indicates that an interface design is stable?  [48/S0/F1]
    * Further evaluation is unlikely to produce many new issues
    - Further design is unlikely to produce many new issues
    - Further coding is unlikely to produce many new issues
    - Further prototyping is unlikely to produce many new issues
    because: Stability is reached when further evaluation is unlikely to reveal many new issues. Further design, prototyping, or coding is not the stated stopping point for the interface design cycle.
  Q Why does an interactive system need an empirical study even after its code has been tested?  [48/S0/F3, 48/S0/F4]
    - Code testing shows documentation, not usability
    * Code testing shows executability, not usability
    - Code testing shows requirements, not usability
    - Code testing shows usability, not executability
    because: Code testing establishes that the system can run, but it does not estimate how usable it is, so an empirical study is still required.
  Q What makes a long path to deployment possible in the traditional interactive system development lifecycle?  [48/S0/F7, 48/S0/F8, 48/S0/F9]
    - Each phase is reviewed and documented before the next phase starts
    - Each phase is prototyped and documented before the next phase starts
    - Each phase is coded and documented before the next phase starts
    * Each phase is completed and documented before the next phase starts
    because: Deployment is delayed because each phase has to be completed and documented before later work can begin, so any delay or paperwork accumulates. Requirements such as coding or prototyping do not apply to every phase.
  judge round 1: 2 of 4 failed

      check: D
      reason: Fact 1 says 'usability requirements primarily come from end users', which makes D the correct and only defensible answer.
    2 FAIL no_giveaway  (Which observation indicates that an interface design is stable?)
      check: A
      reason: Fact 2 supports A, but A is the only option with the hedge 'unlikely' and the qualifier 'many', and it is the longest, so the correct option is signaled by its form. A repair should make all options parallel and similarly qualified.

48/A2  recap  48/S0  "Recap"  (11 facts, 47 concepts)
  The traditional interactive system lifecycle proceeds through requirement gathering, interface design, code design, implementation and code testing, and an empirical usability study. Each stage must be fully completed and documented before the next stage begins, so deployment comes only after all requirements, design, coding, testing, and usability work are done. Because stages take time and require separate documents, this strict process can produce time and cost overruns or client non-acceptance.
  - Requirement gathering collects functional, non-functional, and usability requirements from clients and end users.
  - Interface design uses repeated design, prototyping, and evaluation cycles until the design is stable.
  - Code design is produced through iterative brainstorming and design notations.
  - Implementation's coding and code testing show executability, not usability, so an empirical study with participants tests usability.
  - Long stages, strict completion, and documentation can delay deployment and cause time/cost overruns or client non-acceptance.
  judge round 1: 3 of 6 failed

A repaired version would say requirement gathering collects functional and non-functional requirements, including usability, from clients and end users.
    2 pass  (Interface design uses repeated design, prototyping, and evaluation cycles until the design is stable.)
      check: none
      reason: Fact 2 supports the repeated design-prototype-evaluate cycle and the stopping condition of a stable interface design. The omission of “quick” and the evaluation methods is not needed for the point's main idea.
    3 pass  (Code design is produced through iterative brainstorming and design notations.)
      check: none
      reason: Fact 3 supports that code design is produced through iterations and brainstorming using design notations; the point's shorter phrasing does not add or contradict the fact.
    4 FAIL supported,faithful  (Implementation's coding and code testing show executability, not usability, so an empirical study with …)
      check: code testing shows that a system is executable [4]; usability testing or an empirical study is therefore needed to estimate usability [5]; empirical study requires identifying participants [6]
      reason: It attributes “show executability” to coding as well as code testing, and it says an empirical study “tests usability” rather than estimates usability as stated. A repaired version would say coding is followed by code testing, which shows executability but not usability, and an empirical study with participants estimates usability.
    5 pass  (Long stages, strict completion, and documentation can delay deployment and cause time/cost overruns or …)
      check: none

  Q What is the main delivery difference between agile development and standard ISDLC?  [48/S1/F1]

    - ISDLC keeps delivering features over successive deliveries

  Q Why can an agile sprint run for four to six weeks while a full ISDLC can take six to nine months?  [48/S1/F3]
    - A sprint does not try to test the release
    - A sprint does not try to collect feedback
    - A sprint does not try to train the users
    * A sprint does not try to do everything at once

    - It demos the current backlog and shares quick feedback for the next cycle

    because: Agile teams give a live demonstration after an iteration and use quick stakeholder feedback before the next sprint. The wrong options replace the demonstrated iteration or the quick feedback with something not used that way.

    - Agile targets documentation completeness, while ISDLC targets quick stakeholder feedback

    - feasibility, documentation, coding, and maintenance
    - conceptualization, inception, release, and production
    * requirements, development, testing, and delivery to production

48/A4  recap  48/S1  "Recap"  (7 facts, 23 concepts)
  Agile development is contrasted with the standard Interactive System Development Life Cycle (ISDLC) as a faster, more incremental way to build interactive systems. Instead of completing everything first, it works through short sprints that each move requirements, development, testing, and delivery forward. Daily meetings, demonstrations, and quick customer or stakeholder feedback let the team adjust the next sprint, which supports practical delivery rather than only a textbook lifecycle.
  - Agile development starts small, cuts unnecessary documentation, and aims for quick, client-acceptable projects.
  - Agile development delivers features over successive short sprints, unlike ISDLC's one completed delivery.
  - In the agile process flow, a sprint includes requirements, development, testing, and delivery.
  - The agile development team uses daily meetings, demos, and quick customer and stakeholder feedback to shape the next sprint.
  - Agile methods aim at practical acceptable products, while ISDLC mainly explains the overall lifecycle flow.
  judge round 1: 1 of 6 failed
    1 FAIL supported,faithful  (Agile development starts small, cuts unnecessary documentation, and aims for quick, client-acceptable projects.)
      check: eliminates [1], ensures [1]
      reason: The point weakens fact 1 by saying agile “cuts” unnecessary documentation instead of “eliminates” unnecessary elements and documentation, and “aims for” quick, client-acceptable projects instead of “ensures quick turnaround” of more client-acceptable projects. A repaired version would say: “Agile development starts small, eliminates unnecessary documentation, and ensures quick, client-acceptable projects.”
    2 pass  (Agile development delivers features over successive short sprints, unlike ISDLC's one completed delivery.)
      check: none
      reason: Fact 2 supports delivering features over successive deliveries unlike ISDLC’s completed-then-delivered system, and fact 4 supports calling the sprint short because it is typically four to six weeks. The point is self-contained, one idea, and faithful.
    3 pass  (In the agile process flow, a sprint includes requirements, development, testing, and delivery.)
      check: none
      reason: Fact 5 directly states that an agile sprint includes requirements, development, testing, and delivery, and fact 3 supports calling this part of the agile process flow. The point is standalone, clear, and one idea.
    4 pass  (The agile development team uses daily meetings, demos, and quick customer and stakeholder feedback …)
      check: none
      reason: Fact 6 states that the team holds daily meetings, gives live demonstrations, and collects quick stakeholder and customer feedback that is shared before the next sprint so it can be addressed, which makes “shape the next sprint” a fair summary. The point is standalone, clear, and one idea.
    5 pass  (Agile methods aim at practical acceptable products, while ISDLC mainly explains the overall lifecycle …)
      check: none
      reason: Fact 8 supports the contrast: agile methods are for developing acceptable products for practical purposes, while ISDLC is primarily for understanding the overall flow and pedagogical purposes. “Explains the overall lifecycle flow” is a fair paraphrase of ISDLC’s role.
    0 pass  (Agile development is contrasted with the standard Interactive System Development Life Cycle (ISDLC) as …)
      check: none
      reason: The text coherently explains that agile is contrasted with ISDLC as faster and incremental, works through short sprints covering requirements, development, testing, and delivery, and uses meetings, demos, and feedback to adjust the next sprint. It covers the segment’s main teaching and does not add unsupported claims or source talk.

  design-prototype-evaluate cycle = A cycle in the iterative software development lifecycle for interactive system development that quickly prototypes, evaluates, and refines interface and interaction design …
  implementation = A stage in interactive system development that involves coding followed by code testing.
  stable interface design = An interface design in interactive system development that is reached after repeating a design-prototype-evaluate cycle until further evaluation is unlikely to produce …
  agile development = A development framework that starts small, avoids collecting all requirements initially, and adds features over successive iterations to deliver projects quickly that …
  conceptualization = A part of the agile development process flow; together with inception, it roughly refers to physical feasibility study and requirement gathering.
  inception = A stage of the agile development process flow in which the team is created and funds and resources are arranged.
  sprint = A stage in the agile development process that typically requires four to six weeks and includes requirements, development, testing, and delivery.
  release = A stage in an agile development process in which testing, training, documentation, and deployment occur.

48/A13  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (12 facts, 40 concepts)
  Q Why does the traditional interactive system development lifecycle often delay deployment and risk client non-acceptance, whereas agile sprint-based delivery can be quicker and more acceptable?  [48/S0/F7, 48/S0/F8, 48/S1/F0, 48/S1/F1, 48/S1/F3; interactive system development lifecycle, agile development, deployment, sprint]
    A Traditional deployment waits until requirements, coding, code testing, and usability testing are all complete, and each stage must be fully completed before the next. This rigidity can cause time and cost overruns and non-acceptance. Agile development starts small, keeps delivering by adding features over successive deliveries, and a sprint is shorter because it does not try to do everything.
  Q Why does an interactive system still need an empirical study even after implementation and code testing have shown that it is executable?  [48/S0/F3, 48/S0/F4, 32/S4/F4; implementation, code testing, empirical study, usability testing]
    A Implementation consists of coding followed by code testing, which can show that the system is executable. However, code testing does not show whether the system is usable. An empirical study, also called usability testing, systematically evaluates usability with end users, so it provides the usability evidence that executable code testing alone cannot provide.
  Q How does an agile sprint use customer or stakeholder feedback to keep development iterative and user-centered?  [48/S1/F4, 48/S1/F5, 32/S2/F2, 32/S2/F3; sprint, feedback, requirement, iteration]
    A In a sprint, requirements are based on the sprint backlog and on customer or stakeholder feedback, and the team provides a live demonstration after each iteration. Quick feedback is shared with the team before the next sprint so that it can be addressed. This creates iterative loops in which user needs and expectations can redirect the work instead of forcing a fixed stage sequence.

===== lecture 49: VR experience optimisation

49/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (14 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is locomotion? (lecture 11) -> Locomotion is the motor component of navigation in a virtual world, the actual movement between two locations, carried out by techniques that let a user move and perceive that the movement has taken place.
  What is gait negation technique? (lecture 40) -> A gait negation technique is a walking-based virtual locomotion technique that requires a specialized setup to cancel the user's lateral movements and keep the user's physical position fixed before the movement is mapped to virtual navigation.
  What is extended reality (XR)? (lecture 1) -> Extended reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR).
  What is immersive experience? (lecture 1) -> An immersive experience is a perceived experience through sensory organs that appears real, because a person cannot distinguish the experienced environment from their real environment and perceives it as that real environment.
  What is virtual reality (VR)? (lecture 4) -> Virtual reality (VR) is an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli provided by a computer, in which a person's actions partially determine what happens and which replaces the user's sense of reality without requiring the physical existence of objects or places.
  What is presence? (lecture 8) -> Presence is a subjective psychological state in which an experience generated by human-made technology is perceived as real, because the user fails to acknowledge the technology's role and perceives computer-generated stimuli as coming from the real world.

    * reducing the chance of cybersickness in VR
    - increasing the realism of the environment in VR

The experience side is framed as reducing the chance of cybersickness, while the resource side arises because VR is generally resource-hungry and affordability matters. Resource optimization then balances lower resource needs against preserving immersive experience quality, with experience optimization as the main concern.
  - VR optimization has two perspectives, psychophysiological experience and technological resource optimization, more prominent in immersive XR.
  - VR experience optimization roughly means designing the experience to minimize cybersickness or its induction.
  - XR and VR systems are generally resource-hungry, so high requirements reduce mass-market affordability.
  - Effective VR resource optimization balances resource requirements with immersive experience, avoiding reduced quality where possible.

49/A4  recap  49/S1  "Recap"  (5 facts, 26 concepts)
  Cybersickness is a multicausal condition that can affect users while using virtual reality. Its causes are divided into internal user factors and external hardware or content factors. Reducing cybersickness can improve user experience and broaden VR appeal, but mitigation can undermine presence, so it must preserve presence even if the experience may feel more artificial.
  - Cybersickness, also called visually induced motion sickness, can affect users interacting with virtual reality (VR) and is not single-factor.
  - Cybersickness factors are internal user factors and external hardware or VR content factors.
  - Reducing cybersickness can greatly enhance user experience and make VR appealing to more people.
  - Cybersickness mitigation must preserve presence, although reducing cybersickness may make the experience feel artificial and less immersive.

49/A5  quiz  49/S2  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 15 concepts)
  Q To minimize cybersickness in a VR tour while keeping presence preserved or maximized, what can be reduced?  [49/S2/F0]
    - the field of view or the visual scene complexity
    * the exposure duration or the navigation distance
    - the route-turn count or the virtual walking speed
    - the display resolution or the headset input latency
    because: Cybersickness is minimized by shortening exposure to the virtual world or by reducing the virtual distance travelled, while presence is preserved or maximized. Changing display or scene properties is not the stated reduction strategy for keeping presence high.
  Q What do full-gait, partial-gait, and gait-negation virtual locomotion techniques have in common?  [49/S2/F1]
    - they require selecting destinations from a list
    - they rely on controller-based steering
    - they follow a path decided by the system
    * they involve physical walking by the user
    because: Full-gait, partial-gait, and gait-negation techniques are walking-based virtual locomotion techniques, so they share the use of physical walking. Steering, selection, and system-controlled movement belong to other categories.
  Q How does a system-controlled VR tour differ from a user-controlled VR tour?  [49/S2/F2]
    - the user decides where and how to move with input
    - the user's physical walking decides the movement path
    - the system decides the visual scene but not the motion
    * the system decides where and how the user moves
    because: In a system-controlled tour, the application controls the user's movement, often along a predetermined path, whereas in a user-controlled tour the user controls how and where to navigate.

    - because the system increases the distance covered
    - because the tour requires continuous user input

49/A6  recap  49/S2  "Recap"  (5 facts, 15 concepts)
  Virtual locomotion techniques and virtual tour control modes define how users move through a VR environment. Reducing virtual-world exposure duration or navigation distance can minimize cybersickness while preserving or maximizing presence. User-controlled tours keep navigation with the user, whereas system-controlled tours can lower cognitive demands but may weaken presence because the user cannot control movement.
  - Cybersickness is minimized by reducing virtual-world exposure duration or navigation distance while preserving or maximizing presence.
  - Virtual locomotion techniques for VR tours include walking-based techniques involving physical walking, steering-based, selection-based, and manipulation-based techniques.
  - VR tours are either user-controlled, where the user navigates, or system-controlled, where the system moves the user.
  - System-controlled VR tours often reduce cognitive demands but can weaken presence because user control is absent.

    - It waits for the user to move from one place to another
    - It prompts the user to move from one place to another
    because: A system-controlled virtual reality tour moves the user along the tour, rather than allowing, prompting, or waiting for user-initiated movement.
  Q Why is a realistic walking experience important in a system-controlled virtual reality tour?  [49/S3/F1]

    * It helps the user feel present rather than controlled by the system
    - It helps the user choose a different route while the system moves them
    because: Realistic walking in a system-controlled tour is important because it supports presence and reduces the user's awareness of being controlled. Judging speed is a difficulty in such tours, not the reason realistic walking is needed.

    - Selection of the user's walking speed
    * Change in the user's walking speed
    - Control of the user's walking speed
    - Steadiness in the user's walking speed
    because: A constant optic flow is not very realistic because people rarely walk at constant speed, so the tour should account for changes in the user's walking speed. Steadiness, control, or selection of that speed is not what makes constant optic flow insufficient.

49/A8  recap  49/S3  "Recap"  (6 facts, 15 concepts)
  A system-controlled VR tour moves the user automatically, so realistic walking helps the user feel present rather than controlled. Because such tours usually do not allow continuous user input, it is hard to align user input with speed or judge whether the provided speed is natural. Since movement is perceived through optic flow, realistic walking requires matching that scene-change speed to the user's instantaneous real-world walking speed, motivating a walking-speed model instead of constant optic flow.
  - A system-controlled VR tour is a navigation mode where the system forces the user to move.
  - Realistic walking in a system-controlled VR tour helps the user feel present rather than controlled.
  - System-controlled VR tours usually do not allow continuous user input, making it hard to align input or judge walking speed.
  - In VR tours, optic flow is the scene-change speed that makes movement appear as a constantly changing view.
  - A realistic system-controlled VR tour uses a walking model to match optic flow to the user's instantaneous real-world walking speed.
  judge round 1: 0 of 6 failed
    1 pass  (A system-controlled VR tour is a navigation mode where the system forces the user …)
      check: none
      reason: The point is a faithful, standalone paraphrase of fact 1: a system-controlled VR tour is a navigation mode in which the system forces user movement.
    2 pass  (Realistic walking in a system-controlled VR tour helps the user feel present rather than …)
      check: none
      reason: The point states the core benefit in fact 2, namely that realistic walking supports presence rather than a controlled feeling, and leaves out only an additional detail.
    3 pass  (System-controlled VR tours usually do not allow continuous user input, making it hard to …)
      check: none
      reason: The point is supported by fact 3: such tours typically lack continuous input, making it difficult to align input with speed or judge the provided speed.
    4 pass  (In VR tours, optic flow is the scene-change speed that makes movement appear as …)
      check: none
      reason: The point is supported by fact 4: optic flow is the scene-change speed through which movement is perceived as a changing view.
    5 pass  (A realistic system-controlled VR tour uses a walking model to match optic flow to …)
      check: none
      reason: The point is supported by facts 5 and 6: a realistic walking tour should match optic flow to the user's real-world walking speed using a walking model.
    0 pass  (A system-controlled VR tour moves the user automatically, so realistic walking helps the user …)
      check: none
      reason: The text summarizes the segment as a connected explanation: system-controlled movement motivates realistic walking, the lack of continuous input creates speed-judgment difficulty, and optic-flow matching motivates a walking-speed model. It is supported by facts 1 through 6 and covers the main taught idea.
  judge kept: original

49/A14  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (11 facts, 20 concepts)
  Q How are psychophysiological experience optimization and resource optimization related in virtual reality?  [49/S0/F0, 49/S0/F1, 49/S0/F3; psychophysiological experience optimization, resource optimization, immersive experience]
    A In virtual reality, optimization can be considered from two perspectives: psychophysiological experience optimization and resource optimization. Experience optimization can roughly be taken to mean designing the experience to minimize cybersickness. Resource optimization means minimizing resource requirements while maximizing immersive experience, which requires balancing the trade-offs between resource requirements and experience.
  Q Why can reducing exposure duration or navigation distance to limit cybersickness still harm a virtual reality experience?  [49/S1/F3, 49/S1/F4, 49/S2/F0; cybersickness mitigation, presence, user experience]
    A Cybersickness mitigation often lowers presence because the user may feel more in an artificial environment than in a real one. Since presence is indirectly related to user experience, this can reduce immersion. The design challenge is therefore to shorten exposure or travel while preserving or maximizing presence.
  Q How can a system-controlled virtual reality tour reduce cognitive demands while still threatening the user's sense of presence?  [49/S2/F3, 49/S2/F4; system-controlled virtual reality tour, presence]
    A System-controlled virtual reality tours are often an effortless experience with reduced cognitive demands because the system decides how and where the user moves. Lack of user involvement makes them less realistic and defeats the purpose of presence because the user is unable to control the movement.
  Q Why is matching a walking speed model more realistic than using a constant optic flow in a system-controlled virtual reality tour that assumes walking?  [49/S3/F3, 49/S3/F4, 49/S3/F5; optic flow, constant optic flow, instantaneous walking speed, walking speed model]
    A Optic flow is the scene-change speed through which movement is perceived. If the tour assumes walking, that optic flow should match typical real-world walking speed, not virtual reality walking speed, or movement looks unrealistic. People rarely walk at constant speed, so matching instantaneous walking speed with a walking speed model is more realistic.

===== lecture 50: VR experience optimisation

50/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (16 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is cybersickness (CS)? (lecture 10) -> Cybersickness (CS) is a condition primarily relevant to virtual reality that may be caused by multiple internal and external factors and in which a user may experience symptoms such as nausea, dizziness, headache, or disorientation.
  What is virtual reality tour? (lecture 33) -> A virtual reality tour is a virtual reality experience for visiting a recreated place without physically going there, in which movement from one point to another is either user-controlled or system-controlled.
  What is practice effect? (lecture 46) -> Practice effect is, in a within-subject design, an improvement in task performance from repeated practice that is a confounding variable and adds noise to the data, because performance gains may be due to practice rather than the interface.
  What is p-value? (lecture 46) -> P-value is a probability in a statistical significance test that the data were obtained by chance, with a lower value meaning the result is less likely to have been obtained by chance.
  What is optic flow? (lecture 49) -> Optic flow is the rate at which the visual scene changes, producing the perception of movement as the view of the surroundings changes.
  What is virtual reality (VR)? (lecture 4) -> Virtual reality (VR) is an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli provided by a computer, in which a person's actions partially determine what happens and which replaces the user's sense of reality without requiring the physical existence of objects or places.

50/A7  quiz  50/S3  "Quick quiz"  (6 facts, 12 concepts)
  Q Which property of a Fourier series makes it useful for modeling the slow-in-slow-out walking pattern?  [50/S3/F0, 50/S3/F1]
    - It can remove the slow start and slow finish by keeping the pattern at full height
    - It can replace step frequency with a constant average speed over the walk
    * It can approximate a start-plateau-stop pattern with a few sinusoidal terms
    - It can convert actual walking speed into perceived scene speed with a constant factor
    because: The slow-in-slow-out pattern resembles a pulse that starts, stays approximately constant, and returns to zero, and a Fourier series can approximate such a periodic shape by combining sinusoidal terms.
  Q How are the weights of the sinusoids in the slow-in-slow-out model determined?  [50/S3/F2]
    - They are standard constants for any square-pulse approximation
    * They are calculated from empirical walking data
    - They are chosen from the user's height and visual gain
    - They are set to equal values for every harmonic term
    because: The Fourier model uses empirically obtained weights for its sinusoids rather than fixed, height-based, or equal weights.
  Q In the virtual walking model, what does visual gain do?  [50/S3/F5]
    - It sets the actual walking speed to a constant average value throughout the walk
    - It changes the step frequency used in the Fourier-series expansion
    - It calculates the distance between the source and the destination
    * It scales actual walking speed to produce the perceived scene-change speed
    because: Visual gain multiplies the user's actual instantaneous walking speed to obtain the perceived or visual scene-change speed.
  Q Why should a virtual tour change the scene at a perceived speed different from the user's actual walking speed?  [50/S3/F3, 50/S3/F4, 50/S3/F5]
    - Perceived motion is usually faster than actual movement, so the perceived scene-change speed can be adjusted to feel natural
    * Perceived motion is usually slower than actual movement, so the perceived scene-change speed can be adjusted to feel natural
    - Perceived motion is best represented by a constant average speed, so the perceived scene-change speed can be fixed to that speed to feel natural
    - Perceived motion should match actual movement in natural walking, so the perceived scene-change speed can be left unchanged to feel natural
    because: People generally perceive visual or optic flow more slowly than their actual movement, so the perceived scene-change speed is adjusted away from actual walking speed to make the walking behavior feel natural. 50/A8  recap  50/S3  "Recap"  (9 facts, 13 concepts)
  A walking-behavior model for system-controlled virtual reality navigation represents the observed slow-in-slow-out pattern with a Fourier-series approximation and handles the mismatch between actual movement and perceived visual flow. A visual gain converts actual walking speed into perceived scene-change speed, while actual walking speed is derived from instantaneous step frequency and user height.
  - The square-pulse-like slow-in-slow-out walking pattern is modeled by a few Fourier terms of sinusoids, with empirical weights.
  - Generally, an individual perceives visual or optic flow more slowly than actual movement.
  - A virtual tour makes perceived scene-change speed natural by multiplying actual instantaneous walking speed by visual gain, typically 2.10.
  - Actual walking speed equals instantaneous step frequency times 0.157 times (user height × 1.72) squared.
  - Instantaneous step frequency is computed from a Fourier-series sum of sinusoids using initial frequency and source-destination distance.
  judge round 1: 4 of 6 failed

A repaired point should say the slow-in-slow-out pattern is modeled by a Fourier-series expansion of sinusoids with empirically calculated weights, without asserting 'a few terms'.
    2 FAIL supported,faithful  (Generally, an individual perceives visual or optic flow more slowly than actual movement.)
      check: In virtual walking [4]

A repaired point should say that, in virtual walking, an individual generally perceives optic flow more slowly than actual movement.
    3 pass  (A virtual tour makes perceived scene-change speed natural by multiplying actual instantaneous walking speed …)

50/A9  quiz  50/S4  "Quick quiz"  (7 facts, 21 concepts)
  Q How does the natural walking speed model produce the perceived walking speed?  [50/S4/F0]
    - By dividing the computed natural walking behavior by a visual gain factor
    - By adding the computed natural walking behavior to a visual gain factor
    * By multiplying the computed natural walking behavior by a visual gain factor
    - By averaging the computed natural walking behavior with a visual gain factor
    because: The model forms perceived natural walking by multiplying computed natural walking behavior by a visual gain factor. Adding, dividing, or averaging the behavior with that factor would not give the model's perceived speed.
  Q Which two navigation conditions did the validation study compare?  [50/S4/F1, 50/S4/F3]
    * A constant-speed navigation condition and an instantaneous-speed navigation condition
    - An instantaneous-speed navigation condition and a measured-step-frequency navigation condition
    - A constant-speed navigation condition and a higher-visual-gain navigation condition
    - A constant-speed navigation condition and an actual-walking-speed navigation condition
    because: The study compared system-controlled navigation at constant speed with navigation at the instantaneous natural walking speed. The other pairings are not the conditions used in that comparison.
  Q Why did participants experience the two speed conditions in randomized order with breaks?  [50/S4/F4]
    - To prevent visual-gain drift and display lag from affecting the data
    * To prevent practice effects and rating bias from affecting the data
    - To prevent picture recognition and scene memory from affecting the data
    - To prevent cybersickness and visual fatigue from affecting the data
    because: Randomizing the conditions and giving breaks was intended to avoid practice effects and bias in the collected ratings. The other listed problems are not the stated reason for that design choice.
  Q What did the statistical test show about the instantaneous natural walking speed condition?  [50/S4/F6]
    - It had significantly lower realism and preference ratings
    - It had significantly higher realism but not preference ratings
    - It had significantly higher preference but not realism ratings
    * It had significantly higher realism and preference ratings
    because: The paired sample t-tests indicated that instantaneous speed was rated more realistically and more preferentially than constant speed. Options that isolate one rating or reverse the direction are not supported by the study's result.
  Q Which issue remains unresolved when using the instantaneous natural walking speed model alone?  [50/S4/F7, 50/S4/F8]
    - Producing a natural perceived speed with that model by itself
    - Increasing user preference with that model by itself
    - Increasing perceived realism with that model by itself
    * Minimizing cybersickness with that model by itself
    because: The model is suitable for a realistic walking experience and is likely to increase presence, but it does not by itself solve cybersickness. Therefore, minimizing cybersickness with only that model remains an open issue.

50/A10  recap  50/S4  "Recap"  (9 facts, 25 concepts)
  The natural walking speed model uses a visual gain factor to make computed walking behavior feel natural to the user. A randomized Oculus Rift art-exhibition study then compared constant average speed with instantaneous natural walking speed, rating realism and preference. Instantaneous speed scored significantly higher on both ratings, so the model suits realistic VR walking and may increase presence, but it does not by itself address cybersickness.
  - The natural walking speed model multiplied computed natural walking behavior by a visual gain factor.
  - The study tested whether instantaneous natural walking speed improves perceived realism compared with constant average speed.
  - Thirty-four participants randomly experienced both speed conditions in an Oculus Rift virtual art exhibition.
  - On realism and preference scales, instantaneous speed scored significantly higher than constant speed.
  - The instantaneous natural walking speed model suits realistic VR walking and may increase presence but does not alone address cybersickness.

    3 pass  (Thirty-four participants randomly experienced both speed conditions in an Oculus Rift virtual art exhibition.)

50/A17  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (16 facts, 48 concepts)
  Q Why should a system-controlled virtual reality tour change the scene at a perceived speed different from the user's actual walking speed rather than at the actual speed?  [50/S3/F3, 50/S3/F4, 50/S3/F5, 50/S3/F6; optic flow, perceived movement speed, actual movement speed, visual gain]
    A In virtual walking, an individual generally perceives optic flow more slowly than the actual movement. To make the walking feel natural, the tour should not change the scene at actual speed, but should set the perceived scene-change speed to a visual gain multiplied by the actual instantaneous walking speed. The gain is typically set to 2.10, so the perceived scene-change speed is 2.10 times the actual walking speed.
  Q Why is a Fourier-series expression suitable for modelling the slow-in-slow-out step-frequency pattern observed in the corridor walking study?  [50/S2/F1, 50/S3/F0, 50/S3/F1, 50/S3/F2; slow-in-slow-out walking pattern, fourier series, square pulse wave, sinusoid]
    A The observed step frequency starts low, rises, plateaus, and falls to zero, a shape similar to a square pulse wave. A Fourier series of harmonically related sinusoids can approximate such a pattern, and a practical approximation is obtained by using the first few terms. Its weights are calculated from the empirical walking data.
  Q Why did the validation study randomize the order in which each participant experienced constant speed and instantaneous natural walking speed?  [50/S4/F4, 46/S2/F2, 50/S4/F5; randomized order, practice effect, bias]
    A Randomized order was used to avoid the practice effect and bias in the data collection. In a within-subject design, the practice effect is an improvement from repeated practice that can confound the analysis by adding noise. Because speed was the independent variable with constant and instantaneous levels, randomizing those conditions avoids confounding the collected realism and preference data with practice or bias.
  Q Why can the instantaneous natural walking-speed model be considered useful for virtual reality realism while it still cannot be treated as a solution to cybersickness?  [50/S4/F6, 50/S4/F7, 50/S4/F8, 10/S0/F0, 10/S0/F1; natural walking speed model, cybersickness, realism, user preference]
    A The validation study found that instantaneous speed produced significantly higher realism and user preference ratings than constant speed, supporting a realistic walking experience and likely presence. Cybersickness, however, is a visually induced motion-sickness condition with many symptoms. The model alone does not address cybersickness, so additional measures are required.

===== lecture 51: VR experience optimisation

51/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (13 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is instantaneous step frequency? (lecture 50) -> Instantaneous step frequency is the number of steps per second, where a step is one foot strike to the next foot strike on the ground.
  What is fourier series? (lecture 50) -> Fourier series is a weighted sum of harmonically related sinusoids that can approximate any continuous periodic function to arbitrary precision, with practical approximations using the first few terms.
  What is visual gain? (lecture 50) -> Visual gain is a factor in a natural walking speed model that multiplies actual instantaneous walking speed to compute the desired perceived scene-change speed.
  What is natural walking speed model? (lecture 50) -> Natural walking speed model is a model for a system-controlled virtual reality tour that displays a visual speed, or optic flow, matching the user's perceived instantaneous walking speed by multiplying actual instantaneous walking speed by a visual gain factor, to provide a realistic walking experience.
  What is virtual reality (VR)? (lecture 4) -> Virtual reality (VR) is an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli provided by a computer, in which a person's actions partially determine what happens and which replaces the user's sense of reality without requiring the physical existence of objects or places.
  What is virtual environment? (lecture 4) -> Virtual environment is a non-real, computer-generated graphical representation of a real or imaginary world, populated with artificial objects, that is experienced through computer-generated sensory stimuli.

  Q In a system-controlled virtual tour, which intended effect follows from matching displayed scene change to perceived speed?  [51/S0/F0]
    * a realistic movement sensation
    - a reduced exposure duration
    - a faster virtual tour
    - a smaller virtual world
    because: Matching displayed scene change to perceived speed creates a realistic movement sensation. It is not the optimization target; exposure duration, travel speed, and world size belong to later optimization levers.
  Q Which aspect is not part of the natural walking model's role in a system-controlled virtual tour?  [51/S0/F1]
    * experience optimization
    - realistic walking feel
    - scene-change matching
    - presence enhancement
    because: The natural walking model's role is to support presence through realistic movement, not to optimize the experience. Presence, realistic feel, and scene-change matching are part of that role.

    - the interaction time at each point of interest
    * the duration of exposure in the virtual world
    - the number of points of interest visited
    - the travel speed between points of interest
    because: The optimization approach addresses cybersickness by controlling how long the user is exposed to the virtual world. Travel speed, POI count, and interaction time may influence exposure, but they are not the target named by this approach.

    - because larger virtual worlds increase the need for travel

51/A2  recap  51/S0  "Recap"  (4 facts, 12 concepts)
  The natural walking model is a realism and presence tool for system-controlled VR tours, not an experience-optimization tool. Since cybersickness symptoms rise as VR exposure duration increases, an optimization approach using the model can control exposure duration and help minimize sickness. This links the model's walking-realism role to reducing sickness by limiting how long users are exposed.
  - For a system-controlled VR tour, the natural walking model creates realistic movement by matching visual speed to perceived walking speed.
  - In a system-controlled VR tour, the natural walking model only enhances presence, not optimization of the experience.
  - Using the natural walking model, VR navigation optimization can limit exposure duration, helping reduce cybersickness as symptoms rise with duration.

51/A4  recap  51/S1  "Recap"  (8 facts, 17 concepts)
  VR exposure duration is set by virtual world size, travel speed, travel time, and interaction time. Reducing travel time by arbitrary speed, teleportation, or terrain changes can shorten exposure but may compromise natural movement or spatial understanding. Semi-interactive VR tours further assume automatic travel and restrict interaction to a small set of objects at POIs.
  - VR exposure duration depends on virtual world size, travel speed, travel time, and object interaction time.
  - A larger virtual world increases VR exposure duration, while faster travel reduces it, though walking speed cannot be arbitrary.
  - Teleportation can reduce VR exposure duration by instant movement, but it is not a natural movement.
  - Changing virtual terrain or POI distances can reduce travel time but can impair real-space perception and wayfinding.
  - System-controlled VR tours ignore interaction time; semi-interactive tours use automatic travel and limit interaction to small POI object sets.

      reason: The point directly paraphrases fact 1’s four determinants of VR exposure duration, without adding or strengthening anything. Fact 1 carries it.
    2 FAIL supported,faithful  (A larger virtual world increases VR exposure duration, while faster travel reduces it, though …)

51/A12  recap  51/S5  "Recap"  (6 facts, 16 concepts)
  Travel-time optimisation is set up as a graph path problem. A path’s travel time is the sum of Euclidean distances between consecutive vertices, and the goal is the minimum-time path through all vertices, a TSP variation. Because TSP assumes a complete graph while the travel-time graph may lack edges, missing pairs receive hypothetical edges weighted by shortest-path lengths. The connectedness of the graph makes those shortest-path lengths well-defined, producing a complete TSP instance.
  - The total travel time of a graph path is the sum of Euclidean edge weights between its consecutive vertices.
  - The travel-time minimisation problem seeks the minimum total travel time path through all graph vertices, a TSP variation.
  - The travelling salesman problem seeks the shortest complete-graph path visiting each node once and returning to start.
  - The travel-time graph is not assumed complete, so a Hamiltonian path visiting all nodes exactly once may not exist.
  - The added hypothetical edges use shortest-path length, well-defined because the graph is connected; direct edges keep Euclidean distance.

    3 pass  (The travelling salesman problem seeks the shortest complete-graph path visiting each node once and …)

51/A13  quiz  51/S6  "Quick quiz"  (4 facts, 17 concepts)
  Q What measure is recorded for a hypothetical edge between two unconnected vertices in the points-of-interest graph?  [51/S6/F1]

    * The shortest-path distance between those vertices in the original graph
    - The travel time between those vertices in the original graph
    - The Euclidean distance between those vertices in the original graph
    because: A missing pair of vertices is joined by a hypothetical edge whose value is based on the shortest route between them in the original graph. Euclidean distance is the original direct-edge weight, and travel time is used only after the completed graph is reweighted.
  Q After the points-of-interest graph has been completed, what do the edge weights given to the travelling-salesman solver represent?  [51/S6/F2]

    * The travel times between each pair of vertices
    - The Euclidean distances between each pair of vertices
    - The number of intermediate vertices between each pair of vertices
    because: The completed graph is reweighted so that each edge weight is the travel time between the two vertices, not the Euclidean distance or the raw shortest-path length. The TSP solver therefore optimizes total travel time.

    - It is kept and its endpoints are treated as directly connected in the original graph
    - It is removed and its endpoints are joined by a direct edge in the original graph
    * It is replaced by the shortest path between its endpoints in the original graph
    - It is replaced by the longest path between its endpoints in the original graph
    because: The TSP solution may use hypothetical edges that do not exist in the original graph, so each such edge is expanded into the shortest original path between its endpoints. Removing it or keeping it would not restore a valid original-graph path.

    - Because the optimal travel time can be capped at the cybersickness time threshold
    because: Even when the algorithm finds the minimum-time path, that time can still exceed the cybersickness threshold in a large environment, so the approach may defeat its purpose. The threshold does not cap, set, or ignore the computed minimum time.

51/A14  recap  51/S6  "Recap"  (6 facts, 19 concepts)
  A minimum-time POI tour can be found by reducing the original graph to a complete time-weighted TSP. The graph is first completed with shortest-path hypothetical edges, then reweighted with travel times, so a standard TSP solver can return an optimal time and tour. The solver’s tour is then made valid by replacing hypothetical edges with shortest paths from the original graph. However, the resulting minimum travel time may still exceed the cybersickness threshold in large environments.
  - The POI optimisation algorithm takes original graph G and produces optimal time T and minimum-time path P covering all vertices.
  - The POI optimisation algorithm keeps direct edges, adds shortest-path edges to complete G', then uses travel-time weights to form G''.
  - For G'', a standard TSP solver returns τ_opt and p_opt; hypothetical edges are replaced by original shortest paths, restoring p_dash_opt.
  - The TSP-based minimum travel time for all POIs can still exceed the cybersickness threshold in large environments.

    - Removing each hypothetical edge from the solver's output before presenting the final route
    - Visiting every point of interest in the shortest possible total travel time
    because: The time-limited approach changes the objective from covering every point of interest to visiting as many as possible before the duration runs out; the other options describe steps of the minimum-time method rather than the goal of the time-limited one.
  Q Before a standard TSP solver is used in the minimum-time VR path method, what changes are made to the original POI graph?  [51/S7/F1, 51/S7/F2, 51/S7/F3, 51/S7/F4]
    - Missing pairs are left absent, and the solver works with directly connected edges
    - Existing pairs receive longer distances, and the solver keeps Euclidean weights
    - Missing pairs receive straight-line hypothetical edges, and the edge weights remain Euclidean distances
    * Missing pairs receive shortest-path hypothetical edges, and the edge weights become travel times
    because: The method first makes the graph complete by representing missing links with shortest paths, then reweights the complete graph using travel times so a standard TSP solver can be applied.
  Q Why is the optimal TSP route not used directly as the final route in the virtual world?  [51/S7/F5]
    - It may use a point of interest more than once in the same tour
    - It may use a direct edge whose Euclidean distance was computed incorrectly
    - It may use a walking speed that changes after each vertex
    * It may use hypothetical edges that are not actual direct connections
    because: The TSP solver works on a completed graph, so its optimal route can contain placeholder links that stand for multi-edge shortest paths and must be replaced before the final route is produced.

51/A17  recap  51/S7  "Recap"  (7 facts, 20 concepts)
  Two path strategies can reduce cybersickness: visiting every point of interest as quickly as possible, or visiting as many points as possible before a time limit. In the minimum-time strategy, points become graph vertices, natural walking-speed shortest-path times become complete-graph weights, and a travelling-salesman problem solver returns an optimal tour. Hypothetical edges in that tour are removed before the final solution path is produced, and if the minimum tour still exceeds the cybersickness threshold, the time-limited maximum-point strategy is introduced.
  - Two XR path optimisation approaches minimize cybersickness: cover all points in minimum time, or cover maximum points within a time limit.
  - The minimum-time approach uses a non-complete graph of points of interest, with direct edges weighted by Euclidean distance.
  - Walking-speed shortest-path travel times become complete-graph weights, mapping the minimum-time all-points problem to a travelling salesman problem.
  - A travelling-salesman problem solver returns optimum time and path, and any hypothetical edges are removed before the final solution path.
  - The minimum-time all-point path may exceed the cybersickness threshold, motivating a time-limited maximum-point approach.

51/A23  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (13 facts, 35 concepts)
  Q Why can limiting interaction time at each point of interest in a semi-interactive virtual reality tour help reduce cybersickness?  [51/S0/F3, 51/S1/F0, 51/S2/F0; cybersickness, exposure duration, interaction time, semi-interactive virtual tour]
    A Cybersickness symptoms rise as virtual reality exposure duration increases. Exposure duration includes time spent inspecting, selecting, or manipulating virtual objects. In a semi-interactive tour, the system can cap interaction at each point of interest by forcing the user to move on after an estimated maximum time, so this capped interaction time can reduce total exposure and thus the risk of cybersickness.
  Q Why are travel times in the virtual reality tour optimisation computed with the natural walking-speed model instead of assuming an arbitrarily high virtual travel speed?  [51/S0/F0, 51/S1/F2, 51/S1/F3; natural walking speed model, virtual travel speed, perception of movement, exposure duration]
    A The natural walking-speed model displays optic flow that matches the perceived instantaneous walking speed, producing a realistic perception of movement. Although higher virtual travel speed would lower travel time and exposure duration, virtual travel speed cannot be modified arbitrarily when a realistic walking experience is required. Therefore travel-time estimates use the model's constrained realistic speed rather than an arbitrary maximum speed.
  Q Why must hypothetical edges be added to the original virtual-world graph before it can be solved as a travelling-salesman problem?  [51/S5/F2, 51/S5/F3, 51/S5/F4, 51/S6/F1; travelling salesman problem, complete graph, hypothetical edge, shortest path]
    A A standard travelling-salesman problem is posed on a complete graph, while the original virtual-world graph need not be complete because some vertex pairs may not be directly connected. For such pairs, the algorithm adds a hypothetical edge whose length is the shortest path between the two vertices in the original graph. This makes the graph complete, so a standard travelling-salesman-problem solver can be used.
  Q Why may a minimum-time tour that visits every point of interest still be inadequate for reducing cybersickness?  [51/S6/F5, 51/S7/F0, 51/S0/F3, 51/S7/F6; minimum-time approach, time threshold, cybersickness, alternative path optimization approach]
    A The minimum-time approach finds the shortest possible tour covering all points of interest, but in a large virtual environment the minimum time may still exceed the time threshold associated with cybersickness. Because cybersickness is correlated with exposure duration, minimizing time alone does not ensure the tour remains under that threshold. An alternative approach can therefore choose the maximum number of points of interest that can be experienced within a given time limit.
  judge round 1: 0 of 4 failed
    1 pass  (Why can limiting interaction time at each point of interest in a semi-interactive virtual …)
      check: Limiting interaction time can reduce cybersickness because interaction time contributes to VR exposure duration and cybersickness increases with exposure duration.
      reason: Facts 4, 5, and 13 carry the link: cybersickness rises with exposure duration, exposure duration depends on interaction time, and a semi-interactive tour can cap interaction time at each POI.
    2 pass  (Why are travel times in the virtual reality tour optimisation computed with the natural …)
      check: The model is used because it preserves a realistic perception of movement, while arbitrarily increasing travel speed, though it would shorten exposure, is not allowed if a realistic walking experience is required.
      reason: Facts 1, 7, and 8 supply the needed comparison: the model matches optic flow to perceived walking speed, higher speed would reduce exposure, and speed cannot be arbitrarily modified when realism is required.
    3 pass  (Why must hypothetical edges be added to the original virtual-world graph before it can …)
      check: Hypothetical edges are added because a standard TSP requires a complete graph, whereas the original graph may lack direct edges, so missing pairs are connected by edges weighted by shortest-path lengths.

===== lecture 52: VR experience optimisation

52/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (16 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is natural walking speed model? (lecture 50) -> Natural walking speed model is a model for a system-controlled virtual reality tour that displays a visual speed, or optic flow, matching the user's perceived instantaneous walking speed by multiplying actual instantaneous walking speed by a visual gain factor, to provide a realistic walking experience.
  What is travel time? (lecture 51) -> Travel time is the duration that moving between vertices in a virtual world takes, calculated from their distance and a natural walking-speed model; for a path, it is the sum of the times between consecutive vertices.
  What is original graph? (lecture 51) -> Original graph is the weighted graph input to an optimal-path algorithm that represents a virtual world, with vertices as points of interest, directly connected edges weighted by Euclidean distance, connected but not necessarily complete, and importance and waiting time specified for each node.
  What is vertex set? (lecture 51) -> Vertex set is the set of all points of interest, represented as vertices, in a weighted graph that represents a virtual world.
  What is edge weight? (lecture 51) -> Edge weight is a number assigned to a graph edge that represents the Euclidean distance for directly connected vertices, a very large number for non-directly connected vertices initially, the shortest path length after modification, or travel time in the final time-weighted graph.
  What is complete graph? (lecture 51) -> A complete graph is a graph in which every pair of vertices is connected by an edge; where a direct edge is absent, a hypothetical edge representing the shortest path between the vertices is used.

52/A1  quiz  52/S0  "Quick quiz"  (4 facts, 14 concepts)
  Q What does a time-constrained virtual tour optimisation approach try to find?  [52/S0/F0]
    - a path that uses the least movement before the exposure limit
    * a path that visits the most points of interest before the exposure limit
    - a path that reaches the farthest point of interest before the exposure limit
    - a path that visits every graph vertex before the exposure limit
    because: The optimization goal is to cover as many points of interest as possible while staying within the cybersickness time threshold. It does not require visiting every vertex, and it is not aimed at minimizing movement or reaching a distant point.
  Q What does the cybersickness threshold limit in a virtual tour?  [52/S0/F1]
    - the distance of scene travel, route length, or path length before cybersickness may occur
    * the duration of movement, experience, or VR exposure before cybersickness may occur
    - the count of objects visited, vertices covered, or POIs visited before cybersickness may occur
    - the rate of frames displayed, tracker updates, or scene changes before cybersickness may occur
    because: The threshold is a maximum duration for the VR tour, because exceeding it may cause cybersickness. It is not a limit on distance, object count, or display/update rate.
  Q Why can a tour that covers every vertex in minimum time still be risky for cybersickness?  [52/S0/F2]
    - it can still visit too many vertices and cause cybersickness
    * it can still take too long and cause cybersickness
    - it can still collect too much importance and cause cybersickness
    - it can still cover too much scene and cause cybersickness
    because: Even a minimum-time tour covering all vertices can still be unsafe if its traversal is too long. Excessive duration, not vertex count, importance, or scene coverage, is the cybersickness risk.
  Q Where can a recommended cybersickness time threshold be obtained from?  [52/S0/F3]
    * an empirical user study or pre-existing study results
    - the headset's field of view or frame rate
    - a fixed universal standard or vendor specification
    - the virtual world graph's vertex count or edge count
    because: There is no simple universal way to determine the threshold, so it can come from studying a limited set of users or from earlier study results. Graph metrics or headset specifications do not directly provide it.

52/A2  recap  52/S0  "Recap"  (4 facts, 14 concepts)
  Time-constrained VR tour optimization aims to visit as many points of interest as possible before a fixed time limit is reached. That limit is the cybersickness time threshold TTH, the maximum allowed tour, movement, experience, or exposure duration, and crossing it may cause cybersickness. A minimum-time tour covering all virtual-world graph vertices can still exceed TTH, and TTH is not easy to determine; it may depend on content and movement speed, or come from empirical or pre-existing study results.
  - Time-constrained VR tour optimization seeks the path covering most points of interest within the time threshold TTH.
  - The cybersickness time threshold TTH is the maximum VR tour, movement, experience, or exposure duration; crossing it may cause cybersickness.
  - A minimum-time tour covering all virtual-world graph vertices may still exceed TTH and cause cybersickness.
  - The time threshold TTH is not easy to set; it may depend on content, movement speed, or studies.

    - by multiplying the importance assigned to each node on the path

52/A4  recap  52/S1  "Recap"  (5 facts, 7 concepts)
  Node importance gives a way to value points of interest in a time-limited VR tour. Because a feasible tour need not visit, and may not be able to visit, every node, each node receives a positive real importance value, and a path's total importance is the sum of its node importances. The optimization objective is then to choose a path within the time threshold with the largest total importance.
  - A VR tour within a time threshold need not visit every point-of-interest node and may be unable to.
  - An importance function maps each VR point-of-interest node to a positive real number, with larger numbers meaning higher importance.
  - Node importance is needed to decide which VR nodes to cover within the given time threshold.
  - The total importance of a VR tour path is the sum of the importance of all nodes in that path.
  - The objective is to find, among all VR tour paths within the time threshold, the one with maximum total importance.

52/A8  recap  52/S3  "Recap"  (3 facts, 11 concepts)
  VR tour optimization can be treated as a vehicle routing problem with profit (VRPP), where route profit is node importance and not all nodes must be visited. Existing VRPP solvers can then produce the optimal path that maximizes total node importance within a time threshold. That threshold is the cybersickness limit on user exposure, and the path must still visit as many of the most important points of interest as possible within it.
  - Vehicle routing problem with profit (VRPP) generalizes vehicle routing, allowing unvisited nodes and maximizing node importance within a time constraint.
  - Existing vehicle routing problem with profit solvers can find the path maximizing total node importance within the time threshold.
  - The optimized path must keep user's exposure below the cybersickness time threshold while maximizing most important POI visits within it.
