52/A9  quiz  52/S4  "Quick quiz"  (4 facts, 16 concepts)
  Q What does the optimal path aim to achieve?  [52/S4/F1]
    - minimizing total travel time within the exposure-time threshold
    * maximizing total importance within the exposure-time threshold
    - maximizing total waiting time within the exposure-time threshold
    - balancing travel time and waiting time within the exposure-time threshold
    because: The optimal path is chosen to maximize total importance while keeping the sum of travel time and waiting time under the time threshold. It is not primarily a shortest-travel or waiting-time-balancing path.
  Q What is the first stage of the optimal-path algorithm?  [52/S4/F2]
    - It replaces the shortest path with the absent direct connection between those vertices
    * It replaces the absent direct connection with the shortest path between those vertices
    - It replaces the absent direct connection with the Euclidean distance between those vertices
    - It replaces the Euclidean edge weight with the walking time between those vertices
    because: The algorithm first makes the graph complete by inserting, for each pair of vertices without a direct edge, the shortest path between them. Converting distances to walking times happens afterward.
  Q Why does the algorithm convert the edge weights of the complete graph before the VRPP solver runs?  [52/S4/F3]
    - so each edge weight represents the Euclidean distance for a realistic experience
    - so each edge weight represents the node importance for a realistic experience
    * so each edge weight represents the walking time for a realistic experience
    - so each edge weight represents the waiting time for a realistic experience
    because: Edge weights are changed from Euclidean distances to travel times from the natural walking model so the path costs reflect how long the user actually spends moving. They do not encode importance, waiting time, or raw distance.
  Q Why is the path returned by the VRPP solver changed before the algorithm outputs it?  [52/S4/F5]
    - so each waiting time is replaced by an edge travel time in the original graph
    - so each vertex is replaced by the nearest point of interest in the original graph
    - so each shortest path is replaced by a hypothetical edge in the original graph
    * so each hypothetical edge is replaced by a shortest path in the original graph
    because: The solver works on a complete graph, so its direct edges may be hypothetical. The algorithm re-expands each such edge into the corresponding shortest path in the original environment graph before returning the path.

52/A10  recap  52/S4  "Recap"  (6 facts, 22 concepts)
  The optimal-path algorithm prepares a virtual environment graph for optimal tour planning. First, the original graph is made complete using shortest paths, and its edge weights are changed to realistic walking travel times. The transformed graph, together with node importance and waiting times, is then given to a VRPP solver. The solver's optimal path is finally returned after replacing its hypothetical edges with corresponding shortest paths in the original environment.
  - The optimal-path algorithm starts from a fully connected but not necessarily complete graph G with node importance and waiting times.
  - The optimal path maximizes importance, covers the maximum number of most important POIs, and stays below the exposure-time threshold.
  - The algorithm first creates a complete version of G by replacing missing edges with shortest paths.
  - The algorithm then replaces the complete graph's Euclidean edge weights with natural walking travel times.
  - The final graph with importance and waiting times is solved by VRPP, and hypothetical path edges become original shortest paths.

52/A17  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (12 facts, 32 concepts)
  Q Why can a virtual reality tour that visits every point of interest in minimum time still cause cybersickness?  [52/S0/F1, 52/S0/F2; virtual reality tour, point of interest, cybersickness, time threshold]
    A Because the time needed to traverse all points of interest can exceed the cybersickness time threshold. That threshold is the maximum virtual reality exposure or movement duration, and crossing it may cause cybersickness. Therefore a minimum-time tour covering all vertices is not safe if its traversal time is longer than the threshold.
  Q Why does a virtual reality tour optimizer need an importance value for each point of interest when the tour must be completed within a time threshold?  [52/S1/F0, 52/S1/F2, 52/S1/F3, 52/S1/F4; point of interest, importance, total importance, time threshold]
    A It is needed because visiting every point of interest is neither mandatory nor always possible within the threshold. Importance identifies which points of interest are worth selecting, and the total importance of a path is the sum of the importances of its nodes. The optimizer chooses the path with maximum total importance among paths whose completion time stays within the threshold.
  Q Why must the virtual reality path optimization constraint include waiting time as well as travel time?  [52/S2/F1, 52/S2/F2, 52/S2/F3; waiting time, total completion time, time threshold, virtual reality path optimization model]
    A The revised virtual reality path optimization model constrains total completion time, not only T(P). Waiting time at a node is the maximum time a user requires to inspect or interact with the object there, and the total waiting time W(P) is the sum of these waiting times. Therefore the constraint uses T(P) + W(P), requiring it to be less than or equal to T_H.
  Q How does the natural walking model make the complete time-weighted graph used by the vehicle routing problem with profit solver represent a realistic virtual reality tour?  [52/S4/F3, 52/S4/F4, 51/S0/F0; natural walking speed model, travel time, complete time-weighted graph, vehicle routing problem with profit solver]
    A It supplies travel times computed from the natural walking model, replacing the original Euclidean edge weights, so the final graph's edges are weighted by travel duration. That final graph, with each node's importance and waiting time, is given as input to the VRPP solver. The natural walking model displays optic flow matching the user's perceived instantaneous walking speed, so the solver input represents realistic travel durations rather than raw distances.

===== lecture 53: VR experience optimisation

53/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (19 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is point of interest (POIs)? (lecture 21) -> Point of interest (POI) is a significant spot in a virtual tour, modeled as a graph node or vertex with importance and a maximum waiting time, that need not be a physical object and is visited to inspect or interact with objects.
  What is original graph? (lecture 51) -> Original graph is the weighted graph input to an optimal-path algorithm that represents a virtual world, with vertices as points of interest, directly connected edges weighted by Euclidean distance, connected but not necessarily complete, and importance and waiting time specified for each node.
  What is time threshold (TTH)? (lecture 52) -> Time threshold (TTH) is the maximum duration of user movement, experience, or virtual reality exposure in a virtual tour, beyond which cybersickness may occur; it is the upper time limit used when optimizing a tour path.
  What is vehicle routing problem with profit (VRPP)? (lecture 52) -> Vehicle routing problem with profit (VRPP) is a generalization of the vehicle routing problem, an operations research problem, in which not all nodes must be visited and the route maximizes profit, the importance of the nodes, within a time constraint.
  What is virtual reality (VR)? (lecture 4) -> Virtual reality (VR) is an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli provided by a computer, in which a person's actions partially determine what happens and which replaces the user's sense of reality without requiring the physical existence of objects or places.
  What is virtual environment? (lecture 4) -> Virtual environment is a non-real, computer-generated graphical representation of a real or imaginary world, populated with artificial objects, that is experienced through computer-generated sensory stimuli.

53/A1  quiz  53/S0  "Quick quiz"  (4 facts, 14 concepts)
  Q What remains a problem with the optimal path approach in a very large virtual world?  [53/S0/F0]
    - Its shortest complete tour can still exceed the minimum point count
    - Its shortest complete tour can still exceed the maximum walking speed
    - Its shortest complete tour can still exceed the display frame budget
    * Its shortest complete tour can still exceed the safe exposure duration
    because: Finding the shortest route through all points does not guarantee that the tour fits the user's safe VR exposure time; in a large world the minimum time can still be too long and cause cybersickness.
  Q How does the optimal path under a time constraint differ from the basic optimal path approach?  [53/S0/F1]
    - It adds an upper distance limit and a goal of covering the most important points within it
    - It adds an upper speed limit and a goal of covering every point within it
    - It adds an upper point limit and a goal of covering the least important points within it
    * It adds an upper exposure limit and a goal of covering the most important points within it
    because: The time-constrained approach sets a maximum exposure time and then chooses a path that fits that time while covering as many important points as possible, instead of merely finding the shortest path through all points.
  Q Why is a complete walking-based tour of Auniati's whole site not recommended as a VR experience?  [53/S0/F5]
    * A complete walking visit can last up to a day, and full-day VR exposure can induce cybersickness
    - A complete walking visit can last up to a day, and full-day VR exposure can improve spatial memory
    - A complete walking visit can last up to a day, and full-day VR exposure can reduce the need for navigation
    - A complete walking visit can last up to a day, and full-day VR exposure can increase walking realism
    because: A full walk of the site may take as long as a day, and such a long VR exposure is not advised because it can induce cybersickness.
  Q Why does the system-controlled Auniati VR tour use a natural walking speed model?  [53/S0/F6]
    - To make every point of interest more important
    * To make the walking-based exploration feel realistic
    - To make the shortest navigation path shorter
    - To make the time threshold easier to satisfy
    because: The tour keeps walking-based exploration realistic by using a natural walking speed model; the model is for realism, not for changing the path length, threshold, or point importance.

53/A2  recap  53/S0  "Recap"  (6 facts, 16 concepts)
  The Majuli VR tour must control how long users are exposed to a large virtual site, because Auniati Satra is big enough that a full walk can be unsafe in VR. Since the tour uses walking-based exploration at a natural walking speed, the navigation path directly affects exposure time. The optimal path approach may still take too long, so the time-constrained approach limits exposure by choosing which important points can be covered within a set time.
  - Majuli is a river island, and Auniati Satra has at least 25 points of interest.
  - Exploring all of Auniati Satra by walking can take up to a day, and full-day VR exposure would induce cybersickness.
  - The system-controlled Auniati Satra VR tour uses walking-based exploration with a natural walking speed model.
  - The optimal path approach finds the minimum-time route covering all points, but in Majuli it may still cause cybersickness.
  - The time-constrained approach sets an exposure threshold and covers the most important points within that limit.

    - The maximum wait time at the two point-of-interest locations
    * The Euclidean distance between the two point-of-interest locations
    because: In the Satra graph, edges are weighted by the Euclidean distance between the points of interest they connect. Importance and wait time are attributes associated with points of interest, not with edges.
  Q When are per-point importance values and maximum wait times required in the Satra VR navigation optimization?  [53/S1/F4, 53/S1/F6]
    - When the proposed route has to skip the lake corners because of distance
    * When the all-point minimum-time path is longer than the exposure time threshold
    - When the campus graph has fewer than the stated minimum number of nodes
    - When the field study relied only on interviews with Satra committee members
    because: The second optimization approach is needed when the shortest route through all points of interest still takes too long for a comfortable VR exposure. Then points of interest are ranked by importance and their stopping times are included so that the best route can be found within the time limit.
  Q How was the field-study data for the Satra graph gathered?  [53/S1/F2]
    - By extracting preexisting map coordinates and comparing them with satellite views at the Satra
    - By asking remote users to rate a fixed list of landmarks at the Satra
    - By testing a finished virtual tour and recording comfort reports at the Satra
    * By observing visitors' movement and stopping and interviewing residents at the Satra
    because: The graph was built from on-site contextual inquiry: people's travel and stopping behavior were observed and manually recorded, and campus residents and Satra committee members were interviewed about places people visit and recommend.
  Q What does the maximum wait time at a point of interest cover in the navigation model?  [53/S1/F5]
    - Time to pause, calibrate, and restart the virtual session before resuming navigation
    - Time to choose, compare, and preview the next stop before resuming navigation
    - Time to walk, look around, and take photographs before resuming navigation
    * Time to stop, inspect, and interact with the place before resuming navigation
    because: Maximum wait time is the time needed at a point of interest for the user to stop, inspect it, interact with it if possible, and then continue navigating. It is not the time spent traveling to the next point or performing system setup.

53/A4  recap  53/S1  "Recap"  (7 facts, 16 concepts)
  Turning the Majuli Satra site into a weighted point-of-interest graph enables routing solvers to optimize navigation. The graph is built from field study, and when a simple minimum-time route is too long, a second approach adds POI importance and maximum wait time. A TSP solver can cover all POIs, while a VRPP solver can choose a route within a time limit that favors the most important POIs.
  - The Satra graph has at least 25 point-of-interest nodes, Euclidean-distance edges, and POIs need not be physical.
  - The Satra graph is built iteratively through field study, observing travel behavior and interviewing residents and committee members.
  - If the first path exceeds the time threshold, the second approach assigns each POI importance and maximum wait time.
  - A POI's maximum wait time is the time to stop, inspect, interact, and resume navigation.
  - Using the graph, TSP finds a minimum-time all-node path; VRPP finds a threshold path maximizing important POIs.

53/A10  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (8 facts, 29 concepts)
  Q Why can the optimal path approach for a virtual reality navigation route still be unsuitable for the Auniati Satra tour even though it minimizes travel time?  [53/S0/F0, 53/S0/F5; optimal path approach, cybersickness, Auniati Satra]
    A The optimal path approach finds the minimum-time path that lets a user explore all points of interest. In a very large virtual world such as the Majuli River Island virtual tour, that minimum time can still be very large compared with the expected virtual reality exposure duration. Exploring the whole Auniati Satra by walking may take up to a day, and a full-day virtual reality exposure is not recommended because it would induce cybersickness.
  Q How does the optimal path under a time constraint approach use the time threshold to choose a navigation path for a walking-based virtual reality tour of Auniati Satra?  [53/S0/F1, 52/S0/F1; optimal path under a time constraint approach, time threshold, cybersickness, covering]
    A The approach sets an upper exposure limit, the time threshold, and searches for a path only within that duration. It selects the path that covers the maximum number of the most important points of interest, where covering includes interacting with or inspecting them and navigating between them. Keeping the tour within this threshold matters because exceeding it may cause cybersickness.
  Q Why must points of interest in the time-constrained virtual reality navigation model be assigned relative importance and maximum wait time before a vehicle routing problem with profit solver is used?  [53/S1/F4, 53/S1/F5, 53/S1/F6, 52/S3/F0; relative importance, maximum wait time, vehicle routing problem with profit solver, time threshold]
    A The time-constrained virtual reality navigation model requires each point of interest to have relative importance and maximum wait time. Importance is the profit a vehicle routing problem with profit route maximizes within a time constraint, and wait time is the time to stop, inspect, interact if possible, and resume navigation. These let the solver keep the route within the time threshold, accounting for stopping time, while covering the most important points.

===== lecture 54: VR resource optimization

54/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (19 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is resource optimization? (lecture 49) -> Resource optimization is the technological optimization of resource requirements in extended reality (XR), including virtual reality (VR), that minimizes those requirements while maximizing immersive experience without compromising it. It generally focuses on client-end hardware so users can have a good experience with affordable hardware.
  What is computer? (lecture 13) -> A computer is one of the major components of virtual reality (VR) hardware, a device that processes data from input sensors and activates output devices so that a user can perceive the world.
  What is output device? (lecture 13) -> An output device is an XR hardware component that produces output to stimulate a user's sensory organs, not only a visual display; examples include visual displays, audio output, haptics, motion platforms, and treadmills.
  What is software development kit (SDK)? (lecture 19) -> Software development kit (SDK) is a platform-dependent installable package of software development tools for a specific hardware and operating system combination that provides fundamental tools to design, build, and test virtual or augmented reality experiences.
  What is rendering? (lecture 19) -> Rendering is the multi-stage computational process that creates a scene's visual output as a two-dimensional image that can be displayed, and, in a broad sense, output for other senses.
  What is computer graphics (CG)? (lecture 19) -> Computer graphics (CG) is the area that addresses computer-generated images from synthetic models. It creates or represents objects, synthesizes them into a scene, allows users to manipulate images on a screen, creates the perception of motion, and renders the scene on a display so humans can perceive it.

  Q What is the objective of VR resource optimization?  [54/S0/F0, 54/S0/F1]
    - Increasing resource requirements to make the VR experience more immersive
    - Eliminating resource requirements at any cost to the VR experience
    * Minimizing resource requirements while preserving the VR experience
    - Leaving resource requirements unchanged so that the VR experience is not affected
    because: VR is resource hungry, so optimization aims to reduce the resources needed without weakening the experience. Increasing resources or accepting a worse experience does not match the objective.
  Q Why does VR resource optimization often concentrate on client-end hardware?  [54/S0/F3, 54/S0/F4]

    - It makes software, manpower, and infrastructure the main targets for optimization
    * It gives a direct way to optimize resources without being entangled in many issues
    - It is the only resource type that affects the quality of the VR experience
    because: Client-end hardware is a practical focus because it avoids many of the varied and complex issues involved in optimizing all resource types. It is not the only important resource, and it does not remove all funding or policy concerns.

54/A2  recap  54/S0  "Recap"  (5 facts, 26 concepts)
  Extended reality, especially virtual reality, is resource hungry, so VR resource optimization aims to minimize resource requirements while maximizing the VR experience. XR resources include hardware, software, manpower, and supporting infrastructure, and optimizing each type separately can be difficult because considerations vary widely. Therefore, VR resource optimization generally treats some resources as given and focuses on client-end hardware to support affordable, good user experiences.
  - Extended reality, especially virtual reality, is resource hungry, so VR resource optimization is needed.
  - VR resource optimization aims to minimize resource requirements while maximizing the VR experience without compromise.
  - Extended reality resources can include hardware, software, manpower, and supporting infrastructure.
  - Separately optimizing each XR resource type is difficult because its considerations vary widely.
  - VR resource optimization generally treats some resources as given and focuses on client-end hardware for affordable, good user experiences.

54/A6  recap  54/S2  "Recap"  (9 facts, 15 concepts)
  A generic graphics system places a display controller, video memory, and video controller between a host computer and a display screen. The host CPU sends display commands and passes rendering tasks to the display controller, which generates a digital image and stores it in video memory. A video controller then uses that stored digital image to create analog voltages that excite the screen pixels, producing a colored image.
  - A generic graphics system has a host computer and display with display controller, video memory, and video controller between.
  - The host CPU sends display commands to the display controller and may receive interaction data from it.
  - The display controller, usually a graphics card with a GPU, generates the image to keep rendering off the CPU.
  - The display controller sends the digital image to video memory, a dedicated part of memory sometimes called VRAM.
  - A video controller uses video memory data to create analog voltages that excite screen pixels to show a colored image.

  Q Which pixels are excited when a vector scan device draws a line or curve?  [54/S3/F1]
    * The selected pixels that represent the primitive
    - The pixels chosen at random from the screen
    - The pixels activated in a fixed left-right order
    - The whole grid of pixels in the frame buffer
    because: A vector scan device renders an image by exciting only selected pixels that form geometric primitives such as lines and curves. Activating the whole grid in a fixed order describes raster scan, and “random scan” is a name for vector scan rather than a description of choosing pixels at random.
  Q What feature keeps vector scan devices mainly in specialized, low-quantity applications?  [54/S3/F2]
    - The high precision needed to activate every pixel
    * The high precision needed to excite specific pixels
    - The sequential activation needed to excite every pixel
    - The low precision needed to excite specific pixels
    because: Vector scan devices require high precision to target and excite specific pixels, which makes them costly and unsuitable for mass production. Activating every pixel or doing so in sequence describes raster scan devices, and vector scan devices are not characterized by low precision.
  Q What determines whether a graphic device is a vector scan device or a raster scan device?  [54/S3/F0]
    * The method used for excitation of pixels
    - The amount of video memory used
    - The rate at which pixel light decays
    - The number of pixels in the display grid
    because: Graphic devices are divided into vector scan and raster scan devices by the method used to excite pixels. Grid size, video memory, and pixel-light decay are unrelated to that division.

54/A9  recap  54/S3  "Recap"  (6 facts, 17 concepts)
  Graphic devices are divided into vector scan and raster scan devices by the method used to excite pixels. Vector scan devices excite only selected pixels for geometric primitives, but high precision makes them costly and limited to specialized settings. Raster scan devices activate all pixels in sequence, requiring less precision and much lower cost, so commercial products typically use raster scan displays.
  - Graphic devices are of two types, vector scan and raster scan, by how pixels are excited.
  - Vector scan devices view an image as geometric primitives and excite only selected pixels representing them.
  - Vector scan devices need high precision to excite specific pixels, so they are costly and limited to specialized settings.
  - Raster scan devices activate all pixels in sequence, a less precise and much cheaper method than vector scan.
  - Commercial products, such as smartphones and televisions, typically comprise raster scan displays.

54/A10  quiz  54/S4  "Quick quiz"  (9 facts, 21 concepts)
  Q In a raster scan display, what does the frame buffer hold for each pixel?  [54/S4/F0, 54/S4/F1]
    - a sequential excitation order
    * a bit-string intensity value
    - a geometric primitive position
    - a mixed red-green-blue color
    because: A raster scan frame buffer keeps one memory location per pixel, storing that pixel’s intensity as a bit string. It does not store scan order, a perceived mixed color, or vector primitive positions.
  Q Why does a raster scan display need periodic refreshing even when the image is not changing?  [54/S4/F2, 54/S4/F3, 54/S4/F4]
    - because stored red-green-blue values can fade and the image can become non-uniform
    - because stored frame-buffer bits can fade and the image can become non-uniform
    - because scanned pixel timing can fade and the image can become non-uniform
    * because excited pixel light can fade and the image can become non-uniform
    because: Pixels’ emitted light decays, so a still image would fade; because scanning reaches pixels at different times, that fading can make the image non-uniform. Refreshing re-excites the pixels to keep the displayed image uniform.
  Q Why is a higher refresh rate more useful for a VR display than for a typical computer screen?  [54/S4/F5, 54/S4/F6]
    - the VR headset stores a larger frame buffer
    - the VR scene uses vector scan rendering
    * the VR screen sits much closer to the eyes
    - the VR frame buffer holds more intensity values
    because: A VR screen is much closer to the eyes than a typical computer screen, so refresh-rate differences are more noticeable there; the amount of stored intensity data is not what makes the higher rate more useful.
  Q How does a color display create the color that a viewer sees?  [54/S4/F7, 54/S4/F8]
    - by scanning different intensities of red, green, and blue values in the eye
    * by mixing different intensities of red, green, and blue light in the eye
    - by separating different intensities of red, green, and blue light in the eye
    - by storing different intensities of red, green, and blue values in the eye
    because: A color pixel emits red, green, and blue light at different intensities, and the observed color is formed when those lights are mixed in the eye. The color is not made by separating, storing, or scanning those values in the eye.

54/A11  recap  54/S4  "Recap"  (9 facts, 21 concepts)
  A raster-scan display stores a color image in a frame buffer that matches screen resolution, then re-excites pixels periodically because their light fades and sequential excitation can distort the picture. The refresh rate sets how often the scene is redrawn, with higher rates always preferable for VR because its screen is close to the eyes. Color is created by pixels with red, green, and blue light emitters whose light is mixed in the eye.
  - The raster-scan frame buffer stores each pixel's intensity as bits, one location per pixel, sized to screen resolution.
  - Because raster-scan pixels decay and are excited left-to-right, top-to-bottom, screen refreshing periodically re-excites them, preventing fading and distortion.
  - Refresh rate is scene refreshes per second in hertz; 60 Hz is good, and VR always prefers higher rates.
  - Color display pixels typically have red, green, and blue emitters; the eye mixes their light to perceive color.

      check: light emitted from excited pixel elements decays [3]
      reason: The point says “pixels decay,” but the facts say the light emitted from excited pixel elements decays. A repaired version should say the pixel light or emitted light decays, while keeping the rest.
    3 FAIL faithful  (Refresh rate is scene refreshes per second in hertz; 60 Hz is good, and …)

54/A18  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (10 facts, 40 concepts)
  Q Why is client-end hardware a more practical focus for virtual reality resource optimization than trying to optimize every extended reality resource type?  [54/S0/F1, 54/S0/F2, 54/S0/F3, 54/S0/F4; resource optimization, client-end hardware, resource type, virtual reality experience]
    A Client-end hardware is a more practical focus because optimizing other resource types is difficult, while focusing on client hardware is more straightforward. Virtual reality resource optimization aims to minimize resource requirements while maximizing the immersive experience. Extended reality resources include hardware, software, manpower, and supporting infrastructure, but each can be complicated by funds, availability, policy, and geopolitical issues.
  Q Why is rendering usually carried out by a dedicated graphics component instead of entirely by the central processing unit in a computer graphics system?  [54/S2/F3, 54/S2/F4; rendering, graphics processing unit, central processing unit, display controller]
    A Rendering is usually carried out by a dedicated component because doing all rendering on the central processing unit would leave it little time for other tasks. Image generation is a multi-stage computational process, and the dedicated component is usually a graphics card containing a graphics processing unit. The central processing unit passes rendering tasks to that component, so rendering takes place in the graphics processing unit rather than the central processing unit.
  Q How does the decay of light from excited pixels in a raster scan device make periodic refreshing important, especially in virtual reality?  [54/S4/F2, 54/S4/F3, 54/S4/F4, 54/S4/F6; raster scan device, screen refreshing, refresh rate, virtual reality]
    A Periodic refreshing is important because the light emitted by excited pixels decays, which can make the image fade. Raster scan devices excite pixels sequentially, so fading can make the displayed image non-uniform or distorted, and screen refreshing periodically re-excites the pixels to keep the image uniform. A higher refresh rate is preferable in virtual reality because the virtual reality screen is much closer to the eyes than a typical screen.
  judge round 1: 0 of 3 failed
    1 pass  (Why is client-end hardware a more practical focus for virtual reality resource optimization than …)
      check: Client-end hardware is a practical focus because it is the most straightforward way to optimize VR resources without many issues, while optimizing each XR resource type can be difficult due to funds, availability, policy, and geopolitical considerations.
      reason: Facts 5 and 4 carry the required comparison: fact 5 says VR resource optimization focuses on client-end hardware as the most straightforward approach, and fact 4 explains why optimizing resource types broadly is not easy. The reference answer’s aim statement is supported by fact 2, and the resource list by fact 3.
    2 pass  (Why is rendering usually carried out by a dedicated graphics component instead of entirely …)
      check: Rendering is usually carried out by a dedicated component because CPU-only rendering would consume the CPU’s time and leave it little time for other tasks, while a dedicated component, usually a graphics card with a GPU, can perform the rendering computation.
      reason: Facts 15 and 16 carry the causal link: fact 15 explains that CPU-only rendering would leave the CPU with little time for other tasks, and fact 16 identifies the dedicated component as usually a graphics card containing a GPU that takes over rendering.
    3 pass  (How does the decay of light from excited pixels in a raster scan device …)
      check: Decaying light makes raster-scan images fade and, because pixels are excited sequentially, may become non-uniform or distorted, so periodic refreshing re-excites pixels; in VR a higher refresh rate is preferable because the screen is much closer to the eyes.
      reason: Facts 29 to 31 carry the decay-to-refreshing chain: fact 29 gives fading, fact 30 gives sequential excitation and non-uniformity, and fact 31 gives periodic re-excitation to keep the image uniform. Fact 33 supplies the VR-specific relevance by explaining why a higher refresh rate is preferable.

===== lecture 55: VR resource optimization

55/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (23 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is rendering? (lecture 19) -> Rendering is the multi-stage computational process that creates a scene's visual output as a two-dimensional image that can be displayed, and, in a broad sense, output for other senses.
  What is computer graphics (CG)? (lecture 19) -> Computer graphics (CG) is the area that addresses computer-generated images from synthetic models. It creates or represents objects, synthesizes them into a scene, allows users to manipulate images on a screen, creates the perception of motion, and renders the scene on a display so humans can perceive it.
  What is point of interest (POIs)? (lecture 21) -> Point of interest (POI) is a significant spot in a virtual tour, modeled as a graph node or vertex with importance and a maximum waiting time, that need not be a physical object and is visited to inspect or interact with objects.
  What is edge? (lecture 53) -> An edge is a connection between two nodes or vertices in a graph, which can be weighted by a distance or by a shortest path length.
  What is display controller? (lecture 54) -> Display controller is the rendering component in a generic graphics system that is responsible for image generation, receives display commands from the CPU, uses a GPU for rendering, and sends the generated two-dimensional digital image to video memory.
  What is three-dimensional graphics pipeline? (lecture 54) -> The three-dimensional graphics pipeline is a stage-wise process of computation that starts from object representation and ends by computing pixel intensities for a pixel-grid display, with five stages: object representation, modeling transformation, lighting, a viewing pipeline, and scan conversion.

55/A1  quiz  55/S0  "Quick quiz"  (2 facts, 6 concepts)
  Q Which part of the display controller computes the frame-buffer color values?  [55/S0/F0]
    - The display controller
    * The display processor
    - The frame buffer
    - The graphics processing unit
    because: The display processor, which is part of the display controller, computes the frame-buffer color values. The frame buffer stores those values, while the display controller and the graphics processing unit are not the part that performs this computation.
  Q What does the graphics pipeline refer to for frame-buffer color values?  [55/S0/F1]
    * The distinct stages that compute them
    - The display devices that present them
    - The coordinate systems that transform them
    - The hardware components that store them
    because: The graphics pipeline is the set of distinct stages in which the frame-buffer color values are computed. It is not the storage hardware, the presentation devices, or the coordinate systems used in the process.

55/A2  recap  55/S0  "Recap"  (2 facts, 6 concepts)
  Frame-buffer color values are computed by the display processor, which is part of the display controller. This computation happens in distinct stages. The graphics pipeline is the set of those stages.
  - The display processor in the display controller computes frame buffer color values in distinct stages.
  - The graphics pipeline is the set of distinct stages that compute frame buffer color values.

55/A4  recap  55/S1  "Recap"  (10 facts, 21 concepts)
  The 3D graphics pipeline is a sequence that turns object definitions into displayable pixel values. Its five stages use the coordinate systems local, world, 3D view, 2D view, device, and pixel grid. Modeling, lighting, viewing, and scan conversion successively transform the scene from object definitions through world and view coordinates until it becomes pixels.
  - The 3D graphics pipeline is the stage-wise process that computes pixel intensities for the frame buffer and display.
  - The 3D graphics pipeline stages are object representation, modeling transformation, lighting, viewing pipeline, and scan conversion.
  - The first three pipeline stages define objects locally, place them in world coordinates, and color the scene.
  - The viewing pipeline's sub-stages map the scene to the device coordinate system, equivalent to but not the screen.
  - Scan conversion turns continuous device coordinates into integer pixel-grid coordinates, the final of six coordinate systems.

    * Realistic detail and efficient computation in later pipeline stages
    - Accurate lighting and fewer coordinate transformations in later pipeline stages
    - Simple geometric approximation and reduced storage in later pipeline stages
    - Fast display refresh and reduced hardware cost in later pipeline stages

Point-sample rendering is the simplest, using captured real-world data points that are mapped to pixels, while boundary/mesh representation describes object surfaces with polygons. Meshes approximate surfaces, with more polygons improving accuracy but increasing list complexity, and other representations are converted to mesh before rendering.
  - Broad object-representation categories are point-sample rendering, boundary representation, and space-partitioning-based representation.
  - Point-sample rendering is the simplest category, using real-world points captured with attributes by sensors or computer vision.
  - Point-sample rendering maps captured real-world points to pixels to generate a synthetic image.
  - Boundary representation uses surfaces; meshes approximate curved surfaces with connected polygons, where more polygons improve accuracy but add complexity.
  - Mesh representation is the basic rendered form, with all other representations converted to meshes before rendering.

55/A11  recap  55/S4  "Recap"  (7 facts, 18 concepts)
  Spline representation is a parametric, higher-level boundary representation for curves and surfaces, with mesh as the basic boundary representation. It is usually preferred for artificial scenes because it can express complex surfaces that simple polygons or simple polynomial equations cannot. A spline builds a curve from lower-degree polynomial pieces, commonly third-order, instead of one higher-degree polynomial, and these pieces must join smoothly while satisfying required geometric and other properties.
  - Spline representation is a higher-level boundary representation for curves or surfaces, using parametric forms rather than the basic mesh form.
  - Developers usually prefer spline representation for artificial scenes because it models complex surfaces beyond simple polygons or simple polynomial equations.
  - A spline curve uses several lower-degree polynomial basis functions instead of one higher-degree polynomial, making point computation easier.
  - Third-order polynomials are the most common spline pieces, and all pieces must join smoothly and satisfy geometric and other properties.

55/A12  quiz  55/S5  "Quick quiz"  (4 facts, 6 concepts)
  Q What is the key idea behind a space partitioning representation of an object?  [55/S5/F0]
    - It samples the object's surface as boundary points that represent the object
    - It processes the object's raw scene points into pixels that represent the object
    * It splits the object's occupied space into disjoint regions that represent the object
    - It splits the object's occupied space into overlapping regions that represent the object
    because: A space partitioning representation represents an object by the occupied regions after dividing its occupied space into non-overlapping regions. Overlapping regions would let a point inside the object lie in more than one region.
  Q What is the role of a space partitioning tree in object representation?  [55/S5/F1]
    * It is a hierarchical structure used to create a space partitioning representation
    - It is a set of boundary polygons used to create a space partitioning representation
    - It is a flat list of disjoint regions used to create a space partitioning representation
    - It is a set of smooth polynomial pieces used to create a space partitioning representation
    because: A space partitioning tree organizes the space occupied by an object in a hierarchical tree-like form and is used to build the space partitioning representation. A flat list, boundary polygon set, or spline piece set does not capture that hierarchical tree structure.
  Q Which specialized representation method is suited to a structure whose individual parts repeat in the larger part?  [55/S5/F4]
    - a boundary representation
    - a constructive solid geometric representation
    - a triangular mesh representation
    * a fractal representation
    because: Fractal representation is the specialized method for self-repeating structures, where smaller parts recur in the larger whole. Boundary, mesh, and constructive solid geometric forms represent other kinds of object structure.
  Q Why is particle system representation used for an object such as a waterfall?  [55/S5/F5]
    - because it divides the visible surface of the object
    * because it simulates the physical properties of the object
    - because it repeats the small geometric parts of the object
    - because it records the overall skeletal motion of the object
    because: Particle system representation relies on simulating physical properties, which is why it fits a dynamic object like a waterfall. Repeating parts, skeletal motion, or surface division describes other representation approaches.

55/A13  recap  55/S5  "Recap"  (7 facts, 12 concepts)
  Space partitioning gives a broad object representation method by dividing the 3D space an object occupies into disjoint regions, with space partitioning trees as a hierarchical way to build such a representation. This category includes methods such as the octree method, binary space partitioning, and constructive solid geometry. For application-specific or very complex photorealistic objects, specialized techniques are used rather than these broader categories. Fractal, particle-system, and skeletal representations are specialized examples aimed at self-repeating structures, physically simulated objects, and complex animated characters.
  - Space partitioning represents an object by dividing its occupied 3D space into disjoint, non-overlapping regions.
  - A space partitioning tree hierarchically represents an object's occupied space to create a space partitioning representation.
  - Space partitioning representations include the octree method, binary space partitioning, and constructive solid geometric methods.
  - Application-specific or very complex photorealistic objects often need specialized representation techniques rather than broader boundary or space partitioning.
  - Specialized fractal, particle-system, and skeletal representations serve self-repeating structures, physically simulated objects, and complex animated characters.

    2 pass  (A space partitioning tree hierarchically represents an object's occupied space to create a space …)

55/A21  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (10 facts, 28 concepts)
  Q How does the three-dimensional graphics pipeline support the rendering activity in creating a virtual reality experience?  [19/S2/F0, 54/S5/F0; rendering, three-dimensional graphics pipeline, object representation]
    A Creating a virtual reality experience involves creating the virtual environment and creating the stereoscopic output view, which is called rendering. The three-dimensional graphics pipeline is a stage-wise process that starts from object representation and ends with rendering on the pixel grid. It therefore provides the process by which modeled objects are converted into pixel-level output for the virtual reality experience.
  Q In a three-dimensional graphics pipeline, why can a more realistic object representation create problems for the subsequent stages?  [55/S2/F0, 55/S2/F1; three-dimensional object representation, three-dimensional graphics pipeline, pixel intensity]
    A The fundamental objective of three-dimensional object representation is to balance representing objects of different shapes and sizes with intricate details realistically against making the operations of the subsequent stages efficient in space and time. Pixel intensities depend on the object representation. More complex representations lead to more complex calculations, so realistic rendering can suffer lags or require expensive hardware if the computation is not efficient.
  Q What trade-off does mesh representation face when non-polygonal surfaces are approximated with polygons?  [55/S3/F5, 55/S3/F6, 55/S3/F7; mesh, polygon, triangle, vertex list]
    A Mesh representation assumes object surfaces are polygons, and connected polygons form a mesh. Non-polygonal surfaces can be represented by approximating them with polygonal meshes, typically triangles. Increasing the number of polygons gives a better approximation of the surfaces, but it makes the vertex list more complex and harder to construct, so a trade-off must be maintained.
  Q How does spline representation compute points on a complex curve compared with representing the curve by one higher-degree polynomial?  [55/S4/F2, 55/S4/F3, 55/S4/F5; spline representation, polynomial, polynomial piece, curve segment]
    A A more complex curve can be represented by a polynomial of higher degree, and computing points on a higher-degree polynomial becomes more time-consuming. In spline representation, the complete curve consists of several lower-degree polynomial pieces instead of a single higher-degree polynomial. Each piece is a blending or basis function for a curve segment, so simpler polynomials compute the points on that segment, and the pieces must join smoothly.
  judge round 1: 0 of 4 failed
    1 pass  (How does the three-dimensional graphics pipeline support the rendering activity in creating a virtual …)
      check: The three-dimensional graphics pipeline supports the rendering activity by being the stage-wise computation that goes from object representation to rendering on the pixel grid.
      reason: Fact 41 identifies creating the stereoscopic output view as rendering in a VR experience, and fact 51 states that the 3D graphics pipeline is a stage-wise process from object representation to rendering on the pixel grid; together they give the requested support link.
    2 pass  (In a three-dimensional graphics pipeline, why can a more realistic object representation create problems …)
      check: A more realistic or detailed representation can create problems because pixel-intensity computation depends on the object representation, and more complex representations require more complex calculations that can cause lags or require expensive hardware if inefficient.
      reason: Fact 13 states the need to balance realistic representation with efficiency in subsequent stages, and fact 14 directly links object representation to pixel-intensity computation and to possible lags or expensive hardware when calculations are complex and inefficient.
    3 pass  (What trade-off does mesh representation face when non-polygonal surfaces are approximated with polygons?)

      reason: Fact 23 connects non-polygonal surfaces to polygonal-mesh approximation, and fact 24 states the comparison between better surface approximation and greater vertex-list complexity, which is the trade-off asked for.

56/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (10 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is three-dimensional graphics pipeline? (lecture 54) -> The three-dimensional graphics pipeline is a stage-wise process of computation that starts from object representation and ends by computing pixel intensities for a pixel-grid display, with five stages: object representation, modeling transformation, lighting, a viewing pipeline, and scan conversion.
  What is lighting? (lecture 55) -> Lighting is a stage of the three-dimensional graphics pipeline that assigns color to a constructed scene in the world coordinate system, making the scene's three-dimensional nature more perceptible.
  What is rasterization? (lecture 55) -> Rasterization is the fifth stage of the 3D graphics pipeline that transforms continuous device coordinate descriptions into discrete pixel-grid screen descriptions by choosing the nearest integer-coordinate pixels.
  What is object representation? (lecture 55) -> Object representation is the first stage of the 3D graphics pipeline that defines the objects that form the rendered image in each object's local coordinate system.
  What is local coordinate system? (lecture 55) -> A local coordinate system is an object's own coordinate system in the 3D graphics pipeline, in which objects are defined before modeling transformation transforms them to the world coordinate system.
  What is modeling transformation? (lecture 55) -> Modeling transformation is the second stage of the 3D graphics pipeline that transforms an object’s local coordinate description into the common world coordinate system so that objects can be assembled into a scene.

56/A4  recap  56/S1  "Recap"  (1 facts, 17 concepts)
  The 3D graphics pipeline processes a 3D scene through five stages in a fixed order. It begins with local object representation, then modeling transformation to world coordinates, and lighting in the world coordinate reference frame. The viewing pipeline then converts the scene to device coordinates through viewing transformation, clipping, hidden-surface removal, projection, and window-to-viewport transformation, and scan conversion finally yields screen or pixel-grid coordinates.
  - The 3D graphics pipeline has five ordered stages: object representation, modeling, lighting, viewing pipeline, and scan conversion.

  - The simple lighting model's specular component is direct light from a light source reflected specularly, making a shiny bright spot.

  Reflected light is treated as a fraction of incident light, controlled by surface reflection coefficients. The simple lighting model separates reflection into ambient, diffuse, and specular parts, each using its own coefficient. Ambient reflection is a direct coefficient multiplication, while diffuse reflection uses the surface normal and light direction, counting only positive alignment. Phong specular reflection then uses the viewer direction and an ideal reflected direction, computed from the light direction and normal, raised to a power.
  - A surface's reflection coefficient sets the reflected fraction of incident light reaching the viewer.

  - Phong specular uses cos φ = V dot r: Ks Is (V dot r)^Ns, zero if nonpositive, with r = 2(L dot N)N - L.

    - the human visual system responds to absolute changes between intensity values

56/A23  recap  56/S10  "Recap"  (5 facts, 17 concepts)
  A lighting model’s continuous pixel intensity must be converted into the finite intensities that a display can show. The finite levels are computed from the level count, minimum intensity, and maximum 1 as successive r multiples, because humans perceive relative changes between intensity values rather than absolute intensity changes. A table of these levels and bit patterns then lets each computed intensity choose the nearest level for the frame buffer.
  - A lighting model can compute pixel intensities over a continuous 0-to-1 range, while a display supports only finite intensity values.
  - Successive device-supported intensity levels are I0, rI0, ..., r^nI0, using level count n, minimum I0, and maximum 1.
  - The multiplicative factor r reflects that humans perceive relative changes between intensity values, not absolute intensity changes.
  - A table maps a lighting-model pixel intensity to the nearest device-supported intensity, storing its bit pattern in the frame buffer.
  judge round 1: 2 of 5 failed
    1 pass  (A lighting model can compute pixel intensities over a continuous 0-to-1 range, while a …)
      check: none
      reason: Fact 1 states that the lighting-model pixel intensity can be any value between 0 and 1 while a display supports only a finite set of intensity values; the point paraphrases that without adding unsupported detail.
    2 FAIL faithful  (Successive device-supported intensity levels are I0, rI0, ..., r^nI0, using level count n, minimum …)
      check: I1 = r I0, I2 = r^2 I0, I3 = r^3 I0, and so on up to In = r^n I0 [3]
      reason: Fact 3 lists the successive device-supported values as I1 = rI0 through In = r^nI0; the point adds I0 to that sequence, making it appear as though I0 is one of the listed successive levels rather than only the minimum value used to determine them. A repaired point could say: "The successive device-supported intensity values are I1 = rI0 through In = r^nI0, using n levels, minimum I0, and maximum 1."
    3 pass  (The multiplicative factor r reflects that humans perceive relative changes between intensity values, not …)
      check: none
      reason: Fact 4 states that the multiplicative factor r is based on the psychophysiological property that humans perceive relative rather than absolute intensity changes; the point faithfully paraphrases that idea.
    4 pass  (A table maps a lighting-model pixel intensity to the nearest device-supported intensity, storing its …)
      check: none
      reason: Fact 5 states that a table stores device-supported intensity values and bit patterns, and a lighting-model intensity is mapped to the nearest table intensity so the corresponding bit pattern is stored in the frame buffer; the point is an acceptable condensed paraphrase.
    0 FAIL faithful  (A lighting model’s continuous pixel intensity must be converted into the finite intensities that …)
      check: The use of a multiplicative factor r in the successive device-supported intensity levels is based on the psychophysiological property that humans perceive relative changes between two intensity values rather than absolute changes in intensity values [4]
      reason: The second sentence says the finite levels are computed as successive r multiples because humans perceive relative changes, but Fact 4 supports only the reason for using the multiplicative factor r, not a reason for computing the finite levels from the level count, minimum intensity, and maximum 1. 56/A29  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (16 facts, 52 concepts)
  Q Why does the order of matrices in a composite transformation matrix affect the transformed result?  [56/S4/F0, 56/S4/F3, 56/S4/F6; composite transformation matrix, matrix multiplication, order of application]
    A A world coordinate scene may require several basic transformations, so their matrices are combined into one composite matrix. The first transformation applied is placed rightmost, and later transformations are placed to its left, so the product applies the operations in the intended order. Because matrix multiplication is not commutative, an incorrect order can produce a wrong transformed result.
  Q Why are radial and angular intensity attenuation factors applied to the diffuse and specular components in the modified simple lighting model?  [56/S8/F0, 56/S8/F1, 56/S8/F2, 56/S8/F3, 56/S8/F4; simple lighting model, radial intensity attenuation factor, angular intensity attenuation factor]
    A Radial and angular intensity attenuation are needed because light from a source typically diminishes with distance, and angular intensity attenuation is considered primarily for spotlight effects. The radial factor, typically an inverse quadratic distance function, accounts for that diminishing. The angular factor is 0 outside the angular limit and varies as the cosine of phi raised to the angular attenuation exponent inside. The modified model multiplies the diffuse and specular sum by these factors, leaving the I_M component unchanged.
  Q Why can a shading model be used instead of a lighting model when color is assigned in the computer graphics pipeline?  [56/S5/F0, 56/S5/F1, 56/S5/F2; shading model, lighting model, quality of experience, color]
    A A shading model is an approximation of the color-assignment methods used by a lighting model, and it relies on that lighting model. It can be used to reduce computation without compromising the quality of experience. This still allows colors to be assigned, which helps depth be perceived and can give a more realistic perception.
  Q How does intensity mapping use a multiplicative factor to convert a lighting-model pixel intensity into the value stored in the frame buffer?  [56/S10/F0, 56/S10/F1, 56/S10/F2, 56/S10/F3, 56/S10/F4; intensity mapping, device-supported intensity value, psychophysiological property, frame buffer]
    A A lighting model produces a continuous pixel intensity, while a display supports only finite device-supported values. Because humans perceive relative changes rather than absolute changes, successive device-supported values are powers of a factor times the minimum intensity. A table maps each such value to a bit pattern, and the pixel intensity is mapped to the nearest table value for the frame buffer.

===== lecture 57: VR resource optimization

57/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (16 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is rendering? (lecture 19) -> Rendering is the multi-stage computational process that creates a scene's visual output as a two-dimensional image that can be displayed, and, in a broad sense, output for other senses.
  What is three-dimensional graphics pipeline? (lecture 54) -> The three-dimensional graphics pipeline is a stage-wise process of computation that starts from object representation and ends by computing pixel intensities for a pixel-grid display, with five stages: object representation, modeling transformation, lighting, a viewing pipeline, and scan conversion.
  What is rasterization? (lecture 55) -> Rasterization is the fifth stage of the 3D graphics pipeline that transforms continuous device coordinate descriptions into discrete pixel-grid screen descriptions by choosing the nearest integer-coordinate pixels.
  What is viewing pipeline? (lecture 55) -> The viewing pipeline is the fourth stage of the 3D graphics pipeline that selects a portion of a 3D scene and transforms it from the world coordinate system to the device coordinate system through viewing transformation, clipping, hidden surface removal, projection transformation, and window-to-viewport transformation.
  What is viewing transformation? (lecture 55) -> Viewing transformation is a sub-stage of the viewing pipeline in the three-dimensional graphics pipeline that defines the view coordinate system and maps a scene from the world coordinate system to the three-dimensional view coordinate system.
  What is projection transformation? (lecture 55) -> Projection transformation is a sub-stage of the viewing pipeline in the three-dimensional graphics pipeline that maps objects from a three-dimensional view coordinate system to a two-dimensional view plane or coordinate system.

  - Clipping and hidden surface removal occur in the 3D view coordinate system in the described pipeline.

57/A4  recap  57/S1  "Recap"  (5 facts, 25 concepts)
  Scene points are first defined in the world coordinate system, and the 3D viewing transformation changes that world description into a view description that simulates the camera view. To do this, camera position, view-up point, and look-at point define a view coordinate system whose orthogonal unit axes are N, V, and U. Once those axes exist, a composite translation and rotation matrix built from them transforms world points into view points.
  - The world coordinate system is the reference frame in which all scene points are defined.
  - The 3D viewing transformation converts world coordinates to view coordinates to simulate looking with the camera.
  - The view coordinate system is set up from camera position, view-up point, and look-at point.
  - N opposes the look direction, V follows view-up, and U is their cross product, giving orthogonal unit axes.
  - A view point is the world point multiplied by a composite rotation-translation matrix from the view-coordinate axis vectors.

      check: none

    3 pass  (The view coordinate system is set up from camera position, view-up point, and look-at …)
      check: none
      reason: Fact 3 states that the camera parameters used to set up the view coordinate system are camera position, view-up point, and look-at point.

57/A5  quiz  57/S2  "Quick quiz"  (9 facts, 18 concepts)
  Q Which view-volume shape is used when the projectors converge at a center of projection?  [57/S2/F4, 57/S2/F5, 57/S2/F6]
    - A normalized unit-cube-shaped region
    * A frustum-shaped region
    - A rectangular clipping-window-shaped region
    - A rectangular parallelepiped-shaped region
    because: When projectors converge at a center of projection, the projection is perspective and its view volume is a frustum. Parallel projection uses a rectangular parallelepiped, while a unit cube is the canonical view volume and a clipping window is only one face of the view volume.
  Q What happens to scene objects that lie outside the view volume?  [57/S2/F2, 57/S2/F3]
    - They are scaled into a unit cube
    - They are mapped to the device viewport
    - They are projected onto the view plane
    * They are discarded by clipping
    because: The view volume defines the portion of the scene that is projected, so objects outside it are discarded by clipping. Projection, canonical conversion, and viewport mapping apply to the retained scene content, not to objects outside the view volume.
  Q What is the purpose of converting an arbitrarily defined view volume into a canonical view volume?  [57/S2/F8]
    - To make the projectors converge at a point
    - To discard the objects outside the view volume
    * To simplify the pipeline computations
    - To place the rendered scene on the display
    because: A canonical view volume is a normalized unit cube used to simplify later pipeline computations. Converging projectors describe perspective projection, discarding outside objects is clipping, and placing the scene on the display is related to viewport mapping rather than canonical view-volume conversion.
  Q After a point vector in view coordinates is multiplied by the parallel projection matrix, how are Cartesian coordinates obtained?  [57/S2/F11]
    - By multiplying the homogeneous coordinates by the homogeneous factor w
    - By clipping the point coordinates before the matrix multiplication
    - By multiplying the Cartesian coordinates by the distance D
    * By dividing the homogeneous coordinates by the homogeneous factor w
    because: Parallel projection produces homogeneous coordinate values that are divided by the homogeneous factor w to obtain Cartesian coordinates. The distance D is used inside the projection matrix, and clipping is a separate step rather than the operation that recovers Cartesian coordinates.
  Q What makes converting a perspective view volume to a canonical unit cube more involved than converting a parallel view volume?  [57/S2/F9, 57/S2/F10]
    * It requires scaling with shearing
    - It requires projection without clipping
    - It requires scaling without shearing
    - It requires translation with rotation
    because: A parallel view volume can be scaled into a unit cube, but a perspective frustum must be changed in both size and shape, requiring scaling and shearing. Translation and rotation describe general coordinate transformations, not the extra canonical conversion for a perspective frustum.

57/A6  recap  57/S2  "Recap"  (14 facts, 22 concepts)
  Projection transformation explains how 3D view-coordinate geometry is prepared for display by first limiting it to a view volume. It contrasts perspective and parallel projection, showing that their different view-volume shapes are converted into a canonical unit cube to make clipping and projection easier. The matrix steps then turn selected points into homogeneous coordinates, which are divided by w to produce view-plane coordinates.
  - Projection transformation maps 3D view-coordinate objects to a 2D view plane, usually a rectangular clipping window.
  - A view volume defines the projected scene region, and objects outside it are clipped before projection.
  - Perspective projection uses converging projectors and a frustum view volume; parallel projection uses parallel projectors and a rectangular view volume.
  - To simplify intensive clipping, view volumes become canonical unit cubes by scaling; perspective frustums also require shearing.
  - Projection matrices use D; points multiply through view, canonical, and projection matrices, then homogeneous values are divided by w.

57/A7  quiz  57/S3  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 11 concepts)
  Q In the graphics pipeline, how does a viewport differ from a window?  [57/S3/F0, 57/S3/F1]
    - It is a normalized clipping volume, while the window is a device-space screen region

    * It is a device-space screen region, while the window is an abstract view-plane region
    - It is a camera-space projection region, while the window is a display-defined screen region

    - The three-dimensional view-coordinate position of the point

    - The viewport and window offsets on each axis

57/A8  recap  57/S3  "Recap"  (5 facts, 11 concepts)
  The window, an abstract normalized clipping window or view plane, is set against the viewport, a device-space region of the final screen. The window-to-viewport transformation maps a window point to viewport coordinates using a 3×3 matrix whose scaling and translation come from the window and viewport dimensions. The window point is multiplied by this matrix, and the resulting homogeneous point is divided by W to obtain Cartesian viewport coordinates.
  - A window is the abstract normalized clipping window or view plane, independent of the physical display.
  - A viewport is the device-space screen portion where the scene is rendered, defined by origin and dimensions.
  - The window-to-viewport transformation maps a window point (Wx, Wy) to a viewport point (Vx, Vy).
  - The 3×3 window-to-viewport matrix has Sx, Sy from corresponding x/y dimensions, and Tx, Ty from Sx, Sy, and those dimensions.
  - Multiplying the window point by the window-to-viewport matrix gives a homogeneous point; divide by W for Cartesian coordinates.

57/A10  recap  57/S4  "Recap"  (2 facts, 13 concepts)
  Clipping and hidden surface removal are two ways the VR 3D viewing pipeline avoids processing unnecessary geometry. Clipping removes geometry outside the view volume before projection, reducing the vertices that must be processed. Hidden surface removal removes geometry inside the view volume that is occluded and not visible from the viewer, reducing rendering computation and supporting realistic image generation.
  - Clipping discards geometry outside the view volume before projection, reducing vertices processed and computational complexity.
  - Hidden surface removal removes occluded, viewer-invisible geometry inside the view volume before rendering, reducing computation and supporting realistic images.

57/A19  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (10 facts, 45 concepts)
  Q How do clipping and hidden surface removal reduce computational work in realistic virtual reality scene generation?  [57/S0/F0, 57/S4/F0, 57/S4/F1; clipping, hidden surface removal, view volume, computational complexity]
    A Clipping discards objects or portions of objects outside the view volume before projection, while hidden surface removal removes occluded objects, surfaces, or surface points inside the view volume before rendering. This removes geometry before projection or rendering is applied, reducing computational complexity. That reduction matters because realistic scene generation in virtual reality requires more resources than in augmented reality.
  Q Why does converting a perspective projection view volume to a canonical view volume require more computation than converting a parallel projection view volume?  [57/S2/F8, 57/S2/F9, 57/S2/F10; canonical view volume, perspective projection, parallel projection, frustum]
    A Converting a perspective projection view volume requires more computation because it requires both scaling and shearing, while converting a parallel projection view volume requires only scaling. A canonical view volume is a normalized unit cube used to simplify pipeline computations. For perspective projection, the frustum is changed in size and shape into this cube.
  Q How are camera parameters used to transform a scene from the world coordinate system into a view coordinate system?  [57/S1/F1, 57/S1/F2, 57/S1/F3, 57/S1/F4; camera parameters, viewing transformation, three-dimensional view coordinate system, composite transformation matrix]
    A Camera position, view-up point, and center of interest are used to define three mutually orthogonal unit basis vectors for the view coordinate system. The viewing transformation is then performed by translation and rotation, using a composite transformation matrix formed from these view-coordinate axis vectors. A world-coordinate point vector is multiplied by this matrix to obtain its point in view coordinates.
  judge round 1: 1 of 3 failed
    1 pass  (How do clipping and hidden surface removal reduce computational work in realistic virtual reality …)
      check: Clipping discards outside-view-volume objects before projection and hidden surface removal removes occluded inside-view-volume objects before rendering, reducing computational complexity; this is especially relevant because realistic VR scene generation requires more resources than AR.
      reason: Facts 30 and 31 state what each operation removes and how it reduces computational complexity, and fact 1 supplies the VR resource requirement that connects the reduction to realistic VR scene generation.
    2 FAIL clear  (Why does converting a perspective projection view volume to a canonical view volume require …)

      reason: Facts 19-21 give the comparison: parallel conversion is scaling only, while perspective conversion also requires shearing and therefore more computation. The reference answer fails criterion 6 only because its first sentence defines canonical view volumes instead of giving the direct reason first.

===== lecture 58: VR resource optimization

58/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (13 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is clipping? (lecture 21) -> Clipping is the process in the three-dimensional graphics pipeline that discards objects or portions of objects that are part of the scene but outside the view volume before projection.
  What is world coordinate system? (lecture 55) -> The world coordinate system is the common reference frame in which all scene points are defined and to which objects are transformed from local coordinate systems to construct the scene.
  What is viewing transformation? (lecture 55) -> Viewing transformation is a sub-stage of the viewing pipeline in the three-dimensional graphics pipeline that defines the view coordinate system and maps a scene from the world coordinate system to the three-dimensional view coordinate system.
  What is projection transformation? (lecture 55) -> Projection transformation is a sub-stage of the viewing pipeline in the three-dimensional graphics pipeline that maps objects from a three-dimensional view coordinate system to a two-dimensional view plane or coordinate system.
  What is window-to-viewport transformation? (lecture 55) -> Window-to-viewport transformation is a transformation in the viewing pipeline that maps a point from an abstract window representation to a device-specific viewport representation, transforming the two-dimensional view coordinate system to the device coordinate system.
  What is hidden surface removal? (lecture 57) -> Hidden surface removal is a GPU pixel-processing activity that identifies and removes objects, surfaces, or surface points inside the view volume that are not visible from the viewer because they are occluded, using a depth buffer algorithm before rendering, to reduce computational complexity and support realistic image generation.

58/A6  quiz  58/S2  "Quick quiz"  (6 facts, 27 concepts)
  Q How does point rendering differ from line rendering?  [58/S2/F0, 58/S2/F2]
    - Point rendering avoids integer values, while line rendering selects a set of pixels for a segment
    * Point rendering rounds one point, while line rendering selects a set of pixels for a segment
    - Point rendering rounds both endpoints, while line rendering selects a set of pixels for a segment
    - Point rendering uses a decision parameter, while line rendering selects a set of pixels for a segment
    because: A point is mapped by rounding one real-number coordinate pair to a nearby integer-coordinate pixel, whereas a line segment is represented by a set of selected pixels. Rounding one point does not produce the sequence of pixels needed to approximate a line.
  Q In the Bresenham algorithm for slopes between -1 and +1, when p is less than 0, what happens to x and y?  [58/S2/F4]
    * x is incremented by 1 and y remains unchanged at the next step
    - x is incremented by 1 and y is incremented by 1 at the next step
    - y is incremented by 1 and x remains unchanged at the next step
    - x remains unchanged and y remains unchanged at the next step
    because: For p less than 0, the algorithm advances only in the x direction at the next pixel. It advances both x and y only when the decision parameter is nonnegative.
  Q Why does using integer arithmetic speed up line rendering?  [58/S2/F1, 58/S2/F5]
    - It reduces the number of line pixels that must be selected
    * It avoids floating-point operations when selecting line pixels
    - It lowers the display resolution for line pixels
    - It removes antialiasing for line pixels
    because: Fast line rendering comes from replacing slow floating-point calculations with integer additions and similar operations while choosing pixels. The line is still approximated by a comparable set of pixels, so the gain is not from using fewer pixels or skipping display quality steps.
  Q What makes faster line rendering especially useful in interactive virtual reality?  [58/S2/F6]

    - A lighting model change from user input can demand redrawing many line segments
    because: Interactive virtual reality can change the scene with user input, and a changed scene may require redrawing a large number of line segments. The key reason is the large number of line segments that may need prompt redrawing, not a special calibration, lighting, or headset-orientation requirement.

58/A7  recap  58/S2  "Recap"  (9 facts, 28 concepts)
  Point rendering can use nearest-integer rounding, but line rendering needs a more careful rasterization method because lines cannot be rounded point by point. Bresenham's algorithm chooses the pixels approximating a line from its endpoints by updating a decision parameter with integer arithmetic, so it avoids the slow floating-point operations of naive methods. This matters in VR, where user input can require redrawing many lines, and similar efficient methods are used for other shapes.
  - Point rendering maps real coordinates to the nearest integer pixel, but this method suits points, not lines or circles.
  - Rasterization maps shapes to pixels faster by minimizing floating-point operations; for lines, it can eliminate them.
  - Bresenham's line-drawing algorithm takes endpoints and outputs approximating pixels, described for slopes -1 to +1 with minor modifications.
  - Bresenham's algorithm updates a decision parameter with integer arithmetic to choose each next line pixel without floating-point operations.
  - Faster line rendering makes VR more efficient because user input can require redrawing many lines.

58/A13  recap  58/S5  "Recap"  (2 facts, 15 concepts)
  A VR software stack is organized in layers, from the VR application and SDK down through the VR engine, native rendering libraries, operating system, and GPU hardware. For development, the SDK gives access to the engine rather than direct access to the rendering libraries. This lets the developer use the engine’s interface to the native rendering APIs while the lower layers provide the platform and graphics hardware.
  - The layered VR architecture runs from VR application through SDK, VR engine, native rendering libraries, OS, to hardware, including GPU.
  - A VR developer installs the engine, imports the SDK, and uses native rendering library APIs through the engine, not libraries.
