58/A15  quiz  58/S6  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 34 concepts)
  Q What design feature mainly makes a graphics card well suited to real-time rendering?  [58/S6/F0, 58/S6/F1]
    - One fast core processing vertices one after another during rendering
    - A shared memory pool storing every texture image during rendering
    - A sequential pipeline computing lighting for the whole scene during rendering
    * Many simple cores applying one instruction to many vertices during rendering
    because: GPUs exploit parallelism by using many simple cores that work on the same instruction at the same time, which suits operations like graphics rendering. A single sequential core, a texture-storage pool, or a sequential lighting pipeline does not explain the GPU's main rendering advantage.
  Q What parallel mechanism gives the GPU a large performance advantage when sending vertices to world coordinates?  [58/S6/F3]
    - It applies a different matrix to every vertex vector simultaneously
    - It applies a depth value to every vertex vector simultaneously
    * It applies the same matrix to every vertex vector simultaneously
    - It applies a texture color to every vertex vector simultaneously
    because: World-coordinate placement multiplies one shared matrix with all vertex vectors at once, so the operation is massively parallel. Using a different matrix per vertex, or applying depth or texture data per vertex, is not the parallel mechanism for this stage.
  Q After the composite matrix in the GPU projection stage is applied to vertices, what kind of coordinates do the resulting triangles have?  [58/S6/F7]
    - Local object space coordinates
    - Three-dimensional world space coordinates
    * Screen or device space coordinates
    - Texture image space coordinates
    because: The projection stage combines viewing, projection, and viewport transformations into one composite matrix, producing triangles in screen or device coordinates. World and local coordinates belong to earlier modeling steps, while texture coordinates are used for sampling surface colors.
  Q Why can the rasterization stage determine the colors of many pixels at the same time?  [58/S6/F8]
    - Each pixel has to share its color with nearby pixels before filling
    * Each pixel can be treated independently from other pixels before filling
    - Each pixel has to compare a depth value with the depth buffer before filling
    - Each pixel has to wait for a full triangle to transform before filling
    because: Rasterization can be parallelized because the color of one pixel can be decided without depending on the colors of other pixels. Shared-color propagation, waiting for whole triangles, or depth-buffer comparison are not the reason rasterization itself can run in parallel.
  judge round 1: 1 of 4 failed
    1 pass  (What design feature mainly makes a graphics card well suited to real-time rendering?)
      check: D
      reason: Facts 1 and 2 state that a GPU uses many cores, each capable only of simple arithmetic, that work simultaneously on one single instruction, which matches option D’s parallel simple-core design.
    2 FAIL no_giveaway  (Why does the GPU gain a large performance advantage in the modeling transformation stage?)
      check: D
      reason: Fact 4 states that modeling transformation gives a performance gain by multiplying the same transformation matrix with each vertex vector simultaneously for all vertices, so D is the intended answer; however, the word “transformation” appears in the question and only in the correct option, giving away the answer by form. A repaired question would ask for the parallel mechanism without naming the stage in a way that matches only one option, and D should explicitly say “simultaneously.”
    3 pass  (After the composite matrix in the GPU projection stage is applied to vertices, what …)
      check: C
      reason: Fact 8 states that the projection stage’s composite matrix produces “a stream of triangles in screen or device coordinates,” which is exactly option C.
    4 pass  (Why can the rasterization stage determine the colors of many pixels at the same …)
      check: B
      reason: Fact 9 states that rasterization algorithms exploit “the fact that each pixel can be treated independently from all other pixels” so colors can be determined simultaneously, which is exactly option B.
  judge round 2 (rewrite, ok): 0 of 4 failed
    1 pass  (What design feature mainly makes a graphics card well suited to real-time rendering?)
      check: D
      reason: Facts 1 and 2 state that a GPU is used to exploit the inherent parallelism of graphics operations and that it is a multicore system in which many simple cores work simultaneously on one single instruction, matching D.
    2 pass  (What parallel mechanism gives the GPU a large performance advantage when sending vertices to …)
      check: C
      reason: Fact 4 states that the GPU performs the modeling transformation by multiplying “the same transformation matrix with each vertex vector simultaneously for all vertices” to produce world coordinates.
    3 pass  (After the composite matrix in the GPU projection stage is applied to vertices, what …)
      check: C
      reason: Fact 8 states that the projection stage’s composite matrix produces “a stream of triangles in screen or device coordinates.”
    4 pass  (Why can the rasterization stage determine the colors of many pixels at the same …)
      check: B

58/A16  recap  58/S6  "Recap"  (12 facts, 59 concepts)
  A separate GPU provides many simple cores, streaming multiprocessors, caches, and texture storage so graphics operations can run in parallel. Graphics APIs send triangle-mesh vertices to it, and the GPU applies modeling, lighting, and projection operations to many vertices at once, yielding device-space triangles. Rasterization then determines affected pixels independently, and pixel processing applies textures and removes hidden surfaces in parallel.
  - A separate GPU exploits graphics parallelism with simple cores, streaming multiprocessors, caches, texture storage, and thread management.
  - Graphics APIs send vertices, and the GPU assembles triangle meshes and transforms all vertices in parallel.
  - The GPU applies parallel vertex operations for lighting and for combined viewing, projection, and viewport transformation.
  - Rasterization determines which pixels each device-space triangle overlaps and computes those pixels independently in parallel.
  - Pixel processing applies textures from fast storage and removes hidden surfaces using a depth buffer.
  judge round 1: 1 of 6 failed
    1 pass  (A separate GPU exploits graphics parallelism with simple cores, streaming multiprocessors, caches, texture storage …)
      check: none
      reason: Facts 1, 2, and 3 support the named GPU hardware elements and the point that the GPU is used to exploit graphics parallelism; the sentence is self-contained and stays at that level.
    2 pass  (Graphics APIs send vertices, and the GPU assembles triangle meshes and transforms all vertices …)
      check: none
      reason: Facts 5, 6, and 4 support vertices being sent through APIs, the GPU assembling triangle data, and modeling transformation being applied simultaneously to all vertices; the point remains a single coherent idea about vertex input and transformation.
    3 pass  (The GPU applies parallel vertex operations for lighting and for combined viewing, projection, and …)
      check: none
      reason: Facts 7 and 8 support parallel vertex work for lighting-related vertex color and for the combined viewing, projection, and viewport transformation; the point names the subject and stays within the facts.
    4 pass  (Rasterization determines which pixels each device-space triangle overlaps and computes those pixels independently in …)
      check: none
      reason: Fact 9 directly supports determining the pixels overlapped by device-space triangles and treating pixels independently so their colors can be determined in parallel.
    5 pass  (Pixel processing applies textures from fast storage and removes hidden surfaces using a depth …)
      check: none
      reason: Facts 10, 11, and 12 support that pixel processing includes texturing from high-speed storage and hidden-surface removal using a depth buffer.
    0 FAIL supported,faithful  (A separate GPU provides many simple cores, streaming multiprocessors, caches, and texture storage so …)
      check: fact 8: 'simultaneously'; fact 11: 'in parallel'; fact 12: 'in parallel'
      reason: The text says the GPU applies projection operations 'to many vertices at once' and that pixel processing applies textures and removes hidden surfaces 'in parallel,' but fact 8 does not state that projection is done at once, and facts 11 and 12 do not state that texturing and hidden-surface removal are executed in parallel. A repaired version would say the GPU applies modeling, lighting, and projection operations to vertices, yielding device-space triangles, and pixel processing applies textures and removes hidden surfaces, without asserting simultaneous execution beyond the facts.
  judge kept: original; still failing: [0]

58/A22  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (14 facts, 60 concepts)
  Q Why can using integer arithmetic in line rendering make a virtual reality system more efficient when the user interacts with the scene?  [58/S2/F1, 58/S2/F5, 58/S2/F6; line rendering, floating-point operation, virtual reality, user input]
    A Bresenham's line-drawing algorithm uses integer arithmetic and avoids slow floating-point operations such as rounding and division. In virtual reality, each user input can change the scene and require redrawing hundreds of thousands of lines. Faster line rendering therefore reduces the amount of computation needed for each redraw, making the system more efficient.
  Q Why is a graphics processing unit better suited than a central processing unit to the parallel tasks in modeling transformation and rasterization?  [58/S6/F0, 58/S6/F3, 58/S6/F8; graphics processing unit, central processing unit, modeling transformation, rasterization]
    A A graphics processing unit is designed to exploit the high parallelism of graphics operations, whereas central processing units are generally not designed for large-scale parallel activities. In modeling transformation, the GPU can multiply the same transformation matrix with many vertex vectors at once. In rasterization, each pixel can be treated independently, so the colors of many pixels can be determined simultaneously.
  Q Why can a virtual reality developer rely on the software development kit and engine layer instead of directly calling native rendering libraries?  [58/S4/F2, 58/S4/F3, 58/S5/F0, 58/S5/F1; software development kit, game engine, native rendering library, application programming interface]
    A In a layered virtual reality architecture, the application layer calls the SDK layer, and the SDK layer calls the VR engine layer. The VR engine then calls the application programming interfaces of native rendering libraries to perform rendering. These application programming interfaces are predefined sets of functions that perform specific tasks, and they eliminate the need to know every detail of processor details, memory details, and operating system details, so the developer need not directly access the native rendering libraries.
  Q Why does anti-aliasing both improve visual quality and increase rendering cost?  [58/S3/F0, 58/S3/F1, 58/S3/F2, 58/S3/F3; anti-aliasing, aliasing, quality of experience, pixel intensity]
    A Scan conversion selects pixels that are close to points on an original shape rather than exactly rendering those points, so the approximated shape can produce aliasing distortion. If left unaddressed, this distortion can become visible when resolution changes and reduce quality of experience. Anti-aliasing removes or reduces the distortion, but it adds further computation to the calculation of pixel intensities.

    1 pass  (Why can using integer arithmetic in line rendering make a virtual reality system more …)
      check: Integer arithmetic avoids slow floating-point operations, and because VR user input can require redrawing many lines, faster line rendering makes the system more efficient.
      reason: The cited facts carry the link: fact 13 says integer arithmetic avoids slow floating-point operations and speeds line rendering, and fact 14 says VR interactions can require redrawing many lines, so faster line rendering improves efficiency.
    2 pass  (Why is a graphics processing unit better suited than a central processing unit to …)
      check: A GPU is used to exploit the high parallelism of graphics operations, while CPUs generally are not designed for large-scale parallelism; modeling transformation applies the same matrix to many vertices at once and rasterization treats pixels independently in parallel.
      reason: Facts 30, 33, and 38 state the GPU/CPU parallelism contrast and the simultaneous vertex and pixel operations that answer the question.

      reason: The reference adds 'predefined functions', which is stated in fact 26, but fact 26 is not among the cited key facts; deleting that phrase or adding fact 26 to the key facts would make the answer supported by facts 27-29.

      check: Anti-aliasing reduces aliasing distortion that scan conversion can introduce, improving quality of experience, but it adds computation to calculating pixel intensities, increasing rendering cost.
      reason: Facts 18-20 connect scan-conversion approximation, aliasing distortion, and anti-aliasing's quality benefit, while fact 21 states the added computation.

===== lecture 59: VR resource optimization

59/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (18 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is three-dimensional graphics pipeline? (lecture 54) -> The three-dimensional graphics pipeline is a stage-wise process of computation that starts from object representation and ends by computing pixel intensities for a pixel-grid display, with five stages: object representation, modeling transformation, lighting, a viewing pipeline, and scan conversion.
  What is virtual reality (VR)? (lecture 4) -> Virtual reality (VR) is an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli provided by a computer, in which a person's actions partially determine what happens and which replaces the user's sense of reality without requiring the physical existence of objects or places.
  What is head-mounted display (HMDs)? (lecture 6) -> A head-mounted display (HMD) is a wearable, mobile visual display that integrates electronic, optical, mechanical, and audio components and uses one or two small screens directly in front of the user's eyes to place images for monoscopic or stereoscopic viewing. It can be non-see-through, optical see-through, or video see-through.
  What is latency? (lecture 10) -> Latency is the time delay, or time gap, in virtual reality between a user's movement in the physical world and the corresponding change in the virtual world.
  What is teleportation? (lecture 11) -> Teleportation is a virtual reality locomotion operation in which a user selects a virtual target location and the virtual viewpoint instantly changes from the current location to that target, without physical movement.
  What is rendering? (lecture 19) -> Rendering is the multi-stage computational process that creates a scene's visual output as a two-dimensional image that can be displayed, and, in a broad sense, output for other senses.

59/A2  recap  59/S0  "Recap"  (8 facts, 27 concepts)
  The Majuli VR case study is an immersive, interactive tour of a large river island's ecological and cultural heritage. Its content is extensive because it has many spread-out information points, each with many points of interest and several media types. The island's scale also leads to mixed navigation, with walking inside places and teleportation or vehicle metaphors between places. Because the resulting application is large and its interactive rendering is computationally demanding, regular systems cannot support it, so resource optimization is needed.
  - Majuli is the world's largest inhabited river island, in eastern India on the Brahmaputra.
  - The Majuli VR tour immerses visitors in interactive exploration of the island's ecological and cultural heritage.
  - The Majuli tour's two-level content has many spread-out information points, each with many points of interest and multimodal media.
  - The tour uses walking inside information points and teleportation or vehicle metaphors between them, as the island is large.
  - Regular systems cannot support the near-10 GB Majuli VR app, so resource optimization supports fast storage and computation.

59/A6  recap  59/S2  "Recap"  (7 facts, 17 concepts)
  Adapting the Majuli VR case study to cheap smartphone-based cardboard VR requires reducing its demands. Because an average smartphone cannot support the full system's size and computation, images were compressed and video playback was removed, making the experience less realistic but much smaller. More generally, resource-constrained platforms may require compression, cloud services, or feature removal when a device cannot render a full immersive experience.
  - A cardboard virtual reality headset places a smartphone in a housing to give immersive stereoscopic views cheaply.
  - Deploying Majuli VR on a smartphone/cardboard needed optimization because its full size and computation exceeded average smartphones.
  - Removing video playback and compressing images made Majuli VR less realistic, shrinking it from roughly 10 GB to 0.7 GB.
  - Full immersive VR systems cannot run on platforms that cannot render them; compression, cloud, or feature removal may help.

59/A13  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (8 facts, 38 concepts)
  Q Why can storing videos in the cloud reduce the storage and computation needed for the Majuli virtual tour on an Oculus Quest 2?  [59/S1/F1, 59/S1/F2, 59/S1/F3; Oculus Quest 2, video, cloud-based video loading optimization, computation]
    A Cloud-based video loading keeps videos, which take more space than images, out of the local application. A user can select a video thumbnail and load the chosen video from the cloud instead of storing it on the Oculus Quest 2. This reduces storage and data-access requirements, and because reducing size reduces rendering requirements and memory access, the client application was reduced to 5.1GB, with a corresponding computational reduction.
  Q How do image compression and removal of video playback address the storage problem for the smartphone/cardboard deployment of the Majuli virtual reality system?  [59/S2/F1, 59/S2/F2, 59/S2/F4; smartphone, image compression, video playback, storage requirement]
    A Deploying the full Majuli virtual reality system on a smartphone in a cardboard required optimization because its size and computation exceed what average smartphones typically support. Compressing images reduces the storage requirement, and removing video playback, since most videos could not be utilized, helps reduce the overall size. Together, compressing the images and removing video playback support reduced the overall size from about 10GB to 0.7GB.
  Q Why does the Majuli virtual tour use walking within each information point but teleportation or a vehicle metaphor between information points?  [59/S0/F2, 59/S0/F3; navigation technique, information point, teleportation, vehicle metaphor]
    A The Majuli tour contains many geographically spread information points, each with many points of interest. Walking is used within each information point, while teleportation or a vehicle metaphor is used between points, because a single technique alone may not suit the island's large geographical spread.

===== lecture 60: Linking theory to practice

60/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (14 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is game engine? (lecture 19) -> A game engine is a software development environment and middleware that sits between hardware and higher-level application software, abstracting hardware for developers to build games or extended reality (XR) experiences. It typically provides rendering, physics, audio, scripting, and low-level platform-specific support.
  What is application programming interface (API)? (lecture 58) -> Application programming interface (API) is a predefined set of functions provided by a library that, when invoked with appropriate arguments or parameters, perform specific tasks, allowing a programmer to deal with lower-level tasks without needing to know every detail of the underlying system or platform.
  What is extended reality (XR)? (lecture 1) -> Extended reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR).
  What is augmented reality (AR)? (lecture 1) -> Augmented reality (AR) is an enhanced version of reality created by technology, in which computer-generated digital content is overlaid on the real world in real time and registered in 3D, so the user perceives and interacts with the enhanced environment.
  What is mixed reality (MR)? (lecture 1) -> Mixed reality (MR) is an immersive technology that is the same as augmented reality, in which digital content is overlaid on the view of reality and can be interacted with.
  What is immersive experience? (lecture 1) -> An immersive experience is a perceived experience through sensory organs that appears real, because a person cannot distinguish the experienced environment from their real environment and perceives it as that real environment.

60/A1  quiz  60/S1  "Quick quiz"  (4 facts, 19 concepts)
  Q Which two components make up the Unity platform?  [60/S1/F1]
    - A scene view and a game view
    - A hub application and an installation manager
    - A console window and a status bar
    * A 3D game engine and a developer's interface
    because: The Unity platform comprises the Unity 3D game engine and a developer's interface. Editor windows and Hub tools are not the two top-level components of the platform.
  Q What is the intended effect of Unity's graphics pipeline support for an XR developer?  [60/S1/F2]
    - Managing multiple Unity versions in one place
    - Previewing the scene from the developer's camera
    - Importing external asset files into the project
    * Focusing on building the immersive experience
    because: Unity provides implementation support for graphics pipeline work so the developer can focus on the immersive experience. Managing versions, previewing the scene, and importing assets are other Unity functions, not the effect of its pipeline support.
  Q What kind of output does Unity support across platforms?  [60/S1/F3, 60/S1/F4]
    - 3D games or interactive content on many supported platforms

    - It acts as a primitive shape that can be created directly in the editor in Unity
    because: A game object is the fundamental Unity object that holds components, and those components implement its functionality and give it properties. The other options describe assets, components, or examples of game objects rather than the role of the game object itself.
  Q What is a Unity prefab?  [60/S4/F7]
    * a stored game object template used to make instances for use in a scene
    - a primitive object type created directly within Unity for use in a scene
    - a component that implements functionality for a game object for use in a scene
    - an imported file that supplies visual or audio elements for use in a scene
    because: A prefab is made by configuring and storing a game object, and it lets a developer create instances of that configured object in a scene. Primitive shapes, imported files, and components are related Unity items but are not prefabs.

60/A8  recap  60/S4  "Recap"  (8 facts, 28 concepts)
  Unity's basic project building blocks move from general items to scene content: assets are imported or created, and scenes are assets that contain part or all of the application. Within scenes, game objects gain properties from components, and prefabs store a configured game object so instances of it can be placed in a scene.
  - A Unity asset is any project item used to build the application, imported from outside or created inside Unity.
  - A Unity scene is an asset holding part or all of an application; projects can have many editable scenes.
  - A Unity game object is a component container; built-in or custom components set properties, and primitive types can be made.
  - A Unity prefab is a configured and stored game-object template that can produce instances of that object in a scene.
  judge round 1: 1 of 5 failed

    2 pass  (A Unity scene is an asset holding part or all of an application; projects …)
      check: none
      reason: Facts 3 and 4 support that a scene is a type of asset containing part or all of the application and that a project can contain multiple editable scenes.
    3 FAIL one_idea  (A Unity game object is a component container; built-in or custom components set properties …)
      check: none
      reason: It fails one_idea because it packs several game-object ideas together: that a game object is a component container, that built-in or custom components set properties, and that primitive types can be made. A repaired version would keep only one idea, for example: “A Unity game object is a container whose properties come from added components.”
    4 pass  (A Unity prefab is a configured and stored game-object template that can produce instances …)
      check: none
      reason: Fact 8 supports that a prefab is a template made by configuring and storing a game object and can be used to make instances of that object in a scene.
    0 pass  (Unity's basic project building blocks move from general items to scene content: assets are …)
      check: none

60/A14  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (8 facts, 26 concepts)
  Q How does Unity’s support for the computer graphics pipeline relate to a developer building a realistic immersive environment in the Unity editor?  [60/S1/F2, 60/S2/F2; Unity, computer graphics pipeline, unity editor interface, immersive experience]
    A Unity is intended to provide implementation support for the computer graphics pipeline, so a developer can focus on building the immersive experience rather than mastering the pipeline. The Unity editor interface is essentially an integrated development environment whose menu options provide features for building and deploying a system, and it allows developers to build and deploy realistic immersive environments without having to master and implement that pipeline.
  Q How do the scene view and game view in Unity support different stages of creating and previewing a scene?  [60/S3/F2, 60/S3/F3; scene view, game view, Unity scene, game object]
    A The scene view is the developer's interactive view while a scene is being built, and it lets the developer select, manipulate, and modify the game objects that comprise the scene. The game view is the final preview, because it renders the scene from the camera set by the developer to represent the final published or deployed application.
  Q How does a Unity prefab allow a developer to reuse a configured game object in a scene?  [60/S4/F4, 60/S4/F7; game object, Unity prefab, component, instance]
    A A game object acts as a container for components, and its properties and functionality come from the components added to it. A prefab is created by configuring and storing such a game object as a template, allowing the developer to make instances of that game object in a Unity scene.
  Q How does the Unity Game Engine connect a developer's XR application with the hardware it runs on?  [20/S3/F0, 60/S2/F1; game engine, Unity Game Engine, extended reality system]
    A As middleware, a game engine sits between hardware and higher-level application software and abstracts hardware functionality for developers. The Unity Game Engine uses that middleware role by providing an interface for building XR experiences or XR systems and deploying them on a specific platform.

===== lecture 61: Linking theory to practice

61/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (13 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is Unity scene? (lecture 60) -> A Unity scene is a specific type of Unity asset that contains all or part of a game or application and is composed of game objects. Unity provides a scene interface to create, edit, or modify it.
  What is Unity? (lecture 60) -> Unity is a popular cross-platform game engine and developer environment that provides an editor interface and implementation support for the computer graphics pipeline, enabling developers to create, build, and deploy 2D and 3D interactive content, including XR experiences.
  What is unity editor interface? (lecture 60) -> The unity editor interface is essentially an integrated development environment whose menu options provide developers the features required to build and deploy a system, and it allows developers to build and deploy realistic immersive environments without having to master and implement the computer graphics pipeline.
  What is game object? (lecture 60) -> Game object is a fundamental object in Unity that represents characters, props, or a scenario and acts as a container for components that implement its functionality, so its properties are given by adding components.
  What is component? (lecture 60) -> A component is a Unity asset that can be added to a game object to implement part of the object's functionality or properties, and can be a built-in component type or a custom component created by scripting.
  What is platform? (lecture 19) -> A platform is the combination of hardware and an operating system.

61/A1  quiz  61/S0  "Quick quiz"  (7 facts, 25 concepts)
  Q What kind of tool is Unity for a developer creating an XR system?  [61/S0/F0]
    - A rendering library with a camera interface
    - A user runtime with a player interface
    - A device-driver layer with a hardware interface
    * An implementation platform with an editor interface
    because: Unity is an implementation platform with an editor interface for creating, building, and deploying an XR system. It is not merely a renderer, device-driver layer, or user-side runtime.
  Q In Unity's render-pipeline support, what does a developer have customized control over?  [61/S0/F1]
    - The player input mappings
    * The individual graphics stages
    - The editor scene creation tools
    - The imported model file formats
    because: Unity's render-pipeline support gives customized control over the individual stages of the graphics process, such as camera transforms, lighting, meshes, materials, textures, shaders, and environments. Imported model formats, scene tools, and input mappings are separate Unity capabilities, not the stated pipeline-stage control.
  Q What makes URP a quicker graphics choice than Unity's built-in render pipeline?  [61/S0/F3, 61/S0/F4, 61/S0/F5]
    - It gives photorealism and high-end workstation support
    - It gives manual stage control and detailed optimization support
    * It gives easy customization and stage optimization support
    - It gives fixed options and limited customization support
    because: URP is a quick and easy way to customize graphics, and its implementation optimizes many pipeline stages and minimizes resource requirements. The built-in pipeline has limited customization, and HDRP targets high-end photorealistic graphics rather than quick cross-platform optimization.
  Q What is HDRP in Unity mainly intended for?  [61/S0/F6, 61/S0/F7]
    - Quick customized graphics for a wide range of platforms
    - Optimized graphics for a wide range of platforms
    * High-fidelity photorealistic graphics for high-end platforms
    - Fixed-pipeline graphics for a limited range of platforms
    because: HDRP is a customizable pipeline for cutting-edge, high-fidelity, photorealistic graphics, and it typically requires strong resources such as a good GPU on high-end platforms.
  judge round 1: 1 of 4 failed
    1 pass  (What kind of tool is Unity for a developer creating an XR system?)

  - Unity's main primitives are triangle- or quadrangle meshes; the mesh renderer renders mesh-filter geometry at the transform position.
  - Unity materials specify surface rendering using textures, meshes define shape, and bitmap textures add color and surface properties.

Its default graphics APIs access native libraries such as DirectX, Metal, OpenGL, and Vulkan, depending on which platform APIs are available.   - Unity implements the graphics pipeline through native rendering libraries, not its own, so developers do not manage that implementation.
  - Unity supports major native graphics libraries such as DirectX, Metal, OpenGL, and Vulkan, plus many others.
  - Unity's default graphics APIs access native graphics library APIs, and support depends on platform API availability.
  - In Player Settings, checking AutoGraphics API lets Unity include built-in graphics APIs and choose an appropriate one at runtime.
  - If AutoGraphics API is unchecked, Unity's editor uses the first supported graphics API in the list.

61/A10  quiz  61/S4  "Quick quiz"  (6 facts, 21 concepts)
  Q What does enabling isKinematic on a Unity rigid body allow?  [61/S4/F3]
    - A physics material can set its friction and bounce so it reacts to impacts
    - A collider can define its shape so it can collide with another object
    - A trigger collider can mark it so other colliders can pass through it
    * A script can move it so it does not follow gravity automatically
    because: isKinematic removes the object from automatic physics control, letting a script move it kinematically instead of letting gravity move it. The other options describe collider, trigger, or physics material behavior.
  Q In Unity, which setup can create floors or walls that do not move?  [61/S4/F5]
    - A physics material set for friction and bounce can create a motionless element in the scene
    * A collider without a rigid body can create a motionless element in the scene
    - A trigger collider marked with isTrigger can create a motionless element in the scene
    - A joint connected to a fixed point can create a motionless element in the scene
    because: Static colliders can be added to a game object without a rigid body to make motionless scene elements such as floors and walls. A trigger collider does not behave as a solid object, and a physics material only configures surface response.
  Q In Unity, what does a joint do for rigid bodies?  [61/S4/F8]
    - It removes them from gravity so a script can move them directly in code
    * It connects them to another rigid body or fixed point and limits movement
    - It represents them as a logical tree of constrained joints for structure
    - It defines their collision shape when another object collides in the scene
    because: A joint connects rigid bodies, can apply forces, and has limits that restrict movement. Collision shapes are defined by colliders, script movement without gravity is associated with isKinematic rigid bodies, and a tree of constrained joints describes articulation.
  Q Why is physics articulation useful for moving a complex structure in Unity?  [61/S4/F9, 61/S4/F10, 61/S4/F11]
    * An articulation body can implement joint constraints automatically for a structure represented as a tree of joints
    - A collider can define the shape used when each part of the structure collides with another object
    - A physics material can configure the friction and bounce of each surface in the structure
    - A rigid body can respond to gravity so each part of the structure falls or bounces
    because: Articulation represents a jointed structure as a logical tree and provides automatic support for joint constraints, so a developer does not need to control each joint separately. The other options describe colliders, rigid bodies, and physics materials rather than articulation.

61/A11  recap  61/S4  "Recap"  (12 facts, 34 concepts)
  Unity's physics engine makes objects in a project move realistically by simulating physical laws through its components. Rigid bodies control gravity-driven motion, colliders define collision shapes and surface behavior, and joints connect bodies with forces and limits. Articulation extends this by representing a whole jointed structure as a tree with automatically applied constraints.
  - Unity's physics engine simulates physical laws with rigid bodies, colliders, joints, articulation, and character controllers.
  - A Unity rigid body lets an object respond to gravity; isKinematic can instead let scripts move it.
  - Unity colliders define collision shape with primitive or mesh types; static colliders need no rigid body, trigger colliders are non-solid.
  - Unity physics materials configure the friction and bounce of a surface.
  - Unity joints connect, apply forces to, and limit bodies; articulation models jointed structures as trees with automatic constraints.
  judge round 1: 2 of 6 failed
    1 pass  (Unity's physics engine simulates physical laws with rigid bodies, colliders, joints, articulation, and character …)
      check: none
      reason: Facts 1 and 2 support that Unity's physics engine simulates physical laws and includes the named components; no outside claim is added.
    2 pass  (A Unity rigid body lets an object respond to gravity; isKinematic can instead let …)
      check: none
      reason: Facts 3 and 4 support that a rigid body allows gravity response and that isKinematic can let a script move the object instead of automatic gravity.
    3 pass  (Unity colliders define collision shape with primitive or mesh types; static colliders need no …)
      check: none
      reason: Facts 5, 6, and 8 support the collider-shape/types claim, the static-collider claim, and the trigger/non-solid claim.
    4 pass  (Unity physics materials configure the friction and bounce of a surface.)
      check: none
      reason: Fact 7 directly states that Unity physics materials configure surface friction and bounce.
    5 FAIL faithful  (Unity joints connect, apply forces to, and limit bodies; articulation models jointed structures as …)
      check: 9: 'can apply forces'
      reason: Fact 9 says a joint 'can apply forces', but the point says joints 'apply forces to' bodies, dropping the possibility and making it sound universal. A repaired version would say joints can connect bodies, can apply forces, and have movement limits, while articulation represents jointed structures as trees with automatic constraints.
    0 FAIL supported,faithful  (Unity's physics engine makes objects in a project move realistically by simulating physical laws …)
      check: 7: 'physics materials are used to configure the friction and bounce of a surface'
      reason: The text says 'colliders define collision shapes and surface behavior', but fact 5 assigns shape definition to colliders while fact 7 assigns friction/bounce surface behavior to physics materials, not colliders. A repaired version would separate colliders from physics materials, e.g. colliders define collision shapes while physics materials configure friction and bounce.
  judge kept: original; still failing: [5, 0]

61/A12  quiz  61/S5  "Quick quiz"  (3 facts, 9 concepts)
  Q What does humanoid animation retargeting let a Unity developer do?  [61/S5/F1]
    - Manage transitions between clips before previewing one character model
    * Apply an animation from one character model onto another character model
    - Animate separate body parts with different animation logic on one character model
    - Align several animation clips before previewing one character model
    because: Humanoid animation retargeting is the ability to apply animations from one character model onto another. Aligning clips, managing transitions, and animating body parts with different logics are separate animation capabilities.
  Q What does Unity’s animation system let a developer avoid doing directly?  [61/S5/F2]
    - Animating body parts with different animation logics
    - Aligning animation clips or managing clip transitions
    - Importing animation clips or previewing animation clips
    * Implementing pipeline stages and their computations
    because: Unity handles animation processing with stages similar to 3D graphics pipeline stages, so a developer can work with animations without implementing those stages or computations. The other options describe animation tasks Unity supports rather than pipeline work it removes.
  Q What is the main responsibility of Unity’s audio listener component?  [61/S5/F5]
    - Modify a source output or listener intake to create effects relative to its position
    - Route scene audio to the camera according to the listener's position
    - Make a game object play a standard audio clip at the listener's position
    * Listen to scene audio and send it to speakers relative to its position
    because: The audio listener listens to all audio in the scene and transfers it to the computer speakers, with the heard audio depending on the listener's positioning. Playing sound belongs to the audio source, creating effects belongs to audio filters, and the destination is speakers rather than the camera.

61/A13  recap  61/S5  "Recap"  (7 facts, 20 concepts)
  Unity supports immersive XR animation by giving developers clip tools, retargeting, and direct animation control without manual 3D pipeline work. Its audio side uses dedicated components: a source plays sound, a listener determines what is heard, and filters shape the resulting audio.
  - Unity’s animation system supports importing, aligning, previewing, transitions, humanoid retargeting, visual control, and body-part logics.
  - Unity lets developers work directly with animations without implementing similar 3D graphics pipeline stages.
  - Unity’s audio source component on a game object plays a standard audio clip via mixer, code, or default.
  - Unity’s audio listener, by default one on the camera, gives position-based hearing; audio filters generate effects.

61/A19  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (13 facts, 38 concepts)
  Q How are the Universal Render Pipeline and the High Definition Render Pipeline different in terms of platform support and resource requirements in Unity?  [61/S0/F4, 61/S0/F5, 61/S0/F6, 61/S0/F7; Universal Render Pipeline, High Definition Render Pipeline, resource requirement, high-end platform]
    A The Universal Render Pipeline is a quick and easy way to customize graphics and create optimized graphics across a wide range of platforms. Its pipeline stages are optimized by the pipeline implementation itself, so it minimizes resource requirements. The High Definition Render Pipeline is meant for cutting-edge photorealistic graphics and requires a good amount of resources, typically on high-end platforms with good GPU support.
  Q How do a rigid body and a collider work together to give a Unity game object realistic physical behavior?  [61/S4/F0, 61/S4/F2, 61/S4/F4; rigid body, collider, gravity, collision]
    A The Unity physics engine simulates physical laws so that objects accelerate and respond to collisions. A rigid body attached to the game object lets it respond to gravity, so falling or bouncing appears realistic. A collider defines the game object's shape for physical collisions.
  Q In a Unity model file, how do a mesh, a material, and a texture contribute to the appearance of a 3D object?  [61/S1/F1, 61/S1/F5, 61/S1/F6; model file, mesh, material, texture]
    A A model file can contain mesh, material, and texture data. The mesh describes the object's shape, while the material describes the appearance of the object's surface by specifying how it should be rendered, including references to textures, tiling information, and color tints. Textures are bitmap images applied over the mesh surface to assign color and can represent other surface aspects such as reflectivity and roughness.
  Q How does Unity's AutoGraphics API option let a developer support different platforms without selecting a native graphics library for each platform?     A Unity does not implement the graphics pipeline itself but uses functions of native rendering libraries, and it can support a library when the corresponding API is available on a platform. When AutoGraphics API is checked for a platform, the Unity player build includes a set of built-in graphics APIs. At runtime, Unity uses the appropriate built-in graphics API, so the developer does not need to decide which native graphics library the platform supports.

===== lecture 62: Linking theory to practice

62/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (19 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is Vuforia? (lecture 22) -> Vuforia is a cross-platform augmented reality (AR) software development kit (SDK) that uses computer vision to recognize and track images and objects in the real world for creating AR applications.
  What is Unity? (lecture 60) -> Unity is a popular cross-platform game engine and developer environment that provides an editor interface and implementation support for the computer graphics pipeline, enabling developers to create, build, and deploy 2D and 3D interactive content, including XR experiences.
  What is trigger? (lecture 61) -> A trigger is a Unity collider configured using the isTrigger property that does not behave as a solid object and allows other colliders to pass through.
  What is collider? (lecture 61) -> A collider is a component in a physics engine that defines a game object's shape for physical collisions. It can be static, use primitive or mesh shapes, or be a trigger that other colliders pass through.
  What is augmented reality (AR)? (lecture 1) -> Augmented reality (AR) is an enhanced version of reality created by technology, in which computer-generated digital content is overlaid on the real world in real time and registered in 3D, so the user perceives and interacts with the enhanced environment.
  What is marker? (lecture 3) -> A marker is a real-world object or image placed in the environment that a system detects to identify its position or track a user's motion and to place digital content at that position.

62/A1  quiz  62/S0  "Quick quiz"  (4 facts, 10 concepts)
  Q Why does a programmer write C# scripts for a customized experience in Unity?  [62/S0/F0]
    * To change the built-in support
    - To create a new type of game object
    - To compile scripts in an integrated development environment
    - To install the scripting environment
    because: Unity's built-in support provides only the behavior that the environment already has, so scripts are written to change that behavior for a customized experience. Installing the environment or compiling scripts are setup steps, not the reason for writing a script.
  Q What kind of Unity entity is a newly created C# script?  [62/S0/F3]
    - A new type of game object in Unity
    - A new type of project folder in Unity
    * A new type of component in Unity
    - A new type of prefab in Unity
    because: A Unity C# script is essentially a new component type that can be attached to a game object to control its behavior. It is not itself a game object, prefab, or folder.
  Q What can a C# script component do after it is attached to a game object in Unity?  [62/S0/F4]
    - It can create a new C# script and open it in an IDE while the game runs in Unity
    - It can replace the built-in support and generate game objects while the game runs in Unity
    - It can install the scripting environment and compile scripts while the game runs in Unity
    * It can trigger events and modify component properties while the game runs in Unity
    because: Once attached, the script works when the game is executed and lets the developer trigger events, change component properties over time, and respond to input. It does not perform environment setup, create the script itself, or replace the built-in support.
  Q How are C# scripts usually created in Unity compared with most other assets?  [62/S0/F5]
    - Outside Unity through a separate compiler in Unity
    - In Visual Studio before the Unity project starts in Unity
    - In the Inspector after a game object is selected in Unity
    * Directly in Unity through the IDE interface in Unity
    because: C# scripts are usually created directly within Unity using the interface provided by the IDE. The other options describe separate tools, wrong timing, or a wrong place in the Unity interface.

    - the scene is paused in the editor after five seconds

    - Unity passes control to the function, skips its body, and returns control to Unity

  Unity scripts use prebuilt functions, such as MonoBehaviour's Destroy function, and user-defined functions to control game objects. Event functions are Unity functions activated by gameplay events, including update, initialization, graphical user interface, collision, and trigger events. These event functions can impose realistic physical behavior in physics-event functions and interactive behavior in graphical user interface event functions.
  - Unity's MonoBehaviour Destroy function destroys a game object from the scene after a delay specified in seconds.
  - Unity scripts use prebuilt functions and user-defined functions, with user-defined functions typically part of a good script.
  - Unity event functions are activated by gameplay events, including update, initialization, graphical user interface, collision, and trigger functions.
  - Unity event functions can impose realistic physical behavior in physics-event functions and interactive behavior in GUI event functions.

62/A7  put_in_order  62/S2  "Order the events in Unity event-function activation"  (1 facts, 2 concepts)

    - It gives the inspector window a reference to the prefab for runtime instantiation
    because: The My Prefab field stores a reference in the script so the script can instantiate that prefab at runtime. Dragging the prefab there does not create a scene instance, reverse the reference, or put the reference in the scene or inspector as the operating object.
  Q What distinguishes a do-while loop from a for or while loop?  [62/S3/F3]
    - The condition is checked before the body executes
    - The condition is checked until the body executes
    * The condition is checked after the body executes
    - The condition is checked while the body executes
    because: A do-while loop is exit-controlled: the body runs first and the condition is checked afterward, so the body executes at least once. A for or while loop is entry-controlled, checking the condition before the body can run.
  Q What is a suitable use for a foreach loop?  [62/S3/F4]
    - Working with a polymorphic collection
    - Working with a heterogeneous collection
    * Working with a homogeneous collection
    - Working with a mixed-type collection
    because: A foreach loop is suited to arrays or collections of homogeneous data types because it lets the programmer work with the collection directly instead of dealing with individual data types. Non-homogeneous or mixed-type collections are not the described use case.

  Q How does a Unity coroutine continue after it pauses?  [62/S4/F1]
    - It starts the method again from the beginning on the following frame
    - It waits for a user event before it can resume the method
    * It resumes where the method left off on the following frame
    - It waits for a scene change before it can resume the method
    because: A coroutine pauses, gives control back to Unity, and later continues from the same point on the following frame rather than restarting or waiting for another event.
  Q Why are Unity coroutines not treated as ordinary threads?  [62/S4/F2]
    - They run on separate threads and do not block other scripts
    - They run in separate processes and finish while the game is loading
    * They run on the main thread and do not spawn individual threads
    - They run on worker threads and share work with the hardware
    because: Coroutines are not threads: even when they pause and resume, their work still happens on the main thread and they do not create separate threads.
  Q What makes a gradual opacity fade visible in Unity?  [62/S4/F3]

    - Setting the opacity once so Unity stores the final material
    * Lowering the opacity over several frames so Unity renders intermediate values
    because: A fade is visible only when the opacity changes over a sequence of frames, allowing Unity to render the intermediate values; a one-time change is not perceived as a gradual fade.

    - The pause length and the method's run time, in seconds
    - The start time and the end time, in seconds
    because: InvokeRepeating takes the first time as the delay before the method starts and the second time as the interval between repeated calls, both measured in seconds.

62/A19  quiz  62/S8  "Quick quiz"  (3 facts, 7 concepts)
  Q What allows a basic virtual or augmented reality system to be built with less programming than a customized one?  [62/S8/F0]
    - Hand-written code support for basic functions
    * Menu-based IDE support for basic functions
    - Imported SDK support for basic functions
    - Custom scripting support for basic functions
    because: A basic system can be assembled with menu-based IDE support without scripting, while a customized experience requires scripting and therefore more programming. SDKs are not the reason a basic system needs less code.
  Q In an XR project, importing a software development kit is mainly needed for ?  [62/S8/F1]
    * Functionality that exceeds the support of the Unity development environment
    - Functionality that matches the support of the Unity development environment
    - Functionality that is already included in the support of the Unity development environment
    - Functionality that can be created with the support of the Unity development environment
    because: SDKs are imported when the required functions go beyond what the Unity environment already provides. If the functionality is already available or can be created inside the environment, an SDK is not the main reason for importing one.
  Q What do the Programmer's and Developer's Manuals mainly provide for XR development?  [62/S8/F2]
    * Further details on building and deploying XR systems and writing code
    - Device-specific support for building and deploying XR systems and writing code
    - A customized experience for building and deploying XR systems and writing code
    - Menu-based IDE support for building and deploying XR systems and writing code
    because: The manuals are sources of further details about building, deploying, and coding XR systems. They do not themselves provide device-specific support, menu-based IDE support, or a customized experience.

62/A20  recap  62/S8  "Recap"  (3 facts, 7 concepts)
  Building and deploying virtual and augmented reality systems is primarily programming work. The required amount of scripting varies with functionality, from menu-based basic systems to customized scripted experiences, while device-specific SDKs are imported when Unity development environment support is exceeded. The Programmer's Manual and Developer's Manual provide further details for building, deploying, and writing code.
  - Building XR systems is mainly programming: basic systems can use menu-based IDE support, while customized experiences need scripting.
  - SDKs provide device-specific support for XR systems and are imported when required functionality exceeds Unity development environment support.
  - The Programmer's Manual and Developer's Manual on the respective websites give further details on building, deploying, and writing XR code.

      check: none
      reason: Fact 2 supports that SDKs provide device-specific support for XR systems and are imported when required functionality exceeds Unity development environment support.
    3 pass  (The Programmer's Manual and Developer's Manual on the respective websites give further details on …)

62/A25  odd_one_out  lecture  "Odd one out"  (3 facts, 38 concepts)
  FixedUpdate function | *Start function | Update function | LateUpdate function  (Update, FixedUpdate, and LateUpdate are regular update event functions, while Start is an initialization event function.)  [62/S2/F3]
  OnCollisionStay function | *OnTriggerEnter function | OnCollisionEnter function | OnCollisionExit function  (OnCollisionEnter, OnCollisionStay, and OnCollisionExit are physics event functions, whereas OnTriggerEnter is a physics-related event function for trigger colliders.)  [62/S2/F3]
  Scale | *Opacity | Rotation | Position  (Position, rotation, and scale are the properties stored by a Unity transform property, while opacity is an alpha value used for fading.)  [62/S4/F0, 62/S4/F3]
  judge round 1: 2 of 3 failed

      reason: Fact 15 groups Update, FixedUpdate, and LateUpdate as regular update event functions and places Start in initialization events. It fails only on form: the three intended members all contain 'Update', while Start does not, making the odd item visually obvious.
    2 FAIL no_giveaway  (OnCollisionStay function | OnTriggerEnter function | OnCollisionEnter function | OnCollisionExit function)
      check: Physics event functions, fact 15; no other item is clearly defensible as the odd one from the lecture grouping.
      reason: Fact 15 groups OnCollisionEnter, OnCollisionStay, and OnCollisionExit as physics event functions and places OnTriggerEnter among physics-related trigger events. It fails only on form: the three intended members all begin with 'OnCollision', while the odd item begins with 'OnTrigger', making it visually obvious.
    3 pass  (Scale | Opacity | Rotation | Position)

62/A26  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (9 facts, 29 concepts)
  Q Why is scripting needed for a customized Unity experience even though menu-based integrated development environment support can build a basic system?  [62/S0/F0, 62/S0/F3, 62/S8/F0; scripting, unity script, game object, component]
    A Menu-based IDE support can build a basic system without scripting, but Unity's built-in support provides only the experience the system already provides. A C# script attached as a component to a game object gives the developer a component that behaves as desired rather than according to the built-in support, so a customized experience requires writing such scripts.
  Q Why must a gradual opacity fade in Unity be implemented as a coroutine rather than as a function called once?  [62/S4/F1, 62/S4/F3; coroutine, opacity fade, frame]
    A A gradual opacity fade is visible only when the opacity value is reduced over a sequence of frames so Unity renders the intermediate values. A coroutine can pause execution, return control to Unity, and continue on the following frame, so the change can be spread frame by frame. A function called once cannot produce that visible fade.
  Q Why does the marker-based augmented reality sample use Vuforia instead of relying only on Unity's built-in support?  [62/S6/F2, 62/S6/F3, 62/S7/F4, 62/S7/F9; Vuforia, object recognition, tracking, marker-based augmented reality]
    A Unity's built-in support for object recognition, computer vision, object detection, and tracking is not extensive or very good. Vuforia is an augmented reality software development kit primarily meant to help developers deal with object recognition or computer vision issues, such as object detection, recognition, and tracking. Its setup requires a database containing the marker images, so the Vuforia engine can recognize the marker and display the three-dimensional model in place of the marker.
  judge round 1: 0 of 3 failed
    1 pass  (Why is scripting needed for a customized Unity experience even though menu-based integrated development …)
      check: Scripting is needed because menu-based built-in support only provides the system's default experience, whereas attaching a C# script as a component lets a game object behave as the developer wants.
      reason: Facts 1 and 46 give the limitation of built-in/menu support and the need for scripts for customization, while fact 4 gives the mechanism of attaching a C# script as a component to override built-in behavior.
    2 pass  (Why must a gradual opacity fade in Unity be implemented as a coroutine rather …)
      check: A gradual opacity fade needs a coroutine because only spreading opacity changes over multiple frames makes intermediate values visible, while a function called once cannot.
      reason: Fact 25 states the fade is visible only over a sequence of frames and a one-time fade is not perceivable; fact 23 states a coroutine spreads tasks across frames by pausing and continuing.
    3 pass  (Why does the marker-based augmented reality sample use Vuforia instead of relying only on …)
      check: The sample uses Vuforia because Unity's built-in recognition/tracking is weak, while Vuforia is an AR SDK that can recognize the marker, using a database, and display the model.
      reason: Facts 32 and 33 carry the reason: Vuforia handles recognition/tracking that Unity built-in support does not do well; facts 39 and 44 show the marker database and sample recognition/display.

===== lecture 63: Concluding remarks

63/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (13 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is augmented reality (AR)? (lecture 1) -> Augmented reality (AR) is an enhanced version of reality created by technology, in which computer-generated digital content is overlaid on the real world in real time and registered in 3D, so the user perceives and interacts with the enhanced environment.
  What is mixed reality (MR)? (lecture 1) -> Mixed reality (MR) is an immersive technology that is the same as augmented reality, in which digital content is overlaid on the view of reality and can be interacted with.
  What is extended reality (XR)? (lecture 1) -> Extended reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR).
  What is machine learning-based cybersickness evaluation (ML)? (lecture 11) -> Machine learning-based cybersickness evaluation is an input-based cybersickness measurement technique that uses automated algorithms trained on psychological, physiological, or biometric inputs to automatically determine cybersickness, producing classification labels or a numerical sickness score.
  What is internet of things (IoT)? (lecture 23) -> Internet of Things (IoT) is a current stage in the development of computer systems in which users are surrounded by multiple connected computers that can communicate with each other without the user separately operating them, moving toward making technology disappear from the user's point of view.
  What is resource optimization? (lecture 49) -> Resource optimization is the technological optimization of resource requirements in extended reality (XR), including virtual reality (VR), that minimizes those requirements while maximizing immersive experience without compromising it. It generally focuses on client-end hardware so users can have a good experience with affordable hardware.
